{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.345582+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6e9838daad033267a324612fda93794ababb91013b8c4bcf33990c572760ca95","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Ppn 138 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] If $\psi:\bbR^{d_1}\to\bbR^{d_2}$ is Lipschitz, then $\psi$ preserves $\bbW_2$ convergence.
If $d_1=2,d_2=1$ and $\psi(X,Y)=XY$, then $\psi$ preserves $\bbW_2$ convergence for sequences on which $X$ is uniformly bounded.

\begin{proof}
The first statement follows because $L$-Lipschitz maps increase $\bbW_2$ distances by at most a factor of $L$.
For the second statement, suppose 
$X_N\to X$ and $Y_N\to Y$ in $L^2$, with $|X_N|\leq C$ almost surely for all $N$. 
We will argue that this implies $X_NY_N\to XY$ in $L^2$, and the assertion then follows. First,
the uniform bound on $X_N$ gives
  \[
  \E\Big[(X_NY_N-X_NY)^2\Big]
  \le C^2 \E\Big[(Y_N-Y)^2\Big]
  = o_N(1)\,,
  \]
so $X_NY_N$ and $X_NY$ are close in $L^2$. For $T$ growing sufficiently slowly with $N$, we then bound
  \[
  \E\Big[ (X_NY-XY)^2\Big]
  \le T^2\E\Big[ (X_N-X)^2\Big]
  + 4C^2\E\Big[Y^2; |Y| \ge T\Big]
  \le T^2 o_N(1) + o_T(1)\,,
  \]
where the last term is because $Y^2\in L^1$. Therefore $X_NY$ converges to $XY$ in $L^2$, and the claim follows.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:33:17.699658+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6e9a9d385797667793f19e6403a4855ede982b6a6040e847cbc370e15cd57b82","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 29 (Spectral approximation) of arXiv:2607.10813, '2607.10813'] Under the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:local-wp}, fix a compact
$K\Subset\R^3$ and the fixed localization pair
$(\chi_K^\circ,\rho_K^\circ)$ from
\eqref{eq:reference-localization-and-lifetime}.  Denote the corresponding solution of the localized auxiliary system and its
fixed-point variables by
$(u^\circ,v^\circ,\mathcal N^\circ,Z^\circ)$, and denote their
finite-cutoff counterparts by
$(u_\Lambda^\circ,v_\Lambda^\circ,
  \mathcal N_\Lambda^\circ,Z_\Lambda^\circ)$.
Their restrictions to the backward cone $\mathcal Q_{K,T}$ represent the
local fields and source.

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.45em]
\item \emph{Fixed-profile dyadic cutoffs.}
For every fixed-profile dyadic cutoff there is an event $\Omega_K^\circ$ of
probability one, which may depend on the chosen profile, such that, for every $\omega\in\Omega_K^\circ$ and every
$T<\tau_K(\omega)$, the finite-cutoff fixed point exists for all sufficiently
large dyadic $\Lambda$ and
\begin{align}
  Z_\Lambda^\circ&\longrightarrow Z^\circ
  &&\text{in }\mathcal Z_T,
  \\
  \bigl(\chi_K(u_\Lambda^\circ-u^\circ),
  \chi_K(v_\Lambda^\circ-v^\circ)\bigr)
  &\longrightarrow0
  &&\text{in }C([0,T];\mathcal D'(\R^3))^2
  
\end{align}
for every $\chi_K\in C_c^\infty(\R^3)$ equal to one near $K$.  The three source terms converge in the topology
\eqref{eq:nonlinear-source-topology}.  If
$\eta_K\in C_c^\infty(\R^3)$ satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \eta_K\equiv1\ \text{near }K,
 \qquad \eta_K\chi_K^\circ=\eta_K,
\end{equation}
then
\[
 \eta_Ku_\Lambda^\circ v_\Lambda^\circ
 \longrightarrow \eta_K\mathcal N^\circ
 \quad\text{in }\mathcal D'((0,T)\times\R^3).
\]

\item \emph{Arbitrary admissible cofinal cutoffs.}
Let $(\pi_{\Lambda_n})_{n\ge1}$ be an admissible cofinal cutoff sequence and
let $T\in(0,1]$ be deterministic.  There are Borel events
$\mathcal A_{n,T}^K$ and strongly measurable $\mathcal Z_T$-valued random
variables $Z_{n,T}^\circ$ whose restriction to $\mathcal A_{n,T}^K$ is the
finite-cutoff fixed point.  If $Z_T^\circ$ denotes the strongly measurable
restriction of $Z^\circ$ to $[0,T]$ on $\{T<\tau_K\}$, then
$(\mathcal A_{n,T}^K,Z_{n,T}^\circ)$ converges to $Z_T^\circ$ in probability
on $\{T<\tau_K\}$ in the sense of
Definition~\ref{def:partial-probability-convergence}.  The same conclusion
holds for every continuous seminorm on
$C([0,T];\mathcal D'(\R^3))^2$ and for the source norms in
\eqref{eq:nonlinear-source-topology}.
\end{enumerate}

For any other fixed localization pair $(\chi,\rho)$ adapted to $(K,1)$,
the same conclusions hold on its existence interval, and the limiting fields
and source agree with those obtained from the fixed pair
$(\chi_K^\circ,\rho_K^\circ)$ on every common interval. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:22:59.718645+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6e9ed6e5ef30f0d2eb7273f6ec3c577dceec765ae5f388111327acdec5c4f514","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:ik-non-duality of arXiv:2608.29708, 'Intuitionistic and Constructive Modal Logics for Classical Modal Logicians'] {simpson_proof_1994}}] 
  (1) $\textbf{IK} \nvdash \textsf{Dual}_\Box$. (2) $\textbf{IK} \nvdash \textsf{Dual}_\Diamond$.
  \begin{proof}
    Let $\mathfrak{M} = (\set{ x_0, x_1, y_0, y_1 }, \leq, \sqsubset, V)$, where $\leq$ is the reflexive closure of $\set{ (x_0, x_1), (y_0, y_1) }$,
    $\mathord{\sqsubset} = \set{ (x_0, y_0), (x_1, y_1) }$, and $V(p) = \set{ y_1 }$,
    then $\mathfrak{M}$ is an IK-model.
    The model is visualized in Figure (fig:ik-countermodels of the paper).
    We use it to prove both.

    (1) $x_0 \not \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \Diamond \neg p$ and $x_1 \not \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \Diamond \neg p$ hold, which imply $x_0 \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \neg \Diamond \neg p$.
    Also, $x_0 \not \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \Box p$ holds.
    Therefore, $\textbf{IK} \nvdash \neg \Diamond \neg p \to \Box p$ by completeness.

    (2) $x_0 \not \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \Box \neg p$ and $x_1 \not \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \Box \neg p$ hold, which imply $x_0 \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \neg \Box \neg p$.
    Also, $x_0 \not \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \Diamond p$ holds.
    Therefore, $\textbf{IK} \nvdash \neg \Box \neg p \to \Diamond p$ by completeness.
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:58:53.191597+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6e9f4316f0743dedc3012c9ae8e1ca8090bea5746e3fba9bda64216912d113ae","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 2 of arXiv:2606.31455, 'Discrete time-multidimensional renewal theory and applications'] Let $\mathcal{R}:=\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}^d}$ be the set of all real-valued sequences on $\mathbb{N}^d$.
Equipped with pointwise addition $+$ and the convolution product $*$ in \eqref{eq:conv}, $(\mathcal{R},+,*)$ is a commutative ring
with unity. The identity element (unit) is the sequence $\ez$ defined by

\[
\ez(k)=
\begin{cases}
1, & k=0_d,\\
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]

If there exists $b:\mathbb{N}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ such that $a*b=b*a=\ez$, then $a$ is \emph{convolutionally invertible} and $b$ is called
its \emph{convolutional inverse}, denoted by $a^{(-1)}$.

Moreover, the map $\Phi:\mathcal{R}\to \mathbb{R}[[x_1,\ldots,x_d]]$ defined by $\Phi(a)=P_a$ is a ring isomorphism. In particular,
for all $a,b\in\mathcal{R}$,
\[
P_{a+b}(x_{1:d})=P_a(x_{1:d})+P_b(x_{1:d}),\ \
P_{a*b}(x_{1:d})=P_a(x_{1:d})\,P_b(x_{1:d}),\ \
P_{\ez}(x_{1:d})=1.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:51.726715+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis / Sobolev embedding","id":"claim_6eb2ea7b6a07326d6e5d6688779ae32153ce28e129f99091ad137afef25da73a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: H^s(R^n) embeds into L^∞(R^n) ∩ C^0 only for s > n/2, strictly; the borderline s = n/2 is excluded. Then ∫|∇u|² = 2π ∫_0^{e^{−1}} dr / ( r log²(1/r) ) = 2π < ∞ and ∫ u² < ∞, so u ∈ H¹(R²), yet u is unbounded at the origin. General n: choose f with f̂(ξ) = (1+|ξ|)^{−n} (log(2+|ξ|))^{−1} ≥ 0; then ∫ (1+|ξ|²)^{n/2}|f̂|² dξ < ∞ (radially, ∫ dρ/(ρ log²ρ) converges) so f ∈ H^{n/2}(R^n), while ∫ f̂ dξ = ∞ (∫ dρ/(ρ log ρ) diverges); since f̂ ≥ 0, an L^∞ bound on f would force ∫ f̂ < ∞ (test against a Gaussian approximate identity with positive Fourier transform and use monotone convergence), so f ∉ L^∞. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:18:13.294721+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6ecbc8323de36e2a618c67a1dde402826105a7d6501a410d59a4d8fd1049c06d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:break_loops of arXiv:2507.15589, 'Tightness of approximations to metrics on non-simple conformal loop ensemble gaskets'] {amy-cle-resampling}}]

Suppose that $\Gamma$ is a nested ${\rm CLE}_{\kappa}${} in a simply connected domain $D$. For each $a\in(0,1)$, $b>0$ there exists $p > 0$ such that the following holds. 

Let $z\in D$ and $j_0\in\mathbf{Z}$ be such that $B(z,2^{-j_0})\subseteq D$. There exists a resampling $\Gamma^{\mathrm{res}}_{z,j}$ of $\Gamma$ within $A(z,2^{-j},2^{-j+1})$ for each $j>j_0$ with the following property. Let $G^{\mathrm{res}}_{z,j}$ be the event that
\begin{itemize}
 \item no loop in $\Gamma^{\mathrm{res}}_{z,j}$ crosses the annulus $A(z,2^{-j},2^{-j+1})$,
 \item denoting $\mathcal {C}$ the loops in $\Gamma$ that cross $A(z,2^{-j},2^{-j+1})$, the collection of loops of $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma^{\mathrm{res}}_{z,j}$ remain the same in each connected component of $\mathbf{C} \setminus \bigcup\mathcal {C}$ that is not surrounded by a loop in $\mathcal {C}$ and intersects $B(z,2^{-j})$, and the gasket of $\Gamma$ in these components is contained in the gasket of $\Gamma^{\mathrm{res}}_{z,j}$.

For $k\in\mathbf{N}$, let $\widetilde G_{z,j_0,k}$ be the event that the number of $j=j_0+1,\ldots,j_0+k$ so that
\[ \mathbf{P}[ G^{\mathrm{res}}_{z,j} \,|\, \Gamma ] \geq p\]

\[ \mathbf{P}[(\widetilde G_{z,j_0,k})^c] = O(e^{-b k}) \]

{"assumptions":["Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0058-a-peeling-algorithm-exploring-site-percolation-on-boltzmann-maps","No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:26:45.042388+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6ee908b5f808cca14f04a9496a7df36b77c5fdd7c0ca2b7a7d3ee18a1cb155de","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Design the algorithm and check whether the exploration frontier remains Markov. Result: For bond percolation the peeling frontier is a two-colour boundary (free/blocked edges) and the algorithm peels the edge at the colour change, keeping the unexplored region a Boltzmann map with a boundary of the same type. For site percolation the colour lives on vertices and after peeling a face the newly exposed boundary vertices are uncoloured; the natural algorithm peels the edge whose left endpoint is black and right endpoint is uncoloured, colouring the new vertices as they appear. The unexplored region is then a Boltzmann map with a boundary condition that is a word in {black, white, uncoloured}, and the difficulty is that the length of the black segment is no longer a Markov chain by itself: the future depends on the positions of uncoloured vertices along the boundary. The frontier becomes Markov if one records the boundary word, which is an infinite-dimensional state. On triangulations the problem was solved (Angel-Curien) because degree-3 faces expose at most one new vertex per step, keeping the state finite; for general Boltzmann maps with large faces a peeled face exposes many uncoloured vertices at once. So a Markov site-percolation peeling exists exactly when faces expose boundedly many vertices, i.e. for bounded face degrees, and the general Boltzmann case requires a state space of boundary words; whether the threshold can still be computed from a word-valued Markov chain is the open part. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:47.655725+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6ef2f8b8a657794c791b85a18e34c7c7214aed82b0d2edf0aeed7cc33ac6febf","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 6 of arXiv:2605.07369, '2605.07369'] Let $(X_n)_{n\ge 0}$ be a stochastic process taking values in $\rr$ and satisfying the stochastic approximation algorithm  (\ref{sa-0}).

Then, for any $\varepsilon>0$ and $F>0$, there exists a positive constant $\delta\in(0,1)$ such that for all sufficiently large $n$, we have

\pp\left(b \left|\sum_{i=[\delta n]}^n \frac{U_{i+1}}{i+1}\right|\ge 2\varepsilon\right)\\

Here, $[\delta n]$ denotes the integer part of $\delta n$. The constant $\delta$ can be chosen to satisfy

$$

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:32:38.638852+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6f0e87ad010127afbb6124a8275fc47d14da9e01333dfb0317e56152cdc6db89","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Cor 12 of arXiv:2506.17979, '\large\bf A remark on subharmonicity for symmetric Dirichlet forms'] Let ${\sf d}$ be a distance function consistent with the given topology on 
 $E$.
Suppose that the jumping measure $J$ satisfies $\frac{D_1}{{\sf d}(x,y)^{p_1}}{\m}({\d} x){\m}({\d} y)\leq 
J({\d} x{\d} y)\leq \frac{D_2}{{\sf d}(x,y)^{p_2}}{\m}({\d} x){\m}({\d} y)$ for some $D_1,D_2>0$ and $0<p_1\leq p_2<\infty$.
Assume $1\land\frac{1}{{\sf d}(\cdot,o)^{p_1}}\in L^1(E;{\m})$ for a fixed $o\in E$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:01:48.617912+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6f155acdc0830bd5aeb602e98085e3ef8a1c96bd1fe6b2fcecbea1503a83c8d7","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma l:W.is.subgaussian of arXiv:2607.02013, 'Resolution of the Detection Threshold Conjecture for Random Geometric Graphs in the $d>n$ '] Let
\begin{equation}
{\mathcal{H}} =  \{\|I_n+W\|_{\operatorname{op}}\le 4 \}.
    
\end{equation}
If $d \ge (1+\epsilon) n$ for some arbitrarily small constant $\epsilon>0$, then there exists a constant $c>0$ only depending on $\epsilon$ such that 
$\mathbb{P}_0(W \in {\mathcal{H}}^c) \leq \mathop{\rm exp}(-cn)$ 
and,
for any zero-diagonal symmetric matrix $U$,
\[
\mathbb{E}_{X\sim \mathbb{P}_{0}}[\mathop{\rm exp}( \langle U,W\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal H}\rangle)]\le \mathop{\rm exp}\left(\frac{2 \|U\|^2}{d}\right)+1\le 2\mathop{\rm exp}\left(\frac{2\|U\|^2}{d}\right).
\]

\begin{proof}

Recall that $W=XX^\top -I_n$, so 

${\mathcal{H}}$ is implied by the event
$\{\|X\|_{\rm op} \le 2\}$.
Let $Z$ be an $n\times d$ matrix with i.i.d.\ standard gaussian entries, and let $D$ be the $n\times n$ diagonal matrix with diagonal entries $\|z_1\|,\ldots,\|z_n\|$. Then $X$ is equidistributed as $D^{-1}Z$, so we can bound
    \[\|X\|_{\rm op} \le 
    \frac{\|Z\|_{\rm op}}
        {\min_i \|z_i\|}\,.\]
By the standard concentration inequality for Gaussian matrices~[vershynin2010introduction], we have
\[\|Z\|_{\rm op}
\le\sqrt{d} + \sqrt{n}
+t\]
with probability at least $1-2\mathop{\rm exp}(-t^2/2)$. By the standard concentration bound for chi-squared random variables (Lemma~(l:chi.square.lower.tail of the paper)), we have
    \[
    \min\Big\{ \|z_i\|
    : 1\le i\le n\Big\}
    \ge d-(2d)^{1/2} t
    \]
with probability at least $1-n\mathop{\rm exp}(-t^2/2)$.  Taking $t=cn^{1/2}$, we conclude that with probability at least $1-3n\mathop{\rm exp}(-c^2 n/2)$, we have
\[\|X\|_{\rm op} \le \frac{1+(1+c)/\sqrt{1+\epsilon}}{[1-\sqrt{2}c/\sqrt{1+\epsilon}]^{1/2}} \le 2\,,\]
where the last inequality holds by choosing $c$ to be a sufficiently small constant  depending on $\epsilon$. 

Next, let $W_m$ denote the principal submatrix of $W$ formed by the first $m$ rows and columns. We will truncate on the event
$\mathcal H_m= \{\| I_m+W_m\|_{\operatorname{op}}\le 4 \}$.
Note that ${\mathcal{H}}_{m+1} \subset {\mathcal{H}}_{m}$ for all $1 \le m \le n-1$ and $\mathcal{H} = \mathcal{H}_n$. Abbreviating $u_n$ for the last column of $U$, we can bound
\begin{align*}
     &\ \mathbb{E}_{X\sim \mathbb{P}_{0}}\Big[\mathop{\rm exp}( \langle U,W\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal H}\rangle)\Big]\\
   \le &\ \mathbb{E}_{x_1,\dots,x_n}
   \bigg[\mathop{\rm exp}\bigg( \sum_{i<j}u_{ij}\langle x_i,x_j\rangle\bigg)
   \mathbf{1}\{W_n \in \mathcal H_n\}\bigg]+1\\
   \le&\ \mathbb{E}_{x_1,\dots,x_{n-1}}\bigg[\mathop{\rm exp}\bigg(
   \sum_{i<j<n}u_{ij}\langle x_i,x_j\rangle\bigg)\mathbf{1}\{ W_{n-1} \in \mathcal H_{n-1}\} \mathbb{E}_{x_n}\bigg[\mathop{\rm exp}\bigg(
   \bigg\langle \sum_{i<n} u_{in}x_i,x_n
   \bigg\rangle
   \bigg)\bigg]\bigg]+1\\
    \le&\ \mathbb{E}_{x_1,\dots,x_{n-1}}\bigg[\mathop{\rm exp}\bigg(\sum_{i<j<n}u_{ij}\langle x_i,x_j\rangle\bigg)\mathbf{1}\{W_{n-1}\in \mathcal H_{n-1}\}\cdot \mathop{\rm exp}\bigg(\frac{ (u_n)^\top (I_{n-1}+ W_{n-1}) u_n}{2d}\bigg)\bigg]+1\\
    \le&\ \mathbb{E}_{x_1,\dots,x_{n-1}}\bigg[\mathop{\rm exp}\bigg(\sum_{i<j<n}u_{ij}\langle x_i,x_j\rangle\bigg)\mathbf{1}\{W_{n-1} \in \mathcal H_{n-1}\}\bigg]\cdot \mathop{\rm exp}\left(\frac{2 \|u_n\|^2
    }{d}\right)+1\,,
\end{align*}
where the second-to-last inequality is by Lemma~(lem:beta.mgf of the paper), and the
 last inequality holds because we have $\|I_{n-1}+W_{n-1}\|_{\operatorname{op} }
\le 4$ on the event ${\mathcal{H}}_{n-1}$.
Iterating the above gives the claimed bound.
\end{proof}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:14:57.693479+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6f19676373d88852d3921b106ae320d092f977406e679496eee893efa53daf1d","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm weak_convergence of arXiv:2605.29073, 'Volterra clocks and their pure-jump limits: \\hitting times of curved boundaries'] Let $\left(W^n\,, X^n\right)_{n \geq 0}$ be a sequence of weak solutions to (equation eq:Volterra_clock of the paper) on $[0\,,T]\,$, for the sequence of inputs $(G_0^n\,, K^n\,, f^n\,, \lambda^n\,, \nu^n)_{n \geq 0}\,$, where $\lambda^n\,, \nu^n \geq 0\,$, $f^n$ satisfies Assumption (assumption:f of the paper), $K^n \in L^1_{loc}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}_+\,, \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}_+)$ and $G_0^n : \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}_+ \to \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}_+$ is non-decreasing with $G_0^n(0) = 0\,$, for each $n \geq 0\,$. {"assumptions":["a well-defined Dirichlet form and reversible Markov chain with a reference measure mu","a valid Nash-type functional inequality with a specified effective dimension d","for two-sided estimates: matching volume-growth and effective-resistance-growth bounds on balls","typically also an elliptic Harnack inequality, or comparable regularity, to establish the matching lower heat-kernel bound"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.993577+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6f33033cc6c015e74e17ecf03f84254fb9e59f13180becd49ac22b25d7db440b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). A Nash inequality on a graph with Dirichlet form E and reference measure mu has the form ||f||_2^{2+4/d} <= C E(f,f) ||f||_1^{4/d} for all f in the domain of the form, where d is an effective dimension parameter. Such an inequality is classically equivalent, by results of Nash and later Carlen-Kusuoka-Stroock, to an on-diagonal heat-kernel upper bound p_t(x,x) <= C' t^{-d/2} for the associated Markov semigroup, and combining it with matching volume-growth and effective-resistance-growth estimates, within the general framework relating resistance growth to heat-kernel decay used for fractal-like and random graphs, yields two-sided sub-Gaussian or Gaussian heat-kernel bounds. On graphs where effective resistance to the complement of a ball of radius n grows like n^zeta and volume grows like n^alpha, this gives sub-Gaussian heat-kernel estimates with off-diagonal decay governed by the exponent alpha+zeta, a technique central to analysis on fractals and on random graphs such as critical percolation clusters or random walk among random conductances. The technique does not give the resistance or volume exponents themselves, which are separate geometric inputs, and a full two-sided heat-kernel estimate typically requires both the Nash-type inequality, giving the upper bound, and a separate lower-bound argument, often via a chaining construction or an elliptic Harnack inequality. Typical failure: Assuming ordinary Euclidean Gaussian heat-kernel scaling, of the t^{-d/2} exp(-|x-y|^2/4t) form, transfers automatically to a random or fractal-like graph without re-deriving the resistance exponent zeta; on structures such as the incipient infinite cluster of critical percolation, or random conductance models with heavy-tailed conductances, the correct scaling is sub-Gaussian with zeta != 1, and using the Euclidean exponent silently mis-states both the walk dimension and the tail behavior of the heat kernel. Canonical reference: Nash, 1958, American Journal of Mathematics; Carlen, Kusuoka and Stroock, 1987, Annales de l'Institut Henri Poincare; Barlow, 2004, Annals of Probability; Kumagai, Random Walks on Disordered Media and their Scaling Limits, 2014, Springer.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:35:05.831179+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6f5969aaf7835926aa02b7f7819aefa5a84cbc55192423f4dbdcbcdd24c5f4ea","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary cor:MMi-c of arXiv:2606.24881, 'Queues with Correlated Service Times --- the $M/M_D/c$ Model'] Consider the $M/M_i/c$ queueing model. Let
\[
M:=\sum_{i=1}^c \mu_i.
\]
Then the queue is stable if and only if
\[
\lambda < M.
\]

Moreover, the stationary distribution satisfies the following properties.

\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] For \(n\ge c+1\), the full-busy states satisfy the recursion
\begin{equation}
(\lambda+M)\pi_n
=
\lambda \pi_{n-1}
+
M\pi_{n+1}.
\end{equation}

\item[(ii)] The geometric tail is given by
\begin{equation}
\pi_n=\pi_c r^{\,n-c}, \qquad n\ge c,
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}
r=\frac{\lambda}{M}.
\end{equation}

\item[(iii)] For a subset state \(s\subseteq \{1,\ldots,c\}\) with
\(|s|=m\le c-2\), the balance equation is
\begin{equation}
\Bigl(\lambda+\sum_{i\in s}\mu_i\Bigr)\pi_s
=
\sum_{u:\,a(u)=s}\lambda \pi_u
+
\sum_{j\notin s}\mu_j\,\pi_{s\cup\{j\}}.
\end{equation}

\item[(iv)] For a subset state \(s\subseteq \{1,\ldots,c\}\) with
\(|s|=c-1\), let \(j(s)\) be the unique idle server, i.e.
\[
\{j(s)\}=\{1,\ldots,c\}\setminus s.
\]
Then the balance equation is
\begin{equation}
\Bigl(\lambda+\sum_{i\in s}\mu_i\Bigr)\pi_s
=
\sum_{u:\,a(u)=s}\lambda \pi_u
+
\mu_{j(s)}\,\pi_c.
\end{equation}

\item[(v)] The linking equation at level \(c\) is
\begin{equation}
(\lambda+M)\pi_c
=
\lambda \sum_{|s|=c-1}\pi_s
+
M\pi_{c+1}.
\end{equation}
Using (equation eq:MMi-geo of the paper), this may be written equivalently as
\begin{equation}
M\pi_c
=
\lambda \sum_{|s|=c-1}\pi_s,
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\pi_c
=
r\sum_{|s|=c-1}\pi_s.
\end{equation}

\item[(vi)] The normalization condition is
\begin{equation}
\sum_{\substack{s\subseteq \{1,\ldots,c\}\\ |s|\le c-1}} \pi_s
+
\frac{\pi_c}{1-r}
=
1.
\end{equation}
\end{itemize}

Hence the stationary distribution of the \(M/M_i/c\) queue is determined
by the geometric tail (equation eq:MMi-geo of the paper) together with the finite boundary
system (equation eq:MMi-boundary-subset of the paper)--(equation eq:MMi-link2 of the paper) and the
normalization condition (equation eq:MMi-normalization of the paper).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:09:41.190331+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_6f5cfee93cb76cd8d74924060da891f5b4881b2215fe5aa410d44ee0474d26de","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematics, the term homology, originally introduced in algebraic topology, has three primary, closely related usages. First, there is the homology of a chain complex, a sequence of abelian groups, called homology groups, which are regarded as fundamental invariants of the chain complex. Secondly, when one can associate a chain complex to a different mathematical object, one can also associate its homology to that object. Distinct procedures of associating chain complexes to a given object are grouped into homology theories. Finally, homology is important in the study of topological spaces. Under nice conditions in which distinct homology theories for a single topological space produce the same homology groups, one can define a single homology of a topological space. This last notion of homology is closely related to topological ideas frequently discussed in popular mathematics such as the holes of a surface or the cycles of a graph. There is also a related notion of the cohomology of a cochain complex, giving rise to various cohomology theories, in addition to the notion of the cohomology of a topological space.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:35:04.094911+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6f628d213e948889bebd7b6cc96612958248be05cf576e45b6f16f5b6758c038","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:circuit-primitives of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] For an ordered finite set $S$ of oriented carrier labels, write
$\mathscr H_S=\bigotimes_{u\in S}H_u$, with every factor equipped with
the Euclidean Hilbert norm.  A \emph{normalized Brauer primitive} is a
signed carrier permutation, a wedge reversal, full transpose, a share
turn, a through string, the orthogonal antisymmetrizer, or a cup/cap
normalized so that its operator norm is one.  A share turn is the fixed
signed boundary permutation, possibly followed by full transpose,
induced when a principal pivot reverses one of the two ordered boundary
intervals.  The two coefficient primitives are
\[
 \widehat C_{uv}=\iota_{uv}C\pi_{uv}:H_u\otimes H_v\to H_u\otimes H_v,
\]
where $\pi_{uv}$ is the normalized orthogonal projection and
identification onto $\Lambda^2H$, and $\iota_{uv}=\pi_{uv}^*$; hence
$\widehat C_{uv}$ is zero on $\operatorname{Sym}^2H$ and has norm $K$.
The other coefficient primitive is the restriction/re-expression of
(eq:2.1.3 of the paper) as the Bianchi transfer
\[
 (\Phi_CY)_{ik}=\sum_{m,n}C_{in,mk}Y_{mn},
 \qquad Y\in\Lambda^2H.
\]
The first Bianchi identity identifies the latter with the physical action
of $C$.  A \emph{safe gate} is a typed composite of these primitives,
including the $AA$ words and correctly oriented $AB$ words used below.
Its degree is the number of coefficient primitives.  Thus a degree-$d$
safe gate $G:\mathscr H_S\to\mathscr H_T$ satisfies
$\|G\|_{\rm op}\le K^d$; untouched factors are ancillary identities.

A coefficient box has four darts
$L_{i,0},L_{i,1},R_{i,0},R_{i,1}$.  For a column pairing $q$, a
\emph{packet} is a connected component of the box-incidence graph whose
edges are the $q$-pairs joining different boxes.  A $q$-pair joining the
two darts of one wedge is forbidden and gives zero.  An allowed
\emph{smoothing} chooses at each box either
\[
 h_i^{\parallel}=\{L_{i,0}R_{i,0},L_{i,1}R_{i,1}\},\qquad
 h_i^{\times}=\{L_{i,0}R_{i,1},L_{i,1}R_{i,0}\}.
\]
The alternating circuits of $q\vee h$ are the \emph{smoothing
carriers}; adjoining one carrier means adjoining one identity factor
$I_H$.  The smoothing support $\operatorname{supp}_h(i)$ of a box is the
one- or two-element set of $q\vee h$ carriers containing its two
$h$-passages.  A \emph{ported pair comb} on two chosen carriers consists of all
boxes whose smoothing support is that pair, together with every singleton-support box
assigned to it exactly once; removing all other support groups leaves
their boundary darts as linearly ordered typed ports.  These definitions
fix the domains and codomains of every safe word, fold, comb, and
attachment below.

An \emph{ambient rooted ribbon record} $\Gamma$ consists of a common
finite dart set, its coefficient boxes and local wedge signs, a row
pairing $p$, a column pairing $q$, a rooted trace pairing $r$, and the
declared boundary/root data.  Thus $p\vee r$ is the disjoint union of the
original trace circuits in that record; its components, not temporary
proof cuts, receive the normalization bases below.  The more detailed
Weingarten data carried by $\Gamma$ are specified in
(def:ribbon-record of the paper).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:32:20.037306+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6f7bba6049abfc5c9989de372a714c7cc8c00f70f6a858dbfc6c7896d99ab908","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 41 (The Metropolis--Hastings algorithm converges; Theorem \ref{thm:mhintro}) of arXiv:2608.03353, '\bfseries A Direct Route to Markov Chain Convergence\\[2mm] \Large via Asymptotic Equivale'] Let $(\XX,\XXA)$ be a measurable space, $\lambda$ a $\sigma$-finite measure on it,
and let the target be $\pi(A) = \int_{A} p \dd\lambda$ for a measurable map
$p : \XX \to (0,\infty)$ with $\int_{\XX} p \dd\lambda = 1$. Let the proposal be the
Markov kernel $Q(A \mid x) = \int_{A} q(y \mid x)\,\lambda(\dd y)$, given by an
$\XXA\otimes\XXA$-measurable map $q : \XX\times\XX \to [0,\infty)$ with
$\int_{\XX} q(y \mid x)\,\lambda(\dd y) = 1$ for every $x \in \XX$, define the
acceptance probability
\[
  a : \XX\times\XX \to [0,1], \qquad
  a(y \mid x) := \min\Bigl\{ 1,\ \frac{p(y)\,q(x \mid y)}{p(x)\,q(y \mid x)} \Bigr\}
  \quad\bigl(:= 1 \text{ when } q(y \mid x) = 0\bigr),
\]
and let $T$ be the Metropolis--Hastings kernel
\[
  T(A \mid x) := \int_{A} a(y \mid x)\,q(y \mid x)\,\lambda(\dd y) + r(x)\,\ind_{A}(x),
  \qquad
  r(x) := 1 - \int_{\XX} a(y \mid x)\,q(y \mid x)\,\lambda(\dd y) .
\]
Assume
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),nosep,topsep=3pt]
  \item $q(y \mid x) > 0$ for $(\lambda\otimes\lambda)$-almost every $(x,y) \in \XX\times\XX$;
  \item for every $x \in \XX$ the set $\{ y \in \XX : q(y \mid x) > 0 \text{ and } q(x \mid y) > 0 \} \in \XXA$ has positive $\lambda$-measure.
\end{enumerate}
Then $\pi$ is the unique invariant probability measure of $T$, and
$\tv{T^{n}\circ\mu - \pi} \to 0$ for every initial distribution $\mu \in \Prob$.

Both hypotheses hold in either of the following two cases, which are the ones met in
practice and which give Theorem \ref{thm:mhintro}:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),nosep,topsep=3pt]
  \item $q(y \mid x) > 0$ for every $(x,y) \in \XX\times\XX$;
  \item $q$ is symmetric, $q(y \mid x) = q(x \mid y)$ for all $(x,y)$, and
        $q(y \mid x) > 0$ for $(\lambda\otimes\lambda)$-almost every $(x,y)$.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.351977+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6f97ed2f4a5f62c3336de36c19870ab905777e638f947f2f9b8aabcaf18277b6","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 191 (annealed first moment bounds for 
$E^{\sigma,\tau}$ and $E^{\frozen,\sigma,\tau}$
with $\sigma,\tau\in\{\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let
$Q^{\sigma,\tau}=E^{\sigma,\tau}+\tilde{Q}^{\sigma,\tau}$ as in Definitions~\ref{d:Q} and \ref{d:tQ}. Then, for $N$ large enough, we have
	\[\bbE
	\Big|\Delta E^{\sigma,\tau}(q_d)\Big| 
	\le L^{O(1)}\bigg\{\eta\delta^{1/2} + \frac{\BUCKETS\delta}{N}
	\bigg\}
	\]
for all $\sigma,\tau\in\{\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}$. The same bound holds with $E^\frozen$ in place of $E$.
\begin{proof}
This is similar
to the proof of Corollary~\ref{c:Q.first.quenched}. Recall 
that Lemma~\ref{l:qv.simplification} implies
	\[
	\Big|\Delta E^{\sigma,\tau}(q_d)\Big| 
	\le O\bigg(
	\eta^2
	+\sum_{\rho\in\{\sigma,\tau\}}\bigg[
	\eta\Big(\Delta\tilde{Q}^\rho(q_d)\Big)^{1/2}
	+\Big( \Delta \bar{D}^\rho(q_d)\Big)^2
	\bigg]\bigg)\,.
	\]
By Lemmas~\ref{l:barD.II.second}--\ref{l:barD.Ising.second}, for all $\sigma\in\{\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}$ we have
	\[\E\Big[\Delta\bar{D}^\sigma(q_d)^2\Big]
	\le\frac{ L^{O(1)}\BUCKETS\delta}{N}
	\,.\]
By Lemma~\ref{l:tQ.first.quenched} and the bound $\E[(\MAX_N)^2]\le L^{O(1)}$ from Proposition~\ref{p:Y.kolmogorov}, for all $\sigma\in\{\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}$ we have
	\[
	\E\bigg[\Big(\Delta\tilde{Q}^\sigma(q_d)\Big)^{1/2}\bigg]
	\le L^{O(1)} \delta^{1/2}\,.
	\]
Combining the bounds gives the claim, recalling that $\eta\ll\delta$ from Assumption~\ref{a:params}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:32:34.741762+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6fe65f3f7dfc8306e792ce9578bf5d2ecdb90b93650b9e22b982831c7dbb39b1","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:tropp_moment of arXiv:2411.07878, 'Bernstein-type and Bennett-type inequalities for unbounded matrix martingales'] Let independent random matrices $\mathbf{X}_1, \dots, \mathbf{X}_n \in \mathbb{H}(d)$ satisfy for all $k = 1, \dots, n$, all $p = 2, 3, \dots$, with some $K > 0$ and positive-definite matrices $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k$
    \[
    \E \mathbf{X}_k = 0,
    \quad
    \E \mathbf{X}^p_k \preccurlyeq \frac{p!}{2} K^{p-2} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k.
    \]
    Let $\sigma^2 \coloneqq \norm*{\sum^n_{k = 1} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k}. $ Then for all $t \ge 0$
    \[
    \mathbb{P} \lr{\lambda_{\max}\left(\sum^n_{k=1} \mathbf{X}_k\right) \ge t} \le d \elr{- \frac{t^2}{2 (\sigma^2 + K t)}}.
    \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:36:49.819860+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6ff4d4292755c3eb3d1be3283f166d79c3ecad66f3002c0fae4eb7df642710f2","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:convex-linear-bound of arXiv:2609.02829, 'Quantitative explosion and percolation of the divisible sandpile'] Let $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_N$ be i.i.d.\ mean-zero variables with finite
		variance. Let $F$ be convex in each
		coordinate and suppose that, $\mathbb{P}$-almost surely, for every $1\leq i\leq N$,
		\[
			0\leq\partial_i^+F\leq b_i\, ,
		\]
		where the $b_i$ are deterministic. Then there is a universal
		$C<\infty$ such that, for every $L>0$,
		\[
			\mathbb{E}\left[\left(
			F-\mathbb{E} F-\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbb{E}[\partial_i^+F]\xi_i
			\right)^2\right]
			\leq CL^2\sum_{i=1}^N\Var(\partial_i^+F)
			+C\eta(L)\sum_{i=1}^Nb_i^2\, ,
		\]
		where, for an independent copy $\xi_1'$ of $\xi_1$,
		\[
			\eta(L)\coloneqq
			\mathbb{E}\left[(\xi_1-\xi_1')^2
			\mathbf{1}_{\{|\xi_1-\xi_1'|>L\}}\right]\, .
		\]","status":"unverified"}

   A_N(\xi, \xi) = 1 - \sum_{\eta = \textrm{\tt disp}(\xi) }  A_N(\xi, \eta),

{"assumptions":["alpha is irrational and satisfies ||q alpha|| >= C q^{-tau} for all integers q >= 1, with C > 0 and tau >= 1","||t|| denotes the distance from t to the nearest integer","in part (ii), f is C^infinity on the circle R/Z with mean zero, and the rotation is x -> x + alpha","solutions are sought up to an additive constant; L^2 and distributional solutions are compared by Fourier coefficients"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:09:43.732260+00:00","domain":"Diophantine approximation, small divisors, circle rotations","id":"claim_701f743bb2241950d3a8f90b87a8fd689c27198731a6afd43cc9166321190ecf","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"For a real number t write ||t|| for its distance to the nearest integer. Fix an irrational alpha and suppose alpha is DIOPHANTINE of type (C, tau): there are constants C > 0 and tau >= 1 with

  ||q alpha||  >=  C * q^{-tau}    for every integer q >= 1.

Then:

(i) (the small divisors are only polynomially small) for every nonzero integer q,
      | e^{2 pi i q alpha} - 1 |  =  2 | sin(pi q alpha) |  >=  4 ||q alpha||  >=  4 C |q|^{-tau}.
    The upper bound | e^{2 pi i q alpha} - 1 | <= 2 pi ||q alpha|| always holds, so the two sides are comparable to ||q alpha||.

(ii) (solving the cohomological equation) Let R_alpha(x) = x + alpha on the circle T = R/Z and let f be a C^infinity function on T with mean zero. Then the equation u(x + alpha) - u(x) = f(x) has a C^infinity solution u, unique up to an additive constant, given on Fourier coefficients by u-hat(q) = f-hat(q) / (e^{2 pi i q alpha} - 1) for q nonzero. Quantitatively |u-hat(q)| <= |q|^{tau} |f-hat(q)| / (4C), so one loses tau derivatives: in Sobolev scale ||u||_{H^{s - tau}} <= (4C)^{-1} ||f||_{H^s}, and the analogous statement holds in Holder scale with an epsilon loss.

(iii) (how common the hypothesis is) For every tau > 1, Lebesgue-almost every alpha is Diophantine of type (C, tau) for some C = C(alpha) > 0; for tau = 1 the alpha satisfying the condition are exactly the badly approximable ones (bounded partial quotients), a set of Lebesgue measure zero and full Hausdorff dimension; for tau < 1 no alpha satisfies it at all, by Dirichlet's theorem.

WHERE IT FAILS. If alpha is LIOUVILLE (no such C, tau exist), the conclusion of (ii) fails badly: choose q_1 < q_2 < ... with ||q_k alpha|| < q_k^{-k} and define f by f-hat(q_k) = f-hat(-q_k)-bar = ||q_k alpha||^{1/2} and all other coefficients zero. These coefficients decay faster than any power of q_k, so f is C^infinity with mean zero, yet |u-hat(q_k)| >= ||q_k alpha||^{1/2} / (2 pi ||q_k alpha||) = 1 / (2 pi ||q_k alpha||^{1/2}), which blows up faster than any polynomial in q_k. Hence no solution u exists in L^2, and not even a distributional solution exists. So the Diophantine condition is not a technical convenience: it is what separates solvability from non-solvability. Note also that (ii) gives no information at all about the SPEED of ergodic averages by itself, and that the estimates degrade as C -> 0, so any application that needs uniformity must track C and tau explicitly.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:15:55.030292+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7055b30bffe13cb0d0f8870c5417c476f4eca3705dbf803a0ec718620fda056b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition of arXiv:2608.29708, 'Intuitionistic and Constructive Modal Logics for Classical Modal Logicians'] \leavevmode
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*)]
    \item For every $\Box$-p frame $\mathfrak{F}$, $\beta \mathfrak{F}$ is $\Box$-condensed and $\Box$-brilliant.
    \item For every $\Diamond$-p frame $\mathfrak{F}$, $\delta \mathfrak{F}$ is $\Diamond$-condensed and $\Diamond$-brilliant.
  \end{enumerate}
  \begin{proof}
    (1)
    ($\Box$-condensed)
    Take any $x \leq x' \sqsubset_\beta y''$, then there is $y'$ such that $(x \leq) x' \sqsubset y' \leq y''$.
    By $\Box$-p of $\mathfrak{F}$, there is $y$ such that $x \sqsubset y \leq y' (\leq y'')$,
    then $x \sqsubset y \leq y''$, so $x \sqsubset_\beta y''$.
    ($\Box$-brilliant)
    Take any $x \sqsubset_\beta y' \leq y''$, then there is $y$ such that $x \sqsubset y \leq y' (\leq y'')$.
    then $x \sqsubset y \leq y''$, so $x \sqsubset_\beta y''$.

    (2)
    ($\Diamond$-condensed)
    Take any $x'' \geq x \sqsubset_\delta y$, then there is $y'$ such that $x \sqsubset y' \geq y$.
    By $\Diamond$-p of $\mathfrak{F}$, there is $y''$ such that $x'' \sqsubset y''$ and $y'' \geq y' (\geq y)$,
    then $x'' \sqsubset y'' \geq y$, so $x'' \sqsubset_\delta y$.
    ($\Diamond$-brilliant)
    Take any $x' \sqsubset_\delta y' \geq y$, then there is $y''$ such that $x' \sqsubset y'' \geq y' (\geq y)$,
    then $x' \sqsubset y'' \geq y$, so $x' \sqsubset_\delta y$.
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:16:18.692823+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_705cce3bc3c2f162b4275875c9b9a71f24d78fbec2f616fc38040dcbd9b51005","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 31 (Compatible prefix time) of arXiv:2607.26377, '\textbf{Entire Logarithmic Signatures\\ of Bounded-Variation Paths in Finite Dimensions}'] Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real normed vector space with
$\dim V\geq2$, and let
$\gamma\colon[0,T]\to V$ be a continuous bounded-variation path. Set
\[
l=\log S(\gamma),
\qquad
v=\gamma_T-\gamma_0,
\]
and assume that
\[
R(l)=\infty,
\qquad
v\neq0.
\]
Fix $\ell\in V^*$ such that $\ell(v)=1$, put $W=\ker\ell$, and write
\[
\gamma_t-\gamma_0=x_t v+X_t,
\qquad
x_t=\ell(\gamma_t-\gamma_0),
\qquad
X_t\in W.
\]

Give $W$ an auxiliary Euclidean norm and let $W_{\C}$ be its
complexification. For every finite symmetric set
$\Lambda\subset2\pi\Q$, define the real Hilbert space
\[
E_\Lambda
=
\set{(z_\omega)_{\omega\in\Lambda}
\in\prod_{\omega\in\Lambda}W_{\C}:
 z_{-\omega}=\overline{z_\omega}}
\]
with the norm inherited from the Hilbert direct sum, the decorated
transverse path
\[
B_t^\Lambda(\gamma)
=
\left(
\int_0^t \e^{i\omega x_s}\dd X_s
\right)_{\omega\in\Lambda},
\qquad 0\leq t\leq T,
\]
and the orthogonal map
\[
T_\Lambda\colon E_\Lambda\to E_\Lambda,
\qquad
(T_\Lambda z)_\omega=\e^{i\omega}z_\omega.
\]
Denote by the same symbol the induced graded automorphism of tensor
series, and set
\[
r_t^\Lambda
=S\bigl(B^\Lambda(\gamma)|_{[0,t]}\bigr),
\qquad
h_\Lambda=r_T^\Lambda.
\]

Then there exists $t_*\in[0,T]$ such that, for every finite symmetric
$\Lambda\subset2\pi\Q$,
\begin{equation}
h_\Lambda
=a_\Lambda T_\Lambda(a_\Lambda)^{-1},
\qquad
a_\Lambda=r_{t_*}^\Lambda.
\end{equation}
Equivalently,
\[
r_{t_*}^\Lambda
=h_\Lambda T_\Lambda\bigl(r_{t_*}^\Lambda\bigr)
\]
for every such $\Lambda$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:59:58.457995+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_707a083e05662da9815b61f18d881d65e051872ee20f302eea6356337996e140","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem OSSS of arXiv:2605.14910, 'Sharp Phase Transition for the Formation of Infinite Tubes'] Let $f\colon\{0,1\}^N\to\{0,1\}$ be an increasing Boolean function.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-13T03:42:25.818646+00:00","domain":"probability, Markov chains, random walks on graphs","id":"claim_70883747d2f8094e81f1250f92c005572a73779bc267e33d29fe488ce3c6f103","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign status: candidate_full_solution - author-checked, unrefereed] Aldous and Fill, Reversible Markov Chains and Random Walks on Graphs, Open Problem 7.27 (Chapter 7, p. 259) asks whether, over arc-transitive graphs excluding the n-cycles, tau* = O(n log n), tau2 = O(n) and tau*/(2 tau0) = 1 + o(1). Our result (id P0208, 2026-09-08): all three claims are FALSE. The counterexample is the lexicographic product C_m[Kbar_2] for odd m >= 5 - the m-cycle with every vertex split into two non-adjacent twins - which is connected, 4-regular, arc-transitive and not a cycle, on n = 2m vertices. With g(j) = j(m-j) + m the mean hitting time at cycle-distance j and 2m the twin hitting time: tau* = 2*floor(m^2/4) + 2m ~ n^2/8 (quadratic, not O(n log n)); tau2 = 1/(1 - cos(2 pi/m)) ~ n^2/(8 pi^2), because A(C_m[Kbar_2]) = A(C_m) tensor J_2 so the relaxation time is the m-cycle's own; and tau*/(2 tau0) tends to 3/2, not 1 + o(1). Verification, as the source words it: exact hitting times by linear algebra at m = 5, 7, 9, 11, 15, 21 (all five formulas exact at every size); arc-transitivity checked mechanically at m = 5, 7, 9 (the group generated by the rotation, one reflection and one fibre swap has order 2^m * 2m and its orbit of one arc is all 8m arcs); and a Lean file P0208.lean with nine theorems, no sorry, axioms propext / Classical.choice / Quot.sound only. Not formalised: uniqueness of the solution of (I-P)h = 1 and the tensor eigenvalue computation, both standard and checked numerically. Prior art not cleared. odd m >= 5 simple random walk on the lexicographic product C_m[Kbar_2] (n = 2m vertices, 4-regular, arc-transitive, not a cycle)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:23:25.634591+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7089e0c06e1ce3f0d01d2a2851b0a77e3a83e3072340314f9dac3f0546320bdf","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm Inverse4 of arXiv:2609.01350, 'New classes of trace-form permutation polynomials and their compositional inverses'] Let $q=2^m$ with $m$ odd, and let
$f_2(x)=x+\gamma{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}\big(c_1x+c_2x^2+x^{2q-1}\big)$ with
$c_1,c_2\in\mathbb F_{q^2}$ and $\gamma\in\mathbb F_{q^2}\setminus\mathbb F_q$
satisfying
\[
  \gamma^{3(q-1)}=1,\qquad
  1+{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(c_1\gamma)=\gamma^{2q-1},\qquad
  {\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(c_2\gamma^q)=0,
\]
so that $f_2$ is a permutation polynomial of $\mathbb F_{q^2}$ by
Theorem~(Result2 of the paper)(3). Then
\begin{equation}
  f_2^{-1}(x)=
  \begin{cases}
    0
      & \text{if } x=0,\\[0.8em]
    x+\gamma^{q-1}\Big(h_2(x)+\dfrac{{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(x^3)}{x^{q+1}}\Big)
      & \text{if } x\neq0,\ r=0,\\[0.8em]
    x+\gamma^{q-1}\Big(h_2(x)+\dfrac{{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(x^3)}{x^{q+1}}
      +r^{1/3}+\dfrac{P}{r^{1/3}}\Big)
      & \text{if } x\neq0,\ r\neq0,
  \end{cases}
\end{equation}
where
\[
  P=h_2(x)^2+h_2(x)\,{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}\big(\gamma^{q-1}x^q\big)
    +\frac{{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(\gamma x)^3\,{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(x)^3}{\gamma^3\,x^{2q+2}},
  \qquad
  r=P\Big(h_2(x)+\frac{{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(x)^3}{x^{q+1}}\Big).
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:17:10.022418+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_70aaacc132bf006490a2efbd61e694a78c197fa1fcea406ad4ce694db2ff6bdd","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 3 of arXiv:2608.17374, '\textbf{On the Pseudo-Mixing of Kac's Walk}'] [Distinguishability With Respect to Fixed Sequences] 
Fix two sequences of distributions $\mu_{n}, \nu_{n}$ that take on values in the set $\mathcal{S}_{n}$, and let $f_{n}$ be a sequence of functions from $\mathcal{S}_{n}$ to $\mathbb{R}$.

We say the sequence $f_{n}$ \textit{weakly} distinguishes $\mu_{n}$ and $\nu_{n}$ if
\be 
\sqrt{\max(\Var_{\mu_{n}}(f_{n}),\Var_{\nu_{n}}(f_{n}))} = O(|\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{n}}[f_{n}] - \mathbb{E}_{\nu_{n}}[f_{n}] |),
\ee 
and \textit{strongly} distinguishes if the LHS is 
$o(|\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{n}}[f_{n}] - \mathbb{E}_{\nu_{n}}[f_{n}] |)$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:49:05.363346+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_70f0fb268b1ece30100715ddcfee6caf52d2175e66905d7971576d0c2a24c440","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:orbit_kernel of arXiv:2601.07045, 'From Continuous to Discrete: \\ a No-U-Turn Sampler for Permutations'] Let $(m, b)$ specify a NURS orbit
\[
\mathcal{O} = (\sigma \circ \rho^i)_{i = a}^b,
\qquad a = b - 2^m + 1.
\]
Then the orbit selection kernel of NURS satisfies
\[
p_{\mathrm{orbit}}(m, b \mid \sigma, \rho)
=
\frac{1}{2^m}
\cdot
\mathbf{1}\Biggl(
\Phi(\mathcal{O})
\;\wedge\;
\bigwedge_{s = 1}^{m} \; \bigwedge_{t = 1}^{2^s}
\neg \textsc{Stop}\!\left(\mathcal{O}_{s,t}, \varepsilon, w\right)
\Biggr),
\]
where $\{\mathcal{O}_{s,t}\}$ are the dyadic sub-orbits of $\mathcal{O}$
(Definition~(def:dyadic-suborbit of the paper)), and where $\Phi(\mathcal{O})$ holds if and only if
\[
\textsc{Stop}(\mathcal{O}, \varepsilon, w)
\;\vee\;
\textsc{SubStop}(\mathcal{O}_+^{\mathrm{ext}}, \varepsilon, w)
\;\vee\;
\textsc{SubStop}(\mathcal{O}_-^{\mathrm{ext}}, \varepsilon, w)
\;\vee\;
|\mathcal{O}| = 2^M.
\]

{"assumptions":["f measurable and a.e. finite","|E| < infinity (or E sigma-finite, applied piecewise)","the measure is Borel regular, so that inner regularity by closed sets is available"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.751562+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_70f1790178f49b91f5ee0ff4790936831774e34f8e840b54c67bc80f664a49ab","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f : R^d -> C be Lebesgue measurable and finite almost everywhere, let E be a measurable set of FINITE measure, and let eps > 0. Then there is a CLOSED set F contained in E with |E \\ F| < eps such that the RESTRICTION of f to F is continuous. Moreover one may take g in C_c(R^d) with g = f on F and sup |g| <= sup |f|. The theorem does not assert that f is continuous AT the points of F as a function on R^d: the indicator of the rationals is nowhere continuous on R, yet it agrees with the zero function off a set of measure zero, and Lusin's F can be taken to be any closed set of irrationals of nearly full measure. Finiteness of |E| may be relaxed to sigma-finiteness by exhausting E, at the price of stating the conclusion with |E \\ F| < eps for each piece. [standard; e.g. Rudin, Real and Complex Analysis, 3rd ed., Theorem 2.24]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Two explicitly specified centered covariance-I Gaussian mixture families","0<s sufficiently small; dimension limit before small-SNR expansion","Positive bounded conditional covariance perturbations","Not asserted to satisfy the iid matrix-factor model"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T16:15:57.431274+00:00","domain":"Extensive-rank matrix inference, Gaussian mixtures and high-noise KL expansions","id":"claim_70f4e8e741b41d6bfce9be790f7d9243f6253379eb668f0f080e91fce2b8bc1c","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Own work, proof draft UNAUDITED; no novelty claim. There are two families of centered, covariance-I_d Gaussian mixtures

 log(1+chi^2(P_s||Q))/d =s^4/2+O(s^8)

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:28:49.121797+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_70f93b993bb6bb37c7bfcb078034702d78b2e5b7cd400a6962d5b950db4fff82","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:johnson-spectrum of arXiv:2608.18293, 'Critical tensor covariance at the Marchenko--Pastur threshold'] Assume $1\le q<n/2$. Let $A_q$ be the adjacency matrix of the Johnson graph
$J(n,q)$: two $q$-subsets are adjacent when their symmetric difference has size
two. For a $j$-subset $T$, define
\[
  f_T(I)=\1_{\{T\subseteq I\}},
  \qquad |I|=q,
\]
and let $U_j$ be the span of the functions $f_T$ with $|T|=j$. Then
\[
  U_0\subseteq U_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq U_q.
\]
Set $U_{-1}=\{0\}$. If $H_j=U_j\cap U_{j-1}^{\perp}$, then $A_q$ acts on $H_j$ by the scalar
\begin{equation}
  \alpha_j=(q-j)(n-q-j)-j,
  \qquad 0\le j\le q.
  
\end{equation}
In particular, when $q<n/2$, the largest eigenvalue of $A_q$ on the orthogonal complement of the constant vector is
\begin{equation}
  \alpha_1=q(n-q)-n.
  
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:09:34.497474+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_71012fbc4a10ccd6ccbbd74ad09769b158fb5d1f6cab2bb33003059607417a82","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm conformal_invariance_aut_D of arXiv:2505.14762, 'Multiple radial SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Sutherland system'] Let \( \tau \in \mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{D}) \). The drift term \( b(\boldsymbol{\theta}, u) \) is a pre-Schwarzian form, satisfying:
\[
b_i = \tau' \widetilde{b}_i \circ \tau + \frac{6 - \kappa}{2} \left(\log \tau'\right)'.
\]
\begin{itemize}
    \item[(i)] There exists a smooth function \( F(\tau, u): \widetilde{\mathrm{Aut}}(\mathbb{D}) \times \mathbb{D} \to \mathbb{R} \) such that:
    \[
    \log \psi - \log (\psi \circ \tau) + \frac{\kappa - 6}{2\kappa} \sum_i \log \tau'(\theta_i) = F(\tau, u),
    \]
    where \( F \) satisfies the functional equation:
    
    \begin{equation}
    
    F(\tau_1 \tau_2, u) = F(\tau_1, \tau_2(u)) + F(\tau_2, u).
    \end{equation}

    \item[(ii)] There exists a rotation constant \( \omega \) such that:
    \begin{equation}
    F(A_\theta, 0) = \omega \theta.
    \end{equation}

    If \( \omega = 0 \), \( \mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{D}) \) suffices to describe conformal invariance, and \( F \) reduces to a map \( \mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{D}) \times \mathbb{D} \to \mathbb{R} \).

    \item[(iii)] Suppose \( F_1(\tau, u) \) and \( F_2(\tau, u) \) correspond to partition functions \( \psi_1 \) and \( \psi_2 \). If their rotation constants \( \omega_1 = \omega_2 \), then there exists a function \( g(u) \) such that:
    \[
   \psi_2 = g(u) \cdot \psi_1.
    \]

    \item[(iv)] For \( \tau \in \widetilde{\mathrm{Aut}}(\mathbb{D}) \), let \( \tau(u) = v \). Decompose \( \tau = T_v \circ A_\theta \circ T^{-1}_u \), where \( u, v \in \mathbb{D} \) and \( \theta \in \mathbb{R} \). Using the relations \( T_u'(u) = \frac{1}{1 - |u|^2} \) and \( T_v'(0) = 1 - |v|^2 \), define:
    \[
    \tau'(u)^{\lambda(u)} \overline{\tau'(u)}^{\overline{\lambda(u)}} := \left(\frac{1 - |v|^2}{1 - |u|^2}\right)^{2 \operatorname{Re}(\lambda(u))} e^{-2 \theta \operatorname{Im}(\lambda(u))}.
    \]
    Then:
    \[
    F(\tau, u) = \log \left(\tau'(u)^{\lambda(u)} \overline{\tau'(u)}^{\overline{\lambda(u)}}\right),
    \]
    satisfy the functional equation ((functional equation for F of the paper)), with rotation constant \( \omega = \operatorname{Im}(\lambda(u)) \).
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:10:07.562333+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_711345066701a1faec8680ac5e358ef0500f35056a1690d48cf8aad81b8d8e14","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition eq:Gaussian-divisible-slice of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[proposition]{prop:gaussian-divisible-upper-slice}

\[
 J_{I,N}=\sqrt{1-\tau_N}\,X_{I,N}+\sqrt{\tau_N}\,G_{I,N},
 \qquad \tau_N\in[\tau_0,1],
\]

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:15:34.384394+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_711bc4c5386e203ff4a9457fa6e67176abe8893462a82fbafbc5da524eef141a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 7 of arXiv:2609.03248, 'Connections between colored restricted $b$-ary and ordinary partitions'] Let $b\geq 2$ and $\rho\geq 1$ be integers, and let the finite sequences

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:20:33.752427+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7124a5917977f2ae5f1f94d056ca5a53354973487bc04d551754f7e5081dc684","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop 11 of arXiv:2609.03836, 'Koszul Orlik--Solomon Algebras from Non-supersolvable Arrangements'] Let $M$ be a matroid and $F, G \in \mathcal{L}(M)$.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item Suppose $F \subseteq G$,
        $F$ is modular in $M|_G$, and $G$ is modular in $M$. Then $F$ is modular in $M$.
        \item If $F$ is modular in $M$, then $F \cap G$ is modular in $M|_G$.
        \item If $F, G$ are modular in $M$, then $F \cap G$ is modular in $M$.
        \item If $F$ is modular in $M$, then $(F \vee G)-G$ is modular in $M/G$.
        \item If $F$ is modular in $M$ and $S \subseteq E(M)$ contains $F$, then $F$ is modular in $M|_S$.
        \item If $F$ is modular in $M$ and $M$ is connected, then $M|_F$ is connected.
    \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:09:34.497957+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7136ddb39be635661b82383746e601fad68a079bdd47e3f5f06f6b57b54acc5c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn Monodromy of Coulomb Gas Correlation Differential of arXiv:2505.14762, 'Multiple radial SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Sutherland system'] Let $\boldsymbol{\sigma} = \sum_{j=1}^n \sigma_j \cdot z_j$ be a divisor on $\mathbb{C}$ with associated Coulomb gas correlation differential
\[
C_{(b)}[\boldsymbol{\sigma}] = \prod_{j < k} (z_j - z_k)^{\sigma_j \sigma_k}.
\]
This function is multivalued due to the presence of non-integer exponents. Its multivaluedness is described by the \emph{monodromy representation} arising from analytic continuation around branch points.

To illustrate the basic mechanism, consider the case $n = 2$. Then
\[
C_{(b)}[\boldsymbol{\sigma}] = (z_1 - z_2)^{\sigma_1 \sigma_2},
\]
which is analytic in $z_1$ on $\mathbb{C} \setminus \{z_2\}$. If we analytically continue this function as $z_1$ travels once counterclockwise around $z_2$, the function picks up a multiplicative factor of $e^{2\pi i \sigma_1 \sigma_2}$. 

Thus, the monodromy representation
\[
\rho: \pi_1(\mathbb{C} \setminus \{z_2\}, z_1) \longrightarrow \mathbb{C}^*, \quad \rho(C_2) = e^{2\pi i \sigma_1 \sigma_2}
\]
captures how the function changes under analytic continuation around the singularity at $z_2$, where $C_2$ is the loop encircling $z_2$.

In general, for $\boldsymbol{\sigma} = \sum_{j=1}^n \sigma_j \cdot z_j$, the function $C_{(b)}[\boldsymbol{\sigma}]$ is analytic in $z_1$ on $\mathbb{C} \setminus \{z_2, \ldots, z_n\}$. The fundamental group $\pi_1(\mathbb{C} \setminus \{z_2, \ldots, z_n\}, z_1)$ is the free group generated by loops $C_j$ encircling each $z_j$ ($j = 2, \ldots, n$), and the monodromy representation
\[
\rho: \pi_1(\mathbb{C} \setminus \{z_2, \ldots, z_n\}) \to \mathbb{C}^*, \quad \rho(C_j) = e^{2\pi i \sigma_1 \sigma_j}
\]
describes the multiplicative factor acquired by $C_{(b)}[\boldsymbol{\sigma}]$ when $z_1$ loops around $z_j$ once in the counterclockwise direction.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:20:33.748944+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_71675438816c4663ef4169d1a556ab5a73b0f958f871d72d049f7142464e37be","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 23 (Stable L\'evy functional limit in the heavy-tail regime, see~{\cite[Theorem 7.4.2.) of arXiv:2607.28865, 'First-Passage Percolation on Spread-out line graphs: Microscopic Regime'] {whitt02}}]
Assume Assumption~\textnormal{A.\ref{ass:A2}} holds with $0 < \gc < 2/\lc$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:T1-tail}, $\sfT_1$ is regularly varying with tail index $\alpha := \gc\lc \in (0,2)$. Let $m_n := \lfloor n/\mu_{\sfP} \rfloor$, and choose the scaling sequence $a_n$ and the truncated centering function $b_n(t)$ as
\[
    a_n := \inf\left\{x>0 : m_n\pr(\sfT_1>x)\le 1\right\}, \qquad

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:25:06.127242+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_71676e85fcb95b5d9a2f06cff143c3bf433f9ac32afb94face9d72503635e047","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 20 (Martingale Fourier CLT) of arXiv:2608.22342, 'Completely Positive Entropy and Fourier Central Limit Theorems for Stationary Random Measu'] Let $D\in\mathscr K$ and let $\theta\in\bT^d$ satisfy $2\theta\neq0$. For
$h_1,\ldots,h_m\in C_c^\infty(\bR^d;\bC)$, set
\begin{equation}

    M_R(h_a,\theta)
    :=R^{-d/2}\sum_{k\in\bZ^d}
      h_a(k/R)e^{-2\pi i\langle k,\theta\rangle}U^kD.
\end{equation}
Then there is an $H^m$-valued complex Gaussian random element with mean zero
\[
    G=\bigl(G(h_1),\ldots,G(h_m)\bigr)
\]
such that
\begin{equation}

    (M_R(h_1,\theta),\ldots,M_R(h_m,\theta))\dto G
    \qquad\text{in }H^m.
\end{equation}
Its covariance is
\begin{equation}

    \E\!\left[
      \langle G(h_a),u\rangle_H
      \overline{\langle G(h_b),v\rangle_H}
    \right]
    =\left(\int h_a\overline{h_b}\right)
      \E\!\left[
        \langle D,u\rangle_H
        \overline{\langle D,v\rangle_H}
      \right],
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}

    \E\!\left[
      \langle G(h_a),u\rangle_H
      \langle G(h_b),v\rangle_H
    \right]=0,
    \qquad u,v\in H.
\end{equation}
The covariance operator on $H^m$ determined by
\eqref{eq:innovation-fourier-covariance} is positive and trace class; its trace
is
\[
    \left(\sum_{a=1}^m\|h_a\|_2^2\right)\E\|D\|_H^2.
\]
Thus the Gaussian law in the statement is well defined by
Subsection~\ref{subsec:hilbert-gaussian-weak-convergence}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:47.652013+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7186db882c863ea9073dea828e7af3f00cab1a8dfbe5aaa44a03333a136d9bd8","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 13 ($\ell$-multigraph) of arXiv:2605.07050, 'Universality of the fluctuations of the free energy in generalized Sherrington--Kirkpatric'] We say that a multigraph $\gamma$ with nodes $1, 2, \dots, N$ is an $\ell$-multigraph if any pair of nodes can be connected by at most $\ell$ edges. The multiplicity $m^\gamma_{ij}$ between the nodes $i$ and $j$ is the number of separate edges connecting them, and we let $m^\gamma_{ij} = 0$ if the nodes $i$ and $j$ are not connected. (It is possible that $m_{kk}^{\gamma} > 0$, i.e., self-loops are allowed.) If $m^\gamma_{ij} = 1, 2, 3, 4$, we say that the edge between the nodes $i$ and $j$ is single, double, triple, quadruple, respectively.

The degree of the node $i$ is defined by
\[
	d^\gamma_i = m^\gamma_{ii} + \sum_{j=1}^N m^\gamma_{ij}.
\]
In particular, a single self-loop at the node $i$ increases the degree of the node $i$ by $2$. The size $m^\gamma$ and the length $n^\gamma$ of a multigraph $\gamma$ are defined by
\[
	m^\gamma = \sum_{i\leq j} m^\gamma_{ij} = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^N d^\gamma_i, \quad n^\gamma = \sum_{i\leq j} \indi(m^\gamma_{ij} > 0),
\]
respectively. The number of the single (respectively, double, triple, quadruple) edges $n_1^\gamma$ (respectively, $n_2^\gamma, n_3^\gamma, n_4^\gamma$) is defined by
\[
	n_r^\gamma = \sum_{i\leq j} \indi(m^\gamma_{ij} = r), \quad r=1, 2, 3, 4.
\]
Similarly, the number of the single (respectively, double) self-loops $\tilde n_1^\gamma$ (respectively, $\tilde n_2^\gamma$) is defined by
\[ \tilde n_r^\gamma = \sum_{k=1}^{N}\indi(m^\gamma_{kk} = r), \quad r=1,2.\]

The set of all $\ell$-multigraphs with single and/or double self-loops is denoted by $\caG^\ell$. (The empty graph is a multigraph and included in $\caG^\ell$.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:37:51.453011+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_718e27bf4bbf07fd6d9ca45a921b17a91898532306124df36d052b0aad720960","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 32 of arXiv:2604.03213, 'Asymptotic expansion for transport maps \\ between laws of multimatrix models'] Let $\cX$ be a Banach space and $a \in \R$.
Suppose $f \colon [a,\infty) \times \cX \to \cX$ is a continuous function such that for all $T > a$ and $R > 0$, there exists a constant $c_{T,R} < \infty$ such that
\[
\sup_{a \leq t \leq T}\norm{f(t,x) - f(t,y)}_{\cX} \leq c_{T,R}\norm{x-y}_{\cX} \qquad (x,y \in C_R(x_0)).
\]
If $c \colon [a,\infty) \to \cX$ is continuous, then there exists a $T_{\infty} \in (a,\infty]$ and a continuous function $y_{\infty} \colon [a,T_{\infty}) \to \cX$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),font=\normalfont]
    \item $\displaystyle y_{\infty}(t) = c(t) + \int_a^t f(s,y_{\infty}(s))\,\d s$ for all $t \in [a,T_{\infty})$, i.e., $y_{\infty} = c + \int_a^{\boldsymbol{\cdot}} f(t,y_{\infty}(t))\,\d t$ on $[a,T_{\infty})$;
    \item If $T > a$ and $y \colon [a,T) \to \cX$ is a continuous function such that $y = c + \int_a^{\boldsymbol{\cdot}} f(t,y(t))\,\d t$ on $[a,T)$, then $T \leq T_{\infty}$, and $y_{\infty}|_{[a,T)} = y$.
\end{enumerate}
Moreover, if $T_{\infty} < \infty$, then $\norm{y_{\infty}(t)}_{\cX} \to \infty$ as $t \nearrow T_{\infty}$.
The function $y_{\infty}$ is the \textbf{maximal solution} to the integral equation $y = c + \int_a^{\boldsymbol{\cdot}} f(t,y(t))\,\d t$, and $T_{\infty}$ is its \textbf{lifetime} (or \textbf{blow-up time}). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:48:24.296611+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_71e0d9ba818881c73222688b9d12a1a5628ea07bb86c0ba813ab26f2112a95b4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem optimaliq>1 of arXiv:2605.10452, 'A secretary for Messrs. Luce and Mallows'] Consider the secretary problem
with either  the  Mallows distribution
or the $P_n^{\mathcal{L}_\text{inv};\{q_n^i\}_{i=1}^n}$-type Luce distribution with  $q=q_n\in(0,\infty)-\{1\}$
in the case that the smallest number is  of highest rank.

\noindent i. Let $q_n=1-\frac cn$, where $c>0$. Then the asymptotically optimal strategy is $\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
\begin{equation}
M_n^*\sim n\Big(\frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{1-e^{-c}}{e-1+e^{-c}}\big)\Big),
\end{equation}
 and the corresponding  limiting probability of success
is $\frac1e$

\noindent Also, $\lim_{c\to\infty} \frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{1-e^{-c}}{e-1+e^{-c}}\big)=0$ and $\lim_{c\to0} \frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{1-e^{-c}}{e-1+e^{-c}}\big)=\frac1e$.

\noindent ii.
Let $q_n=1-\frac c{n^\alpha}$, where $c>0$ and $\alpha\in(0,1)$. Then the asymptotically optimal strategy  is $\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
$$
M_n^*\sim\frac1c\left(1-\log(e-1)\right)n^\alpha\approx0.459\frac{n^\alpha}c,
$$
 and the corresponding limiting probability of success
is $\frac1e$.

\noindent iii.
Let $q\in(0,1)$.  Then the asymptotically optimal strategy  is $\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M^*)$, where
$$
M^*=\begin{cases}&\max\left\{M\ge1: \sum_{j=M}^\infty\frac{q^j}{1-q^j}\ge\frac 1{1-q}\right\}, \ \text{if}\ \sum_{j=1}^\infty\frac{q^j}{1-q^j}\ge\frac1{1-q};\\
&0,\ \text{if}\ \sum_{j=1}^\infty\frac{q^j}{1-q^j}<\frac1{1-q}.\end{cases}
$$
(If  $\sum_{j=M^*}^\infty\frac{q^j}{1-q^j}=\frac 1{1-q}$, then $M^*-1$ is also optimal.)

\noindent The corresponding limiting probability of success is given by
$$
\begin{cases}&(1-q)(1-q^{M^*})\sum_{j=M^*}^\infty\frac{q^j}{1-q^j}\ge(1-q^{-M^*}),\ \text{if}\ M^*\ge1;\\
&1-q>\frac1e,\ \text{if}\ M^*=0.\end{cases}
$$
This limiting probability is always greater or equal to $\frac1e$ and is
strictly greater than $\frac1e$ for all but at most a countable number of $q$ with no accumulation points in $(0,\infty)$.

\noindent iv. Let $q_n=1+\frac cn$, where $c>0$. Then the asymptotically optimal strategy is $\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
\begin{equation}
M_n^*\sim n\Big(\frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{e^c-1}e\big)\Big),
\end{equation}
 and the corresponding  limiting probability of success
is $\frac1e$.

\noindent Also, $\lim_{c\to\infty} \frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{e^c-1}e\big)=1$ and $\lim_{c\to0} \frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{e^c-1}e\big)=\frac1e$.

\noindent v.
Let $q_n=1+\frac c{n^\alpha}$, where $c>0$ and $\alpha\in(0,1)$. Then the asymptotically optimal strategy  is $\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
$$
n-M_n^*\sim\frac{n^\alpha}c,
$$
 and the corresponding limiting probability of success
is $\frac1e$.

\noindent vi. Let $q>1$.  Then the asymptotically optimal strategy  is $\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
$$
M_n^*=n-L, \ \text{where}\ L \ \text{satisfies}\ \frac1{q-1}\le L<\frac q{q-1}.
$$
The corresponding limiting probability of success is given by
$$
\frac{q-1}{q^L}L>\frac1e.
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:36:31.223822+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_71e98425fe4dbb8a7802a7e1bee535b588fa33d6d2fd777225f303dfc5d1e2f2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 17 (Unique Pinkall-modulus limit) of arXiv:2609.00501, 'Uniqueness of Finite-Time Varifold Limits for the M\"obius-Invariant Willmore Flow'] Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:anchored-profile}, orient the
profiles consistently with the reduced flow.  Let
\(\mathcal A_t\in\R/4\pi\mathbb Z\) be the oriented area class
enclosed by \(\gamma_t\), and let \(\mathcal A_T\) be the corresponding area class for
\(\gamma_T\).  Then
\begin{equation}
 
 \mathcal A_t\longrightarrow\mathcal A_T
 \qquad\text{in }\R/4\pi\mathbb Z .
\end{equation}
For \(t\) sufficiently close to \(T\), choose compatible real
representatives such that \(\mathcal A_t\to\mathcal A_T\).  Pinkall's
lattice is
\begin{equation}
 
 \Gamma_t=
 \operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Z}
 \left\{(2\pi,0),
 \left(\frac{\mathcal A_t}{2},\frac{L(\gamma_t)}2\right)\right\},
\end{equation}
and the corresponding modulus is
\begin{equation}
 
 \tau_t=\frac{\mathcal A_t+iL(\gamma_t)}{4\pi}\in\mathbb H .
\end{equation}
It satisfies
\[
 \tau_t\longrightarrow
 \tau_T:=\frac{\mathcal A_T+iL_T}{4\pi}.
\]
Its imaginary part satisfies the quantitative bounds
\begin{equation}
 
 \frac14\leq\operatorname{Im}\tau_T\leq\frac2\pi.
\end{equation}
Consequently the conformal classes
\[
 [\tau_t]\longrightarrow[\tau_T]
 \qquad\text{in }\mathcal M_1=\mathbb H/\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb Z)
\]
have a unique finite-time limit, independent of the approaching time
sequence.  With the orientation induced by the fixed oriented profile
and the positively oriented Hopf fibres, the class \([\tau_T]\) is the
intrinsic oriented conformal class of the limiting \(C^1\) Hopf torus.
In particular, no conformal
degeneration occurs at the finite endpoint.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:14:37.598093+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_71f4a4e7ad75fadec7819c97164eaddbc6037a3c91022cb2c0b3be00e86c7196","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 12 of arXiv:2608.18688, 'Regularity Preservation for Jump-Type Stochastic Transport Equations with Singular Drift'] Given a $\mH^{1}$-function $h(x)$ on $\mR^d$, a local random field $u_t(x)$, $x\in\mR^d$, $t\in [0,\tau(x))$ is called a local solution of equation (\ref{SPDE-2}) with initial condition $u_0(x,\omega)=h(x)$, if the following conditions are satisfied:
 	
 	(i) $\tau(x)=\tau(x,\omega)$ is an accessible, lower semicontinuous stopping time.
 	
 	(ii) $u_t(x)$, $t\in [0,\tau(x))$ is a local $\mH^{1,\alpha}$-semimartingale for some $\alpha>0$ and satisfies 
 	\ce 
 	u_t(x)
 	&=&h(x)+\int_0^t \bar{F}_0(r,x,u_r(x),\nabla u_r(x))\,dr+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\int_0^t F_i(r,x,u_r(x),\nabla u_r(x))\circ dW_r^i\no\\
 	&&+\int_0^t\int_{\mR^d_0} G(r,x,u_{r-}(x),z)\, N_R(dr,dz),
 	\de 
 	for all (t,x) such that $0\leq t<\tau(x)$ a.s..
 	
 	If there is a solution of equation (\ref{SPDE-2}) such that the terminal time $\tau(x)$ is infinite for all $x$ a.s, we will call it a global solution of equation (\ref{SPDE-2}).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:22:48.869147+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_71ff7ae56de7e3b8e2ef15f7c1fcaedf08696e3b657cfbd34e6e235e8d2a9323","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 7 of arXiv:2608.29148, '2608.29148'] A Lorentzian metric $g'$ on $X'$ is called an {\it $S^1$-invariant Poincar\'e metric} with conformal infinity $(\mathcal{C}, [g^{\mathrm{F}}_\th])$ if the following conditions are satisfied:
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] $g'$ is $S^1$-invariant.
\item[(ii)] The Killing vector field 
\[
K:=\frac{n+2}{2}\frac{\pa}{\pa s}
\]
satisfies 
\[
g'(K, K)=-1.
\]
Here, $\pa/\pa s$ is the infinitesimal generator of the $S^1$-action on $X'$. In particular, the integral curves of $K$ are geodesics.
\item [(iii)]$g'$ is a conformally compact metric with conformal infinity $(\mathcal{C}, [g^{\rm F}_\th])$, that is, for any boundary defining function $r\colon \ol{X'}\to [0, \infty)$, the metric $r^2 g'$ extends smoothly to a Lorentizan metric on $\ol{X'}$ satisfying $[(r^2 g')|_{T\mathcal{C}}]=[g^{\rm F}_\th]$.
\item[(iv)] $g'$ is ``asymptotically hyperbolic'' in the sense  that it satisfies
\[
\Bigl|\frac{dr}{r}\Bigr|^2_{g'}\bigl(=|dr|^2_{r^2 g'}\bigr)=\frac{1}{4}\quad {\rm on}\ \mathcal{C}
\] 
for an arbitrary boundary defining function $r\colon \ol{X'}\to [0, \infty)$.
\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:57:16.074012+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_720d26bdf3825ca4fa044d0ed818e8336754d3f37d85f57f49d0f220d8ec314b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theo excha of arXiv:2507.00737, 'Dispersion models on a circle: universal properties and asymptotic results'] Consider a valid {\sf CDM}\xspace $A$, and some deterministic masses $m[k]=(m_0,\cdots,m_{k-1})$, which are either positive or zero and satisfy the total weight condition  $W(m[k])  <1$. Let $({\sf IR}_j^A,0\leq j \leq k-1)$ denote the interval relaxation processes associated with $A$. We have  
	\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
		\item For a fixed $k$, the law of $\left(\textbf{O}^{(k)},\textbf{F}^{(k)}\right)$ does not depend on $A$ (it is the same for all valid {\sf CDM}\xspace that are designed to treat the masses $(m_0,\cdots,m_{k-1})$.
		\item  The law of $\left(\textbf{O}^{(k)},\textbf{F}^{(k)}\right)$ is invariant under the permutation of the masses:
		For any permutation $r\in {\bf S}_k$ (the symmetric group on $\{0,\cdots,k-1\}$),
		\[{\cal L}\left (\left(\textbf{O}^{(k)},\textbf{F}^{(k)}\right)~|~ (m_0,\cdots,m_{k-1})\right)={\cal L}\left (\left(\textbf{O}^{(k)},\textbf{F}^{(k)}\right)~|~ (m_{r(0)},\cdots,m_{r(k-1)})\right)\]
		(where we have written, as a condition, the successive masses that are used).
		\item For $k\geq 1$, the number of free CC,  ${\bf N}_k$, has (almost) a binomial distribution:
		\begin{equation}
		 {\bf N}_k \sur{=}{(d)} 1+ B(m[k]), \textrm {~~where~~} B(m[k])\sim {\sf Binomial}(k-1,R_k) 
		\end{equation}
		where $R_k=1-W(m[k])$ is the final free space available after the deposition of the first $k$ masses.
		\item Take a uniform element $\theta$ in $\{0,\cdots,b-1\}$ (independently of everything). Conditional on ${\bf N}_k=b$, 
		\begin{equation}\left(\left|\textbf{F}^{(k)}_{i+\theta {~\sf mod~} b}\right|,0\leq i \leq b-1\right)\sur{=}{(d)} R_k\, ({\bf D}_0,\cdots,{\bf D}_{b-1})\end{equation}  where $({\bf D}_0,\cdots,{\bf D}_{b-1})\sim{\sf Dirichlet}(b;1,\cdots,1)$. 
		Hence, the sequence $\left(|\textbf{F}^{(k)}_{i}|,0\leq i \leq b-1\right)$ taken according to a uniform independent rotation, is unbiased. 
		\item 
		The process $({\bf N}_k,k\geq 0)$ is a Markov chain, and its transition matrix can be computed explicitly (see (sec:qefgrethry of the paper)). 
	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:37:51.461737+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_723ad6b0fc4c418480ceff7855f9a1f82bb50dbef869d87ffa6e86fd1b67d24f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 3 (Long-time behavior in the scalar case) of arXiv:2604.04100, '\LARGE Learning Equilibrium Fluctuation Expansions from Overdamped Langevin Dynamics'] Assume $d=1$. Let $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ and let $X_\varepsilon$,  $(\bar{X}_m)_{0\leq m\leq n}$,  $(a_m)_{0\leq m\leq n}$ be as in Proposition \ref{thm-weak-exp-intro}. If we further assume that Assumption \ref{A2} holds, then for every $F \in C^{n+1}(\mathbb{R})$ satisfying \eqref{assump-F}, the following assertions hold:\begin{enumerate}

\item[(i)] The limit
$$
b_0(F) := \lim_{t\to\infty} a_0(t,F)
$$
exists, and satisfies
\begin{equation}
b_0(F) = \mathbb{E}\Bigl[ \lim_{t\to\infty} F\bigl(\bar{X}_0(t)\bigr) \Bigr]
= F(1)\mathbb{P}(\xi_0>0) + F(-1)\mathbb{P}(\xi_0<0).
\end{equation}
\item[(ii)] For each $m \in \{1, \dots, n\}$ and $i \in \{1, \dots, m\}$, define
$$
S_{m,i}(t) := \sum_{(j_1,\dots,j_i)\in\mathcal{D}_i^m} \prod_{k=1}^{i}\bar{X}_{j_k}(t),\quad t\ge0.
$$
We adopt the convention that a sum over the empty set is equal to $0$, and hence
$$
S_{m,i}(t):=0
\quad\text{whenever }m<0,\ i<0,\ \text{or } i>m.
$$Then the conditional limits
$$
c_{m,i} := \lim_{t \to \infty}\mathbb{E}[S_{m,i}(t)\mid\xi_0>0],
\quad
\bar{c}_{m,i} := \lim_{t \to \infty}\mathbb{E}[S_{m,i}(t)\mid\xi_0<0]
$$
exist and are uniquely determined by the recursion formula
\begin{equation}
    c_{m,i} = \frac{i-1}{2}c_{m-2,i-2} - \frac{3}{2}c_{m,i+1} - \frac{1}{2}c_{m,i+2}, 
    \quad 
    \bar c_{m,i} = \frac{i-1}{2}\bar c_{m-2,i-2} + \frac{3}{2}\bar c_{m,i+1} - \frac{1}{2}\bar c_{m,i+2},
\end{equation}
with $c_{1,1}=\bar c_{1,1}=0$, $c_{2,2}=\bar c_{2,2}=\frac12$ and the convention that $c_{0,0}=\bar c_{0,0}=1$, and
		$$c_{k,j}=\bar c_{k,j}=0 \quad\text{whenever } (k,j)\notin \{(0,0)\}\cup\{(k,j): k\ge1,\ 1\le j\le k\}.$$ 
The recursion \eqref{eq-c-n-intro} is understood as a nested induction: one first increases the order $m$, and for each fixed $m$, computes $c_{m,i}$ backward in $i$ from $i=m$ to $1$. The same procedure applies to $\bar c_{m,i}$.

\item[(iii)] For each $m \in \{1, \dots, n\}$, the limit
\begin{equation}
b_m(F) := \lim_{t \to \infty} a_m(t,F)
\end{equation}
exists and is given by
\begin{equation}
    b_m(F) = \mathbb{P}(\xi_0>0)\sum_{i=1}^{m} \frac{c_{m,i}}{i!} F^{(i)}(1)
    + \mathbb{P}(\xi_0<0)\sum_{i=1}^{m} \frac{\bar{c}_{m,i}}{i!}F^{(i)}(-1).
\end{equation}
In particular, $b_m(F)=0$ for all odd $m$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-05T06:00:09.358321+00:00","domain":"ensemble learning","id":"claim_725b1291163158659b5a95f154eb99cbd5bf0e3c3895a5a6a7c646f4cd804d39","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In a multi-output stacking problem scored by the mean per-sample relative error $\\frac{1}{n}\\sum_i \\|\\hat y_i - y_i\\|/\\|y_i\\|$, the per-output least-squares stack minimises the unweighted squared error, which is dominated by the cases with the largest $\\|y_i\\|$, while the score is dominated by the cases with the smallest. Interpolating the per-output weights toward one pooled simplex weight vector fitted on the relative error therefore improves the score even IN-SAMPLE on the very calibration rows on which least squares is optimal in squared error - the signature that distinguishes an objective mismatch from a generalisation (variance) effect, which can only appear out of sample. Measured on the EMIT lookup-table pool (seed 101, component Y2, 23 members, 932 calibration rows, 285 outputs): in-sample relative error 0.1105 for least squares against 0.1026 at interpolation weight 0.4 (-7.2 percent), the in-sample optimum at the same weight as the out-of-sample optimum (0.1292 to 0.1186), while the in-sample squared error is minimal at least squares (8.8e-5 against 1.2e-4); the out-of-sample gain is +15.9 percent in the smallest-norm quartile of targets and -9.6 percent in the largest, and 45 percent of the least-squares score comes from its worst decile of cases. Consequently no model of the sampling noise of the weight rows reproduces the cross-validated interpolation weight: the known-noise James-Stein amount is 0.00 and the heteroscedasticity-robust amount 0.03-0.05 where cross-validation chooses 0.10-0.40. Shrinking toward the pooled UNCONSTRAINED least-squares weights (entries up to 90 in magnitude) or toward the mean of the rows is much worse; the simplex constraint together with the relative objective carries the effect. The practical rule: when a stack is scored in a metric that weights cases differently from the fitting loss, the first question is the objective, not the estimator's variance.","status":"unverified"}

(1) Commutativity cannot be dropped: for the 2×2 matrices A = [[0,1],[0,0]] and B = [[0,0],[1,0]] one has e^A = I + A, e^B = I + B, so e^A e^B = [[2,1],[1,1]], whereas A + B = [[0,1],[1,0]] gives e^{A+B} = [[cosh 1, sinh 1],[sinh 1, cosh 1]] ≠ e^A e^B (and e^B e^A = [[1,1],[1,2]] ≠ e^A e^B, so the two products differ as well). For non-commuting A, B the product e^A e^B is instead described by the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff series e^{A+B+[A,B]/2+…} when it converges, and by the Lie–Trotter formula e^{A+B} = lim_{n→∞} (e^{A/n} e^{B/n})ⁿ. (2) The converse is false in general: e^A e^B = e^{A+B} does not imply AB = BA (there are non-commuting complex matrices with e^A = e^B = e^{A+B} = I); it does hold for Hermitian (self-adjoint) matrices A, B, because then e^{A+B} Hermitian forces e^A e^B = (e^A e^B)* = e^B e^A, so the positive definite matrices e^A and e^B commute, and hence so do their unique Hermitian logarithms A and B. (3) For UNBOUNDED operators (generators of semigroups) the series definition is unavailable and 'commuting' must be formulated with care (e.g. commuting resolvents / commuting semigroups); this statement is only about bounded operators and Banach algebras.","status":"unverified"}
