{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:40:21.317862+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7761191fa7e4868bbb24d30f2148d6800f0c1d094815b57ec26f431c705d0009","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 1 (Exact reduction to \texorpdfstring{$L_p$}{Lp}) of arXiv:2604.09933, 'Explicit cutoff profiles for colored top-\texorpdfstring{$m$}{m}-to-random shuffles'] Let \(\mu\) be a probability mass function on \(\{0,1,\dots,n\}\), and define
\[
\widetilde Q_{\mu,p}:=\sum_{u=0}^{n}\mu(n-u)\,\widetilde Q_{n-u,p},
\qquad
S_\mu(\ell):=\sum_{u=0}^{\ell}\mu(n-u)\,u!\,p^u.
\]
Then
\[
\frac{\widetilde Q_{\mu,p}(x)}{U(x)}=S_\mu(L_p(x))
\qquad(x\in G_{n,p}),
\]
and, for every \(\Phi:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R\) for which the sums are finite,
\[
\sum_{x\in G_{n,p}}U(x)\,
\Phi\!\left(\frac{\widetilde Q_{\mu,p}(x)}{U(x)}\right)
=
\sum_{\ell=0}^{n}U\{L_p=\ell\}\,\Phi\!\bigl(S_\mu(\ell)\bigr).
\]
Moreover,
\[
\sep(\widetilde Q_{\mu,p},U)=
\begin{cases}
1-\mu(n)-\mu(n-1), & p=1,\\[4pt]
1-\mu(n), & p\ge2,
\end{cases}
\]
and
\[
\left\|\frac{\widetilde Q_{\mu,p}(\cdot)}{U(\cdot)}-1\right\|_{L^\infty(U)}
=S_\mu(n)-1
=\sum_{u=0}^{n}\mu(n-u)\,u!\,p^u-1.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:11:09.317987+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7769ad35ea798402e2d9dfb68648b26bba59b5f29562b4786a3e123a8f4beb65","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:vrjp-on-G-r-pos-rec of arXiv:2411.06195, 'Restrictions of some reinforced processes to subgraphs'] Let $G=(\Lambda,E)$ be a connected undirected graph without self-loops

  respect to some probability measure with corresponding expectation ${\mathbb E}$. Its restriction
  $(X^{\Lambda_l\neq},T^{\Lambda_l\neq})$ to $\Lambda_l$

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:55:37.821677+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_777c1f8dc11f0b211f115acdab510f10051796e40714785ffd737fbc7203d710","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defi defCBDI of arXiv:2605.06488, 'Continuous-state branching processes with L\'evy-Khintchine drift-interaction: Laplace dua'] \
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
    \item  We call $\mathrm{CBDI}$ any $[0,\infty]$-valued càdlàg Markov process $\big(X, (\mathbb{P}_x)_{x\in [0,\infty]}\big)$, solution to the following martingale problem $\mathrm{MP}\big(\mathcal{X},\mathrm{C}^2_c((0,\infty))\big)$:
\[\forall x\in (0,\infty), \ f\in \mathrm{C}^2_c((0,\infty)), \quad \left(f(X_t)-\int_0^{t}\mathcal{X}f(X_s)\mathrm{d} s,\ t\geq 0 \right) \text{ is a } \mathbb{P}_x\text{ - martingale}.\]
\item  We call minimal and denote by $X^{\mathrm{m}}$, any $\mathrm{CBDI}$ process  whose boundaries $\{0,\infty\}$ are absorbing, namely: 
\[\forall x\in [0,\infty], \ \mathbb{P}_x-\text{a.s.}\  X^{\mathrm{m}}_t=\begin{cases} 0 &\text{ if } t\geq \sigma_0^{-} \text{ and }  \sigma_0^{-}<\sigma_\infty^{+}, \\
\infty  &\text{ if } t\geq \sigma_\infty^{+} \text{ and }  \sigma_\infty^{+}<\sigma_0^{-}.
\end{cases}
\]
\item  For $\Delta\in \{0,\infty\}$, we say that a process $\big(X^{\mathrm{e}\Delta},(\mathbb{P}_x)_{x\in [0,\infty]}\big)$ is a $\mathrm{CBDI}$ extended at $\Delta$, if it is a $[0,\infty]$-valued  Markov process, which once stopped at the boundary $\Delta$, has the same law as the minimal process: namely, if one sets  $\zeta^{\Delta}:=\inf\big\{t\geq 0: X_{t-} \text{ or } X_t =\Delta\big\}$, then one has
\[\forall x\in [0,\infty]\setminus \{\Delta\}, \ \  (X^{\mathrm{e}\Delta}_{t\wedge \zeta^{\Delta}},t\geq 0)\overset{\mathrm{law}}{=}(X^{\mathrm{m}}_t,t\geq 0)\ \text{ under } \mathbb{P}_x.\]
\begin{itemize}
\item[-]The process $X^{\mathrm{e}\Delta}$ is said furthermore to be a continuous extension if its boundary $\Delta$ is continuous in the sense of Definition~(def:boundary of the paper)-(def:continuous of the paper). 
\item[-] It is a Fellerian extension of $X^{\mathrm{m}}$ if  its semigroup $(P^{\mathrm{e}\Delta}_t)_{t\geq 0}$ satisfies for any $f\in \mathsf{C}([0,\infty])$,
    $P^{\mathrm{e}\Delta}_tf(x) \underset{t\rightarrow 0+}{\rightarrow} f(x),\ x\in [0,\infty]$ 	and $P^{\mathrm{e}\Delta}_tf \in \mathsf{C}([0,\infty])$.
\end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["U ⊂ C is open","all members of the family are holomorphic (respectively meromorphic) on the same open set U"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:42.483658+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_778fb0bb31baea70fbabe9efe4cbc496909f379fa127979c6c8cf41293005128","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let U ⊂ C be open and F a family of holomorphic functions on U. F is normal (in the finite sense) if every sequence in F has a subsequence converging uniformly on every compact subset of U; the limit is then automatically holomorphic, and it need not belong to F. F is normal in the extended sense if every sequence in F has a subsequence which, on each connected component of U, either converges uniformly on compact subsets to a holomorphic function or tends to ∞ uniformly on compact subsets (equivalently, the reciprocals tend to 0 uniformly on compact subsets). For families of meromorphic functions, normality means that every sequence has a subsequence converging uniformly on compact subsets with respect to the chordal metric of the Riemann sphere; restricted to holomorphic families this coincides with the extended sense, because a spherical limit of zero-free reciprocals is, by Hurwitz's theorem, either holomorphic or identically ∞ on each component. Normality is a local property: F is normal on U if and only if every point of U has a neighborhood on which F is normal. Normality asserts the existence of convergent subsequences only; it does not assert convergence of the family itself, and the limit function may leave the family (for instance the limit of injective functions may be constant).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:51:11.969356+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_779af4b65f168c330570cd29cf153b943f59e61fb27b908aa1167f04f96b0e42","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 14 (Filtered BCH and the initial ancestry symbol) of arXiv:2608.08756, 'Infinite-Dimensional L\'evy Area and Spectral Ancestry'] Let \(A:V\to V\) be linear and write \(L(A)\) for its functorial action
on \(L\).  Then
\[
 L(A)\gamma_r(D)\subseteq\gamma_r(D),
 \qquad
 [\gamma_r(D),\gamma_s(D)]\subseteq\gamma_{r+s}(D).
\]
Consequently every truncation in ordinary tensor degree is nilpotent and
filtered for
\(F_0L=L\), \(F_rL=L\cap J^r=\gamma_r(D)\).  It therefore defines BCH
laws on the ordinary-degree completions of \({\operatorname{gr}}_FL\) and of the extended
Rees Lie algebra
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal R_F(L):=
 \sum_{r\geq0}F_rL\,z^{-r}\mathbf k[z]
 \subseteq L[z,z^{-1}],
 \qquad
 \mathcal R_F(L)/z\mathcal R_F(L)\cong{\operatorname{gr}}_FL,
 
\end{equation}
Reduction modulo \(z\) records the associated-graded deformation.  If
\(x\in F_rL\setminus F_{r+1}L\),
its full initial symbol is the nonzero class
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{in}^{\mathrm{full}}_F(x)
 :=x+F_{r+1}L\in{\mathfrak L}_r(Q).
 
\end{equation}
Thus filtration order cannot decrease under linear transport (with the
value \(+\infty\) if the transported element vanishes), and
\begin{equation}
 \nu_F([x,y])\geq\nu_F(x)+\nu_F(y)
 
\end{equation}
for nonzero \(x,y\), with the convention \(\nu_F(0)=+\infty\).  Exact
valuation is preserved
by transport precisely when the induced associated-graded map does not kill
the initial symbol; injectivity of that map on the containing graded layer
is sufficient.  Likewise,
equality holds in \eqref{cc:eq-valuation-superadditive} precisely when
the associated-graded bracket of the two initial symbols is nonzero.
Otherwise transport,
bracketing, cancellation in a sum, or a BCH component may raise the order
or annihilate the element.  A full Rees lift of a causal logarithm requires
a Rees jet or a splitting and is not supplied canonically by the filtration.

In the ordinary-degree completion, exponentiation identifies the special
fibre with
\begin{equation}
 \exp\!\left(V_{\mathrm{ab}}\ltimes_\rho\widehat{{\mathfrak L}}(Q)\right).
 
\end{equation}
Here
\(\widehat{{\mathfrak L}}(Q)=\prod_{n\geq1}{\mathfrak L}(Q)_n\) denotes completion in
ordinary tensor degree.
Moreover, the associated-graded bracket induces
\begin{equation}
 \mathfrak b_{a,b}:G^{\mathrm{full}}_{n,a}(V)\otimes
 G^{\mathrm{full}}_{m,b}(V)
 \longrightarrow G^{\mathrm{full}}_{n+m,a+b}(V),
 \qquad \mathfrak b_{a,b}([x],[y])=[x,y],
 
\end{equation}
and this is the mixed quadratic symbol of BCH:
\begin{equation}
 \left.\partial_s\partial_t\right|_{s=t=0}
 {\operatorname{BCH}}(sx,ty)=\tfrac12[x,y].
 
\end{equation}
If the three layers in \eqref{cc:eq-ancestry-bracket} are finite
dimensional, duality gives
\begin{equation}
 \mathfrak b_{a,b}^{\vee}:E^{\mathrm{full}}_{n+m,a+b}(V)
 \longrightarrow E^{\mathrm{full}}_{n,a}(V)\otimes
 E^{\mathrm{full}}_{m,b}(V).
 
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}\big|\mathbb P(\widetilde X_n\le x)-e^{-e^{-x}}\big|
=
\frac{25(\log\log \alpha_n)^2}{16e\log \alpha_n}(1+o(1))
\]
for all sufficiently large \(n\).

\item If \(\alpha=0\), then
\[
\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}\big|\mathbb P(\widetilde X_n\le x)-\Phi(x)\big|
=
(1+o(1))
\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}
\phi(x)\big|
\frac{\sqrt{2}+4\ln 2}{2}\sqrt{\alpha_n}
-\frac{x}{4n}
\big|
\]
as \(n\to+\infty\).

\item If \(\alpha\in(0,+\infty)\), then for each fixed \(x\in\mathbb R\), the
infinite-dimensional matrix \(\widetilde M(x,\alpha)\) defines a trace-class operator on

\[
\widetilde\Phi_\alpha(x):=\det({\rm I}-\widetilde M(x,\alpha))
\]
is well defined. Moreover, \(\widetilde\Phi_\alpha\) is a distribution function and
\[
\lim_{n\to+\infty}\mathbb P(\widetilde X_n\le x)=\widetilde\Phi_\alpha(x),

The family \(\{\widetilde\Phi_\alpha\}_{\alpha>0}\) interpolates continuously between the
Gaussian and Gumbel laws, and its boundary asymptotics are given by
\[
\lim_{\alpha\to0^+}
\frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha}}
\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}\left|\widetilde\Phi_\alpha(x)-\Phi(x)\right|
=
\frac{\sqrt{2}+4\ln 2}{2\sqrt{2\pi}},
\]
and
\[
\lim_{\alpha\to+\infty}
\frac{\log\alpha}{(\log\log\alpha)^2}
\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}\left|\widetilde\Phi_\alpha(x)-e^{-e^{-x}}\right|

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:48:43.463233+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_77d47a96f45be9ed781038dd32eb03ccaf72ea883fc8205a829579749f75d2fd","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 1 (Asymptotics of the solutions) of arXiv:2608.06565, 'Smoothness of the survival probability in models with a random environment: the annuity an'] Let $\sigma>0$, $c<0$, $\lambda>0$ and
$\mathcal L^0\psi:=\sigma^2u^2\psi''/2+(au+c)\psi'$. Consider the equation
$\mathcal L^0\psi-\lambda\psi=0$. It has a fundamental system of solutions
$\{\pup,\pdn\}$ with $\pup(0+)=0$ and $\pdn$ bounded at infinity, and as
$u\to0+$
\begin{equation}
    
    \pup(u)=C_\uparrow\,u^{\beta}\exp\left(-\frac{\kappa}{u}\right)
    \bigl(1+O(u)\bigr),\quad \kappa=\frac{2|c|}{\sigma^2},\quad
    \beta=2-\frac{2a}{\sigma^2},
\end{equation}
where $C_\uparrow>0$, while $\pdn(0+)$ is finite and non-zero. As
$v\to\infty$ one has $\pdn(v)\sim C_\downarrow v^{\rho_-}$, where $\rho_-<0$
is the smaller root of
$$
    \tfrac12\sigma^2\rho^2+\bigl(a-\tfrac12\sigma^2\bigr)\rho-\lambda=0 .
$$
The solutions may be chosen positive; then $\pup$ is strictly increasing,
$\pdn$ is strictly decreasing, they are linearly independent, the Wronskian
$\mathcal W=\pup\pdn'-\pup'\pdn$ is strictly negative, and by Liouville's
formula
\begin{equation}
    
    \mathcal W(v)=C_{\mathcal W}\,v^{-2a/\sigma^2}\,e^{2c/(\sigma^2v)},
    \qquad C_{\mathcal W}<0 .
\end{equation}
For $c\ge0$ the behaviour of the solutions is different. Zero is inaccessible,
$\pdn(0+)=+\infty$, and the role of $\pup$ is played by the solution bounded at
zero. For $c>0$ such a solution is unique up to a factor and satisfies
$\pup(0+)>0$, while every solution not proportional to it grows like
$u^{\beta}e^{2c/(\sigma^2u)}$. For $c=0$ the equation is of Euler type and
$\pup(u)=u^{\rho_+}$, $\pdn(u)=u^{\rho_-}$, where $\rho_+>0$ is the larger root
of the same equation. Formula \eqref{eq:liouville} and the negativity of the
Wronskian hold for every sign of $c$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Independent arrays and standard Gaussian channel noise; N,P>=2,M>=1; X=UV^T/sqrt(N)","Fixed centered unit-variance factor laws with finite fourth moments; bounded tau_U,tau_V","E[u h]=E[tau_U h'], E[(u^2-1)h]=E[eta_U h']; corresponding V identities and E[(tau_V-1)h]=E[zeta_V h'] for bounded C1 h with bounded derivative","Square-integrable eta_U,eta_V,zeta_V; precise constants and all rate bounds are in proof Eqs2,13","Positive finite convergent aspects only for limiting coefficient; no information-limit existence assumed"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T16:16:13.028659+00:00","domain":"probability; Gaussian channels; extensive-rank matrix factorization","id":"claim_77f6ac5e73d28069a2817defb72ab668c6f3bbc97c7a3b33f41566584c157634","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Own work, proof (unaudited), novelty unestablished.

U in R^(N by M), V in R^(P by M), N,P>=2,M>=1, have independent
iid real entries within each array; the arrays are independent.
Their fixed scalar laws u,v are centered with variance one and
finite fourth moments u4,v4. Assume measurable scalar functions
tau_U,eta_U,tau_V,eta_V,zeta_V satisfy, for bounded C1 functions h
with bounded derivative, including their bounded smooth compositions
in the proof,

 E[u h(u)]=E[tau_U(u) h'(u)],
 E[(u^2-1)h(u)]=E[eta_U(u) h'(u)],
 E[v h(v)]=E[tau_V(v) h'(v)],
 E[(v^2-1)h(v)]=E[eta_V(v) h'(v)],
 E[(tau_V(v)-1)h(v)]=E[zeta_V(v) h'(v)].             (1)

Assume |tau_U|<=T_U, |tau_V|<=T_V almost surely and
E eta_U^2,E eta_V^2,E zeta_V^2 finite. No differentiability of
these five functions and no posterior independence is assumed.
Bounded truncation of h(x)=x gives E tau_U=E tau_V=1.
Define the finite scalar constants

 t_U=E tau_U^2, t_V=E tau_V^2,
 e_U=E eta_U^2, e_V=E eta_V^2, z_V=E zeta_V^2,
 a_U=E[tau_U u^2], a_V=E[tau_V v^2],
 b_U=E[tau_U u], b_V=E[tau_V v],
 h_U=E eta_U, h_V=E eta_V,
 L_N=N-2+2*a_U^2+2*b_U^4.

Let independent Z have iid standard Gaussian entries, X=UV^T/sqrt(N),
Y=sqrt(s)X+Z, d=NP, alpha=P/N, beta=M/N, v_s=1+beta*s.
Set g=beta/v_s, m_N=E||X-E[X|Y]||^2/d and
B_N=log(v_s)/2-I(X;Y)/d, with natural logs.

## Explicit constants and result

Put A=beta^2*(N-1)*(P-1)/N^2 and

 E3=6*(N-1)*(P-1)*M*(t_U^2*t_V-1)/N^4,
 Ec=6*(N-1)/N^4 *
       [M*T_U^4*T_V^2*(v4+2*(P-1))+M*(M-1)*a_V^2],
 Eeta=2/N^3 * [M*P*e_U*T_V^2+M*(M-1)*h_U^2*b_V^2],
 Ezeta=2*N*M*z_V/N^3,
 E4=24*(N-1)*(P-1)/N^5 *
       [M*T_U^4*T_V^2*e_V*N+2*M*(M-1)*b_U^2*h_V^2],
 W=120*(N-1)*(P-1)*(P-2)/N^6 *
       [M*T_U^4*T_V^6*N*(N-1+u4)+M*(M-1)*L_N],
 F2=2*(Eeta+Ezeta), F3=2*(E3+Ec), F4=E4.            (2)

All constants are nonnegative. For all s>0,delta>0,

 g-m_N <= (1+delta)*s^3/v_s^2*(sqrt(A)+s*sqrt(W))^2
       +3*(1+1/delta)/v_s^2*(s^2*F2+s^3*F3+s^4*F4). (3)

For the exact R_N in038(10), define

 a=(N+u4-3)/N, b=(P+v4-3)/N,
 Q(s)=v_s^3+beta*(a+b)*v_s*s^2+beta*a*b*s^3,
 D(s)=v_s^2*Q(s), delta_N=1/floor(sqrt(N)),
 eps_N=delta_N*A+3*(1+1/delta_N)*(F2+F3+F4),
 K_N=A*(Q(1)-1)+(1+delta_N)*(A+2*W).

For 0<=s<=1 the requested estimate and its integral are

 0<=R_N(s)<=eps_N*s^2+K_N*s^4,                      (4)
 half integral_0^s R_N(t)dt<=eps_N*s^3/6+K_N*s^5/10. (5)

In particular the full finite-N two-sided information bound is

 -A*(D(1)-1)*s^5/10
 <= B_N(s)-A*s^4/8
 <= eps_N*s^3/6+K_N*s^5/10.                         (6)

For fixed priors with positive aspect ratios bounded above,
F2,F3,F4=O(1/N), W,A,Q(1) are uniformly bounded,
eps_N=O(N^(-1/2)), and K_N is uniformly bounded.
If alpha_N->alpha>0,beta_N->beta>0, every limiting information
envelope therefore satisfies

 B(s)=alpha*beta^2*s^4/8+O(s^5), 0<=s<=1,            (7)

with the explicit remainder constants in (6). Existence or uniqueness
of the information limit is not required. The finite-N error in (6)
is additive O(N^(-1/2)*s^3), not a pure uniform Taylor remainder
after dividing by s^4 arbitrarily close to zero.

Equivalently the normalized mutual information has the explicit
finite-N polynomial

 P4_N(s)=beta*s/2-beta^2*s^2/4+beta^3*s^3/6
                              -(beta^4+A)*s^4/8,

and

 -eps_N*s^3/6-K_N*s^5/10
 <= I(X;Y)/d-P4_N(s)
 <= [beta^5+A*(D(1)-1)]*s^5/10.                     (6a)

The elementary identity log(1+x)=x-x^2/2+x^3/3-x^4/4
+integral_0^x t^4/(1+t)dt, valid for all x>=0, pays the log remainder.
Thus the limiting quartic term in I/(NP) is
-(beta^4+alpha*beta^2)*s^4/8, and no prior fourth cumulant enters
at that order within this class. The channel parameter is s=1/Delta;
I(UV^T;Y)=I(X;Y) because deterministic nonzero rescaling of the
input is invertible.

## Non-Gaussian example and whole-family scope

Both priors may independently be uniform on [-sqrt(3),sqrt(3)].
For either law take tau(x)=(3-x^2)/2, eta(x)=x-x^3/3;
for the V law take zeta(x)=-eta(x)/2. Their endpoint values vanish,
and their negative derivatives are x, x^2-1, and tau(x)-1,
respectively. Ordinary one-dimensional integration by parts proves
(1), without a Gaussian prior or a boundary contribution.
Exact constants are T=3/2, fourth moment9/5, t=6/5,
e=8/35, z=2/35, a=3/5, b=h=0.
Gaussian priors also satisfy (1) with tau=1,eta=x,zeta=0.
The result applies to every fixed law satisfying the stated kernel
conditions, not just these examples. Discrete Rademacher priors do
not satisfy (1) for arbitrary smooth tests and are not covered.
Specifically choose a compact smooth cutoff of (3*x-x^3)/2 which
equals that polynomial near {-1,1}. At a Rademacher input, h(u)=u
and h'(u)=0, so E[u*h(u)]=1 while E[tau(u)*h'(u)]=0 for every
finite function tau on its support. This is an obstruction to
applying the present derivative-transfer route to that law, not a
counterexample to quartic universality for discrete priors.

More concretely, each of U and V may have any standardized beta
law, with its own arbitrary fixed positive shape parameters p,q.
Let k=p+q, C=1/k, B=(q-p)*sqrt(k+1)/(k*sqrt(p*q)), and
x=(t-p/k)/sqrt(p*q/[k^2*(k+1)]) for t~Beta(p,q). Then

 tau(x)=1+C+B*x-C*x^2,
 eta(x)=tau(x)*(x+B)/(1+C),
 zeta(x)=B*tau(x)-C*eta(x).

The beta density times tau vanishes at both endpoints, including
when the density itself is unbounded there, because p,q>0.
Direct integration of its derivative proves E[x h]=E[tau h'].
Writing Q=x^2-1, the identity tau-1=B*x-C*Q and applying this
first identity to x*h(x) give
(1+C)E[Q*h]=E[tau*(x+B)*h']; this proves the eta identity.
The zeta identity follows by the same linear relation tau-1.
All kernels are bounded on the compact standardized support, so
every hypothesis of (1) is paid. This covers two asymmetric beta
priors as well as the symmetric subfamily. For an asymmetric exact
check, Beta(2,3) standardized as x=5*t-2 has
tau=(6+x-x^2)/5, eta=tau*(1+5*x)/6, zeta=tau*(1-x)/6.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:15:36.157488+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_77fdca3bb28312596952beb32b6bebf13676562a75fe0943c5ce0317951c7fab","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 1 (Methodological scope and structural innovations) of arXiv:2609.01589, 'Uniform stability of expanding simple waves for Euler--Poisson--Boltzmann: a singular comp'] \normalfont
Write $\mathrm{N1}$--$\mathrm{N6}$ for the defining features of \cref{thm:main}:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(N\arabic*)},leftmargin=*]
\item the warm-ion Euler--Poisson system with Maxwell--Boltzmann electrons,
  $p_i'(n)\ge p_*>0$;
\item the boundaryless cylinder $\R\times\T$ and a prescribed smooth
  expanding planar simple wave connecting two distinct neutral end states;
\item fully two-dimensional $H^s$ perturbations, completely removing any 
  irrotationality or zero-vorticity hypothesis;
\item stability under relative perturbations that are strictly independent of 
  $\eps$; $\eps$-preparedness is imposed only to capture the expansion rate;
\item for every finite $M$, the construction of an even Debye composite through 
  order $\eps^{2M}$ yielding a residual of $O(\eps^{2M+2})$;
\item a uniform lifespan on every fixed $[t_0,T]$, $t_0\ge0$, based on a novel 
  compensated topology that directly controls $\norm\psi_{H^s}+\eps\norm{\nabla\psi}_{H^s}$ 
  without $\eps^{-1}$ losses over the distinct end states.
\end{enumerate}
Contextualized against the existing literature, these contributions advance the 
state of the art in the following ways:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)},leftmargin=*]
\item Cordier--Grenier \cite{cordier2000quasineutral} laid the rigorous 1D foundation 
  for the ion--Boltzmann quasineutral limit. The present work substantially advances 
  this theory by capturing fully two-dimensional rotational dynamics \textup{(N3)} 
  and simultaneously managing the distinct distinct-end-state geometry \textup{(N2)} 
  over an arbitrary finite-order hierarchy \textup{(N4)}--\textup{(N5)}.

\item Wang \cite{wang2005quasineutral} provided multidimensional uniform-lifespan theories for 
  periodic problems yielding incompressible Euler and Navier--Stokes limits. Our 
  framework successfully addresses the distinct analytical challenges of a 
  compressible flow limit connecting heterogeneous far fields.

\item Peng--Wang--Yong \cite{peng2006quasi} rigorously justified finite-order 
  expansions for periodic non-isentropic flows. We pioneer this hierarchical expansion 
  for the compressible ion--Boltzmann limit \textup{(N1)}, introducing the relative 
  compensated topology \textup{(N6)} strictly required to handle the dispersing background.

\item G\'erard-Varet--Han-Kwan--Rousset \cite{gerard2013quasineutral,gerard2014quasineutral} 
  masterfully resolved the multidimensional half-space problem, where boundary data 
  generate Debye layers. We complement this by solving the Cauchy stability problem 
  for a boundaryless wave \textup{(N2)}, where the analytical stiffness stems entirely 
  from the internal singular electric transition.

\item Slemrod--Sternberg \cite{slemrod2001quasi} provided a comprehensive 
  center-to-wall asymptotic analysis for bounded plasmas. In contrast, our focus is 
  the Cauchy stability of the class \textup{(N2)}--\textup{(N4)} on an unbounded cylinder, 
  avoiding boundary layers to isolate the wave asymptotics.
\end{enumerate}
In summary, the present paper develops a novel compensated energy topology that 
rigorously isolates the stability of the smooth expanding wave from the singular 
Debye scaling. By establishing uniform nonlinear stability over a heterogeneous 
background, this framework provides a critical analytical stepping stone toward 
the full global geometric theory of multidimensional quasineutral rarefactions. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:16:33.595011+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_780a34cf99432152b10899cdd580dbdd2b800f24e54f58db93caaf547e75a987","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Abstract of arXiv:2609.02362, '\\textbf{Farthest-cell triplet entropy: high-dimensional shell limits and hyperbolic...'] We introduce farthest-cell triplet entropy, the conditional Shannon entropy of the farthest-prototype label given three random prototypes. For independent queries and prototypes, its estimator records only the farthest label, not coordinates or numerical distances. The statistic is bounded by $\\log 3$, is invariant under common strictly increasing transformations of the dissimilarities, and has an exact mutual-information interpretation. In high-dimensional isotropic radial models $X_d=R_dU_d$, the Euclidean ordering reduces to scores $\\lambda_d\\xi_{i,d}-Z_i$, where $\\lambda_d=\\sqrt d\\,\\operatorname{sd}(R_d)/\\E R_d$ and the $Z_i$ are independent standard Gaussian variables. This gives angular-dominated, intermediate, and radial-dominated entropy limits $\\log 3$, $\\Hinf(\\lambda;F)$, and $0$. In hyperbolic space of curvature $-\\kappa_d^2$, the same master curve appears at $\\lambda_{d,\\mathbb H}=\\sqrt d\\,\\tau_d A(s_d)$, where $\\tau_d=\\operatorname{sd}(R_d)/\\E R_d$, $s_d=\\kappa_d\\E R_d$, and $A(s)=s\\coth s$. With a calibrated radial law and $\\tau_d$, and a monotone operating interval, entropy inversion identifies the scale-invariant target $s_d^2$; absolute curvature requires an external length unit. CPU simulations give Euclidean and hyperbolic master-curve RMSEs of $0.0164$ and $0.0209$. Inversion from observed synthetic latent coordinates has a median relative error in $\\kappa$ of $6.6\\%$, while angular anisotropy increases this error to $68.9\\%$. Thus the entropy statistic is comparison-based, whereas curvature recovery remains model-calibrated, is not graph-only, and is not robust to anisotropy.","status":"unverified"}

The \emph{generator} $A:D(A) \to L^2(X,\mu)$ is the linear operator with domain
		\[
		D(A):= \{ f\in \mathcal{F} \vert \mbox{there exists $C>0$ such that $\abs{\mathcal{E}(f,g)} \le C \norm{g}_{L^2(\mu)}$ for all $g \in \mathcal{F}$}\}.
		\]
		For any $f \in D(A)$, the element $A(f) \in L^2(X,\mu)$ is defined by
		\[
		\mathcal{E}(f,g)= -\langle A(f), g \rangle_{L^2(\mu)}.
		\] 
		
		We define the \emph{energy measure} as $\Gamma(f,g)= \gamma(f,g)\cdot \mu$ for all $f,g \in \mathcal{F}$, where $\gamma: \mathcal{F} \times \mathcal{F} \to L^1(X,\mu)$ is the associated carr\'e du champ.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:15:45.377679+00:00","domain":"set theory","id":"claim_783ee34fc14e104fa620373620d7e9f6dc197a014b894eb8ac44b832183c96a2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Two sets A and B are equinumerous (have the same cardinality, written |A| = |B|) when there exists a bijection from A onto B. One writes |A| <= |B| when there is an injection from A into B. Equinumerosity is an equivalence relation, and <= is reflexive and transitive; by the Schroder-Bernstein theorem it is antisymmetric up to bijection (|A| <= |B| and |B| <= |A| imply |A| = |B|), all without the axiom of choice. With the axiom of choice any two sets are comparable (trichotomy), and every set is equinumerous with a unique initial ordinal, its cardinal number. A set is finite if it is equinumerous with {1, ..., n} for some natural number n; countably infinite if equinumerous with the set N of natural numbers; countable if finite or countably infinite; uncountable otherwise. Strict inequality |A| < |B| means |A| <= |B| and there is no bijection between A and B.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:43:55.659303+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_78777a494d1ebb937c61f3d2519ec1a462cfff8698b75503205e420678fb79a0","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem LAN of arXiv:2604.07183, 'Stopping on the last success with unknown odds: asymptotic minimax optimality of the plug-'] Fix~$h>0$ and an integer~$k\ge2$, let
$$

The model consists of discrete variables that represent magnetic dipole moments of atomic \"spins\" that can be in one of two states. The spins are arranged in a graph, usually a lattice, allowing each spin to interact with its neighbors. Neighboring spins that agree have a lower energy than those that disagree; the system tends to the lowest energy but heat disturbs this tendency, thus creating the possibility of different structural phases. The two-dimensional square-lattice Ising model is one of the simplest statistical models to show a phase transition. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:07:48.561153+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_78a6b372d2caafb8dcaa94c4880f0bf813456055361755f18780b8e73bb6314e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 2 (The transference principle) of arXiv:2609.01460, 'On cost-induced Santal\'o-type inequalities \\ in Polish measure spaces'] For $m\in\N$, let $(X_1,\mu_{X_1}),\dots, (X_m,\mu_{X_m})$ be Polish measure spaces. Let $c \colon X_1 \times\cdots \times X_m \to (-\infty,\infty)$ be a continuous cost function. Fix $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_m \in (0,1)$ such that $\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1$.

Consider collections, for $i=1,\dots,m$, $\mathcal{C}_{X_i}$ of $\mu_{X_i}$-measurable subsets of $X_i$. Let $a,b\in \R\cup\{\pm\infty\}$ be such that for all non-empty $A_i\in \mathcal{C}_{X_i}$, $\sup_{\substack{x_i\in A_i \\ 1\leq i \leq m}} -c(x_1,\dots,x_m) \in [a,b]$ and consider a continuous, non-decreasing function $F \colon (a,b]\to [0,\infty)$ satisfying $F(a^+)=0$.

Then, the following are equivalent:\begin{enumerate}
    \item For every non-empty $A_1\in \mathcal{C}_{X_1},\dots,A_m\in\mathcal{C}_{X_m}$, one has
    \[
\prod_{i=1}^m\mu_{X_i}(A_i)^{\lambda_i} \leq F\left(\sup_{\substack{x_i\in A_i \\ 1\leq i \leq m}} -c(x_1,\dots,x_m) \right).
\]
\item For every $(m+1)$-tuple of measurable functions $f_1 \in \mathcal{F}(\mathcal{C}_{X_1}),\dots, f_m\in \mathcal{F}\left(\mathcal{C}_{X_m}\right)$ and $\Omega \colon (a,b]  \to [0,\infty)$, where $\Omega$ is non-increasing, that satisfy
\begin{align*}
\prod_{i=1}^mf_i(x_i)^{\lambda_i} &\leq \Omega(-c(x_1,\dots,x_m)) \text{ for all } 
\\
&(x_1,\dots,x_m)\in X_1\times\cdots\times  X_m, \text{ with } -c(x_1,\dots,x_m)\in (a,b],
\end{align*}
one has
\[
\prod_{i=1}^m\left(\int_{X_i} f_i(x) d\mu_{X_i}(x) \right)^{{\lambda_i}} \leq \int_{a}^b \Omega(r) dF(r).
\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.197231+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_78b5f2af63677a8e0ff36d9d7c03fa4cefc36487dd925193649690b73fcabe8d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 117 (temporal smoothing of budget constraint) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Analogously to \eqref{e:budget.constraint.Ising.plus.coarse} and the bound from Lemma~\ref{l:sp.smooth.budget}, with high probability we have 
	\begin{align*}
	\breve{C}^N(t)
	- \frac{\bar{W}^N(t)^2}{\alpha} 
	\le
	\bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2 \TMAX_N \tep^{1/2}
	+ 3\epsilon^\circ
	\end{align*}
for all $t\in[q_*,1]$. Additionally, with $J^N\equiv J(p^N,\tep,\lambda)$ as  defined by \eqref{e:bad.times.J}, we have
	\[
	\Big|\breve{C}^N(t)
	-\bar{C}^N(t)
	\Big|
	\le \bigg(\frac{ \trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2
	\lambda^{1/2}
	\]
for all $t\in[q_*,1] \setminus J^N$.

\begin{proof}
We continue to use the abbreviations introduced above. The function $\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}$ is convex on the expanded domain $\{(b,v,u) : v \ge u^2-2\bar{\lambda}\}$. Recall $\tGam^N\equiv(\tbbb,\tvvv,\tuuu)^N$
and $\TGam^N\equiv(\Tbbb,\Tvvv,\Tuuu)^N$: we have from Lemma~\ref{l:t.smooth.domain} that
(with high probability)
 $\TGam^N(t,y)$ lies in the expanded domain for all $(t,y)\in[q_*,1]\times \R$, while
$\tGam^N(t,y)$ lies in the expanded domain for all $(t,y)\in ([q_*,1]\setminus J^N)\times \R$. Lemma~\ref{l:t.smooth.domain} implies, for $(t,y)\in ([q_*,1]\setminus J^N)\times \R$,
	\[
	\bigg|
	\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}
	\Big( \tGam^N(t,y)\Big)
	-\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}
	\Big( \TGam^N(t,y)\Big)
	\bigg|
	\le
	\bigg(\frac{ \trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2
	\lambda^{1/2}\,.
	\]
Integrating with respect to $\overline{\varrho_{\vY,N,t}*\sphi(y)}\,dy$ proves the second conclusion. For all $(t,y)\in[q_*,1]\times\R$, we can bound
	\begin{align*}
	& \Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}
	\Big(\TGam^N(t,y)\Big)
	=
	\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}\bigg( \tE \Big[\sGam(t-\sss,y)\Big]\bigg) \\
	&\qquad\le \tE\bigg[
	\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}\Big( \sGam(t-\sss,y)\Big)\bigg]
	= \int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)
	\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}( \sGam(s,y) )\,ds\,.
	\end{align*}
Integrating with respect to $\overline{\varrho_t*\sphi}(y)\,dy$ gives
	\begin{align*}
	&\breve{C}^N(t)
	=
	\int_{\R} \Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}\Big(\TGam^N(t,y)\Big)
	\overline{\varrho_t*\sphi}(y)\,dy
	\le
	\int_{\R}
	\bigg[
	 \int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)
	\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}( \sGam(s,y) )\,ds\bigg]
	\overline{\varrho_t*\sphi}(y)\,dy \\
	&\qquad=
	\int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)
	\bigg[\int_{\R}
	\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}( \sGam(s,y) )
	\overline{\varrho_s*\sphi(y)} \,dy\bigg]\,ds
	+O\bigg[ \bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2 \TMAX_N
	\tep^{1/2}\bigg]\\
	&\qquad=
	\int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)
	\tilde{C}^N(s)\,ds
	+O\bigg[ \bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2 \TMAX_N
	\tep^{1/2}\bigg]
	\,,
	\end{align*}
where the error estimate uses the bounds on $\sGam=(\sbbb,\svvv,\suuu)$ proved in Lemma~\ref{l:sp.smooth.reg}, along with the regularity of the map $t\mapsto \overline{\varrho_s*\sphi}$ proved in Lemma~\ref{l:sp.smooth.cty}. 
 Similarly, note that
	\[
	S_t(w)
	\equiv
	\bigg( \int_{\R} w(y)^{1/2} \varsigma_t*\sphi(y)\,dy\bigg)^2
	\]
is a concave function. It follows that
	\begin{align*}
	&\bar{W}^N(t)^2 
	=\bigg(\int_{\R} \twww(t,y)^{1/2} \varsigma_t*\sphi(y)\,dy\bigg)^2
	= S_t\bigg(\tE\Big[ \swww(t-\sss,\cdot)\Big]\bigg)
	\ge \tE\bigg[ S_t\Big( \swww(t-\sss,\cdot)\Big)\bigg]\\
	&\qquad= \int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)
	\bigg( \int_{\R} \swww(s,y)^{1/2} 
		\varsigma_t*\sphi(y)\,dy\bigg)^2\,ds\\
	&\qquad=
	\int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)
	\bigg( \int_{\R} \swww(s,y)^{1/2} 
		\varsigma_s*\sphi(y)\,dy\bigg)^2
	\,ds
	+
	O\bigg[ \bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2 \TMAX_N \tep^{1/2}\bigg]
	\\
	&\qquad=
	\int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)
	\tilde{W}^N(s)^2\,ds
	+
	O\bigg[ \bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2 \TMAX_N \tep^{1/2}\bigg]
	\end{align*}
where the error estimate again follows from Lemmas \ref{l:sp.smooth.reg} and \ref{l:sp.smooth.cty}. The claim then follows by combining with

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:31:49.903450+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_78b8151fd8a506bf10bc33657c81d9bd8f046318b73a8610cc25eb24ce0b1758","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma of arXiv:2608.25065, 'Detection of first homology via random geometric graphs in the thermodynamic regime'] \label[lemma]{induction}

    To reduce clutter, 
    write $K = 4Q \rho r|\log r|$.

    $z \in Z_1(\mathring{G}^n_M(r))$,

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:49:05.487850+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_78d7fcd70ba4df873666c92a5ed8a3bfe8077d4e2f6dec93806c45f83c40bee8","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem convolution-sup-bounds of arXiv:2601.19145, 'Stochastic Persistence in Infinite Dimensions'] Fix $2 \leq r < \infty$ and $\mathcal{B} \coloneqq L^r$. For all $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$, $\epsilon \in (0,1/2)$, $p > \epsilon^{-1}$, $T > 0$ the following hold:
    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
        \item For $y \in L^p([0,T]; \mathcal{B}_{\alpha - 1 + \epsilon})$,
        $$[0,T] \ni t \mapsto (S*y)_t \in \mathcal{B}_\alpha$$
        is continuous and
        $$
        \sup_{t \leq T} \|(S * y)_t\|^p_\alpha \lesssim \int_0^T \|y_t\|^p_{\alpha - 1 + \epsilon} dt \,.$$
        \item For $Z \in L^p(\Omega \times [0,T];\gamma(\mathcal{U}, \mathcal{B}_{\alpha - 1/2 + \epsilon}))$,

        is continuous and
        $$\mathbb{E}\Big[\sup_{t \leq T} \|(S \diamond Z)_t\|^p_\alpha \Big] \lesssim \mathbb{E}\Big[\int_0^T \|Z_t\|^p_{\gamma(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{B}_{\alpha - 1/2 + \epsilon})} dt\Big] \,.$$
    \end{enumerate}
    In the above, the constants in $\lesssim$'s do not depend on $x,y,Z$, and the dependence on $T$ is uniform over bounded subsets of $(0,\infty)$.","status":"unverified"}

Let G be a countable connected locally finite graph with p_c(G)>0 and sample iid Bernoulli bond percolation at p_c(G). Almost surely every infinite open component C, regarded as a fixed graph after conditioning on the sampled field, has quenched bond threshold p_c(C)=1. For rational r<1, independent r-thinning of the sampled open bonds is unconditionally iid bond percolation at p_c(G)r<p_c(G), so its probability of any infinite component is zero. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:27:36.746601+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_78e2f4c4bd764b472e1b3af25a9b61a824cdb200d4bfcd7ad72185ff9e942529","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Df 7 of arXiv:2511.18861, 'Correlation Decay for Maximum Weight Matchings on Sparse Graphs'] Let $G$ be a finite graph with fixed (non-random) edge weights $(w_e)_{e \in E(G)}$, and let $M$ be a matching.  
An augmenting path for $M$ is a finite self-avoiding path or cycle  
\[
P = e_1 \sim e_2 \sim \cdots \sim e_n
\]
where $e \sim e'$ means that the edges are adjacent in $G$ (and, if $P$ is a cycle, we also have $e_n \sim e_1$), such that the following hold:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The edges of $P$ alternate between those in $M$ and those not in $M$.  In particular, if $P$ is a cycle, then $n$ must be even.
    \item Writing $e_i = (x_{i-1}, x_i)$ for $i = 1, \ldots, n$, if $P$ is not a cycle and if $e_1$ (respectively $e_n$) is not in $M$, then $x_0$ (respectively $x_n$) is unmatched in $M$.
    \item The edge weights on $P$ satisfy
    \[
        \sum_{e \in P \cap M} w_e \;<\; \sum_{e \in P \cap M^c} w_e.
    \]
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:10:07.451152+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_78e7f9001e04ec0a27742070218a07fa32e55e4e094660e1750dd00ce2833cd7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem eq:abstract-pressure-bridge of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[theorem]{thm:conditional-transfer}
For all sufficiently large \(N\), suppose
\(\widehat Q_{N,L}\) and
\(\widehat P_{N,L}(\varepsilon,\eta)\) are finite for every
\(\varepsilon,\eta>0\).  Suppose also that there exist \(\Phi\in\mathbb R\) and a
function \(F\) on \((0,\infty)^2\) such that
\begin{equation}
 \widehat P_{N,L}(\varepsilon,\eta)\longrightarrow F(\varepsilon,\eta)
 \quad\text{for every fixed }\varepsilon,\eta>0,
 \qquad
 F(\varepsilon,\eta)\longrightarrow\Phi
 \quad\text{as }(\varepsilon,\eta)\to(0,0).
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{align}
 \limsup_{N\to\infty}\widehat Q_{N,L}
 &\le\Phi+\delta_{L,\mathrm{dr}}^{J,\mathrm{up}}(V),
 \\
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\widehat Q_{N,L}
 &\ge\Phi-\delta_{L,\mathrm{dr}}^{J,\mathrm{low}}(V).
 
\end{align}
Consequently,
\begin{align}
 \limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathscr C_N^J(V)
 &\le
 \max\{\Phi+\delta_{L,\mathrm{dr}}^{J,\mathrm{up}}(V),
            \overline\Lambda_L^J(V)\},\\
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathscr C_N^J(V)
 &\ge
 \max\{\Phi-\delta_{L,\mathrm{dr}}^{J,\mathrm{low}}(V),
            \underline\Lambda_L^J(V)\}.
 
\end{align}
If both de-regularization defects vanish, then
\begin{equation}
 \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N
 \log\widehat{\mathscr C}_{N,L}^J(V)=\Phi
\end{equation}
and the exact identities
\begin{align}
 \limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathscr C_N^J(V)
 &=\max\{\Phi,\overline\Lambda_L^J(V)\},
 \\
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathscr C_N^J(V)
 &=\max\{\Phi,\underline\Lambda_L^J(V)\}
 
\end{align}
hold.  In particular,
\begin{equation}
 \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathscr C_N^J(V)=\Phi
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \overline\Lambda_L^J(V)\le\Phi.
\end{equation}

A concrete sufficient condition for (equation eq:abstract-pressure-bridge of the paper)
is that, for any fixed \(L>0\), the disorder array and \(V\) satisfy the
hypotheses of (thm:bulk-universality of the paper) with \(m=2\).
Indeed, (equation eq:point-Haar-zero-cost of the paper) is automatic.  In this concrete
case,
\[
 \Phi=\Phi_p^{\rm bulk}(V)
 =\sup_{u\in\mathbb R}\{\theta_p(u)-V(u)\}.
\]
When the two de-regularization defects vanish,
(equation eq:exact-universality-iff-localized-defect of the paper) therefore gives a
criterion for the localized branch that is both necessary and sufficient. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.188849+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7921c02af68dc652942368cd5bb06586646634155ca82d789995c416a9b6cf61","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 101 (coordinate sum) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any measure $\rho$ on $[0,1]\times\R^d$, let $\bar{\rho}$ be the measure on $[0,1]\times\R$ that satisfies
	\[
	\int_{t,y} f\bigg(t, \sum_{i=1}^d y^i\bigg)
	\,\rho(dt\,dy)
	= \int_{t,x} f(t,x)
	\,\bar{\rho}(dt\,dx)\,,
	\]
where $t\in[0,1]$, $y\in\R^d$, and $x\in\R$.
As above, let $\vY$ be an $\R^d$-valued semimartingale with drift $\vD$ and covariation $\vQ$. We now consider the one-dimensional projections
	\[
	Y = \sum_{i=1}^d Y^i\,,\quad
	\sum_{i=1}^d D^i\,,\quad
	\sum_{i,j=1}^d Q^{ij}\,.
	\]
Then $Y$ is a (one-dimensional) semimartingale with drift $D$ and covariation $Q$. We hereafter abbreviate $\rho\equiv\rho_{\vY}$ for the occupation measure of $\vY$ defined in Definition~\ref{d:intro.cts.occ}.
Then the occupation measure of $Y$ is $\bar{\rho}$. The occupation measures associated to the drift and covariation of $Y$ are
	\[
	\sum_{i=1}^d
	\bar{\rho}_{D^i}\,,\quad
	\sum_{i,j=1}^d
	\bar{\rho}_{Q^{ij}}\,.	
	\]
Let $\hvY$ be as defined by Lemma~\ref{l:ideal.smoothed.occ.msr},
and let $\iY$ be the one-dimensional projection, so $\iY(t)=Y(t-\sss)+\mathfrak{x}$ where $(\sss,\mathfrak{x})\sim\bar{\varphi}$ (the density $\varphi$ integrated over $x^1 + \ldots + x^d=\mathfrak{x}$). It follows that $\iY$ has occupation measure $\overline{\rho*\varphi}=\bar{\rho}*\bar{\varphi}$. Similarly, the occupation measures associated to the drift and covariation of $\iY$ have densities
	\[
	\sum_{i=1}^d
	\overline{\rho_{D^i}*\varphi}
	\,,\quad
	\sum_{i,j=1}^d
	\overline{\rho_{Q^{ij}}
		*\varphi}\,.	
	\]
Then, analogously to \eqref{e:intro.occ.ratio.drift} and \eqref{e:intro.occ.ratio.qv}, we define (with $x$ now a scalar)
	\begin{align}
	
	B(t,x) 
	&\equiv
	\sum_{i=1}^D \frac{
	\overline{\rho_{D^i}*\varphi}(t,x)
	}
		{\overline{\rho*\varphi}(t,x)}\,,\\
	A(t,x)
	&\equiv
	\sum_{i,j=1}^D \frac{
	\overline{\rho_{Q^{ij}}*\varphi}(t,x)
	}
	{\overline{\rho*\varphi}(t,x)}\,.
	
	\end{align}
Let $\iX$ be the solution to the (one-dimensional) SDE
	\[
	d\iX(t)
	= B(t,\iX)\,dt
	+A(t,\iX)^{1/2}\,dW(t)\,,
	\]
where $W$ is a one-dimensional standard Brownian motion.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["a sequence of (random) rooted graphs with controlled local neighborhoods, such as bounded degree, sufficient for tightness","existence of a limiting infinite, typically unimodular, random rooted graph as the local weak limit","the functional of interest is expressible as, or well approximated by, a sum or average of local, root-based quantities","for extensive functionals: an additional argument, such as subadditivity or concentration, to pass from the local limit to a law of large numbers for the global sum"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.994267+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_793f7dca888660c8d4669b9e22cd3be3e733262e6b2906c64e5ca49d47cf39e4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For a sequence of finite, possibly random, rooted graphs G_n, local weak (Benjamini-Schramm) convergence means that for every finite radius r, the distribution of the isomorphism class of the r-ball around the (uniformly, or otherwise canonically) chosen root converges weakly to that of a limiting, typically infinite, random rooted graph (G*, o). The objective method, due to Aldous and Steele, is the broader program of analyzing this limiting infinite object directly, such as a Poisson weighted infinite tree or a unimodular Galton-Watson tree, to compute limiting constants for combinatorial optimization functionals on the finite graphs, such as the minimum spanning tree constant or the limiting value in the random assignment problem, by solving a recursive distributional (fixed-point) equation on the infinite limit rather than working with finite-n computations directly. It does not by itself establish that a given sequence converges locally weakly, which typically must be separately verified via a subsequential compactness argument together with uniqueness of subsequential limits, and it does not directly give convergence of global, extensive functionals without an additional concentration or summation argument beyond the purely local statement. Typical failure: Assuming that local weak convergence of the underlying random graph automatically implies convergence of a global extensive functional, such as the total weight of a minimum spanning tree, at the same per-vertex limiting rate; local convergence controls only typical local neighborhoods, and passing to a global average requires an additional uniform-integrability or concentration argument, often the genuinely hard part of an objective-method proof, which is easy to overlook once the local limit has been identified. Canonical reference: Benjamini and Schramm, 2001, Electronic Journal of Probability; Aldous and Steele, 2004, in Probability on Discrete Structures, Springer; Aldous and Lyons, 2007, Electronic Journal of Probability.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(X, M) is a measurable space","mu and nu are positive measures on M (for signed or complex measures the definition is applied to their total variations)","the separating set E is required to belong to M"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:13:10.402012+00:00","domain":"measure theory, decomposition of measures","id":"claim_7949ee76619d07edbf68d03f6116561c0881f49a0a0bfc5d35c33818a908ff98","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, M) be a measurable space and let mu and nu be positive measures on M. One says that mu and nu are MUTUALLY SINGULAR, written mu perp nu, if there exists a set E in M with mu(E) = 0 and nu(X minus E) = 0; equivalently, X splits into two measurable pieces, one carrying all of nu and mu-null, the other carrying all of mu and nu-null. The relation is symmetric. For signed or complex measures the definition is applied to the total variations: mu perp nu means |mu| perp |nu|. Basic consequences: mu perp mu holds if and only if mu = 0; if nu is absolutely continuous with respect to mu (nu << mu) and nu perp mu, then nu = 0; if nu_1 perp mu and nu_2 perp mu then (nu_1 + nu_2) perp mu. CAUTIONS. (1) Mutual singularity is much stronger than 'nu is not absolutely continuous with respect to mu': a measure can fail to be absolutely continuous without being singular, and in general a measure splits into an absolutely continuous and a singular part (Lebesgue decomposition). (2) Singularity is a measure-theoretic, not a topological, smallness statement: the measure sum over n of 2^(-n) times the Dirac mass at the n-th rational is mutually singular with Lebesgue measure on R yet has full support, and the Cantor-Lebesgue measure is mutually singular with Lebesgue measure while being atomless. (3) The witness set E must be measurable; without that requirement the notion is vacuous or ill-posed. (4) Mutual singularity is not preserved by arbitrary uncountable sums of measures.","status":"unverified"}

A rank-one bounded PSD kernel on [-1,1], k(x,xprime)=1{x>=0}1{xprime>=0}, with observation noise variance 1, prevents every continuous raw-input Gaussian predictor from achieving uniform forward KL below log(9/8)/4 > 1/36. # Raw-input obstruction for Target 1

Claim T336-w727-C003 v1. Status: proof (unaudited). This is a scope obstruction to the literal bounded-kernel raw-input statement; it does not contradict C002's supplied-feature theorem. No novelty or Lean certification is claimed.

## Statement

There is a rank-one bounded positive-semidefinite kernel on the compact raw-input domain [-1,1], observation-noise variance s=1, and bounded context labels, such that every predictor with continuous Gaussian output parameters (mu(x),v(x)), v(x)>0, has worst-case noisy predictive forward KL at least

    c0=(1/4) log(9/8)>1/36.

The conclusion applies in particular to every finite transformer whose raw-input encoding and subsequent operations are continuous and whose output is a Gaussian with positive continuous variance. It applies to normalized ReLU attention and softmax attention under these conditions. Therefore boundedness, compactness, finite rank, and positive observation noise alone cannot imply the raw-input version of Target 1 for arbitrarily small eps.

## Kernel and posterior

Define phi(x)=0 for x<0 and phi(x)=1 for x>=0. Set k(x,x')=phi(x)phi(x'). For any finite coefficients a_i,

    sum_{i,j} a_i a_j k(x_i,x_j)=(sum_i a_i phi(x_i))^2>=0.

Thus k is positive semidefinite, bounded by 1, and of rank exactly one (because k(0,0)=1). The GP can be represented as f(x)=Z phi(x), with Z~N(0,1). Observations add independent N(0,1) noise.

Use the empty context if allowed. Alternatively, for any n>=1 use one observation at x=-1 with label y=0, which satisfies every B>=0. This observation is pure noise independent of Z, so the posterior law of Z remains N(0,1). For either context, the new noisy predictive distribution is

    P_x=N(0,1) for x<0; P_x=N(0,2) for x>=0.

Hence the example does not rely on whether a context of length zero is included.

## Continuity forces two incompatible approximation requirements

Fix this context and any continuous output mu(x),v(x)>0. Let E=sup_x KL(P_x || N(mu(x),v(x))). If E is infinite the bound is immediate. Otherwise put mu0=mu(0),v0=v(0)>0. At x=0,

    D_2:=KL(N(0,2)||N(mu0,v0))<=E.

Take x_j=-1/j tending to zero from below. Since mu,v are continuous and v0>0, the explicit Gaussian KL formula is continuous along this sequence; all denominators remain positive near the limit. Therefore

    D_1:=KL(N(0,1)||N(mu0,v0))<=E.

No dominated convergence, probabilistic conditioning argument, or exchange of a supremum with a limit is used: every term in this deterministic convergent sequence is <=E.

For a>0 define

    D_a=(1/2)(log(v0/a)+(a+mu0^2)/v0-1).

Writing w=3/(2v0)>0 and combining logarithms gives the exact identity

    (D_1+D_2)/2
      = (1/4)log(9/8)+(1/2)(w-1-log w)+mu0^2/(2v0).

The inequality log w<=w-1 follows by integrating 1/t from 1 to w, separately for w>=1 and 0<w<=1, or by differentiating w-1-log w. Both additional terms are nonnegative. Consequently

    E >= (D_1+D_2)/2 >= (1/4)log(9/8).

Finally log(9/8)=integral_1^{9/8} dt/t > (1/8)(8/9)=1/9, since 1/t>8/9 except at the right endpoint. Thus c0>1/36. Every denominator and logarithm argument above is strictly positive.

## Interpretation for the dossier

C002 supplies phi as an input, so its input encoding itself is discontinuous as a function of raw x in this example; the continuity hypothesis here then fails. There is no contradiction. To close Target 1, the architecture must explicitly permit the fixed feature map in the input representation, or the theorem must add assumptions that make raw-input feature computation possible and account for its cost. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:16:49.564661+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7994b8eb14afe8df4ccbb96e64ddbced16fb44ee3fe5f57fd62aa626e183d505","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 17 (Inversion of the surrogate objectives) of arXiv:2608.25188, 'Transforms for LLM Quantization:\\ The Great Inversion and Format Co-Design'] Regard both distortions as functionals of the transformed energy vector $v$ at
fixed $E=\sum_k v_k$, the shared-scale one on a \emph{uniform} grid.
\begin{itemize}
\item The \textbf{allocation-flexible} coding surrogate (\Cref{sec:classical})
$D_{\mathrm{vr}}(v)\propto(\prod_k v_k)^{1/d}$ is the geometric mean, the form the
variable-rate distortion takes while every coordinate draws positive rate
(\Cref{prop:schur}(i); once the water level of \Cref{prop:waterfill} rises above a
coordinate's energy the true distortion is floored by the un-coded coordinates' energy,
so the vanishing limit below is an idealization of the surrogate). It is strictly
Schur-\emph{concave} wherever all coordinates are positive and identically zero elsewhere; it decreases under majorization, so it is driven down by
\emph{concentration}, the direction in which the KLT moves the profile, reaching the
majorization-maximal \emph{reachable} one, the spectrum (\Cref{thm:klt}).
\item The \textbf{shared-scale AbsMax} surrogate (\Cref{sec:inv-flatness})
$D_{\mathrm{fr}}(v)=\sum_g\max_{k\in g}v_k$ obeys the max-vs-mean bound of
\Cref{prop:schur}(ii), so among all $v$ of fixed sum it is minimized at the
\emph{flat} $v$, the direction in which incoherence processing and the Hadamard move the
profile (\Cref{prop:rht}), and maximized under within-group concentration.
\end{itemize}
Over all $v$ of fixed total energy, then, the two surrogates are driven apart. The
geometric mean is strictly Schur-concave on the positive orthant, so every majorization
step toward concentration strictly lowers $D_{\mathrm{vr}}$ while every coordinate remains
positive, and it is maximized at the flat $v$;
while $E/G\le D_{\mathrm{fr}}\le E$, the lower bound attained exactly when every group
is internally uniform and the upper bound when each group's mass sits on a single
coordinate. Concentrating energy \emph{within} a group therefore strictly lowers the first whenever every coordinate remains positive, and never lowers the second, strictly raising it as soon as the group maximum rises; flattening within groups does the reverse. Along no \emph{within-group} step of the order do the two objectives move the same way.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a compact metric space","T : X -> X is continuous and surjective","the definition quantifies over all nonempty OPEN subsets U"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.090776+00:00","domain":"topological dynamics, mixing properties of non-invertible maps","id":"claim_79ea44cf7b3dcd7452df709c8e293198d63314337814289a89d9a84e9a0edffe","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a compact metric space and T : X -> X a continuous surjection. T is TOPOLOGICALLY EXACT, also called locally eventually onto, if for every nonempty open set U there is an integer n >= 1 with T^n(U) = X. Two consequences are what proofs actually use. (a) UNIFORMITY IN n: if T^n(U) = X then T^m(U) = X for every m >= n, because T is onto; hence for each nonempty open U there is N with T^n(U) = X for ALL n >= N. (b) DENSE BACKWARD ORBITS WITH ALL LARGE PERIODS: for every x in X and every nonempty open U there is N with U intersect T^{-n}(x) nonempty for every n >= N; in particular the full backward orbit of any point is dense. Property (b) is a genuine aperiodicity statement that topological transitivity does not give and that even topological mixing of an invertible system cannot give. Relations: topological exactness implies topological mixing, which implies topological transitivity; the converses are false. An invertible map is never topologically exact unless X is a single point, since T^n(U) = X forces U = X for a homeomorphism, so exactness is a hypothesis reserved for genuinely non-invertible maps: expanding maps of the circle or of a compact manifold, one-sided mixing subshifts of finite type, and Chebyshev-like interval maps are the standard examples.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:58:01.575452+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_79efc22e2efdf6b3517514085c1069b95d1e98df1cf7e1f83fb4c240025e816a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2608.27372, 'Universality and sharp thresholds for ellipsoid fitting'] Let $(x_i)_{1\leq i\leq n}\in \R^d$ be i.i.d. random vectors such that $x_1=(x_{1j})_{1\leq j\leq d}$ has indpenedent coordinates satisfying
	\begin{equation}
		\E[x_{1j}]=0,\qquad \E \left[x_{1j}^2\right]=1,\qquad
		\E \left[x_{1j}^4\right]=\kappa,\qquad \sup_{j\le d}\|x_{1j}\|_{\psitwo}\le K_x,
	\end{equation}
    where $\kappa>1$ and $K_x>0$ do not depend on $n,d$. Let
	$n,d\to\infty$ with $n/d^2\to\alpha\in(0,\infty)$.  There is an explicit
	threshold $\alpha_\star(\kappa)$, defined in Eq.~\eqref{eq:alpha-star-def},
	which depends only on $\kappa$, such that the following holds.
	\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
		\item If $\alpha<\alpha_\star(\kappa)$, then with probability tending to one, there exists an ellipsoid fitting all $(x_i)_{1\leq i\leq n}$:
		\[
		\exists R\succ 0,\quad\textnormal{such that}\quad x_i^{\top}R x_i=1\quad \textnormal{for all}\quad 1\leq i\leq n.
		\]
		Moreover, such $R\in \R^{d\times d}$ can be chosen to be well-conditioned: $\lambda_{\max}(R)/\lambda_{\min}(R)=O(1)$. 
		\item If $\alpha>\alpha_\star(\kappa)$, then with probability tending to one
		there is no $R\succeq0$ such that $x_i^\top R x_i=1$ for all $1\leq i\leq n$. Moreover, the optimal squared fitting error converges in probability:
		\begin{equation}
			\Gamma_X:=\inf_{R\succeq0, \operatorname{Tr}R=d}\,\inf_{r\geq 0}\,
			\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\frac{x_i^\top Rx_i}{\sqrt{d}}-r\right)^2
			\pto e_\star(\alpha,\kappa),
		\end{equation}
        where $e_\star(\alpha,\kappa)$ is defined in Eq.~\eqref{eq:optimal-fitting-error-main}. For $\alpha>\alpha_\star(\kappa)$, $e_\star(\alpha,\kappa)>0$ holds, thus an approximate ellipsoid fitting is not possible with any $R\succeq 0$ with $\Tr R=d$.
	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["K ⊂ ℝⁿ is nonempty and closed","the Euclidean norm is used (for the eikonal equation |Du| = 1 the ball of the same norm is the unit speed set)","the eikonal equation is taken in the form |Du| − 1 = 0"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:57:26.110904+00:00","domain":"Hamilton–Jacobi equations, optimal control, distance functions","id":"claim_7a06bdbc5ba6d57f83322f14777c062b65834326f61029190ba7a9d22b579f18","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let K ⊂ ℝⁿ be nonempty and closed and let d(x) := dist(x, K) = min_{y ∈ K} |x − y| (the minimum is attained because K is closed). Then: (a) d is 1-Lipschitz, d ≥ 0, and d(x) = 0 exactly when x ∈ K. (b) [minimal-time / control representation] d(x) = inf { T ≥ 0 : there is an absolutely continuous ξ: [0,T] → ℝⁿ with |ξ'(s)| ≤ 1 for a.e. s, ξ(0) = x, ξ(T) ∈ K } = inf { ∫_0^T |ξ'(s)| ds : ξ absolutely continuous, ξ(0) = x, ξ(T) ∈ K, T ≥ 0 } — the distance is the value function of the minimal-time problem for the control system ξ' = α, |α| ≤ 1, with target K, and the straight segment from x to a nearest point of K is an optimal trajectory. (c) [variational characterization] d is the largest 1-Lipschitz function that is ≤ 0 on K: if u: ℝⁿ → ℝ is 1-Lipschitz and u ≤ 0 on K then u ≤ d everywhere, and d itself is admissible; equivalently d(x) = max { u(x) : u 1-Lipschitz, u ≤ 0 on K }. (d) [eikonal equation] d is a viscosity solution of |Du| − 1 = 0 in the open set ℝⁿ \\ K, and a viscosity subsolution of |Du| − 1 ≤ 0 on all of ℝⁿ. Sharp edges. (1) The sign convention matters: d solves |Du| − 1 = 0 but is in general NOT a viscosity solution of 1 − |Du| = 0 (for K = {−1, 1} ⊂ ℝ, d = 1 − |x| on (−1,1) has a concave kink at 0 which is admissible for the first form only). (2) Uniqueness of viscosity solutions of |Du| = 1 in ℝⁿ \\ K vanishing on K FAILS without a sign or growth restriction: for K = {0}, the function u(x) = −|x| is a classical (hence viscosity) solution of |Du| − 1 = 0 in ℝⁿ \\ {0} with u(0) = 0, different from d(x) = |x|. The distance is singled out among solutions by (c), or by nonnegativity/boundedness-below conditions that this lemma does not assert. (3) For K not closed the minimum in the definition of d must be replaced by an infimum and d vanishes on the closure of K, not only on K.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:17:04.322958+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7a112d984414996beb1871b3c4a78c359f37fdfc7dd3eb7542762ba4b443e657","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition of arXiv:2606.01683, 'Singular-value gap of nonreversible Markov processes'] For a Banach couple $(E_0, E_1)$, denote by $\mathcal{F}(E_0, E_1)$ the class 
    of functions $F: \Bar{S} \to E_0 + E_1$ satisfying
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $F$ is continuous on $\Bar{S}$ and analytic on $S$
        \item $F(it) \in E_0$ and $F(1+it) \in E_1$ for all $t \in \mathds{R}$
        \item $\|F\|_{\mathcal{F}(E_0, E_1)} \coloneqq 
        \max \Big\{ \sup_{t \in \mathds{R}} \|F(it)\|_{E_0}, \sup_{t \in \mathds{R}} \|F(1+it)\|_{E_1}           \Big\} < \infty$ 
    \end{itemize}
    Then, for $0 \leq \theta \leq 1 $, the \textbf{complex interpolation space} $[E_0, E_1]_\theta$ is the 
    Banach space defined by
    \[
        [E_0, E_1]_\theta \coloneqq \{h \in E_0 + E_1: h = F(\theta) \ \ \text{for some} \ F \in \mathcal{F}(E_0, E_1)\}
    \]
    equipped with the norm
    \[
        \|h\|_{[E_0, E_1]_\theta} \coloneqq \inf_{\substack{F \in \mathcal{F}(E_0, E_1) \\
        F(\theta) = h}} \|F\|_{\mathcal{F}(E_0, E_1)}
    \]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:33:17.740358+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7a118bd39237e36f9cf206734f90190f5bd46dea6d841e3f5d3c658a95681f87","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 104 (Passage of finite propagation to the cutoff limits) of arXiv:2607.10813, '2607.10813'] Let $(\chi_1,\rho_1)$ and $(\chi_2,\rho_2)$ be adapted to $(K,T_0)$, and let
$(u_\jmath,v_\jmath,\mathcal N_\jmath)$, $\jmath=1,2$, be the corresponding
limiting localized solutions with existence times $\tau_1,\tau_2$.  Fix
$T<\tau_1\wedge\tau_2$.  Choose
$\eta\in C_c^\infty(\R^3)$ such that $\eta=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$ and
$\operatorname{supp}\eta\subset K^{[1]}$.  For every sufficiently large
integer $J$, on the finite intersection of the two fixed-profile dyadic
probability-one events,
\begin{equation}
 \eta(u_1-u_2)=\eta(v_1-v_2)=0
 \quad\text{in }C_TH^{-J},
 \qquad
 \eta(\mathcal N_1-\mathcal N_2)=0
 \quad\text{in }L_T^1H^{-J}.
\end{equation}
For an arbitrary admissible cofinal cutoff sequence and deterministic
$T$, the same conclusion holds on the event
$\{T<\tau_1\wedge\tau_2\}$ in the partial convergence sense of
\cref{def:partial-probability-convergence}: the two localized approximations
converge in probability in the same Banach spaces to the common triple in
\eqref{eq:limit-localization-comparison}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:56:36.587912+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7a13d8024428def817be185b12010821d20c2bbe75867199b2938a788f55a9d2","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn defi_kin_sol of arXiv:2608.30548, 'Finite speed of propagation and waiting time phenomena for stochastic porous media equatio'] Let $u_0\in L^1(\mathbb{T}^d)$ be non-negative and assume  (equation equation_n_m_together of the paper)  and (equation Eq_ass_B1 of the paper)--(equation Eq_ass_B3 of the paper). 	\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
	\item mass is conserved, i.e., $\mathbb{P}$-a.s, we have  $\|u(t)\|_{L^1(\mathbb{T}^d)} = \|u_0\|_{L^1(\mathbb{T}^d)}$ for all $t\in [0,T]$,
	\item it holds $\sigma(u) \in L^2(\Omega \times [0,T]\times \mathbb{T}^d)$,
	\item  we have $((K\wedge u )\vee 1/K) \in  L^2(\Omega \times [0,T]; H^1(\mathbb{T}^d))$ for all $K\in \mathbb{N}$,
	\end{enumerate}  
and there exists  a kinetic measure $q$ with 
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
	\setcounter{enumi}{3}
	\item $\mathbb{P}$-a.s, $m\delta(v - u)v^{m-1} |\nabla u|^2 \le q $ in the sense of measures on $\mathbb{T}^d \times (0,\infty) \times [0,T]$,
	\item  $q$ vanishes at infinity in the sense that $\lim_{M\to\infty} \mathbb{E} [ q(\mathbb{T}^d \times [M,M+1] \times [0,T])] = 0$,
	\item and for every $\psi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{T}^d\times (0,\infty ))$, it holds $\mathbb{P}$-a.s.\ 
	\begin{align}\begin{split}&\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}
		\mathbf{1}_{\{0<v <u(t,x)\}} \psi(x,v)

		\\&\qquad -\,\int_0^t  \int_{\mathbb{R}} \int_{\mathbb{T}^d} \partial_v \psi (x,v) \,\mathrm{d} q\,+\,\frac{1}{2}\int_0^t \int_{\mathbb{T}^d} \bigl(
		\sigma(u)\sigma'(u)\nabla u \cdot \Psi_2 \,+\, \Psi_3 \sigma^2(u)\bigr) (\partial_v\psi)(x,u) 
		\,\mathrm{d} x
		\mathrm{d} s
		\\&\qquad - \sum_{i=1}^d\sum_{k=1}^\infty \int_0^t \int_{\mathbb{T}^d} \psi(x, u) \partial_i ( \psi_k \sigma (u)) \,\mathrm{d} x \,\mathrm{d} \beta_k^{(i)}(s)		
		,
		\end{split}
	\end{align}
	for all $t\in [0,T]$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:47.659910+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7a37ce8165404fc566d24822af83b22605397f94fcfe11efc17e4145e45ac5d6","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 20 of arXiv:2605.08844, 'Signature Kernel and Schwinger-Dyson Kernel Equations as Two-Parameter Rough Differential '] For every \(n\in [1:\kappa+\zeta]\), let \(\ell=\lceil n/2\rceil\). Then the homogeneous components of the Schwinger--Dyson kernel satisfy
\begin{equation}
K_0(s,t)=1 +  \int_s^t  K_{1}(s,u) d\mathbf{X}_u du,
\qquad
K_n(s,t)
=
-\int_s^t \sigma_n\bigl(K_{\ell-1}(s, \cdot),K_{n-\ell}(\cdot, t)\bigr)_u\,d\mathbf X_u .
\end{equation}
Here, for every word \(I=i_1\cdots i_n\) over the alphabet \(\{1,\dots,d\}\), we set
\(
\tilde I:=i_1\cdots i_{\ell-1},\,
\hat I:=i_{\ell+1}\cdots i_n,
\)
and,given a basis \(e_1,\dots,e_d\) of \(V\), define
\begin{align*}
&\sigma_n:
\mathrm{Hom}\bigl(V^{\otimes(\ell-1)},\mathbb R\bigr)\boxtimes
\mathrm{Hom}\bigl(V^{\otimes(n-\ell)},\mathbb R\bigr)
\to
\mathrm{Hom}\bigl(V,\mathrm{Hom}(V^{\otimes n},\mathbb R)\bigr),\\
&\sigma_n(\eta,\xi)[e_j](e_I)
=
\sigma_n(\eta,\xi)[e_j](e_{\tilde I}\otimes e_{i_\ell}\otimes e_{\hat I})
=
\eta(e_{\tilde I})\,\delta_{i_\ell j}\,\xi(e_{\hat I}),
\end{align*}
for every word \(I\) of length \(n\), and extend linearly on \(V^{\otimes n}\).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:21:06.856933+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7a45d4128093f4c2b60093ff4b5157307344efbd140da82fb749f74ee8fc0c65","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2608.21063, '\textbf{Non-bijective scaling limits and phase transitions of planar maps}'] All limits below are taken in the Gromov--Hausdorff--Prokhorov sense as $n\to\infty$, restricted to $n\equiv0 \mod d_\omega $.
	
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item Suppose that Condition~\eqref{eq:bwfvv} holds, or that $\nu=1$ and Condition~\eqref{eq:bwregvar} holds for some $\frac{5}{4} < \alpha \le 2$. Then $\kappa < \infty$ and
		\[
			\left( \mM_n^\omega, \frac{2^{1/\alpha-1}}{\kappa}\frac{b_{n}}{n} d_{\mM_n^\omega}, \mu_{\mM_n^\omega} \right) \convd (\mathbf{T}_\alpha, d_{\mathbf{T}_\alpha}, \mu_{\mathbf{T}_\alpha}).
		\]
		\item Suppose that $\nu=1$, that Condition~\eqref{eq:bwregvar} holds with $\alpha=5/4$, and that the limit  \[

		\]

		\[
		   \left( \mM_n^\omega, \frac{1}{\mathfrak d_{\mathbf{M}}} \left(\frac{6}{d_\omega}\right)^{1/4} \left(\frac{5\Gamma(3/4)^4}{c_\omega}\right)^{1/5} \frac{1}{n^{1/5}\log n} d_{\mM_n^\omega}, \mu_{\mM_n^\omega} \right)

		\]
		\item Suppose that $\nu=1$ and that Condition~\eqref{eq:bwregvar} holds for some $1 < \alpha < \frac{5}{4}$.	 Then
		\[
			\left( \mM_n^\omega, \left( \frac{3}{2^{2 + 1/\alpha} b_{n}} \right)^{1/4} d_{\mM_n^\omega}, \mu_{\mM_n^\omega} \right) \convd \left(\mathbf{T}^{\mathrm{dec}}_\alpha(\mathbf{M}), d_{\mathbf{T}^{\mathrm{dec}}_\alpha(\mathbf{M})}, \mu_{\mathbf{T}^{\mathrm{dec}}_\alpha(\mathbf{M})}\right).

		\item Suppose that $\nu=1$ and that Condition~\eqref{eq:bwregvar} holds with $\alpha=1$. Then
		\[

		\[

		\]
	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:19:56.712514+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7a49b705a1eff1d6d56361f2585346d775af33fe4ef1039f67e9fc5640c798e0","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 26 of arXiv:2608.30991, 'A block-Toeplitz approach to the spectrum of the Neumann-Poincaré operator on self-similar'] Let $a:\mathbb{T}\to\mathcal{L}(X)$. A \emph{right Wiener--Hopf factorisation} of $a$ with respect to the unit circle $\mathbb{T}$ is a representation
	\[
	a(z)=a_-(z)\Lambda(z)a_+(z),
	\qquad z\in\mathbb{T},
	\]
	in which $a_+$ and $a_+^{-1}$ extend holomorphically to the interior unit disk $\mathbb{D}$, $a_-$ and $a_-^{-1}$ extend holomorphically to the exterior domain $\mathbb{E} = \{z : |z| > 1\} \cup \{\infty\}$, all four with continuous boundary values on $\mathbb{T}$, and
	\[
	\Lambda(z)=I-\Pi+\sum_{j=1}^{J}z^{\nu_j}\Pi_j,
	\qquad
	\Pi:=\sum_{j=1}^{J}\Pi_j,
	\]
	where $\Pi_1,\dots,\Pi_J$ are rank-one idempotents with $\Pi_i\Pi_j=0$ for $i\neq j$ and $\nu_1,\dots,\nu_J\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}$ are the \emph{non-zero partial indices}, not necessarily distinct. The factorisation is \emph{canonical} if $J=0$, that is $\Lambda\equiv I$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.153335+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7a4b687052c31d21a374350800babbe1e0bb54804bb21e625501c86003d4f73f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 1 of arXiv:2608.29406, 'Partially Totally Real Submanifolds of Sasakian Manifolds'] A submanifold $M$ of a Sasakian manifold, tangent to $\xi$, is called a \emph{partially totally real (PTR) submanifold} if there exists a nonzero constant-rank totally real distribution $\Dperp\subset TM\cap\ker\eta$, i.e.
\[
 \phi\Dperp\subset\Tperp.
\]
If $\Dtilde$ denotes the orthogonal complement of $\Dperp\oplus\langle\xi\rangle$ in $TM$, then
\begin{equation}
 TM=\Dperp\oplus\Dtilde\oplus\langle\xi\rangle.
\end{equation}
Following the K\"ahler PTR terminology, $\Dtilde$ is called the
\emph{ambiguous distribution}.  The PTR structure refers to this chosen
decomposition; maximality of \(\Dperp\), when needed, is imposed later
and is not part of the definition.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:34:33.538462+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7a97ad96f4b81f30399ab986caeac2453c3307cc069e9dec1196571c81a009e1","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 5 of arXiv:2603.28702, 'Distribution of the magnetization of the critical Ising model on sparse random graphs'] \begin{itemize}
\item 
Let $G$ be a graph with vertex set $V$. The Ising model on this graph with inverse temperature $\beta$ is the probability measure $\mu$ on $\{-1,1\}^V$ satisfying
$$\mu_{\beta}(\sigma)=\dfrac{1}{Z_{\beta,G}}\exp\left(\beta\SL{u\sim v}\sigma_u\sigma_v\right).$$
\item
Fix a measure $\nu$ on $\{-1,1\}^V$. For a configuration $\sigma\in\{-1,1\}^V$ and for some $v\in V$, let $\sigma^{\oplus v}$ be the configuration $\sigma$ in which the spin at vertex $v$ is flipped. For two configurations $\sigma,\tau\in\{-1,1\}^V$, we write $\sigma\sim\tau$ if $\tau=\sigma^{\oplus v}$ for some $v\in V$. The continuous time Glauber Dynamics on $G$ for $\nu$ at rate 1 is a Markov chain with transition rates, for $\sigma\neq\tau$, equal to
$$q(\sigma,\tau)=\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\nu(\tau)}{\nu(\sigma)+\nu(\tau)},\ \ \text{if}\ \ \sigma \sim \tau
\\ \\
0,\ \ \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}$$
Informally, every vertex gets updated at rate one, and the update happens conditionally on the configuration in the rest of the vertices.
\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:46:26.252202+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7aa3c8b1005683c1ef4fd5fc4e7f3fa59cc78590af426c95614b31f7da091b9f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theo 3 of arXiv:2605.23292, 'Second-order Poincaré inequalities and localization on the Poisson space'] (rates of normal convergence for sums of $BL$-space-time localizing scores on metric spaces)

\[

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:02:17.985904+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7abd5943eeca0508bf674af20b2bef2fa66b54442080048fa79fc8c4ef9c274c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:standard-twostream of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] Fix $\lambda \in (0,1)$
and a \emph{send sequence}  
$\overline{p}$ with $p_0=1$.
Let $Z=(Z^A,Z^B)$ be the two-stream process with birth rate~$\lambda$, send sequence~$\overline{p}$ and start time~$0$  
where for all $D\in \{A,B\}$ and all
positive integers~$k$,
$\mathbf{arr}_k^{Z^D}(\tau) = \emptyset$. 
Let $X$ be the backoff process with birth distribution~$\mathsf{Po}(\lambda)$, send sequence~$\overline{p}$, and cohort set $\mathcal{C}=\{A,B\}$ (Definition~(def:backoff-cohorts of the paper)).
The standard coupling of~$Z$ and~$X$ has the following invariants for every $i\geq 1$ and $t\geq 1$.
\begin{description}  
\item  [Inv-$b_i(t)$:] For each stream $D\in \{A,B\}$, $\mathbf{b}_i^{Z^D}(t-1) \subseteq \mathbf{b}_i^{X^D}(t-1)$.
\item  [Inv-$B_i(t)$:] For each stream $D\in \{A,B\}$, $\mathbf{B}_i^{Z^D}(t) \subseteq \mathbf{B}_i^{X^D}(t)$.
\item [Inv-$s_i(t)$:] 
For each stream $D\in \{A,B\}$, $\mathbf{s}_i^{Z^D}(t) \subseteq \mathbf{s}_i^{X^D}(t)$.
\end{description}
Initially, Inv-$b_i(1)$ holds for every $i\geq 1$ since all of these sets are empty.

For any $t$ assuming Inv-$b_i(t)$, the coupling at step~$t$ proceeds as follows.
For each $D\in \{A,B\}$, $\mathbf{n}^{Z^D}(t) = \mathbf{n}^{X^D}(t)$, so for all $i\geq 1$, 
Inv-$B_i(t)$ holds.
For every   
$D\in \{A,B\}$ and
$i\geq 1$, $\mathbf{S}^{X^D}_i(t)$ is formed by including each ball in 
$\mathbf{B}_i^{X^D}(t) \setminus \mathbf{B}_i^{Z^D}(t)$ 
independently with probability~$p_i$.
Then $\mathbf{s}^{X^D}_i(t) = \mathbf{S}^{X^D}_i(t) \cup \mathbf{s}^{Z^D}_i(t)$, establishing Inv-$s_i(t)$.

 
  

  
The assignments to $\mathbf{e}_i^{X^D}(t)$ follow deterministically, using  Definition~(def:backoffasgen of the paper)
and the assignments to $\mathbf{e}_i^{Z^D}(t)$  are chosen  following Definition~(def:two-stream of the paper).

Since $\mathbf{s}_i^{X^D}(t) \cap \mathbf{B}_i^{Z^D}(t) = \mathbf{s}_i^{Z^D}(t)$, Inv-$b_i(t+1)$  follows from  
$ \mathbf{s}_i^{Z^D}(t) \cap \mathbf{e}_i^{X^D}(t) \subseteq \mathbf{e}_i^{Z^D}(t)$, which holds:
If a ball~$\beta$ is in $ \mathbf{s}_i^{Z^D}(t) \cap \mathbf{e}_i^{X^D}(t) $ then
$\mathbf{s}^{X^A}(t) \cup \mathbf{s}^{X^B}(t)= \{\beta\}$ so
$\mathbf{s}^{Z^A}(t) \cup \mathbf{s}^{Z^B}(t) = \{\beta\}$ so

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:59:24.052460+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7acf4cebcdf3320b4a885a7f1398cec5bd1f2ceb7be521f238958e306f2b4758","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:pathbound of arXiv:2608.30888, 'Three-term asymptotics for discrete\\ Hardy--Rellich constants in high dimension'] Fix $J$ and two finite sets of partitions.  Uniformly for $0\leq j\leq J$ and
for all partitions $\lambda,\mu$ in those sets or reachable from them in at
most $J$ steps,
\begin{equation}
 \left|\ip{A_N^j\psi_\lambda}{\psi_\mu}\right|
 \leq C_J N^{a_j(\lambda,\mu)/2},

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:56:37.651622+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7ad26847ff861be199c6bd05ca3ce9408dd4e7aec539420e2a44e52a20c91d27","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:openpath of arXiv:2608.24830, 'Motion helps the contact process: survival below\\ the percolation threshold on Poisson Br'] Let $\lambda\in(0,\infty]$, $\mu\in(0,\infty]$ and $\mathfrak r\in\{\mathrm{u},\mathrm{i}\}$. An \emph{open
path} from $(u_0,t_0)$ to $(u_n,t_{n+1})$ consists of particles $u_0,\dots,u_n$, such that
consecutive particles are distinct, and times $t_0<t_1<\dots<t_{n+1}$, such that
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item for $1\le j\le n$ there is an active transmission mark from $u_{j-1}$ to $u_j$ at time
  $t_j$; when $\lambda=\infty$ this says that $u_{j-1}$ and $u_j$ are in contact at $t_j$;
\item for $0\le j\le n$ there is no effective recovery mark of $u_j$ in $(t_j,t_{j+1}]$.
\end{enumerate}
Its \emph{trace} is the c\`adl\`ag path $\gamma$ on $[t_0,t_{n+1}]$ given by $\gamma(t)=X_{u_j}(t)$
for $t\in[t_j,t_{j+1})$ and $0\le j\le n-1$, and by $\gamma(t)=X_{u_n}(t)$ for
$t\in[t_n,t_{n+1}]$. Its jumps have size at most $2r$. The path is \emph{contained} in a
space-time region $D$ if $(\gamma(t),t)\in D$ for every $t\in[t_0,t_{n+1}]$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:15:54.983664+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7b1174403ad43db638eb1b9310108ffb2faefa813439da61246dbc94ae3e0994","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:prenosil-diamond of arXiv:2608.29708, 'Intuitionistic and Constructive Modal Logics for Classical Modal Logicians'] {simpson_proof_1994}}] 
  On an f-model $\mathfrak{M} = (W, \leq, \sqsubset, V)$, consider the diamond clause
  \[
    x \Vdash^{\mathrm p}_\mathfrak{M} \Diamond \varphi
    \mathrel{\;\ratio\Longleftrightarrow\;}
    \exists x', y \in W \,
      (x' \leq x \mathrel{\text{\&}} x' \sqsubset y \mathrel{\text{\&}} y \Vdash^{\mathrm p}_\mathfrak{M} \varphi).
  \]
  Thus $\Diamond \varphi$ holds at $x$ when $\varphi$ holds at an ${\sqsubset}$-successor
  of some ${\leq}$-predecessor of $x$.
  Simpson attributes this clause to unpublished work of Plotkin and Stirling.
  P\v{r}enosil later developed the corresponding operation on upsets [prenosil_duality_2014].","status":"unverified"}
