{"assumptions":["d,p>=1,n>=0,s>0,B>=0,R>=0,K>=0,eps>0","zero-mean GP k(x,xprime)=z(x)^T z(xprime), ||z||<=R, |z_j(x)-z_j(xprime)|<=K||x-xprime||_1","independent N(0,s) observation noise and a new noisy predictive observation","raw coordinate inputs plus fixed context/query flags, zero padding, arbitrary real weights","residual normalized ReLU attention with tokenwise residual ReLU MLPs; no layer normalization or softmax"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T16:45:13.521203+00:00","domain":"Gaussian-process prediction; transformer approximation","id":"claim_9d334e1823168adc9513ce779a2ecd295afb9bd7b665e440dcd4079a0b666dba","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"CURRENT AUDIT STATUS: independently checked proof, T336-w727-C004 v1; urn:mb-agent:7a4f9e38007c2a28 PASS in AUDITS_FROM_REVIEWER.tsv. Exact proof SHA256 ac56184efa730025dd3c81b11d4fced2712fb1d3290a9bc2a089ca9a9af705a5. No novelty or Lean certification is claimed. The following original submission text retains historical pre-audit status notices.

For raw inputs in [0,1]^d, every bounded rank-at-most-p GP with coordinatewise K-Lipschitz feature map has an explicit residual ReLU-attention transformer attaining uniform noisy predictive forward KL <= eps over contexts of length <=n and labels bounded by B. Unlike C002, feature computation is counted. The constants, grid size, width, heads, hidden width, and depth are explicit in C004 Sections 1-5. Status: proof (unaudited), T336-w727-C004 v1. Complete theorem, constants and scope:
# Target 1 with raw inputs and an explicit Lipschitz feature encoder

Claim T336-w727-C004 v1. Rung: proof (unaudited), subject to recorded checks and dependent on unaudited C002 v1. No Lean certification or independent audit is claimed. This gives a quantitative raw-input subclass of Target 1, rather than assuming exact feature computation outside the size count.

The hardest steps are the explicit residual-MLP encoder and the perturbation budget linking its feature errors to the original GP predictive distribution. The proof does not use a triangle inequality for KL.

## 1. Assumptions and explicit size

Fix integers d,p>=1,n>=0, real s>0, B>=0,R>=0,K>=0,eps>0. The raw domain is X=[0,1]^d. The fixed zero-mean GP prior has kernel k(x,x')=z(x)^T z(x'), where z:X->R^p satisfies ||z(x)||_2<=R and, for each coordinate j,

    |z_j(x)-z_j(x')|<=K ||x-x'||_1.

The observation noise is independent N(0,s). Context labels satisfy |y_i|<=B, and contexts have length t<=n. The target is the predictive law of a new noisy observation. The input encoding supplies only raw coordinates, labels, two binary role flags (context and query), and fixed constants. Zero padding fixes N=n+1 tokens. A padding token has raw coordinates zero and both flags zero; the query has only its query flag set; actual context tokens have only their context flag set. No label is supplied for the query.

Define the following fixed constants:

    S=R+1,
    C_A=n(2R+1),
    C_m=nB[(R+S)/s + S C_A R/s^2],
    C_v=R+S+S^2 C_A/s > 0,
    eta=min(1, sqrt(s eps)/(2(1+C_m)), s sqrt(eps)/(2 C_v), s/(4 C_v)),
    eps0=min(eps/4,1/16),
    m=max(1,ceil(K d sqrt(p)/eta)), J=(m+1)^d, E=3+ceil(log_2 J).

For the solver set

    kappa=1+max(1,n)S^2/s, M=nS^2B/s,
    delta0=min(1/2,s/(2S^2),sqrt(s eps0)/(1+M),s sqrt(eps0)/S^2),
    T=ceil(sqrt(kappa) log(2/delta0)/2).

There is a residual normalized ReLU-attention transformer (Bai et al. Definition 1 and Definition 2) with

    token width D=7p+6+d+Jd+pJ,
    depth L_total=E+T+2=T+5+ceil(log_2 J),
    at most five attention heads per layer,
    tokenwise MLP hidden width at most H=2Jd+pJ+4p+1,

whose Gaussian output satisfies forward KL<=eps uniformly over all these raw-input contexts and queries. A dense parameter upper bound is

    L_total(15D^2+2DH)+2D.

Fixed affine input placement is not counted; all nonlinear feature computation is counted. Every weight is specified below or in C002 v1 and depends only on the fixed prior feature map (through finitely many grid samples) and the displayed bounds, never on observed contexts, query labels, or future data. This is a real-weight size theorem, not a finite-bit complexity theorem or training guarantee.

## 2. Posterior perturbation caused by an approximate feature map

First suppose a map ztilde satisfies sup_x ||ztilde(x)-z(x)||<=eta<=1. Then ||ztilde||<=R+eta<=S. For any fixed admissible context and query, put

    A=sI+sum_i z_i z_i^T, b=sum_i z_i y_i, q=z(x_*),
    Atilde=sI+sum_i ztilde_i ztilde_i^T, btilde=sum_i ztilde_i y_i, qtilde=ztilde(x_*).

Both matrices are symmetric positive definite with inverse operator norm <=1/s. For vectors u,v,

    ||uu^T-vv^T||_op
      =||(u-v)u^T+v(u-v)^T||_op
      <=||u-v|| (||u||+||v||).

Thus

    ||A-Atilde||<=n(2R+eta)eta<=C_A eta,
    ||b-btilde||<=nB eta, ||b||<=nRB,
    ||A^{-1}-Atilde^{-1}||
      =||A^{-1}(Atilde-A)Atilde^{-1}||<=C_A eta/s^2.

The true and perturbed noisy predictive parameters are

    mu=q^T A^{-1}b, v=s+s q^T A^{-1}q,
    mutilde=qtilde^T Atilde^{-1}btilde,
    vtilde=s+s qtilde^T Atilde^{-1}qtilde.

Both variances are >=s. Add and subtract qtilde^T A^{-1}b and qtilde^T Atilde^{-1}b. Cauchy-Schwarz and the preceding bounds give

    |mu-mutilde|
      <=eta nRB/s + S C_A eta nRB/s^2 + S nB eta/s
      =C_m eta.

For the variance, first replace both q factors while retaining A^{-1}, and then replace the inverse. This gives

    |v-vtilde|
      <=s[eta(R+S)/s+S^2 C_A eta/s^2]=C_v eta.

The definition of eta ensures

    |mu-mutilde|<=sqrt(s eps)/2,
    |v-vtilde|<=min(s/4,s sqrt(eps)/2).

No probabilistic context distribution or independence between observed features is needed here.

## 3. A finite-grid cone encoder

Let G={0,1/m,...,1}^d, so |G|=J. For each feature coordinate define

    ztilde_j(x)=min_{a in G}[z_j(a)+K sum_{r=1}^d |x_r-a_r|].

The Lipschitz assumption shows every term in this minimum is >=z_j(x). Choose a nearest grid point coordinate by coordinate; its L1 distance is <=d/(2m). The same Lipschitz bound then gives

    0<=ztilde_j(x)-z_j(x)<=Kd/m.

Consequently ||ztilde(x)-z(x)||<=sqrt(p)Kd/m<=eta. This also holds for K=0, when the error is zero and m=1. In particular |ztilde_j(x)|<=||ztilde(x)||<=S on the whole input cube.

The encoder is exact as an implementation of this finite minimum, including all absolute values. It is not a numerical approximation to the finite minimum.

## 4. Exact tokenwise residual-MLP construction

Use the 7p+4 core registers of C002. Add d registers for raw x, Jd zero-initialized absolute-value registers, pJ zero-initialized cone registers, and two role flags. This is D=7p+6+d+Jd+pJ. Initially the feature registers z_c,z_q are zero. The core constant is one=1; the variance-output register starts at s, and the query/padding label register is zero. Encoder MLP layers preserve raw x, the flags, and all core constants.

Each MLP has the residual form h^+=h+W2 ReLU(W1 h), with a constant register implementing affine biases. All unspecified matrix entries are zero. The attention block in each encoder layer is the identity (all value matrices zero).

Layer 1 uses 2Jd hidden units for ReLU(x_r-a_r) and ReLU(a_r-x_r), for all a in G,r. Their sums are written into the initially zero absolute-value registers, yielding |x_r-a_r| exactly.

Layer 2 uses Jd identity-ReLU units on the nonnegative absolute registers and one unit on the constant one. Its output matrix writes

    F_{j,a}=z_j(a)+K sum_r |x_r-a_r|

into each initially zero cone register. Negative fixed grid values cause no difficulty: they occur in the output matrix applied to the constant unit.

Next compute the minimum independently for each coordinate j by a balanced binary tournament on the J cone registers. A pair of current registers u,v is replaced in the first slot by

    u-ReLU(u-v)=min(u,v),

leaving the other slot unused thereafter. This is one residual MLP unit: W1 reads u-v and W2 subtracts its ReLU from the u register. Distinct pairs at the same level use disjoint output slots. An unpaired register passes unchanged. After ceil(log_2 J) levels one designated cone slot contains ztilde_j(x). Each level uses at most p floor(J/2) units, bounded by pJ. This works for signed cone values and for every J, not only powers of two.

One final gating layer writes the feature registers. For any |f|<=S and binary flag r define

    g(f,r)=ReLU(f+S(r-1))-ReLU(-f+S(r-1)).

If r=1, this equals f; if r=0, both arguments are <=0 and it equals zero. Apply g to every computed feature with the context flag to populate z_c, and with the query flag to populate z_q. The registers start at zero, so the residual connection adds precisely the desired values. This uses 4p units. Query, padding, and context feature routing now matches C002 exactly. Both flags and the raw x registers are preserved throughout.

There are E=3+ceil(log_2 J) MLP encoder layers. The stated H bounds every hidden width. Biases are realized through the constant register, rather than being omitted from the construction. All grid feature values are fixed weights of the known prior; no context-dependent parameter is selected.

## 5. Solver composition and KL budget

Apply C002 v1 to ztilde with feature bound S and accuracy eps0. Its core 7p+4 registers embed in the larger width D; all additional registers are preserved by zero extension of its matrices. The solver uses its one-head broadcast layer, T five-head Chebyshev layers, and four-head readout layer. All solver MLPs are identities. The resulting parameters muhat,vhat obey

    vhat>=s,
    |mutilde-muhat|<=sqrt(s eps0)<=sqrt(s eps)/2,
    |vtilde-vhat|<=s sqrt(eps0)<=min(s/4,s sqrt(eps)/2).

Combine these with Section 2 using ordinary triangle inequalities for scalar errors, not for KL:

    |mu-muhat|<=sqrt(s eps),
    |v-vhat|<=min(s/2,s sqrt(eps)).

Since v,vhat>=s, put h=(v-vhat)/vhat in [-1/2,1/2]. As proved directly in C002 Section 5,

    KL(N(mu,v)||N(muhat,vhat))
      <=(mu-muhat)^2/(2s)+(v-vhat)^2/(2s^2)<=eps.

The depth is E+T+2. There are at most five heads, each with three D-by-D matrices. Counting two D-by-H/H-by-D MLP matrices at every layer, even when they are zero, and a two-coordinate linear readout, gives the stated dense parameter bound.

## 6. What this does and does not settle

This is a quantitative raw-input theorem for every bounded finite-rank GP feature map satisfying the displayed Lipschitz assumption, in every fixed input dimension. It counts the encoder rather than treating it as a free feature oracle. The bound is deliberately explicit and can be very large because J=(m+1)^d.

C003 shows that dropping all raw-feature regularity makes the literal bounded-kernel statement false for continuous Gaussian-output transformers. C004 therefore supplies a precise constructive assumption, while C002 remains the smaller theorem when features are supplied directly.

The finite-grid envelope and ReLU min/max identities are classical elementary constructions, not claims of new approximation theory. The claimed target contribution is their fully costed composition with the accelerated posterior solver and a uniform original-posterior forward-KL budget. C004 remains a proof candidate dependent on C002 until independent review passes both exact versions.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:38:04.490628+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9d64110588c97f543ef87ca2bf4754e5229218909260b2e282aba9ad1f7798f6","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma impr_upper_bnd of arXiv:2607.05054, 'Root Dynamics of Differentiated Polynomials with Rotationally Invariant Structure'] Let $Q$ be a polynomial of degree $n \geq 1$ with positive real roots, and let 
$(r_j)_{1 \leq j \leq n}$ be a strictly increasing sequence of positive real numbers. We assume that for $\alpha \in (0,1)$, 
$$ \max_{1 \leq j \leq n-1} (r_j/r_{j+1}) \leq \alpha$$
and we define
$$y := \frac{2 + \log_- (\log (\alpha^{-1}))}{\log (\alpha^{-1})},$$
where $\log_-$ denotes the negative part of $\log$, i.e. the maximum of $0$ and $- \log $. 
Suppose the $ j $-th smallest root of $ Q $ is at most $ r_j $ for $ 1 \leq j \leq n $. Then, for integers $m \geq 1$, $ 1 \leq q \leq m-1 $ and $ 1 \leq j \leq n $, all roots of the polynomial $S$ given by 
$$S(z) = q Q(z) + m z Q'(z)$$
are real and positive, and the $ j $-th smallest root of $S$ 
is at most  
\begin{align*}
\left(1 - \frac{\alpha}{  j+2 + 2y }\right) r_j.
\end{align*}  
For $ 2 \leq j \leq n $, the $ (j-1) $-th smallest root of $ Q' $, which has all real and positive roots, is at least  
\begin{align*}
\left(1 - \frac{\alpha}{  j+2 +2y }\right) r_j.
\end{align*}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.348330+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9d9940d5d71c04317ee6bf6c7af44330e25833e47c30d0a08c189418c3460668","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 161 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For all $1 \leq \ell\leq \ubl$ we have:
  \begin{align}
  
  \bbE[\hat U^{\ell}-\hat U^{\ell-1}
  \,|\,
  \cF^{\hat U,\tilde U}(\ell-1)]
  &=0\,,
  \\
  
  \bbE[\hat Y^{\ell}-\hat Y^{\ell-1}
  ~|~
  \cF^{\hat Y,\tilde Y,\hat{\prxY},\tilde{\prxY}}(\ell-1)]
  =
  \bbE[\hat Y^{\ell}-\hat Y^{\ell-1}
  ~|~
  \cF^{\hat U,\tilde U}(\ell-1)]
  &=
  0\,,
  \\
  
  \bbE[\hat V^{\ell}-\hat V^{\ell-1}
  ~|~
  \cF^{\hat V,\tilde V}(\ell-1)]
  &=0\,,
  \\
  
  \bbE[\hat M^{\ell}-\hat M^{\ell-1}
  ~|~
  \cF^{\hat M,\tilde M}(\ell-1)]
  =
  \bbE[\hat M^{\ell}-\hat M^{\ell-1}
  ~|~
  \cF^{\hat V,\tilde V}(\ell-1)]
  &=
  0
  \,.
  \end{align}

\begin{proof}
  We will show inductively that
  \eqref{eq:pair-u-increments-orthogonal} implies
  \eqref{eq:pair-y-increments-orthogonal}, which implies
  \eqref{eq:pair-v-increments-orthogonal}, which implies
  \eqref{eq:pair-m-increments-orthogonal}, which implies
  \eqref{eq:pair-u-increments-orthogonal} with $\ell+1$ in place of $\ell$.
We therefore proceed with the inductive argument: 

\begin{itemize}
\item \eqref{eq:pair-u-increments-orthogonal} $\Rightarrow$
  \eqref{eq:pair-y-increments-orthogonal}: 
for this we use
the recursion \eqref{e:state.evol.x.y.increments.CHAOTIC}. Note that $w^{\ell-1}(\hat{\prxY}^{\ell-1})$ is measurable with respect to the $\sigma$-field $\cF^{\hat Y,\tilde Y,\hat{\prxY},\tilde{\prxY}}(\ell-1)$, which in turn is contained in the $\sigma$-field 
$\cF^{\hat U,\tilde U}(\ell-1)$. Therefore
  \[
  \bbE[\hat Y^{\ell}-\hat Y^{\ell-1}
    ~|~
    \cF^{\hat U,\tilde U}(\ell-1)]
  = \frac{w^{\ell-1}(\hat{R}^\eta\hat{\prxY}^{\ell-1}) }
    {\hat{\gamma}(\ell,\delta,\eta)}
  \E[\hat{U}^\ell-\hat{U}^{\ell-1}
  ~|~ \cF^{\hat U,\tilde U}(\ell-1)
  ]=0\,,
  \]
where the last step is by the inductive hypothesis \eqref{eq:pair-u-increments-orthogonal}. This implies
\eqref{eq:pair-y-increments-orthogonal}.

\item \eqref{eq:pair-y-increments-orthogonal} $\Rightarrow$ \eqref{eq:pair-v-increments-orthogonal}:
it follows from the state evolution definition that the random variables $\hat{V}^{\ell,k}$ and $\tilde{V}^{\ell,k}$ are jointly gaussian. Using the covariance formula \eqref{eq:state-evolution-setup}, for $0\le k\le s \le \ell-1$ we have
  \begin{align*}
  \E[(\hat{V}^{\ell,k}-\hat{V}^{\ell-1,k})
  \tilde{V}^{s,k}]
  &\stackrel{\eqref{eq:state-evolution-setup}}{=} \E\bigg[
   \Big(h_{\chaos,\ell,k}(\hat{U}[[\ell]])-
  h_{\chaos,\ell-1,k}
  (\hat{U}[[\ell-1]])
  \Big)
    h_{\chaos,s,k}
    (\tilde{U}[[s]])
    \bigg]\\
  &\stackrel{
  \eqref{e:f.h.l.k.explicit.CHAOTIC}
  }{=} (a_k)^2
  \E[(\hat{Y}^\ell-\hat{Y}^{\ell-1})
    \tilde{Y}^s]
  = 0\,,
  \end{align*}
where the last step is by the inductive hypothesis \eqref{eq:pair-y-increments-orthogonal}. A similar calculation gives the same identity but with $\hat{V}^{s,k}$ in place of $\tilde{V}^{s,k}$. Since the $V$ are jointly gaussian, this implies \eqref{eq:pair-v-increments-orthogonal}.

\item \eqref{eq:pair-v-increments-orthogonal} $\Rightarrow$ \eqref{eq:pair-m-increments-orthogonal}: this follows from the recursion \eqref{e:state.evol.x.y.increments.CHAOTIC}, by the same reasoning as for \eqref{eq:pair-u-increments-orthogonal} $\Rightarrow$ \eqref{eq:pair-y-increments-orthogonal} above.

\item
\eqref{eq:pair-m-increments-orthogonal}
$\Rightarrow$
\eqref{eq:pair-u-increments-orthogonal}:
this follows by similar reasoning as for
\eqref{eq:pair-y-increments-orthogonal}
$\Rightarrow$
\eqref{eq:pair-v-increments-orthogonal} above.
\end{itemize}
The above steps give one complete round of the induction, and the claim follows.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:01:15.321162+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9d9ae8a1780512450e7be376ea0339c654dfea0a9a749db538cea12dc5781d95","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 15 (A sufficient deletion-chord curvature bound) of arXiv:2608.30261, 'Estimating Population-Risk Curves Along Nonconvex Gradient Flows from the Training Sample'] \label[corollary]{cor:cpp-bound}
Fix $\kappa\in[0,\infty)$.
For every $i\in[n]$, $0\leq\alpha_0\leq(n-1)^{-1}$, and
$P=P_n+\alpha_0 h_i\in\mathfrak P_S$ with $h_i\ne0$, define the
sample-dependent realized normalized deletion direction
$\widetilde h_i:=h_i/\|h_i\|_{\TV}\in\mathcal M_0$.  For every $\lambda\in\Lambda$ and
$t\in[0,T]$, suppose there is an interval containing zero on which the flows
trained under $P+\alpha\widetilde h_i$ exist, the map
$\alpha\mapsto\theta_t^{P+\alpha\widetilde h_i,\lambda}$ is twice
continuously differentiable, and the first and second $\alpha$-derivatives of
$\theta_t^{P+\alpha\widetilde h_i,\lambda}$ commute with the time derivative
and may be passed through the training and population-risk integrals.  Suppose
there are
$G_h,H_h,J_3,G_0,H_0\in[0,\infty)$, possibly depending on the realized sample
$S$, such that, uniformly over
$i\in[n]$ with $h_i\ne0$, $\alpha_0\in[0,(n-1)^{-1}]$, $\lambda\in\Lambda$, and
$t\in[0,T]$,
\[
\begin{gathered}
 \left\|\int\nabla\ell^{\rm tr}_{\lambda,z}(\theta_t^{P,\lambda})
          \,\dd\widetilde h_i(z)\right\|\leq G_h,\quad
 \left\|\int\nabla^2\ell^{\rm tr}_{\lambda,z}(\theta_t^{P,\lambda})
          \,\dd\widetilde h_i(z)\right\|_{\op}\leq H_h,\\
 \|\nabla_\theta^3F_{P,\lambda}(\theta_t^{P,\lambda})\|_{\op}\leq J_3,
 \quad \nabla^2F_{P,\lambda}(\theta_t^{P,\lambda})\succeq-\kappa I,\\
 \|P_0\nabla\ell^{\rm ev}_{\lambda,Z}(\theta_t^{P,\lambda})\|
 \leq G_0,\quad
 \|P_0\nabla^2\ell^{\rm ev}_{\lambda,Z}(\theta_t^{P,\lambda})\|_{\op}
 \leq H_0.
\end{gathered}
\]
The averaged first-order cancellation condition
\eqref{eq:average-first-order-cancellation} holds, and the curvature condition
\eqref{eq:measure-curvature-bound} holds with
\begin{equation}
 C_{PP}=H_0G_h^2\phi_\kappa(T)^2
 +G_0\{2H_hG_h\chi_\kappa(T)+J_3G_h^2\mathcal J_\kappa(T)\}.
\end{equation}
If $h_i=0$, then $P_n+\alpha_0 h_i=P_n$ for every
$0\leq\alpha_0\leq(n-1)^{-1}$.  Consequently, the scalar chord map
$\alpha_0\mapsto\psi_{i,t,\lambda}(\alpha_0)$ in
\eqref{eq:deletion-chord-functional} is constant, so
$\psi_{i,t,\lambda}''(\alpha_0)=0$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:28:31.956840+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9d9b0b9fca3fd9626f8242630d713c23a815ac23022fe8fe06de411303fb4066","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 18 of arXiv:2512.01483, 'Scaling Limits of Line Models in Degenerate Environment'] Let $(\xi(t))_{t \geq 0}$ be a one-dimensional, simple random walk with generator given by
    \begin{equation}
 
\mathcal{L} f(x) = f(x+1) - 2 f(x) + f(x-1), \qquad x \in \mathbb{Z}, 
\end{equation}
for all $f: \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{R}$. Let, for all $T>0$,
    \[\ell^{\xi,T}_t(x) := \frac{1}{\sqrt{T}} \int_0^{Tt} \mathbf{1}_{\{\xi(s) = \lfloor \sqrt{T} x \rfloor \}} \, ds, \qquad  t \geq 0, \quad x \in \mathbb{R},\]
    and let $(\tilde{\ell}^{T}_t(x))_{x \in \mathbb{R}, t \geq 0}$ be the continuous version, obtained by a linear interpolation in space
    \[\tilde{\ell}^{\xi, T}_t(x) = \left(\lceil \sqrt{T} x \rceil - \sqrt{T} x\right)\ell^{\xi,T}_t(x) + \left(\sqrt{T} x - \lfloor \sqrt{T} x \rfloor \right) \ell^{\xi, T}_t(x+1),  \qquad t \geq 0,
    \quad x \in \mathbb{R},\]
    where $\lfloor x \rfloor$ designates the integer part of $x$, and $\lceil x \rceil := \lfloor x \rfloor + 1$.
    Then, we have the joint convergences in law 
    \[ \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}} \xi(Tt) \right)_{t \geq 0} \Longrightarrow (B_t)_{t \geq 0} \qquad \hbox{in} \quad D  \]
     for the Skorohod topology and 
    \[(\tilde{\ell}^{\xi,T}_t(x))_{x \in \mathbb{R}, t \geq 0} \Longrightarrow  (L^B(t,x))_{x \in \mathbb{R}, t \geq 0} \qquad \hbox{in} \quad C([0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R}) \]
    for the topology of uniform convergence on compact sets. Here $(B_t)_{t \geq 0}$ is a Brownian motion started from $0$ with diffusion coefficient $\sqrt{2}$ and $(L^B(t,x))_{x \in \mathbb{R}, t \geq 0}$ is its family of local times.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:04:39.234179+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9d9ca9d05527293c0e35936140dd1bfc8cecee92700c485101ee18003b5b732f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 38 (A confluence-safe residue determinant in one variable) of arXiv:2608.14475, '\vspace{-1.2cm}\textbf{Finite Gaussian Reconstruction of Polynomial Orbits:\\ From Correla'] Let
\[
 g(x)=a_\mu x^\mu+a_{\mu-1}x^{\mu-1}+\cdots+a_0,
 \qquad a_\mu\neq0,
\]
and define the global residue functional on \(\C[x]/(g)\) by
\[
 \operatorname{Res}_g(f)
 =
 -\operatorname{Res}_{x=\infty}\frac{f(x)\,\mathrm d x}{g(x)}.
\]
In the basis \(1,x,\ldots,x^{\mu-1}\), the residue Gram matrix
\[
 R_g=
 \bigl(\operatorname{Res}_g(x^{i+j})\bigr)_{0\leq i,j<\mu}
\]
satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \det R_g
 =
 (-1)^{\mu(\mu-1)/2}a_\mu^{-\mu}.
 
\end{equation}
Thus this residue pairing remains nondegenerate when critical points
coalesce; it can lose rank only when the leading coefficient vanishes.

For \(P=H_3\), take
\[
 g_t(x)=x-itH_3'(x)
 =-3itx^2+x+3it.
\]
In the basis \(1,x\),
\begin{equation}
 R_{g_t}
 =
 \begin{pmatrix}
  0&i/(3t)\\
  i/(3t)&1/(9t^2)
 \end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 \det R_{g_t}=\frac1{9t^2}.
 
\end{equation}
In particular the residue pairing stays nondegenerate at the finite
confluence points \(1-36t^2=0\); its only rank boundary in this family is
\(t=0\).","status":"unverified"}

\[

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:51:26.730004+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9e422d4608cc0dee24fad17871092c60bbee41500f0d3abcf32ac100adefa6fc","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:blocks of arXiv:2606.08325, 'Digit Mixing under Polynomial Maps'] Fix integers \(d\ge2 , r\), and a positive real number $\beta>0$. 
			We define the functions
			$s :=\lfloor \beta n\rfloor+r$.
			and  $L:=\lfloor(\log n)^2\rfloor$.
			Given an integer $R$, we define the scale function
			$$H:= H(R) =\left\lfloor \frac{s}{L^R}\right\rfloor.$$
			Provided \(R=R(d)\) is chosen large enough, for
			all sufficiently large \(n\), there exist pairwise disjoint integer intervals
			\[ I_{j,k}\subset\mathbb N, \qquad 1\le j\le d,\quad 1\le k\le L,
			\]
			and an absolute constant $c_d$ (only depending on $d$)  with the following properties. \\	
			First, every \(i\in I_{j,k}\) satisfies
			\begin{equation}
				i\asymp_{\beta,d} n.

			\begin{equation}
				|\left\{(i_1,\ldots,i_d)\in I_{1,k}\times\cdots\times I_{d,k}:

				\asymp_d H^{d-1}.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-12T06:09:38.198131+00:00","domain":"general topology","id":"claim_9e45874fad796149c5ac8f2b58760157b9ee22954ae7f56d86aa7e03bdd65509","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"For a subset A of a topological space X: the interior int(A) is the union of all open sets contained in A (the largest open set inside A); the closure cl(A) is the intersection of all closed sets containing A - which is closed, being an arbitrary intersection of closed sets, contains A, and lies inside every closed superset of A, hence is the smallest closed set containing A; the boundary is cl(A) minus int(A), equivalently cl(A) intersect cl(X\\A). Then A is open iff A = int(A) and closed iff A = cl(A). Point characterization: x is in cl(A) iff every open neighborhood of x meets A (if not, X\\cl(A) is an open neighborhood of x missing A; conversely a neighborhood U of x missing A makes X\\U a closed superset of A avoiding x). The closure operator satisfies the Kuratowski axioms - cl(empty)=empty, A subset of cl(A), cl(cl(A))=cl(A), cl(A union B)=cl(A) union cl(B) - and these four axioms on a set determine a unique topology whose closed sets are exactly the closure-fixed subsets.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-05T06:00:09.358132+00:00","domain":"ensemble learning","id":"claim_9e61da057eaeb025bf9b0a1a12c2abb9dc57a71c46d36c74687a9ef959f51016","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $M$ predictors produce, on $n$ calibration cases with vector-valued targets $y_i \\in \\mathbb{R}^D$, the per-case error vectors $e_{im} \\in \\mathbb{R}^D$ (member $m$'s prediction minus $y_i$). {"assumptions":["Fixed theta in (0,pi/2]","Original Gaussian pool N/(d-1)->beta>0","Noiseless labels","Linear unit-normal output; rotation equivariant for fixed-teacher specialization","Latitude prior for the general learner bound","No teacher information beyond pool labels, q and theta","Output is a unit normal of a linear classifier"],"created_at":"2026-10-22T02:44:05.557283+00:00","domain":"statistical learning theory","id":"claim_9e6db015d647e96bcee4d5352b41eef77048683e9487556d34a1f90c8c29a454","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Own work draft, proof (unaudited), classical counting application with novelty unverified. {"assumptions":["uniform measure","g Boolean (+-1) or f Boolean (0/1)"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T08:56:10.274379+00:00","domain":"analysis of Boolean functions","id":"claim_9e81508c49e2ccdd2e2ecdb8ada748163b44b2755a35246deadeafd619e23393","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let g: {-1, 1}^n -> {-1, 1}. Then Var(g) = I(g) if and only if g is constant or g = +-x_i for some i. Equivalently, for f: {0, 1}^n -> {0, 1} with flip influence I_flip(f) = sum_i P(f(X) != f(X with bit i flipped)) under the uniform measure, I_flip(f) = 4 Var(f) if and only if f is constant or f is the indicator of a half-cube {x_i = 0} or {x_i = 1}. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:09:15.288976+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9e879b789abe8bbeec6add85bb74e471fe94f7dcca6740d489076dd7598496eb","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem verif of arXiv:2411.04802, 'Dynkin ghost games with asymmetry and consolation'] Let two continuous functions $u_1,u_2:\mathcal I\times[0,1]^2\to[0,\infty)$ and a pair $(\Gamma^1,\Gamma^2)\in\mathcal A^2$ be given. 
Assume that $u_i\leq V^{g_i}$, and that $\Gamma^i_{\tau_{g_i}}=1$, $i=1,2$. Define on $[0,\infty)$ two processes
		\[M^1_t:=
			e^{-rt}(1-p_{1}\Gamma^{2}_{t})u_1(X_{t},\Pi^{1}_{t}, \Pi^2_{t}) + p_{1}\int_{[0,t]} e^{-rs}V^{h_1}(X_s)\,d\Gamma^{2}_s\]
   and 
   	\[M^2_t:=
			e^{-rt}(1-p_{2}\Gamma^{1}_{t-})u_2(X_{t},\Pi^{1}_{t-}, \Pi^2_{t-}) + p_{2}\int_{[0,t)} e^{-rs}V^{h_2}(X_s)\,d\Gamma^{1}_s,\]
and assume that 
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)]
$M^i$ is a supermartingale, and it is a martingale 
on $[0,\gamma_i(u)]$ for any $u<1$, $i=1,2$;
\item[(i')] 
$M^2$ is continuous on $[0,\tau_{g_2}]$ and on $(\tau_{g_2},\infty)$, with 
$M^2_{\tau_{g_2}+}-M^2_{\tau_{g_2}}\leq 0$;
\item[(ii)]
$u_1(X_t,\Pi^1_{t},\Pi^2_{t})\geq g_1(X_t)$ and $u_2(X_t,\Pi^1_{t-},\Pi^2_{t-})\geq g_2(X_t)$ for all $t\geq 0$ $\mathbb P_x$-a.s.;
\item[(iii)]
$\Gamma^1_t=\int_{[0,t]} 1_{\{u_1(X_s,\Pi^1_{s},\Pi^2_{s})=g_1(X_s)\}}\,d\Gamma^1_s$ and $\Gamma^2_t=\int_{[0,t]} 1_{\{u_2(X_s,\Pi^1_{s-},\Pi^2_{s-})=g_2(X_s)\}}\,d\Gamma^2_s$.
\end{itemize}
Then $(\Gamma^1,\Gamma^2)$ is a Nash equilibrium, 
and the equilibrium values are given by 
\[M^1_0=(1-p_1\Gamma_0^2)u_1(x,\Pi^1_0,\Pi_0^2) + p_1\Gamma^2_0 V^{h_1}(x)\]
and $M^2_0=u_2(x,p_1,p_2)$, respectively.","status":"unverified"}

where, as before, $\Delta$ denotes the diameter of $(T,d)$. If $X$ is a Gaussian process, 
then there exists a probability measure $\mu\in \eP(T)$, such that 
\begin{align*}
\eF_\beta(X;\mu_\beta^*) + \Delta
&\gtrsim \sup_{t\in T}\int_0^\Delta 
 \Big(\sM_{\delta_t}(\mu,\epsilon)\wedge \beta \epsilon\Big) \dif \epsilon
\end{align*}
In particular,
\begin{align*}
\Ex X_{\uptau_\beta^*}+ \Delta \gtrsim 
\sup_{\nu\in\eP(T)}\int_0^\Delta 
\Big(\sM_\nu^*(\epsilon)\wedge

\end{align*}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:30:28.826168+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9e921c133639f91577ad1e61903f1b2c770594171ef59a29710ffce4f1dafedf","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 5 of arXiv:2609.02105, 'Contact fundamental forms and \\ adjoint varieties'] Let $\fh = \fh_1 + \fh_2$ be a graded Heisenberg algebra.  Let $U(\fh) = \oplus_{k \geq 0} U_k(\fh)$ be its  universal enveloping algebra with the grading induced by the grading of $\fh$ and let $U(\fh)^* = \oplus_{k \geq 0} U_k(\fh)^*$ be its graded dual.
We can identify $U(\fh)^*$ with the space of polynomial functions on the Heisenberg group $\sH$ of $\fh$ by regarding $U(\fh)$ as the space of left-invariant differential operators on $\sH$ (see Remark \ref{r.jet}). Let $\iota:\fh_2\hookrightarrow U_2(\fh)$ be the natural inclusion and let $\rho_2:=\iota^*:U_2(\fh)^*\to\fh_2^*$ be the restriction map.  
 A finite-dimensional graded subspace $$S = \oplus_{k \geq 0} S^k \subset U(\fh)^*, S^k \subset U_k(\fh)^*,$$ is called a {\em contact symbol system} on $\fh$,
if $S^0 = \C, S^1 = \fh_1^*$, $\rho_2(S^2)=\fh_2^*$, and $S$ is preserved under the operation of right-invariant vector fields on $\sH$.  The {\em rank} of a contact symbol system $S$ is ${\rm rk}(S):=\max\{k\mid S^k\ne0\}.$","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.164817+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9e9fc1f22fbbd6aed0546c786bb0cc9eb865e002d311d3614d9fe68ef5df37cd","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 36 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] The following functions are $C_6$-Lipschitz, with $C_6 = 2/\iota$:
    \begin{enumerate}[(a)]
        \item  $z \mapsto m^{-1}(1/z)$, on $(0,+\infty)$.
        \item  $\gamma \mapsto g(\gamma^2)$, on $[0,+\infty)$.
        \item  $\gamma \mapsto \beta_\star(\gamma^2)$, on $[0,+\infty)$.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{proof}
    A routine calculation and application of Lemma~\ref{l:fp-m-fns-conversion} implies
    \[
        \frac{d}{dz} m^{-1}(1/z) = \frac{1/z^2}{m_2(m^{-1}(1/z))}
        \le \frac{1/z^2}{\iota / z^2} = \frac{1}{\iota}\,.
    \]
    This proves part~\eqref{i:fp-m-inv-lipschitz}.
    Since $m$ is strictly decreasing, and $\beta_\star \ge \beta_{
    \min}$, we also have, for $\gamma > 0$,
    \[
        \frac{d}{d\gamma} g(\gamma^2) 
        = 2\gamma m(\beta_\star(\gamma^2))
        \le 2\gamma m(\beta_{\min}(\gamma^2))
        = 2\gamma m(s_2(1/\gamma^2))
        \le \frac{2}{\iota^{1/2}}\,,
    \]
where the final inequality is by Lemma~\ref{l:fp-m-fns-conversion}.
This shows that $\gamma \mapsto g(\gamma^2)$ is $2/\iota^{1/2}$-Lipschitz on $(0,+\infty)$, and the estimate extends to $[0,+\infty)$ since $g$ was defined to be continuous on $[0,\infty)$ (see the comments below \eqref{e:freeprob.g.of.gamma}). 
    This proves part~\eqref{i:fp-g-sq-lipschitz}. For part~\eqref{i:fp-betast-sq-lipschitz}, it suffices to prove that the function
    \[
        \gamma \mapsto \beta_{\min}(\gamma^2)
        = s_2\bigg(\frac1{\gamma^2}\bigg)
    \]
    is $O(1)$-Lipschitz on $[0,+\infty)$. Similarly as above, a routine calculation and application of Lemma~\ref{l:fp-m-fns-conversion} shows that at any $\gamma > 0$, 
    \[
        \frac{d}{d\gamma} 
        s_2\bigg(\frac1{\gamma^2}\bigg)
        = \frac{1/\gamma^3}
            {m_3(s_2(1/\gamma^2))}
        \le \frac{1/\gamma^3}{\iota / \gamma^3}
        = \frac{1}{\iota}\,.
    \]
This shows that $\gamma \mapsto \beta_{\min}(\gamma^2)$ is $1/\iota$-Lipschitz on $(0,+\infty)$, and the estimate extends to $[0,+\infty)$ since the function $\beta_{\min}$ was defined to be continuous on $[0,\infty)$ (again we refer to the comments below \eqref{e:freeprob.g.of.gamma}). 
This proves part~\eqref{i:fp-betast-sq-lipschitz}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Omega open in R^n","A measurable and uniformly elliptic; b, c in L^infinity(Omega)","u in H^1_loc(Omega)","f in L^2_loc(Omega), or more generally in H^{-1}"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:46.146784+00:00","domain":"elliptic partial differential equations","id":"claim_9ea2ee1ebfc2341ed6666c0de202fa3fcddc26d6ef74a9f9346e7802ea76d630","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Omega in R^n be open, L = -div(A grad u) + b.grad u + c u uniformly elliptic with A measurable and b, c in L^infinity(Omega), and f in L^2_loc(Omega). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:18:54.371335+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9edab7a4b69da7064491fee98243307eeedc86c96af59570444be65b938df1b2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Any Hilbert space $H$ has an orthonormal basis $\{e_i\}_{i\in I}$, which is by definition a set of vectors whose span is dense in $H$, and which satisfy
$$<e_i,e_j>=\delta_{ij}$$
with $\delta$ being a Kronecker symbol. The cardinality $|I|$ of the index set, which can be finite, countable, or uncountable, depends only on $H$, and is called dimension of $H$. We have
$$H\simeq l^2(I)$$
in the obvious way, mapping $\sum\lambda_ie_i\to(\lambda_i)$. The Hilbert spaces with $\dim H=|I|$ being countable, such as $l^2(\mathbb N)$, are all isomorphic, and are called separable.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T00:52:17.596335+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9eebc4177620ac3121a2065128933e4a2935e831646282d3ac79bcd84d8f1395","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm lower final of arXiv:2411.15724, 'Wasserstein Convergence Rates for Empirical Measures of Random Subsequence of $\{nα\}$'] Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots$ be integer-valued i.i.d. random variables with characteristic function $\varphi$, and let $S_j = \sum_{i = 1}^{j} X_i$. Let $\alpha$ be an irrational number such that
$$\| q \alpha \| \leq C q^{-\gamma}$$
holds for infinitely many $q \in \mathbb N$ with some constants $\gamma \ge 1$ and $C > 0$. Suppose that
$$|1 - \varphi(x)| \leq c |x|^\beta $$
holds for any $x \in \mathbb R$ with constants $c > 0$ and $0 < \beta \leq 2$. Set $\mu_n = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{j = 1}^{n} \delta_{\{ S_j \alpha \}}$, $n \geq 1$. Then there exists $C' > 0$ such that
$$
\mathbb E \big[ \mathbb W_1(\mu_n, \mu) \big] \geq \frac{C'}{n^{1/(\beta \gamma)}}
$$
holds for infinitely many $n \in \mathbb N$. In other words,
$$
\limsup_{n \rightarrow \infty} n^{1/(\beta \gamma)} \mathbb E \big[ \mathbb W_1(\mu_n, \mu) \big] > 0.
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

  \end{align}

    any finite subset of polymers converges absolutely. Moreover, for
  all $\gamma \in \mathcal P$ we have
  \begin{equation}
    
    \sum_{\substack{X \in \mathcal X :\\ \exists \gamma' \in X, \gamma' \nsim

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:02:17.985539+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9f1c64c712eae10a20f6b2e05f07c1cff9f14a011e6a4e76aa8bf2e7b57643c0","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:two-stream of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] Fix $\lambda \in (0,1)$,
a \emph{send sequence}  
$\overline{p}$ with $p_0=1$, and a non-negative integer~$\tau$.
A \emph{two-stream process} 
with birth rate~$\lambda$, send sequence~$\overline{p}$ and start time~$\tau$ 
is a pair $Z=(Z^A,Z^B)$ of generalised backoff processes with 
send sequence~$\overline{p}$, start time~$\tau$, 
birth distribution
 $\mathcal{D} =  \mathsf{Po}(\lambda/2)$
and some initial populations $\overline{\mathbf{arr}}^{Z^A}(\tau)$ and $\overline{\mathbf{arr}}^{Z^B}(\tau)$. 
We refer to $Z^A$ and $Z^B$ as the \emph{streams} of~$Z$. 
The streams
evolve independently  
except 
that $\mathbf{e}_j^{Z^A}(t)$ and $\mathbf{e}_j^{Z^B}(t)$ are defined as follows for $t> \tau$. 
\begin{itemize}
    \item  
If there are distinct $C$ and $D$ in $\{A,B\}$ such that
$s^{Z^C}(t) = 0$ and $s^{Z^{D}}(t)>0$ then for all $j$, $\mathbf{e}_j^{Z^C}(t)=\emptyset$. In this case, a bin~$J^D$ is chosen with probability proportional to $s^{Z^{D}}_{J^D}(t)/s^{Z^{D}}(t)$ and $\mathbf{e}_{J^D}^{Z^D}(t)$
contains a single uniformly-chosen ball from 
$\mathbf{s}^{Z^D}_{J^D}$.
Also, 
for all $j\neq J^D$, $\mathbf{e}_j^{Z^D}(t)=\emptyset$. 
\item Otherwise, for   all $j$, $\mathbf{e}_j^{Z^A}(t)= \mathbf{e}_j^{Z^B}(t)=\emptyset$.
\end{itemize}
There are no end-of-step arrivals after step~$\tau$. That is, for all $D\in \{A,B\}$, all $t> \tau$, and all positive integers~$j$, $\mathbf{arr}_j^{Z^D} = \emptyset$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:38:37.404623+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9f2d587caff488ee4b6cbc40da3bc5a5222c2231869c7d00bbf014685b39182a","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 17 of arXiv:2605.15501, 'Well-posedness of the obstacle problem for generalized Dean--Kawasaki equation\thanks{ The'] (Existence of solutions to the approximated penalized equation)
Let Assumption \ref{assu:assu for existence} and Assumption \ref{assu:assum for F} hold.
For $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\alpha,\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, there exists a solution $u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}$ of \eqref{eq:appro penalized eq}, defined on the original probability space $\Omega$, in the sense of Definition \ref{def:Weak solution approximating penalized}.
Furthermore, let $\chi_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}(x,\xi,t):=\mathbf{1}_{\{0<\xi<u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}(x,t)\}}$ be the kinetic function of $u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}$.
Then, $u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}$ satisfies that, almost surely for every $\phi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{d}\times(0,\infty)\times[0,T))$,
\begin{align}
& -\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\chi_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}(x,\xi,s)\partial_s\phi(x,\xi,s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}\xi\mathrm{d}s\\
 & =\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\bar{\chi}(u_{\mathrm{init}},\xi)\phi(x,\xi,0)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}\xi-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\Phi^{\prime}(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})\nabla_x u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}\cdot(\nabla_x\phi)(x,u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon},s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber \\
  & \quad-\alpha\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\nabla_{x}u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}\cdot(\nabla_{x}\phi)(x,u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon},s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber\\
 & \quad-\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\big(F_{1}(x)[\sigma_n^{\prime}(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})]^{2}\nabla_x u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}+\sigma_n(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})\sigma_n^{\prime}(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})F_{2}(x)\big)\cdot(\nabla_x\phi)(x,u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon},s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber\\
 & \quad-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\partial_{\xi}\phi(x,\xi,s)\mathrm{d}m_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}(x,\xi,s)-\int_0^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\phi(x,u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon},s)\nabla_x\cdot g(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber \\
 & \quad+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\Big(\sigma_n(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})\sigma_n^{\prime}(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})\nabla_x u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}\cdot F_{2}(x)+\sigma_n^{2}(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})F_{3}(x)\Big)(\partial_{\xi}\phi)(x,u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon},s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber \\
 & \quad-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\phi(x,u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon},s)\frac{1}{\varepsilon}(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}-\psi)^+\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\phi(x,u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon},s)\nabla_x\cdot(\sigma_n(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})f_{k})\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}B_{s}^{k},\nonumber
\end{align}
where the kinetic measure $m_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}$ is
\begin{align}\notag
m_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}&:=\delta_{0}(\xi-u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})\Big(\Phi^{\prime}(\xi)|\nabla u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}|^{2}+\alpha|\nabla u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}|^{2}\Big).
\end{align}
It follows from  (\ref{eq:priori}) that the $\{m_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}\}_{(\alpha,n)\in(0,1)\times\mathbb{N}}$ are finite kinetic measures.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:35:57.303096+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9f590952359f5d25106964bae057c1e4fa8f95fdb7e4b3fdbe79e26b70ae1fda","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn def: DP of arXiv:2604.10446, 'Least singular values of shifted sparse random combinatorial matrices'] Let $n, m\geq 1$ and

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:47.651277+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9f5a771b1ffe3a4acbf98295922ef93fd51f56c64993cc38d5117c6b2577103d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 2 of arXiv:2605.07050, 'Universality of the fluctuations of the free energy in generalized Sherrington--Kirkpatric'] Suppose that Assumption \ref{assump:decay} holds for $W$. Suppose that $\sqrt{N} x_k$  $(1 \leq k \leq N)$ are i.i.d., symmetric, and strictly sub-Gaussian random variables with variance $1$, independent of $W$. Define the likelihood ratios by
\beq
	 \caL(\SNR) := \E_\caX \left[ \prod_{i<j} \frac{p(\sqrt{N} W_{ij} - \sqrt{\SNR N} x_i x_j /\| \bsx \|^2)}{p(\sqrt{N} W_{ij})} \prod_k \frac{p_d(\sqrt{N} W_{kk} - \sqrt{\SNR N} x_k^2  /\| \bsx \|^2)}{p_d(\sqrt{N} W_{kk})} \right]
\eeq
and
\beq
	\ol \caL (\SNR) := \E_\caX \left[ \prod_{i<j} \frac{p(\sqrt{N} W_{ij} - \sqrt{\SNR N} x_i x_j)}{p(\sqrt{N} W_{ij})} \prod_k \frac{p_d(\sqrt{N} W_{kk} - \sqrt{\SNR N} x_k^2)}{p_d(\sqrt{N} W_{kk})} \right].
\eeq
Define
\[
	F_p:= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{(p'(x))^2}{p(x)} \dd x, \quad F_d:= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{(p_d'(x))^2}{p_d(x)} \dd x, \quad G_p:= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{(p''(x))^2}{p(x)} \dd x.
\]
Then, for any $\SNR \in (0, 1/F_p)$,
\[
	\log \caL(\SNR) \Rightarrow \caN(-\rho_L, 2\rho_L), \quad \log \ol \caL(\SNR) \Rightarrow \caN(-\rho_L, 2\rho_L),
\]
as $N \to \infty$, i.e., $\log \caL(\SNR)$ and $\log \ol\caL(\SNR)$ converge in distribution to the Gaussian with mean $-\rho_L$ and the variance $2\rho_L$ as $N \to \infty$, where
\[
	\rho_L:= -\frac{1}{4} \left( \log (1-\SNR F_p) + \SNR(F_p- 2F_d) + \frac{\SNR^2}{4} (2F_p^2 - G_p) \right).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

\]
where $H(\alpha) = -\alpha \log_2 \alpha - (1-\alpha) \log_2 (1-\alpha)$ is the binary entropy function and some constants $C,c \geq 0$ independent from $\kappa, \zeta$ and $d$.

In the special case $d=1$, we have
\[

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:45:38.343650+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9fae422480548998f819fa444ad8fe4df075c9584a72529655a646137cd0b828","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 5 of arXiv:2604.20617, 'Structured random perturbations of \\ tridiagonal twisted Toeplitz matrices'] Let $R_k^{(j)}$ be the $j$-th principal block of $R_n(a)$. Then, for a.e. $z \in \C$ and any $\varepsilon>0$,
\[
\prob \left( \bigl| \log |\det(R_k^{(j)} - zI)| - k \gamma(jk/n,z) \bigr|  \geq k \varepsilon \right) = o(1).
\]
\begin{proof}
Let us fix $z \in K$ and $j \in \N$, with $1 \leq j \leq n/k$. Denote by $\alpha_r^{(n)}$, $\beta_r^{(n)}$, and $\zeta_r^{(n)}$ the entries of $X_n$ on the lower, main, and upper diagonals, respectively. In light of Theorem \ref{thm:approx}, it is enough to prove that
\begin{multline*}
\varepsilon_k=\max_{1\le r \le k} \bigg(
\left| d\left( \frac{(j-1)k+r}{n} \right) + \sigma_n \alpha_r^{(n)} - d\left( \frac{jk}{n} \right) \right|
+\left| b\left( \frac{(j-1)k+r}{n} \right) + \sigma_n \beta_r^{(n)} - b\left( \frac{jk}{n} \right) \right| \\
+\left| c\left( \frac{(j-1)k+r}{n} \right) + \sigma_n \zeta_r^{(n)} - c\left( \frac{jk}{n} \right) \right|
\bigg) \longrightarrow 0
\end{multline*}
in probability.

By the triangle inequality,
\[
\left| b\left( \frac{(j-1)k+r}{n} \right) + \sigma_n \beta_r^{(n)} - b\left( \frac{jk}{n} \right) \right|
\le
\left| b\left( \frac{(j-1)k+r}{n} \right) - b\left( \frac{jk}{n} \right) \right|
+ \sigma_n |\beta_r^{(n)}|.
\]
Since $b$ is uniformly continuous on $[0,1]$, its modulus of continuity
\[
\omega_b(\delta):=\sup_{|x-y|\le\delta}|b(x)-b(y)|
\]
satisfies $\omega_b(\delta)\to0$ as $\delta\to0$. Hence, uniformly in $j$ and $1\le r\le k$,
\[
\left| b\left( \frac{(j-1)k+r}{n} \right) - b\left( \frac{jk}{n} \right) \right|
\le \omega_b\!\left(\frac{k}{n}\right)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}0.
\]

For the random term, Chebyshev's inequality gives, for every $\epsilon>0$,
\[
\prob\!\left(\sigma_n |\beta_r^{(n)}|\ge \epsilon\right)
\le \frac{\sigma_n^2 \operatorname{Var}(\beta_r^{(n)})}{\epsilon^2}
\le \frac{C\sigma_n^2}{\epsilon^2},
\]
where $C>0$ is independent of $r$ and $n$. Therefore, by the union bound,
\[
\prob\!\left(\max_{1\le r\le k}\sigma_n |\beta_r^{(n)}|\ge \epsilon\right)
\le \sum_{r=1}^k \prob\!\left(\sigma_n |\beta_r^{(n)}|\ge \epsilon\right)
\le \frac{Ck\sigma_n^2}{\epsilon^2}.
\]
Since $k\sigma_n^2\to0$, it follows that
\[
\max_{1\le r\le k}\sigma_n |\beta_r^{(n)}| \longrightarrow 0
\qquad\text{in probability.}
\]

Applying the same argument to the lower and upper diagonals, we conclude that $\varepsilon_k\to0$ in probability. The claim now follows from Theorem \ref{thm:approx}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:18:54.265445+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9fb3d7c7e3380b87aa0aacb38e6551cc9cba0f9aac1a9ed10b9655e3774cd5cd","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] A variable $f:X\to\mathbb R$ follows the exponential law of parameter $\lambda>0$ precisely when the following happens, for any measurable function $\phi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$:

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:42:55.342419+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9fbd7d9be9908aedf937e9455b4532f61cc4bf1e15963c5e6f0d01ba8ebb5f39","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 33 of arXiv:2609.02416, '2609.02416'] For later perturbation arguments we also record the adjoint critical limit and the resulting first-variation limit.

\textup{(i)} Let $\phi_\sigma^*>0$ be the positive adjoint eigenfunction of $\cA_{\sigma,2,L}$. Normalize it by $\|\phi_\sigma^*\|_{L^2(-L,L)}=1$. Then
\[
\phi_\sigma^*\longrightarrow\phi_0^*\quad \hbox{strongly in }L^2(-L,L),
\]
where $\phi_0^*>0$ is the normalized Dirichlet principal eigenfunction of
\[
d_Jv''-(qv)'+av+\lambda_0v=0\quad \hbox{in }(-L,L),\qquad v(-L)=v(L)=0.
\]
The zero-extension energies satisfy
\[
E_\sigma(\phi_\sigma^*)\longrightarrow d_J\int_{-L}^{L}|(\phi_0^*)'|^2\,dx,
\]
and $\phi_\sigma^*(L)\to0$.

\textup{(ii)} Let $h\in C([-L,L])$ and, for $|\tau|$ small, replace $a$ by $a+\tau h$. Denote the corresponding principal eigenvalue by $\lambda_\sigma(\tau)$. Then
\[
\partial_\tau\lambda_\sigma(0)=-\frac{\int_{-L}^{L}h(x)\phi_\sigma(x)\phi_\sigma^*(x)\,dx}{\int_{-L}^{L}\phi_\sigma(x)\phi_\sigma^*(x)\,dx}.
\]
After normalizing the direct and adjoint eigenfunctions in $L^2$,
\[
\partial_\tau\lambda_\sigma(0)\longrightarrow-\frac{\int_{-L}^{L}h(x)\phi_0(x)\phi_0^*(x)\,dx}{\int_{-L}^{L}\phi_0(x)\phi_0^*(x)\,dx}.
\]
The right-hand side is the first variation of the local Dirichlet principal eigenvalue.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:42:16.246834+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9ff5276764c10b875ca3fcef2c066361f40ab3eda94506de199d6274f55670d1","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:P_j of arXiv:2607.01946, 'Second-order fluctuations for a phase transition in random partitions'] Let $(P_j^\downarrow)_{j\in{\mathbb N}}$ follow the Poisson--Dirichlet distribution with parameter $(\alpha,\theta)$, and $S_\alpha$ be as in (equation eq:S_alpha 2 of the paper). Set
\begin{equation}
\Gamma_j:=\frac{S_{\alpha}}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)}\pp{P_j^\downarrow}^{-\alpha}, j\in{\mathbb N}.
\end{equation}
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item When $\theta=0$, the sequence $(\Gamma_j)_{j\in{\mathbb N}}$ has the law of consecutive arrival times of a standard Poisson process.
\item More generally for all $\theta>-\alpha$, 
the law of $(P_j^{\alpha,\theta,\downarrow})_{j\in{\mathbb N}}$ is absolutely continuous with respect to the law of $(P_j^{\alpha,0,\downarrow})_{j\in{\mathbb N}}$. 
More precisely, for every continuous and bounded function $f:\Delta_\infty\to{\mathbb R}$, we have 
\[
{\mathbb E} f\pp{(P_j^{\alpha,\theta,\downarrow})_{j\in{\mathbb N}}} = {\mathbb E} \pp{\frac{\Gamma(\theta+1)}{\Gamma(\theta/\alpha+1)}S_\alpha^{\theta/\alpha}f\pp{(P_j^{\alpha,0,\downarrow})_{j\in{\mathbb N}}}},
\]
where $S_\alpha$ on the right-hand side is defined via (equation eq:S_alpha 2 of the paper) using $P_j^\downarrow\equiv P_j^{\alpha,0,\downarrow}$. 

\end{enumerate}
In particular,  by (equation eq:S_alpha 2 of the paper) and (equation eq:Gamma_j of the paper), for all $\alpha\in(0,1)$ and $\theta>-\alpha$, as $j\to\infty$
\[
P_j^\downarrow =  \pp{\frac{S_{\alpha}}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)}}^{1/\alpha} \Gamma_j^{-1/\alpha}    \sim \pp{\frac{S_{\alpha}}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)}}^{1/\alpha} j^{-1/\alpha}, \mbox{ almost surely.}
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["All paired four-point model definitions and restrictions of C010","Noise-to-signal Walsh variance ratio rho>0 fixed as e decreases; actual noise standard deviation tends to zero","Width tends to infinity before feature scale decreases; nonlinear comparison is only through finite T_e for each fixed e","Clean risk averages over all sixteen training-label-noise sign patterns"],"created_at":"2026-10-22T00:34:45.041953+00:00","domain":"learning theory","id":"claim_9ffa636677134a5540e6a704a86f6f5fe37015b52ad2241f167a16f3bc581359","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"# Co-scaled noise phases: double descent versus preference for late stopping

T267 / Target 2 / C011 / proof draft (unaudited); novelty unestablished.
This is an asymptotic phase comparison in C010's restricted model, not
an exact finite-scale two-critical-noise-level theorem.

## 1. Model and statement

Keep the four-point design, unit-norm centered-ReLU teacher, paired
nonzero initialization and both-layer GD of BOUNDED_RELU_PAIRED.md.
Write alpha=alpha_e and replace label noise +/-2alpha by
+/-2alpha sqrt(rho), for any fixed rho>0. Thus the noise standard deviation
is c_e sqrt(rho), which tends to zero. Each Walsh noise variance is
rho alpha^2. Average clean risk over the sixteen noise patterns as before.
All width limits are over even widths m=2N, before e decreases to zero.

Let b_h be the full-kernel rates of C009, q_h=exp(-b_h), and define

K_e=ceil(e^(-3/2)), T_e=ceil(e^(-5/2)),
E(rho)=rho+2+rho/(1+rho),
L(rho)=2rho+2rho/(1+rho).

For small e, K_e<T_e. The following minima of the ACTUAL nonlinear risk
converge in probability in the iterated width-then-scale sense:

min_(0<=k<=K_e) Q_(m,e)(k)/alpha^2 -> min{3,E(rho)},
min_(K_e<=k<=T_e) Q_(m,e)(k)/alpha^2 -> L(rho),
min_(0<=k<=T_e) Q_(m,e)(k)/alpha^2 -> min{3,L(rho)}.

Here convergence means for every epsilon>0, lim_(e->0) limsup_(N->infinity)
P(absolute discrepancy>epsilon)=0. These statements do not control actual
nonlinear risk after T_e or exchange the two limits.

Moreover there are strict descent-rise-descent witnesses at every fixed
rho>0. With k0=ceil(e^(-1/2)),
k1=floor(log(1+1/rho)/b1), k2=K_e,
k3=floor(log(1+1/rho)/b2), their risks divided by alpha^2 converge to

rho+3, E(rho), 2rho+2, L(rho).

Their three limiting strict margins are
1/(1+rho), rho^2/(1+rho), 2/(1+rho).
For all fixed rho<1, the best risk in the late phase is strictly lower
than the best in the early phase with probability tending to one.
For all fixed rho>1, the early phase is strictly better. At rho=1 the
leading phase minima tie at 3; no finite-e ordering is asserted.

Thus rho=1 is the limiting late-versus-early preference boundary in this
model, whereas strict double descent survives on both sides. No lower
critical-noise rate or exact finite-e second threshold is established.

## 2. Exact frozen risk and nonlinear transfer

The frozen zero-output curve is

F_e(k)=Q_e^0(k)/alpha^2
      =rho(1-q0^k)^2
       +sum_(h=1,2,12)[q_h^(2k)+rho(1-q_h^k)^2].

This follows from Walsh Parseval, identical teacher coefficients alpha
and Walsh noise variances rho alpha^2. The paired initialization gives
zero output exactly. Let p_r(q)=q^2+rho(1-q)^2. Completing the square,

p_r(q)=(1+rho)(q-rho/(1+rho))^2+rho/(1+rho).

For each fixed e and rho the labels are bounded; indeed max|y_i| is at
most (3+2sqrt(rho))alpha, which tends to zero. For all sufficiently small
e the residual bound R_0=2 used in C010 is therefore valid. Its pairwise
finite-horizon transfer applies uniformly through T_e (a finite integer
for this fixed e), and over all noise patterns. It follows that

max_(k<=T_e)|Q_(m,e)(k)/alpha^2-F_e(k)| ->0 in probability as N->infinity.

For this step alpha^2 is a FIXED positive number; no uniform-in-e width
bound is inferred. Consequently it suffices to prove the deterministic
frozen limits for the two ranges and the four witnesses.

## 3. Early-phase minimum

At k=0, F_e=3 exactly. At
k1=floor(log(1+1/rho)/b1), the constant mode has learned, q1^k1 tends to
rho/(1+rho), and q2^k1,q12^k1 tend to one. Hence F_e(k1)->E(rho).
These give the upper bound min{3,E(rho)} for the limiting early minimum.

For the lower bound, take any sequence e->0 and early-phase integers
k_e<=K_e. Choose a subsequence such that k_e is bounded or tends to
infinity, and such that b1 k_e converges in [0,infinity].
If k_e is bounded, all nonconstant q_h^k_e tend to one, so liminf F_e>=3.
If k_e tends to infinity, q0^k_e tends to zero. Uniformly for k<=K_e,
b2 k and b12 k tend to zero, since b2 K_e=O(e^(1/2)). Thus the slow-mode
contribution tends to two, while the fast-mode contribution is at least
rho/(1+rho) by the exact completed square. The limit inferior is at least
E(rho), whether the fast scaled time is finite or infinite. This proves
the matching early lower bound. The subsequence argument applies to
minimizers, which exist because the integer range is finite.

## 4. Late-phase minimum

Uniformly for k>=K_e, q0^k and q1^k tend to zero, since b1 K_e tends to
infinity. Their combined risk tends to 2rho, uniformly in this range.
Each of the two slow contributions is bounded below by rho/(1+rho),
so the late minimum has limit inferior at least L(rho).
For k3=floor(log(1+1/rho)/b2), both slow q's tend to rho/(1+rho), because
b12/b2->1. Also K_e<k3<T_e for all small e, since b2 K_e->0 and
b2 T_e->infinity. Thus F_e(k3)->L(rho), proving the matching upper bound.
Combining Sections 3-4 gives the full finite-horizon minimum as
min{3,E(rho),L(rho)}. The simplification in Section 6 proves the stated
min{3,L(rho)} form.

## 5. Strict double-descent witnesses

At k0 all nonconstant modes remain at one and the constant noise mode
has saturated, so F_e(k0)->rho+3. At k1 the limit is E(rho).
At K_e fast q1 tends to zero and the slow q's to one, giving 2rho+2.
At k3 the limit is L(rho). Subtraction gives exactly the three positive
margins in Section 1. This applies to every fixed rho>0, including rho>1.
The strict finite-e margins transfer to nonlinear GD by Section 2.

For rho=0 the frozen curve is sum_(h=1,2,12)q_h^(2k), strictly decreasing.
This zero-noise frozen statement does not imply monotonic actual nonlinear
risk for all times, nor locate a finite-e onset as rho_e tends to zero.
Pointwise positive-rho results must not be promoted to such a uniform
noise-window theorem.

## 6. Which phase wins?

Exact subtraction yields

E(rho)-L(rho)=(2-rho^2)/(1+rho),
L(rho)-3=(rho-1)(2rho+3)/(1+rho).

If 0<rho<1, then L<3 and L<E, so late training beats the entire early
phase, not just its fast-mode stationary point. If rho>1, then L>3,
so the early phase containing k=0 beats the late phase. Also E>3 for
rho>1, since E-3=(rho^2+rho-1)/(1+rho)>0. Consequently the overall
minimum is min{3,L}. At rho=1 the leading early and late values both
are 3, so a finer expansion is needed to decide finite-scale ordering.

Comparing ONLY E and L would instead produce sqrt(2). That would be the
wrong early-stopping boundary because it omits the allowed initialization
time k=0. This is why the early-phase minimization includes every time
from zero rather than only the first fast-signal minimum. The tiny initial
transient may shift the finite-e preference threshold; it does not change
these strict comparisons for rho bounded away from one.

## Scope and source distinction

Stephenson--Lee, arXiv:2108.12006, Section4, EDD-NES/EDD-ES phases and
P3/P4, distinguish onset of double descent from the higher noise level
where early stopping is preferable. This source does not supply this
model's threshold. Our computation is self-contained and restricted to
the paired four-point model. The lower onset at finite scale, its rate,
a full two-threshold window, iid Gaussian inputs, fixed-positive-noise
unit-teacher dynamics, high probability over label noise, and actual
nonlinear convergence after T_e remain open. Mathematical and novelty
review are pending; no independent audit or full Target2 solution.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:51:11.481789+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9ffaf82fc3ee8484462ec0f4b23141b14e93c763064333c37a470c703675f4c6","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 52 of arXiv:2609.02561, 'NON-NEF LOCI IN MIXED CHARACTERISTIC'] Let $(R,\Delta)$ be a BCM-regular pair.
\begin{enumerate}
\item 
The BCM-regular threshold $\bcmt(R,\Delta;r)$ of $(R,\Delta)$ with respect to $0\neq r\in\m$ is defined as
\begin{align*}
\bcmt(R,\Delta;r)
&:=\sup\{t\in\Q_{\geq0} \mid \text{$(R,\Delta+t\cdot\divi(r))$ is BCM-regular} \} \\
&=\inf\{t\in\Q_{\geq0} \mid \text{$(R,\Delta+t\cdot\divi(r))$ is not BCM-regular} \}.
\end{align*}
\item
The local BCM-alpha invariant $\alpha_{\BCM}(R,\Delta)$ of $(R,\Delta)$ is defined as
\[ \alpha_{\BCM}(R,\Delta) := \inf_{0\neq r\in\m} \bcmt(R,\Delta;r)\cdot\nord_{\m}(r), \]
where $\nord_{\m}(r)$ denotes the normalized order of $r$.
\end{enumerate}
When $R$ is of characteristic $p>0$,
the BCM-regular threshold coincides with the $F$-pure threshold, and
the local BCM-alpha invariant $\alpha_{\BCM}(R,\Delta)$ coincides with the local $F$-alpha invariant $\alpha_{F}(R,\Delta)$ recently introduced by Takagi and Yamaguchi \cite[Definition~3.3]{TY}.","status":"unverified"}

solution of \eqref{eq:penalized eq} is a nonnegative, almost surely continuous $L^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{d})$-valued $\mathcal{F}_{t}$-predictable function $u_\varepsilon\in L^{1}(\Omega\times[0,T];L^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{d}))$ satisfying following properties.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] Preservation of mass: almost surely for every $\phi\in C_c^{\infty}([0,T))$,
\begin{align}
    -\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d} u_\varepsilon\partial_s\phi(s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s+\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\phi(s)\varepsilon^{-1}(u_\varepsilon-\psi)^{+}\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s=\int_{\mathbb{T}^d} u_{\mathrm{init}}\phi(0)\mathrm{d}x

\item[(ii)] $\sigma(u_\varepsilon)\in L^{2}(\Omega;L^{2}(Q_T))$,\quad $g(u_\varepsilon)\in L^{1}(\Omega;L^{1}(Q_T;\mathbb{R}^d))$.
\item[(iii)] For every $K\in\mathbb{N}$,
\[
[(u_\varepsilon\land K)\lor(1/K)]\in L^{2}(\Omega\times[0,T];H^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{d}))).
\]
Furthermore, there exists a kinetic measure $m_\varepsilon$ satisfying the following properties.
\item[(iv)] Almost surely as a nonnegative measure, $m_\varepsilon$ satisfies
\[
\delta_{0}(\xi-u_\varepsilon)\Phi^{\prime}(\xi)|\nabla u_\varepsilon|^{2}\leq m_\varepsilon\quad\text{on}\quad\mathbb{T}^{d}\times(0,\infty)\times[0,T].
\]
\item[(v)] (Vanishing)
\[
\lim_{N\to\infty}\mathbb{E}\big[m_\varepsilon(\mathbb{T}^{d}\times[N,N+1]\times[0,T))\big]=0.
\]
\item[(vi)] Preservation of energy: for every $\phi\in C_c^{\infty}([0,T))$,
\begin{align}
&-\mathbb{E}\int_0^T\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}u_\varepsilon^2(x,s)\partial_s\phi(s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s+\frac{2}{\varepsilon}\mathbb{E}\int_0^T\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\phi(s)\psi(x,s)(u_\varepsilon-\psi)^+\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\\

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:51:11.974254+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a06edd131f68ab808402010b08cf6af0c8cfcf68bf60438ed8420e09f623f3d2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 38 (Finite certificates and the Rees observability Gramian) of arXiv:2608.08756, 'Infinite-Dimensional L\'evy Area and Spectral Ancestry'] Let $G$ be a finite-dimensional exact layer and let a labelled native reader
family have full support on $G$.  Then at most $\dim G$ scalar contractions of
allowed reader coordinates suffice to detect $G$.  Thus there are
$\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m\in G$, $m\leq\dim G$, spanning $G$, and a scalar
analysis map
\[
 \mathsf C_G:G^*\longrightarrow\mathbf k^m,
 \qquad q\longmapsto(q(\sigma_1),\ldots,q(\sigma_m)).
\]
After fixing Hilbert norms, write
\[
 \kappa(A):=\inf_{\|x\|=1}\|Ax\|
\]
for the minimum modulus of a linear map $A$, and define the finite Rees
observability Gramian
\begin{equation}
 \Gamma_G:=\mathsf C_G^*\mathsf C_G,
 \qquad
 \kappa_G:=\kappa(\mathsf C_G)
 =\lambda_{\min}(\Gamma_G)^{1/2}.
 
\end{equation}
Then full support is equivalent to $\Gamma_G\succ0$, equivalently
$\kappa_G>0$.  For another analysis map $\widetilde{\mathsf C}_G$,
\begin{equation}
 |\kappa(\widetilde{\mathsf C}_G)-\kappa(\mathsf C_G)|
 \leq\|\widetilde{\mathsf C}_G-\mathsf C_G\|.
 
\end{equation}
Consequently full support is stable under perturbations smaller than
$\kappa_G$, and operator-norm convergence of finite reader maps transports a
uniform positive Gramian gap between Galerkin models and their limit.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:57:07.195470+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a07189e4565bb2e03cc6c8ca76610f610b0d06d46c1290d122574b7a11b44785","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:gamma of arXiv:2509.04333, 'The limiting law of the Discrete Gaussian level lines'] Let $\\phi$ be a\n\t\t$\\mathbb Z$-valued height function on the vertices of a connected domain $V\\subset \\mathbb Z^2$. We say the bond $e$ is a \\emph{disagreement bond} of $\\phi$ if $(\\nabla\\phi)_e\\neq 0$ (including when $\\phi_x$ or $\\phi_y$ are specified by the boundary conditions). For brevity,  we denote labeled disagreement polymers by $\\gamma$ (omitting the $\\{h_i\\}$ from the notation).","status":"unverified"}

 \mathcal R_i(X,Z)&=\{X,[A_i,Z]\}a_i,&
 U_i(X,Z)&=\{X,Z\}a_i,\\
 E_i(X,Z)&=\{[A_i,X],Z\}a_i,&
 \bar E(X,Z)&=\frac1N\sum_iE_i(X,Z).
\end{aligned}
\tag{3.2.10a}
\]
Put $\Psi(T)=\sum_jA_jTa_j$.  Then, with no projection onto curvature
summands,
\[
 \mathcal R_i=A_iU_i-(E_i-\bar E)-\bar E,
 \qquad
 \bar E=\frac1N\sum_jA_jV_j+H(X,Z),\qquad V_j=XZa_j,
\tag{3.2.10b}
\]
where
\[
 H(X,Z)=\frac1N\{-X\Psi(Z)+Z\Psi(X)\}.
\tag{3.2.10b$'$}
\]
Moreover, writing $\|\cdot\|_2$ for Hilbert--Schmidt norm,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \frac1N\sum_i\|U_i\|^2
 &\le\frac4N\|X\|_2^2\|Z\|_\mathrm{op}^2,\\
 \frac1N\sum_j\|V_j\|^2
 &\le\frac1N\|X\|_2^2\|Z\|_\mathrm{op}^2,\\
 \frac1N\sum_i\|E_i-\bar E\|^2
 &\le\frac{16(n-2)}N\|X\|_2^2\|Z\|_\mathrm{op}^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{3.2.10c}
\]
The residue satisfies
\[
 \|H(X,Z)\|
 \le\frac{\sqrt{n-2}}N
 \bigl(\|X\|_\mathrm{op}\|Z\|_2+\|Z\|_\mathrm{op}\|X\|_2\bigr).
\tag{3.2.10e}
\]
If $X$ and $Z$ are symmetric, then $\Psi(X)=\Psi(Z)=0$, so $H=0$.
The identities and estimates remain valid when all maps are tensored by
an ancillary identity and the Hilbert--Schmidt norm is taken on the
amplified space.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:48:25.155607+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a0e3b2a9f13d4c62b85164b1133d5c15b78a0d6de402091428644b66c32f802c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:biinf of arXiv:2607.05671, 'Bi-infinite systems of singularly interacting Brownian particles and the KPZ equation'] \normalfont

Let $X = \{X_i(t), t \in [0,\infty)\}_{i \in \mathbb{Z}}$, $L = \{L_{(i,i+1)}(t), t \in [0,\infty)\}_{i \in \mathbb{Z}}$ be collections of continuous, real-valued $\{\mathcal{F}_t\}$-adapted processes having the properties 
\begin{enumerate}[label = \arabic*.]

\item  For all $t \in [0,\infty), i \in \mathbb{Z}$,
\begin{equation} 
X_i(t) = x_i + B_i(t) + pL_{(i-1,i)}(t) - qL_{(i,i+1)}(t).
\end{equation} 

\item  For all $t \in [0,\infty)$, the sequence $\{X_i(t)\}_{i \in \mathbb{Z}}$ is non-decreasing.

\item  For all $i \in \mathbb{Z}$, $L_{(i,i+1)}$ is a continuous, non-decreasing process such that $L_{(i,i+1)}(0) = 0$ and $L_{(i,i+1)}$ can only increase at times $t \in [0,\infty)$ such that $X_{i+1}(t) = X_i(t)$, i.e. 
\[
\int_0^\infty (X_{i+1}(t) - X_i(t))dL_{(i,i+1)}(t) = 0.
\]
\end{enumerate}
We refer to $X = \{X_i\}$ as a \textit{bi-infinite system of singularly interacting Brownian particles with parameter $p$, initial condition $x$, and driving Brownian motions $\{B_i\}$.} The processes $\{L_{(i,i+1)}\}$ are called the \textit{local times} associated with the system $X$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:22:08.431923+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a0faa08291f0afb4392666fec2ece3bad2d30bf661bd3210c2cf8a2f2d00b47f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma Closure under subtraction of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'] \label[lemma]{lem:closure_under_subtraction}
Let $f,g \in \Sym$ with $\supp(g) \subseteq \supp(f)$. 
Let $C = \inf_{z \in \supp(g)} \frac{f(z)}{g(z)}$ and let $c \in [0,C]$. 
Then $h = \frac{f-cg}{1-c} \in \Sym$. 

Moreover, $\supp(h) \subseteq \supp(f)$, and if $\@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{\supp(f)} < \infty$ then the inclusion is proper if and only if $c = C$. 
\begin{proof}
Let $f,g \in \Sym$. 
First note that for $z \in \supp(g)$, $cg(z) \le Cg(z) \le f(z)$, so $f - cg \ge 0$ by construction. 
Also, $1-c = \sum_{z \in \supp(f)} (f(z) - cg(z))$, so $h$ is a PMF with $\supp(h) \subseteq \supp(f)$. 

Observe that for every $z \in \mathbb{R}$, both $\varphi = f$ and $\varphi = g$ solve the symmetry equation
\[ 

(\phi * f_X)(-z) = (\phi * f_X)(z) 

\]

This equation is linear in $\varphi$, so $\varphi = h$ is also a solution. 
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["g a norm on R^2, even in the transversal coordinate"],"created_at":"2026-08-10T03:39:47.000000+00:00","domain":"convex geometry / first-passage percolation limit shapes","id":"claim_a12c2b183a67ea70d9e183fc859334195570a83942c6e5d103a55a95913d7a60","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let g be a norm on R^2 that is even in the first coordinate (g(-h, m) = g(h, m)), as every lattice-symmetric FPP limit-shape norm is. For fixed m, the map h -> g((h, m)) is even and convex, hence minimized at h = 0, so g((h, m)) >= g((0, m)) = |m| g(e_2). Consequently, for a dogleg from (0,0) through v = (h, j) to (0, r) with j = r + m, m > 0 (longitudinal overshoot past the far endpoint): g(v) + g((0,r) - v) - g((0,r)) >= (r + m) g(e_2) + m g(e_2) - r g(e_2) = 2 m g(e_2), and symmetrically for j = -m < 0. The dogleg excess grows at least LINEARLY in the overshoot, with the explicit constant 2 g(e_2), using convexity and symmetry alone - no curvature hypothesis of any kind. The bound is tight as h -> 0. Use: in localization arguments it kills union sites with longitudinal overshoot at a rate no curvature assumption needs to fund, letting curvature windows be quoted only where they are literally assumed. Numerical attack: 0 violations in 300,000 trials on an anisotropic convex norm, worst ratio 1.000019.","status":"derived_in_campaign_refereed"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:22:48.866139+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a1666659cde4c8dd8f37c476cd3c618c7d1faff23f0aec462c6b13d9a65b70bc","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 7 (Quadratic local objective under scalar CFG) of arXiv:2608.29107, 'PathGuide: Dynamic Classifier-Free Guidance via On-Policy Transport Alignment'] Assume scalar CFG:
\begin{equation}
    v_t^\theta(x\mid y;\omega)
    =
    v_t^\theta(x\mid \varnothing)
    +
    \omega
    \Bigl(
        v_t^\theta(x\mid y)-v_t^\theta(x\mid \varnothing)
    \Bigr).
\end{equation}
For fixed \(y,\vec\omega_i,\psi\), define
\begin{equation}
    A_i(\psi)
    :=
    \int_{\R^d}
    \Bigl(
        u_{t_i}(x\mid y)
        -
        v_{t_i}^\theta(x\mid \varnothing)
    \Bigr)\cdot
    \grad\psi(x)\,
    \hat p_{t_i}(x\mid y;\vec\omega_i)\,\dd x
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
    B_i(\psi)
    :=
    \int_{\R^d}
    \Bigl(
        v_{t_i}^\theta(x\mid y)
        -
        v_{t_i}^\theta(x\mid \varnothing)
    \Bigr)\cdot
    \grad\psi(x)\,
    \hat p_{t_i}(x\mid y;\vec\omega_i)\,\dd x .
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}
    \mathcal L_i(\omega_i\mid y;\vec\omega_i,\psi)
    =
    \bigl|A_i(\psi)-\omega_i B_i(\psi)\bigr|^2 .
\end{equation}
In particular, the exact local objective is quadratic in \(\omega_i\).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:16:18.676229+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a1b49fdcb6d4316afd4d7ae2f3d16649cdccbc77c04ff4bfc4b36e6e221a1d6d","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 17 (Log-Lipschitz stability of the PF-ODE) of arXiv:2607.25685, 'Mimicking diffusion processes with differential equations'] Assume \textup{(E1)}, \textup{(D$_{\mathrm S}$)}, \textup{(I)}, \textup{(S)} with \textup{(S2$_p$)}, and

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:05:09.627170+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a1d55e952d07500eddd791b6124027d5f42c43b5ff6768105d409d84ee9fd11c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def5.2 of arXiv:2411.03528, '\textbf{On a boundary of the central limit theorem for strictly stationary, reversible Mar'] Suppose $\varepsilon$ and $\theta$ satisfy ((eq5.111 of the paper)).

{"assumptions":["n,L,M,D positive integers; D'>=0; B,R>0; B_y>=1; 0<xi<1","The n pretraining instances are iid from the same meta-distribution and the query label is bounded by B_y","Normalized ReLU attention, residual ReLU MLP, input and hidden-token Euclidean projection at radius R, and prediction clipping at B_y","The specified transformer parameter norm is at most B and hat theta is an exact constrained empirical risk minimizer"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T15:33:17.892015+00:00","domain":"transformer generalization; pretraining; in-context learning","id":"claim_a2089af688f2246e22d6df8c528ce0527f4e59ab5605bc65d29b77cbe833c673","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Choose positive integers n,L,M,D and D'>=0, parameter bound B>0, token clipping radius R>0, a label bound B_y>=1, and confidence 0<xi<1. Consider fixed-length in-context prediction instances Z=(H,y), with |y|<=B_y almost surely, drawn independently from one meta-distribution. In the paper's setting one first draws a task distribution P, then draws the context and query example iid from P. A transformer has L residual blocks, each consisting of normalized ReLU attention followed by a residual two-layer ReLU MLP; it has token dimension D, at most M attention heads per block, and MLP hidden width at most D'. For S tokens, attention sends h_i to h_i+(1/S) sum_m sum_j ReLU(<Q_m h_i,K_m h_j>) V_m h_j. The MLP sends h to h+W_2 ReLU(W_1 h). Project every input token and every block's output token onto the Euclidean radius-R ball. Read out the designated label coordinate of the final query token and clip it to [-B_y,B_y]. Restrict parameters to the class Theta with norm max_block(max_m{||Q_m||op,||K_m||op}+sum_m ||V_m||op+||W_1||op+||W_2||op)<=B. Write L(theta)=E[(y-prediction_theta(H))^2/2] and let hat theta be any exact empirical minimizer of the same loss over Theta on n independent instances. There is a universal C such that, with probability at least 1-xi, L(hat theta)<=inf_(theta in Theta) L(theta)+C B_y^2 sqrt((L^2(M D^2+D D') log(2+max{B,R,B_y})+log(1/xi))/n). This is an expected loss over the meta-distribution. Source: arXiv:2306.04637, Section 5.1 and Theorem 20, PDF pages 14–15; proof Appendix J.2, PDF page 89. The harmless choice B_y>=1 is stated explicitly here; any smaller valid label bound may be enlarged to one.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["weights in [a,b], a > 0","nearest-neighbour lattice paths"],"created_at":"2026-08-10T02:29:08.000000+00:00","domain":"probability (first-passage percolation)","id":"claim_a20ea460b9385928f93a270c12abee9681fa07dacff1bba16272f9d26d17697d","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"In first-passage percolation on Z^2 with edge weights confined to [a, b] with a > 0, any geodesic from the origin to (0, r) satisfies a DETERMINISTIC bound on its transversal excursion: it never attains transversal level D > r(b - a)/(2a). {"assumptions":["Allen-Cahn on the 1-d torus with 1-d quadratic noise, critical gamma^2 = 2","deterministic constant initial data u_0 = a > 0"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:11:19.448302+00:00","domain":"stochastic partial differential equations, critical spaces","id":"claim_a215289259f9cccbe1cb7c19d537e22e0c0239f3b17a21caf7771d147f98140b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Agresti and Veraar, Nonlinear parabolic stochastic evolution equations in critical spaces (journal version 2025, p. 130), Problem 4 asks whether in the variational setting of their Theorem 6.4 there is a constant C_T with E sup_{t <= T} ||u(t)||_H^2 <= C_T (1 + E ||u_0||_H^2) for all u_0 in L^2(Omega; H). Our result (id P0266, 2026-09-08): the bound FAILS, on the authors' own named unresolved example - Allen-Cahn on the one-dimensional torus with one-dimensional quadratic noise, du = (Laplacian u + u - u^3) dt + gamma u^2 dW, at the critical gamma^2 = 2. With deterministic constant data u_0 = a > 0 the solution stays spatially constant, and the substitutions Y = 1/U, Y = e^{-t} V, time change s = (e^{2t} - 1)/2 and R = V / sqrt 2 turn the SDE into R being a four-dimensional Bessel process started at R_0 = 1/(sqrt 2 a), with U_t = e^t / (sqrt 2 R_s). Since sup_{t <= T} U_t^2 >= 1/(2 inf_{s <= S} R_s^2) and a BES(4) enters a ball of radius x with probability of order x^2 (Newtonian capacity), P(sup U^2 > y) is of order 1/y - tail index one - so E sup_{t <= T} ||u(t)||_H^2 = infinity for every T > 0 while E ||u_0||_H^2 = a^2 is finite. Verification as the source words it: checked in the reverse direction by Ito as well; and an instrument note - a first simulation appeared to contradict the x^2 scaling, but refining the steps at fixed x drives P/x^2 toward the exact constant 2.0 (1.204, 1.579, 1.697 at x = 0.2 and 0.725, 1.285, 1.455 at x = 0.1), so the scaling is real. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:31:02.815831+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a2166a98ab376a45c0d5df2ab5b5538d1c7067d53f83ae87c0936aa4c267691f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary cor:iterated-suspension of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Let $t\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}$ and put $A^{(0)}=A$.  For each $1\leq i\leq t$, choose an
integer $\ell_i\geq2$ and a specified $c_i$ having a length-$\ell_i$
representation by points of $A^{(i-1)}$ with $\gcd(c_i,\ell_i)=1$, and set
$A^{(i)}=\Sigma_{\ell_i,c_i}A^{(i-1)}$.  Put
$R=\prod_{i=1}^t\ell_i$, with the empty product equal to one.  Then, for
$q\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}$,
\begin{align}
 \mathcal H_{A^{(t)}}(z)
 &=\mathcal H_A(z)\prod_{i=1}^t[\ell_i]_z,
 \\
 |qA^{(t)}|
 &=\sum_{\substack{0\leq j_i<\ell_i\\
                    j_1+\cdots+j_t\leq q}}
   |(q-j_1-\cdots-j_t)A|,
 \\
 \mathcal K_{A^{(t)}}(z)
 &=\mathcal K_A(z)\prod_{i=1}^t(1-z^{\ell_i}),
 \\
 \mathcal B_{A^{(t)}}(\xi,z)
 &=\mathcal B_A(\xi,z)\prod_{i=1}^t(1+\xi z^{\ell_i}),
 \\
 \operatorname{ndiam}(A^{(t)})&=R\operatorname{ndiam}(A).
 
\end{align}
If every $\ell_i\leq q$, then
\[
 r_q(A^{(t)})=r_q(A)+t,\qquad
 \operatorname{fdim}_q(A^{(t)})=\operatorname{fdim}_q(A).
\]
If the starting projective coordinate ring is ACM, then the ACM property
and Cohen--Macaulay type are preserved.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:44:27.936604+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a2320fde1b7f0f8261dfeaa5a2285693580446691cfe5b5d62e619fea82210a0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 2 (Voter consensus) of arXiv:2607.13183, '2607.13183'] Consider the continuous-time voter model on the component specified below,
where each vertex updates at rate $1$ by copying a uniformly chosen neighbor,
and suppose that the initial opinions are all distinct. Let $\cons$ be the
consensus time. There are absolute constants $0<c<C_{\rm sup}<\infty$ such that
the first two assertions below hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item In the fixed-supercritical case, let $H_\lambda$ be the giant component of
$G(n,\lambda/n)$ for a fixed $\lambda>1$. Then, with high probability,
\[
        c n \le \E^{H_\lambda}\cons \le C_{\rm sup} n.
\]

\item In the slightly supercritical case, let $H_{\rm ER}$ be the giant component
of $G(n,(1+\eps)/n)$, where $\eps\to0$ and $\eps^3n\to\infty$. Then, with high
probability,
\[
        c n \le \E^{H_{\rm ER}}\cons \le C_{\rm sup} n.
\]

\item In the critical window, fix $A_0\ge0$ and suppose that
$|n^{1/3}(np_n-1)|\le A_0$. Let $\mathcal C_1$ be the largest component of $G(n,p_n)$.
For every $\eta>0$ there are constants
$0<c_{A_0,\eta}<C_{A_0,\eta}<\infty$, depending only on $A_0$ and $\eta$, such
that, for all sufficiently large $n$,
\[
        \Pbb\left(
        c_{A_0,\eta} n
        \le \E^{\mathcal C_1}\cons
        \le C_{A_0,\eta} n
        \right)\ge1-\eta .
\]
\end{enumerate}
In all three cases, the same displayed bounds hold for the full coalescence
