{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:05:27.627182+00:00","domain":"real analysis","id":"claim_ac75738e8e3dabce1159fdd76643746f5142db1f8704a7114eee97125f9e99b8","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A function f: [a, b] -> R has bounded variation if its total variation V(f; [a, b]) = sup over all partitions a = x_0 < x_1 < ... < x_n = b of sum_{i=1}^{n} |f(x_i) - f(x_{i-1})| is finite; the space of such functions is BV[a, b]. Facts (Jordan, Lebesgue): (1) f is of bounded variation if and only if f = g - h with g and h nondecreasing on [a, b] (Jordan decomposition; one may take g(x) = V(f; [a, x]), the variation function, and h = g - f, both nondecreasing); (2) a BV function is bounded, has one-sided limits at every point, has at most countably many discontinuities, all of them jumps, and is differentiable Lebesgue-almost everywhere with f' integrable and integral_a^b |f'(x)| dx <= V(f; [a, b]), with equality if and only if f is absolutely continuous; (3) monotone functions and Lipschitz functions are BV (a Lipschitz function with constant L has V <= L (b - a)), while a continuous function need not be: x sin(1/x) on (0, 1] (extended by 0) has infinite variation, and the Cantor function is continuous, nondecreasing, BV, yet has f' = 0 almost everywhere with total variation 1 (so it is not absolutely continuous); (4) BV[a, b] is a Banach space under ||f|| = |f(a)| + V(f; [a, b]); (5) f is BV exactly when the Riemann-Stieltjes integral integral_a^b g df exists for every continuous g, and then g -> integral g df is a bounded linear functional on C[a, b] of norm V(f; [a, b]) - the Riesz representation of the dual of C[a, b] (normalised BV functions correspond to finite signed Borel measures). In higher dimensions BV functions are those whose distributional gradient is a finite vector measure.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:46.149510+00:00","domain":"elliptic regularity, L^p theory","id":"claim_ac7bfef65ba08df89da6d269b48b216132d2600e11e7ada5844f2602810376eb","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: in the Calderon-Zygmund theory for Lu = sum a^{ij}D_{ij}u + b.Du + cu the leading coefficients must be continuous (uniform continuity on the relevant compact set), or at least of vanishing mean oscillation; only then does the freezing-and-absorption step work for every 1 < p < infinity. Mere measurable uniform ellipticity is not enough, and the failure is not a technicality: both the estimate and uniqueness fail. Counterexample (Gilbarg-Serrin type): on the unit ball B_1 in R^n, n >= 2, fix lambda in (0,1) and set a^{ij}(x) = delta^{ij} + beta x_i x_j/|x|^2 with 1 + beta = (n-1)/(1 - lambda) > 0. These coefficients are bounded, symmetric, uniformly elliptic (eigenvalues 1 with multiplicity n-1 and (n-1)/(1-lambda)) and continuous except at the origin. For radial u, D_{ij}u = u''(r) x_i x_j/r^2 + (u'(r)/r)(delta_{ij} - x_i x_j/r^2), hence Lu = (1 + beta) u'' + (n-1) u'/r, and u(x) = |x|^lambda gives Lu = r^{lambda - 2} [ (1 + beta) lambda(lambda - 1) + (n-1) lambda ] = 0. Now w = |x|^lambda - 1 lies in W^{2,p}(B_1) for every p < n/(2 - lambda), lies in W^{1,p}_0(B_1) for those p, satisfies Lw = 0 almost everywhere, and is not identically zero (w(0) = -1). Consequences: the Dirichlet problem is not uniquely solvable in W^{2,p} intersect W^{1,p}_0 for p < n/(2 - lambda), so no global estimate ||w||_{W^{2,p}} <= C ||Lw||_{L^p} can hold there; the maximum principle also fails for such strong solutions (w attains its minimum -1 at an interior point while Lw = 0 and w = 0 on the boundary). Note n/(2 - lambda) < n and lambda may be taken as close to 1 as desired, so the failure reaches every exponent below n. What survives with only measurable coefficients: the Aleksandrov-Bakelman-Pucci estimate and Krylov-Safonov theory, both of which require the solution to be in W^{2,n}_loc - which is exactly the class this example escapes.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.357576+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ac81b303f3d1341ca273c97542be91edbaf419690548b6ea7476e7328eb55d4a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 242 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Fix any $\phi \in C_b(\R,\R)$ and define the domain
	\[
		\ocM^{\Ising+}(\alpha) = \Big\{
			\mu \in \cP_2(\R,C'(\alpha)) : \bbW_1(\mu, \ocM^{\Ising}(\alpha)) \le 1
		\Big\}\,.
	\]
	Then the function
	\[
		f_\phi(\mu) \equiv \int \phi\,d\mu
	\]
	is uniformly continuous on $\ocM^{\Ising+}(\alpha)$ equipped with the $\bbW_1$ metric.

\begin{proof}
The set $\ocM^{\Ising+}(\alpha)$ is clearly closed with respect to the $\bbW_1$ metric. It thus suffices to show that $f_\phi$ is continuous. In fact, since we are on a metric space, it suffices to show that $f_\phi$ is sequentially continuous. To this end,  consider any sequence $\mu_n$ in $\ocM^{\Ising+}(\alpha)$ converging to $\mu$ in $\bbW_1$. Then $\mu_n$ also converges weakly to $\mu$. Since $\phi$ was assumed to be a bounded continuous function, we obtain 
	 \[\lim_{n\to\infty} f_\phi(\mu_n) = f(\mu)\,.\]

\lim_{p\uparrow 1} W^{\mathrm{rtb}}_{A,B}(p)=
\begin{cases}
1,& t(A)<t(B),\\
0,& t(A)>t(B),\\
\tfrac12,& t(A)=t(B)>0,\\
\mathbf{1}_{\{L_A<L_B\}}+\tfrac12\,\mathbf{1}_{\{L_A=L_B\}},& t(A)=t(B)=0.
\end{cases}
\]
Let $\Delta_h=|h(A)-h(B)|$ and $\Delta_t=|t(A)-t(B)|$. Then the first nonzero terms near the endpoints have orders
\[
\bigl|W^{\mathrm{rtb}}_{A,B}(p)-\mathbf{1}_{\{h(A)<h(B)\}}\bigr|=\Theta\bigl(p^{\Delta_h}\bigr)\quad (p\downarrow 0),
\]
\[
\bigl|W^{\mathrm{rtb}}_{A,B}(p)-\mathbf{1}_{\{t(A)<t(B)\}}\bigr|=\Theta\bigl((1-p)^{\Delta_t}\bigr)\quad (p\uparrow 1),
\]
and if $h(A)=h(B)\ge 1$ (resp.\ $t(A)=t(B)\ge 1$) then
\[
g_{A,B}(p)=O(p)\quad(p\downarrow 0),\qquad
g_{A,B}(p)=O(1-p)\quad(p\uparrow 1).

In particular, if $(h(A)-h(B))(t(A)-t(B))<0$ then $g_{A,B}$ has at least one zero in $(0,1)$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:58:53.193852+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_acbce9fb6240111ab0a4e688c3ae2425f85bb1ad052738787989095fdd4d4f42","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 25 of arXiv:2606.31455, 'Discrete time-multidimensional renewal theory and applications'] Let $\lambda_1,\lambda_2>0$ and $\rho\in[-1,1]$.
Let
\[
F_X(x_1)=1-e^{-\lambda_1 x_1},\qquad
F_Y(x_2)=1-e^{-\lambda_2 x_2},\qquad x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{R}_+.
\]
The FGM bivariate exponential distribution is defined by the joint cdf

\begin{equation}
F(x_1,x_2)
=
F_X(x_1)F_Y(x_2)\Big[1+\rho\,(1-F_X(x_1))(1-F_Y(x_2))\Big],
\qquad (x_1,x_2)\in\mathbb{R}_+^2,
\end{equation}

whose joint density is

\begin{equation*}
f(x_1,x_2)
=
\lambda_1\lambda_2\,e^{-(\lambda_1 x_1+\lambda_2 x_2)}
\Big[1+\rho\,(1-2e^{-\lambda_1 x_1})(1-2e^{-\lambda_2 x_2})\Big],
\qquad x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{R}_+.
\end{equation*}
Equivalently, \eqref{eq:fgm-cdf} is obtained by combining the exponential marginals
with the FGM copula \cite{morgenstern1956einfache,nelsen2006introduction}.
The case $\rho=0$ corresponds to independence.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X a normed space; no completeness of X is needed","for metrizability and sequential compactness of the ball: X separable","Tychonoff (hence a form of the axiom of choice) in the general case"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.752423+00:00","domain":"functional analysis","id":"claim_ad0f3a207b3c5379410429f086bcbbeb1babd7dfb64560bd3c03ab098d3b5d3e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a normed vector space over R or C. The closed unit ball B of the dual space X^* is COMPACT in the weak-* topology, that is the topology of pointwise convergence on X. Two refinements matter. (a) If X is SEPARABLE then the weak-* topology restricted to B is metrizable and B is weak-* SEQUENTIALLY compact, so bounded sequences of functionals have weak-* convergent subsequences; without separability compactness need not give sequential compactness. (b) The general theorem uses Tychonoff's theorem for a product of compact scalar discs and therefore, in ZF, is not provable without some choice; the separable case needs only a diagonal argument. The theorem does NOT say the ball is norm-compact: by Riesz's lemma the closed unit ball of a normed space is norm-compact if and only if the space is finite-dimensional. Nor does it say the ball of X itself is weakly compact - that characterises reflexivity (Kakutani). [standard; e.g. Rudin, Functional Analysis, 2nd ed., Theorem 3.15]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:26:26.807268+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ad2577d53d461574b2aa13e7c5473ca3510eb25e4462f7d955d961221f62d0ed","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:read-k of arXiv:2608.06159, 'Majority Dynamics on Resampled Sparse Erd\H{o}s--R\'enyi Graphs:\\[0.5ex] Gaussian Winner '] {gavinsky2015tail}}]
    
     Let \(\{\rY_j\}_{j\in[r]}\) be a read-\(k\) family of indicator random variables with \(p_j \coloneqq\P(\rY_j=1)\), and denote their average by \(\bar p \coloneqq r^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^r p_j\).
    If \(0<\bar p<1\), then
    \begin{subequations}
    \begin{align}
    \P\bigg(
    \sum_{j=1}^r \rY_j\ge (\bar p+\varepsilon)r
    \bigg)
    &\le
    \exp\bigg(
    -\frac{r}{k}\D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\bar p+\varepsilon\|\bar p)
    \bigg),
    &&0<\varepsilon\le1-\bar p,
    \\
    \P\bigg(
    \sum_{j=1}^r \rY_j\le (\bar p-\varepsilon)r
    \bigg)
    &\le
    \exp\bigg(
    -\frac{r}{k}\D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\bar p-\varepsilon\|\bar p)
    \bigg),
    &&0<\varepsilon\le\bar p.
    \end{align}
    \end{subequations}
    where the Kullback-Leibler divergence is defined as
    \[
    \D_{\mathrm{KL}}(u\|v)\coloneqq
    u\log(u/v)+(1-u)\log((1-u)/(1-v)).
    \]
    We use the standard convention \(0\log0=0\) at \(u\in\{0,1\}\).
    If \(\bar p\in\{0,1\}\), all the indicators are almost surely constant and
    the corresponding tail statements are trivial. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:13:18.504023+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ad453d4166c9bb1b07d7d7d64a96e9f84f071a56917ecc29dc401a4b7e0dbc0a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 3 (Conditional Fisher-information convergence) of arXiv:2608.30579, '2608.30579'] \hfill\break
Let $\{(X_n,Y_n)\}_{n\geq 1}$ be a sequence of pairs of random variables such that, for each $n$, 
the conditional distribution of $X_n$ given $Y_n$ is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure almost surely. 
Suppose that
\begin{equation}
	    X_n=X_{0,n}+G_{a,n},
\end{equation}
where $G_{a,n}\sim\mathcal N(0,a)$ for some $a>0$, and $G_{a,n}$ is independent of $(X_{0,n},Y_n)$.

Assume that there exists a nonnegative function $l:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ such that $l(R)\to0$ as $R\to\infty$ and
\begin{equation}
    \mathbb{E}L_{X_n\mid Y_n}(R)\leq l(R),
    \qquad \forall n\in\mathbb N^+,\ R\geq 0.	
\end{equation}
Let $(X_n',Y_n')$ be an independent copy of $(X_n,Y_n)$. 
Suppose further that the limits
\begin{equation}
    \lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{E}h(X_n\mid Y_n)
    \quad\text{and}\quad
    \lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Var}(X_n\mid Y_n)
\end{equation}
exist, and that, for some $\lambda\in(0,1)$,
\begin{equation}
    \left|
    \mathbb{E}h(X_{n+1}\mid Y_{n+1})
    -
    \mathbb{E}h(X_n\mid Y_n)
    \right|
    =
    \mathbb{E}\left[
    h(X_n*_{\lambda}X_n'\mid Y_n,Y_n')
    -
    h(X_n\mid Y_n)
    \right],
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}
    X_n*_{\lambda}X_n'
    \triangleq
    \lambda X_n+\sqrt{1-\lambda^2}\,X_n' .
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}
    \lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{E}J(X_n\mid Y_n)
    =
    \frac{1}{\sigma^2},
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}
    \sigma^2
    =
    \lim_{n\to\infty}
    \mathbb{E}\operatorname{Var}(X_n\mid Y_n).
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.352755+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ad9dfddf35a21438c5a228b87c7e72dd3e4305df306e0f8d536a222ca14e5549","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Ppn 197 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any subsequential limit $\Q$ as obtained by Proposition~\ref{p:tightness}, let $\mu\sim\Q$ and $(\Gamma,\Upsilon,\mathcal{E})\sim\mu$ (so $\mathcal{E}\equiv0$). Denote the limiting processes as 
	\begin{align}\nonumber
	\Gamma
	&\equiv \Big(
	D^{\RomI}=D=Y^{\RomI},
	Q^{\RomII},Q^{\RomII,\RomIII},Q^{\RomIII},Q^{\Ising}
	\Big)\,,\\
	\Upsilon
	&\equiv\Big( 
	Z^{\RomII}=Y^{\RomII},
	Z^{\RomIII}=Y^{\RomIII},
	Z^{\Ising}=Y^{\Ising}
	\Big)\,.
	
	\end{align}
Then $\Gamma$ is a finite-variation process, while $\Upsilon$ is a martingale. For each $\sigma,\tau\in\{\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}$, the covariation of $Z^\sigma$ with $Z^\tau$ is given by $Q^{\sigma,\tau}$, where
$Q^{\sigma,\Ising}\equiv0$ for $\sigma\in\{\RomII,\RomIII\}$. 
 The ``$\frozen$'' variant of the statement also holds. 

\begin{proof}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:05:37.767829+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ada6bb71336f4aa0c91cf431aef1484ec65aaca39e0ec609d1a09018c2f84dc8","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition regulated process of arXiv:2607.29548, 'Generalized reflected BSDEs with irregular obstacles driven by RCLL increasing processes o'] \begin{itemize}
			\item A process
			\[
			\mathcal{X}:\Omega\times[0,T]\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}
			\]
			is called a \emph{regulated process} if, for
			$\mathbb{P}$-almost every $\omega\in\Omega$, the mapping
			\[
			t\longmapsto\mathcal{X}_t(\omega)
			\]
			admits a finite right limit at every $t\in[0,T)$ and a finite
			left limit at every $t\in(0,T]$.
			
			\item Let $\mathcal{X}$ be a process with regulated trajectories.
			For $s\in(0,T]$, we define its left limit and left jump by
			\[
			\mathcal{X}_{s-}
			:=
			\lim_{u\uparrow s}\mathcal{X}_u,
			\qquad
			\Delta_-\mathcal{X}_s
			:=
			\mathcal{X}_s-\mathcal{X}_{s-},
			\]
			with the convention $\Delta_-\mathcal{X}_0=0$.
			
			For $s\in[0,T)$, we define its right limit and right jump by
			\[
			\mathcal{X}_{s+}
			:=
			\lim_{u\downarrow s}\mathcal{X}_u,
			\qquad
			\Delta_+\mathcal{X}_s
			:=
			\mathcal{X}_{s+}-\mathcal{X}_s,
			\]
			with the convention $\Delta_+\mathcal{X}_T=0$.
			
			The trajectories of a regulated process have at most countably
			many discontinuities; see
			[DudleyNorvaisa2011].
			
			\item Let
			\[
			\mathsf{K}:\Omega\times[0,T]\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}
			\]
			be a regulated process of finite variation. Then $\mathsf{K}$
			admits the decomposition
			\[
			\mathsf{K}
			=
			\mathsf{K}^c+\mathsf{K}^d+\mathsf{K}^g,
			\]
			where $\mathsf{K}^c$ is continuous, the càdlàg pure-jump process
			$\mathsf{K}^d$ is defined by
			\[
			\mathsf{K}^d_t
			:=
			\sum_{0<s\leq t}\Delta_-\mathsf{K}_s,
			\qquad t\in[0,T],
			\]
			and the càglàd pure-jump process $\mathsf{K}^g$ is defined by
			\[
			\mathsf{K}^g_t
			:=
			\sum_{0\leq s<t}\Delta_+\mathsf{K}_s,
			\qquad t\in[0,T].
			\]
			The above sums converge absolutely along each trajectory since
			$\mathsf{K}$ has finite variation.
			
			In particular,
			\[
			\mathsf{K}_t
			=
			\mathsf{K}^{\ast}_t
			+
			\sum_{0\leq s<t}\Delta_+\mathsf{K}_s,
			\qquad t\in[0,T],
			\]
			where
			\[
			\mathsf{K}^{\ast}
			:=
			\mathsf{K}-\mathsf{K}^g
			=
			\mathsf{K}^c+\mathsf{K}^d
			\]
			is the càdlàg, or right-continuous, part of $\mathsf{K}$.
			The process $\mathsf{K}^g$ is the left-continuous pure-jump part
			of $\mathsf{K}$.
		\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Omega is a compact metric space and T: Omega -> Omega is a homeomorphism","(Omega, T) is minimal","V: Omega -> R is continuous","H_omega is the discrete Schrodinger operator with potential n -> V(T^n omega) on l^2(Z) (equivalently, the continuum Schrodinger operator over a minimal flow)","E is a real energy","uniform hyperbolicity is understood with constants uniform over all of Omega"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:07:38.814897+00:00","domain":"spectral theory of ergodic Schrodinger operators, hyperbolic cocycles","id":"claim_ae02788a467b182215c0322bd89b1ed9531f9fb0c3a5dbf18d877ba74f12ef05","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (Omega, T) be a MINIMAL topological dynamical system, Omega a compact metric space and T a homeomorphism, and let V: Omega -> R be continuous. For each omega in Omega let H_omega be the discrete Schrodinger operator on l^2(Z) given by (H_omega u)(n) = u(n+1) + u(n-1) + V(T^n omega) u(n). By minimality the spectrum sigma(H_omega) is one and the same compact set Sigma contained in R for every omega. For an energy E in R define the Schrodinger cocycle (T, A^E) over (Omega,T), where A^E(omega) is the SL(2,R) matrix with rows (E - V(omega), -1) and (1, 0); its iterates are A^E_n(omega) = A^E(T^{n-1}omega) ... A^E(omega), and they transfer solutions of the difference equation u(n+1) + u(n-1) + V(T^n omega)u(n) = E u(n). The cocycle is UNIFORMLY HYPERBOLIC if there is a continuous T-invariant splitting R^2 = E^s(omega) + E^u(omega) and constants C > 0, lambda > 1 with ||A^E_n(omega)v|| <= C lambda^{-n}||v|| for v in E^s(omega) and ||A^E_{-n}(omega)v|| <= C lambda^{-n}||v|| for v in E^u(omega), for all n >= 0 and all omega; equivalently (for SL(2,R) cocycles over a compact base) ||A^E_n(omega)|| >= C lambda^n for all omega and all n >= 0. THEOREM (R. Johnson): E belongs to R \\ Sigma if and only if the cocycle (T, A^E) is uniformly hyperbolic. Equivalently, Sigma is exactly the set of real energies at which the Schrodinger cocycle fails to be uniformly hyperbolic. The same statement holds in the continuum setting for Schrodinger operators -u'' + V(T_t omega)u on the line with a minimal flow, which is Johnson's original formulation, and it is the standard dictionary between spectral theory and the dynamics of the transfer-matrix cocycle. SHARP EDGES. (a) UNIFORM hyperbolicity is far stronger than a positive Lyapunov exponent, and this is the single most often misused point. In the supercritical almost Mathieu operator, and more generally in the localisation regime, the Lyapunov exponent L(E) is positive at EVERY energy of the spectrum; those energies are in Sigma, so the cocycle there is non-uniformly hyperbolic. 'Positive exponent' therefore does NOT imply 'in the resolvent set'; only uniformity does. (b) Minimality of the base is used twice: to make sigma(H_omega) independent of omega, and to propagate the exponential dichotomy from one orbit to all of Omega. For a non-minimal base the spectrum can genuinely depend on omega and the statement must be reformulated (typically with the union of the spectra over the support of an ergodic measure, or over the whole base), so do not apply the equivalence verbatim outside minimality. (c) The theorem characterises the RESOLVENT set, which is open; correspondingly uniform hyperbolicity is an open condition in E and in the cocycle, whereas positivity of the Lyapunov exponent is not open. (d) The statement is for real E; for non-real E the operator is invertible anyway and the associated cocycle is not an SL(2,R) cocycle.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a topological space","f takes values in the extended reals (-infinity, +infinity]","for the liminf characterisation, X is first countable (e.g. metric)","for the attainment-of-the-infimum statement, X is compact","for the approximation by Lipschitz functions, X is metric and f is bounded below"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:07:38.814277+00:00","domain":"general topology, real analysis, calculus of variations","id":"claim_ae0d76cf084a3679aa5c60bc21a5f1aa5a7d55e81a31da780dbc20178aa9cae5","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a topological space and f: X -> (-infinity, +infinity] an extended-real function. f is lower semicontinuous (lsc) at a point x0 if for every real a < f(x0) there is a neighbourhood U of x0 with f(x) > a for all x in U. f is lsc on X iff any one of the following equivalent conditions holds: (i) the superlevel set {x : f(x) > a} is open for every real a; (ii) the sublevel set {x : f(x) <= a} is closed for every real a; (iii) the epigraph {(x,t) in X x R : t >= f(x)} is closed in X x R. If X is first countable (in particular metric), lower semicontinuity at x0 is equivalent to liminf_{x -> x0} f(x) >= f(x0). f is upper semicontinuous iff -f is lsc, and f is continuous iff it is both. Standard facts, each of which is the reason lsc is worth naming: (1) the pointwise SUPREMUM of an arbitrary family of lsc functions is lsc; (2) a sum of finitely many lsc functions is lsc provided no (+infinity) + (-infinity) occurs, and a nonnegative multiple of an lsc function is lsc; (3) a nondecreasing pointwise limit of continuous functions is lsc, and conversely on a METRIC space every lsc function bounded below is the pointwise nondecreasing limit of a sequence of Lipschitz functions (Baire); (4) the indicator 1_A is lsc iff A is open; (5) WEIERSTRASS FORM: if X is compact and f is lsc then f attains its infimum on X, because the sublevel sets {f <= a} are closed and have the finite intersection property. This is the form in which lsc is used in the direct method of the calculus of variations: coercivity plus lsc on a compact (or weakly compact) set yields a minimiser. SHARP EDGES, i.e. what is NOT true. (a) lsc buys you MINIMA only, never maxima: on the compact space [0,1] the function f(x) = x for x < 1, f(1) = 0 is lsc (every superlevel set {f > a} is (a,1) or [0,1] or empty), its supremum is 1 and it is not attained. (b) The supremum of lsc functions is lsc but the INFIMUM of infinitely many lsc functions need not be: on R the continuous functions f_n(x) = max(0, 1 - n|x|) have pointwise infimum the indicator of {0}, whose superlevel set {f > 1/2} = {0} is not open. (c) 'lsc at every point' is genuinely weaker than continuity; an lsc function may be discontinuous on a dense set. (d) Statement (3) uses metrizability of X; on a general topological space an lsc function need not be a pointwise limit of continuous functions (it is a supremum of continuous functions on compact Hausdorff or, more generally, normal spaces, by Urysohn/Katetov-Tong, but for arbitrary X no such representation is available). (e) In integration theory the useful instance is Fatou's lemma, which says exactly that f -> integral f is lsc along pointwise convergence of nonnegative measurable functions; no upper semicontinuity holds there without a domination hypothesis.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T21:02:38.607107+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ae2f62daa02f830834a94395dafeac40a3fe4f5f5f4c4e48dd98095791eb2a7a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2607.08242, 'Convergence of random sums in non-commutative probability'] Suppose $(\mathcal{A}, \varphi)$ is an NCP. 

Let $\{a_i\}$ be self-adjoint variables such that, $\varphi(a_i)=0, \varphi(a_i^2)=1$, and  $\sup_i|\varphi(a_i^m)| < \infty$ for every positive integer $m$. 
Then the following hold for $S_n:=a_1+\cdots +a_n$.\vskip5pt

\noindent (i) If $\{a_i\}$ are free, then $S_n/\sqrt{n}\stackrel{*}{\to} s$.

\vskip5pt

\noindent (ii) If $\{a_i\}$ are independent, then $S_n/\sqrt{n}\stackrel{*}{\to} z$.

\vskip5pt

\noindent (iii) If $\{a_i\}$ are half-independent, then $S_n/\sqrt{n}
\stackrel{*}{\to} r_S$.

\vskip3pt

\noindent In other words, $\varphi(S_n/\sqrt{n})^m$ in (i), (ii) and (iii) respectively, equal $\varphi(s^m)+o(1)$, $\varphi(z^m)+o(1)$, $\varphi(r_S^m)+o(1)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:49:02.090002+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ae325f24040744b8f8cf7d064e76b80897dacb51b2bfa623c2b875071b1074db","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 25 (Amplification via many macroscopic subtrees) of arXiv:2604.25877, 'Asymptotic height of Plancherel random trees'] Fix $\theta>0$ and let $H_n$ denote the height of the Ewens tree $\mathcal T_n$.
Assume that there exist constants $p_0\in(0,1)$ and $m_0\ge 1$ such that
\begin{equation}
\inf_{m\ge m_0}\Pp\left(H_m\ge h(m)\right)\ \ge\ p_0,
\end{equation}
for some function $h:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$.
Fix any $\delta\in(0,1)$ and set $m:=n-1$ and the macroscopic threshold
\[
t_n := \lceil m^{1-\delta}\rceil,
\qquad
h_{\min}(n):=\min(\{h(j):\ t_n\le j\le m\}).
\]
Then, for all $n$ large enough so that $t_n\ge m_0$,
\begin{equation}
\Pp\left(H_n \ge 1+h_{\min}(n)\right)
\ \ge\
1-\E\left[(1-p_0)^{N_0}\right].
\end{equation}
Moreover,
\begin{equation}
\E[(1-p_0)^{N_0}]\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}0
\qquad\text{and therefore}\qquad
\Pp\left(H_n \ge 1+h_{\min}(n)\right)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}1.
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["A is a square real matrix with nonnegative entries"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T02:00:35.438555+00:00","domain":"linear algebra, nonnegative matrices","id":"claim_ae5c6a4cb8084ef24a18e45632bcc8943945094a5e71de887f9245aa6e393816","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A real $n \\times n$ matrix $A = (a_{ij})$ is nonnegative ($A \\ge 0$) if all entries are $\\ge 0$, and positive ($A > 0$) if all entries are $> 0$. Associate to $A \\ge 0$ the directed graph $G(A)$ on vertices $1, \\dots, n$ with an edge $i \\to j$ iff $a_{ij} > 0$; then $(A^m)_{ij} > 0$ iff there is a walk of length $m$ from $i$ to $j$. $A$ is irreducible if $G(A)$ is strongly connected (every vertex reaches every other), equivalently if there is no permutation matrix $P$ with $P A P^{\\mathsf T} = \\begin{pmatrix} B & C \\\\ 0 & D\\end{pmatrix}$ with $B, D$ square nonempty blocks, equivalently (for $n \\ge 2$) if $(I + A)^{n-1} > 0$; a $1 \\times 1$ matrix is irreducible by convention (some authors exclude the zero $1\\times1$ matrix). The period (index of imprimitivity) $h$ of an irreducible $A$ is the greatest common divisor of the lengths of all closed walks in $G(A)$; it does not depend on the vertex, and $h = 1$ iff $A$ is aperiodic. $A$ is primitive if $A \\ge 0$ and $A^m > 0$ for some $m \\ge 1$; for nonnegative matrices, primitive $\\iff$ irreducible and aperiodic, and then $A^m > 0$ for all $m \\ge (n-1)^2 + 1$ (Wielandt's bound). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T21:00:30.493350+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ae79d6812b4fb7ffa2c3b33c08d4e0e8ba3daead3a304e5986b32ed89a84c3f7","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 11 (Octahedron recurrence) of arXiv:2607.04138, 'Hives from deformed GUE minor processes'] \lab{def:oct}
We use the max-plus form of the octahedron recurrence, in the sense of
\cite{KTW,Speyer,NarSheffTao}.  One starts with real values assigned to a
stepped surface in the parity sublattice of \(\mathbb Z^3\).  A local move
replaces one face of an elementary octahedron by the opposite face.  If the
six vertices of this octahedron are
\[
(i,j,k\pm 1),\qquad (i\pm 1,j,k),\qquad (i,j\pm 1,k),
\]
and all values except \(F(i,j,k+1)\) are already known, then the missing value
is defined by
\[
F(i,j,k+1)
=
\max\{F(i+1,j,k)+F(i-1,j,k),\,
F(i,j+1,k)+F(i,j-1,k)\}
-F(i,j,k-1).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
F(i,j,k+1)+F(i,j,k-1)
=
\max\{F(i+1,j,k)+F(i-1,j,k),\,
F(i,j+1,k)+F(i,j-1,k)\}.
\]
Iterating these local moves transports the data from one stepped surface to
another.  In the hive setting this transport is the
Knutson--Tao--Woodward/Speyer piecewise-linear, volume-preserving bijection
between the two hive decompositions corresponding to associativity
\cite{KTW,Speyer,NarSheffTao}; we denote it by \(\oct\).

For the applications below, Proposition~\ref{gt-rem}(iv) first lets us regard
Gelfand--Tsetlin patterns as hives with one large-gap side.  With this
identification, \(\oct\) sends a pair of Gelfand--Tsetlin patterns, equivalently
a double hive, to an augmented hive, or to a pair of hives glued along their
common boundary.  Throughout the paper \(h_n\) denotes the hive component of

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:05:57.798777+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ae7f4f491c57f1500da9e1c3e081a5803ad42a846738f1d551392e0ac265ad19","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 6 of arXiv:2608.30551, 'Critical Discrete Hardy Inequalities in $L^p$'] Let $\Omega\subseteq X$. $$

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:33:46.767216+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ae806e2d14ac53d071e815421fa3fd8d8dd630356962ffc4f1102a910336673a","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 8 of arXiv:2603.24616, 'Pinning in non-critical half-space geometric last passage percolation'] Let $\\Sigma \\subseteq \\mathbb{Z}$ and $\\Lambda \\subseteq \\mathbb{R}$ be an interval. A {\\em $\\Sigma$-indexed line ensemble $\\mathcal{L}$} is a random variable defined on a probability space $(\\Omega, \\mathcal{F}, \\mathbb{P})$ that takes values in $\\left(C (\\Sigma \\times \\Lambda), \\mathcal{C}_{\\Sigma}\\right)$. Intuitively, $\\mathcal{L}$ is a collection of random continuous curves (sometimes referred to as {\\em lines}), indexed by $\\Sigma$, each of which maps $\\Lambda$ into $\\mathbb{R}$. We will often slightly abuse notation and write $\\mathcal{L}: \\Sigma \\times \\Lambda \\rightarrow \\mathbb{R}$, even though it is not $\\mathcal{L}$ which is such a function, but $\\mathcal{L}(\\omega)$ for every $\\omega \\in \\Omega$. For $i \\in \\Sigma$, we write $\\mathcal{L}_i(\\omega) = (\\mathcal{L}(\\omega))(i, \\cdot)$ for the curve of index $i$ and note that the latter is a map $\\mathcal{L}_i: \\Omega \\rightarrow C(\\Lambda)$, which is $\\mathcal{F}/\\mathcal{C}$ measurable. \n\nWe say that a line ensemble $\\mathcal{L}$ is {\\em non-intersecting} if $\\mathbb{P}$-almost surely $\\mathcal{L}_i(t) > \\mathcal{L}_j(t)$ for all $i < j$ and $t \\in \\Lambda$. We say that a line ensemble $\\mathcal{L}$ is {\\em ordered} if $\\mathbb{P}$-almost surely $\\mathcal{L}_i(t) \\geq \\mathcal{L}_j(t)$ for all $i < j$ and $t \\in \\Lambda$. If $[a,b] \\subseteq \\Lambda$, we let $\\mathcal{L}_i[a,b]$ denote the restriction of $\\mathcal{L}_i$ to $[a,b]$, and note that the latter is a measurable map $\\mathcal{L}_i[a,b]: \\Omega \\rightarrow C([a,b])$. If $\\Sigma_1 \\subseteq \\Sigma$ and $[a,b] \\subseteq \\Lambda$, we let $\\mathcal{L}\\vert_{\\Sigma_1 \\times [a,b]}$ denote the restriction of $\\mathcal{L}$ to $\\Sigma_1 \\times [a,b]$, which is a measurable map $\\mathcal{L}\\vert_{\\Sigma_1 \\times [a,b]}: \\Omega \\rightarrow C(\\Sigma_1 \\times [a,b])$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:35:05.840784+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_aea72b18dcb932a62bfc9db753e0b5d07eff52cade4b16d67f04282cda035690","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition Entropy functional of arXiv:2606.27073, 'Retention Profiles and KL Contraction Bounds in Finite Markov Chains'] The \emph{entropy functional} relative to~$\pi$ is
\[
  \mathrm{Ent}_\pi(f)
  := \sum_{x\in S} f(x)\log f(x)\,\pi(x)
     - \Bigl(\sum_{x\in S} f(x)\pi(x)\Bigr)
       \log\Bigl(\sum_{x\in S} f(x)\pi(x)\Bigr)
\]
for non-negative functions $f\ge 0$ on $S$.

$\mathrm{Ent}_\pi(f) = D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mu\|\pi)$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:33:17.715370+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_aec5ed6aa70646774a71b991d3bc8ec8622ecedde2d6c90a83dfd0b2457fc234","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 56 (Scalar Wiener realization of a centered block) of arXiv:2607.10813, '2607.10813'] Fix a concrete pulled-back dyadic form $\mathbf H^\sharp$ and assume that its

 \mathfrak k_{f,g}(F,G):=\mathbf H^\sharp(F,G,f,g).
\]
Then $\mathfrak k_{f,g}\in\mathcal G_b\otimes_2\mathcal G_c$ and

 \|\mathfrak k_{f,g}\|_{\mathcal G_b\otimes_2\mathcal G_c}
 \le \|F_1^\sharp\|_{\Sch_2}\|f\|_{\mathcal C_{0,Q}}
 \|g\|_{\mathcal E_M}.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:17:17.069216+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_aec7556d43c449fffb08ec6df68bed9c20534e0822f9c8bdb504100ae3e497ef","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 4 (ULDP) of arXiv:2608.19753, 'Uniform large deviation principles for the stochastic heat equation over unbounded sets of'] Let $\mathcal{E}$ be a Polish space, completely metrized by a metric $d$. 
Let $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})$ be a probability space.  Let $ \mathcal{E}_0$ be any set, and let $\{X^\eps_x: \eps>0,x\in \mathcal{E}_0\}$ be a family of $\mathcal{E}$-valued random variables. Let $\{I_x : x \in \mathcal{E}_0\}$ be a collection of lower-semicontinuous maps $I_x : \mathcal{E} \to [0,+\infty]$. 
Let $\mathscr{A}$ be a collection of subsets of $\mathcal{E}_0$.  
Then, the family $\{X^\eps_x: \eps>0,x\in \mathcal{E}_0\}$ is said to satisfy a \emph{Freidlin--Wentzell uniform large deviation principle (ULDP) with respect to the rate functions $I_x$ uniformly over $\mathscr{A}$}, if
\begin{itemize}
\item For any $A \in \mathscr{A}$, $s_0 > 0$, and $\delta > 0$,
\[
\liminf_{\eps \to 0} \inf_{x \in A} \inf_{\varphi \in \Phi_x(s_0)} \big(\eps\log \mathbb{P}(d(X^\eps_x, \varphi) < \delta) + I_x(\varphi)\big) \geq 0.
\]
\item For any $A \in \mathscr{A}$, $s_0 > 0$, and $\delta > 0$,
\[
\limsup_{\eps \to 0} \sup_{x \in A} \sup_{s \in [0,s_0]} \big(\eps \log \mathbb{P}(\mathrm{dist}_d(X^\eps_x, \Phi_x(s)) \geq \delta) + s\big) \leq 0,
\]
\end{itemize}
where $\Phi_x(s) \ceqq \{\varphi \in \mathcal{E} : I_x(\varphi) \leq s\}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:59:45.010040+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_aeccbf6ce826c51a465cad74a5ca5f3282abbd81222730df0bb8d668db4d29dc","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem ordinary-factorial-bispectrum of arXiv:2605.13004, 'Orientation in Poisson Cluster Processes via Imaginary Bispectra'] Assume that the reduced second factorial cumulant measure and the reduced third factorial and complete cumulant measures are finite signed measures, so that the Fourier--Stieltjes transforms below are ordinary bounded functions. Let $B_{\mathrm{comp}}$ denote the Fourier--Stieltjes transform of $\gamma_3^{\mathrm{red}}$, the reduced complete, or ordinary, third cumulant measure, and let $B_{\mathrm{fac}}$ denote the transform of $\kappa_3^{\mathrm{red}}$, the reduced third factorial cumulant measure, under the same Fourier convention. When the latter measure has an $L^1$ density, $B_{\mathrm{fac}}$ is its factorial bispectrum. Then
\begin{equation}
B_{\mathrm{comp}}(\omega_1,\omega_2)
=
B_{\mathrm{fac}}(\omega_1,\omega_2)
+\Gamma(\omega_1)+\Gamma(\omega_2)+\Gamma(\omega_1+\omega_2)-2\lambda.
\end{equation}
In particular, since the second reduced factorial cumulant is symmetric and $\Gamma$ is real-valued,
\[
\mathrm{Im} B_{\mathrm{comp}}=\mathrm{Im} B_{\mathrm{fac}}.
\]
The finite-measure formulation above is the one used below; distributional variants require a separate specification of test-function classes and diagonal embeddings. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:28:08.695139+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_aed1fab15c9d67b31049b6a6f2a26369e3c64b13cf4bb97b66319a49981952a1","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 5 of arXiv:2607.29536, 'Multi-hop visibility through the vacant set of Poissonian obstacles'] Let $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ be lines in $\R^d$ intersecting in a single point $z$, and let $\theta\in(0,\frac\pi2]$ be the angle between them. 
Let $u_1$ be a unit vector parallel to $\ell_1$. 
Then for any $\delta>0$,  
\[
B(\ell_1,\delta)\cap B(\ell_2,\delta)\subseteq 
z + \Big\{x\in B(\ell_1,\delta)\,:\,\big|\langle x,u_1\rangle\big|\leq \frac{\delta}{\tan(\theta/2)}\Big\}.
\]
In words, the intersection of $\delta$-neighborhoods of the two lines is contained in the finite cylinder centered at $z$ of radius $\delta$ and length $2\frac{\delta}{\tan(\theta/2)}$ whose axis is aligned with $\ell_1$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["H is a complex Hilbert space","every A_n and A is self-adjoint (so the resolvent set contains C minus R and the resolvent norm bound 1/|Im z| holds)","no relation between the domains of the A_n and of A is assumed","convergence is of the resolvents, applied to a fixed vector (strong) or in operator norm (norm)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.090914+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, unbounded self-adjoint operators","id":"claim_aefd17250c9ea1190635da34d922379fe94928d2718e0131592cbabceafdf37c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A_n (n = 1, 2, ...) and A be self-adjoint operators on a Hilbert space H, each on its own dense domain; the domains are not assumed equal or even comparable. One says A_n -> A in the STRONG RESOLVENT SENSE if for every psi in H and every z in C with nonzero imaginary part, (A_n - z)^(-1) psi converges in norm to (A - z)^(-1) psi. Because each operator is self-adjoint, the resolvent (A_n - z)^(-1) is bounded with norm at most 1 / |Im z|, so the family is uniformly bounded and it is enough to verify the convergence for a SINGLE non-real z: one z in the upper half plane suffices, the conjugate point following by taking adjoints and the remaining z by the resolvent identity together with the uniform bound. The NORM RESOLVENT SENSE is the same statement with convergence in operator norm; it implies the strong resolvent sense and is strictly stronger. Practical criterion: if all the A_n and A are essentially self-adjoint on a common core D and A_n psi -> A psi for every psi in D, then A_n -> A in the strong resolvent sense. Without such a hypothesis convergence on a dense subspace says nothing, which is precisely why the resolvent formulation, and not naive pointwise convergence of unbounded operators, is the notion that interacts with the spectral theorem.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:49:24.959351+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_af0675e3c299f956c629841a008c19c5efa33b754f94cecdf1d207dc71f119da","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:convergence of arXiv:2609.03264, 'Certified Spherical MUSIC for 3D Localization under Adversarial Subspace Perturbations'] Assume all the hypotheses and numerical inequalities in the statement
of (thm:certified-music-landscape of the paper), and define
\[
    m:=C_0^-\kappa^2,
    \qquad
    M:=C_0^+\kappa^2.
\]
For a fixed step size \(h\) satisfying
\begin{equation}

    0<h\leq\frac{2}{(C_0^-+C_0^+)\kappa^2}
    =\frac{2}{m+M},
\end{equation}
let
\[
    T_h({\bm z}):={\bm z}-h\nabla\widetilde q({\bm z}).
\]
Then, for every \(j=1,\ldots,s\),
\[
    T_h\left(\overline{B_\rho({\bm x}_j)}\right)
    \subset B_\rho({\bm x}_j).
\]
Moreover, \(T_h\) is a contraction on
\(\overline{B_\rho({\bm x}_j)}\) with contraction factor
\[
    r_h:=1-hm=1-hC_0^-\kappa^2\in[0,1).
\]
Consequently, every initialization
\({\bm z}^{(0)}\in\overline{B_\rho({\bm x}_j)}\) generates iterates
\[
    {\bm z}^{(n+1)}=T_h({\bm z}^{(n)})
\]
that remain in \(B_\rho({\bm x}_j)\) and converge to the unique local
minimizer \(\widetilde{\bm x}_j\). More precisely,
\begin{equation}

    |{\bm z}^{(n)}-\widetilde{\bm x}_j|
    \leq
    r_h^n|{\bm z}^{(0)}-\widetilde{\bm x}_j|,
    \qquad n\geq0,
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}

    0
    \leq
    \widetilde q({\bm z}^{(n)})-\widetilde q(\widetilde{\bm x}_j)
    \leq
    \frac{M}{2}r_h^{2n}
    |{\bm z}^{(0)}-\widetilde{\bm x}_j|^2.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:33:43.752886+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_af148899ad2568e533147c56514327fd2e5213c38adeef15b4543cbbba0efd5a","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:prop_of_bessel_space of arXiv:2609.01984, 'Instantaneous shrinking of supports for stochastic PDEs\footnote{JY was supported by a KIA'] Let $p>1$ and $\eta\in\mathbb{R}$.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item 
 
The space $C_c^\infty$ is dense in $H_p^\eta$. 
\item 
 
Let $\eta-\frac1p=n+\nu$ for some $n=0,1,\ldots$ and $\nu\in(0,1]$. Then, for every
$i\in\{0,1,\ldots,n\}$,
\begin{equation}
    \|D^i u\|_{C(\mathbb{R})}
    +
    \|D^n u\|_{\mathcal C^\nu(\mathbb{R})}
    \le
    N\|u\|_{H_p^\eta},
\end{equation}
where $N=N(p,\eta)$, and $\mathcal C^\nu$ is the Zygmund space.
\item 

For every integer $i\ge0$, the operator $D^i:H_p^\eta\to H_p^{\eta-i}$ is bounded. Moreover, for every $u\in H_p^{\eta+i}$,
\[
    \|D^i u\|_{H_p^\eta}
    \le
    N\|u\|_{H_p^{\eta+i}},
\]
where $N=N(p,\eta,i)$.

\item 

Let $p\in(1,\infty)$ and $\mu\le\eta$. If $u\in H_p^{\eta}$, then $u\in H_p^{\mu}$ and
\[ \|u\|_{H_p^{\mu}}\le\|u\|_{H_p^{\eta}}. \]
Moreover, if $q\in(1,\infty)$ satisfies $\eta-\frac{1}{p}=\mu-\frac{1}{q}$, then
\[ \|u\|_{H_q^{\mu}}\le N\|u\|_{H_p^{\eta}}, \]
where $N=N(\eta,\mu,p,q)$.

\item 

Let
\[
\varepsilon\in[0,1],
\qquad
p_i\in(1,\infty),
\qquad
\eta_i\in\mathbb{R},
\qquad i=0,1,
\]
and suppose
\[
    \eta=\varepsilon\eta_0+(1-\varepsilon)\eta_1,
    \qquad
    \frac1p=\frac{\varepsilon}{p_0}+\frac{1-\varepsilon}{p_1}.
\]
Then 
\[
    \|u\|_{H_p^\eta}
    \le
    \|u\|_{H_{p_0}^{\eta_0}}^\varepsilon
    \|u\|_{H_{p_1}^{\eta_1}}^{1-\varepsilon}.
\]
In particular, for every $\delta>0$,
\[
    \|u\|_{H_p^\eta}
    \le
    \delta\|u\|_{H_{p_0}^{\eta_0}}
    +
    N(\delta)\|u\|_{H_{p_1}^{\eta_1}} .
\]

\item  If $u\in H_p^\eta$, $a\in B^{|\eta|+\alpha}$ and $b\in B^{|\eta|+\alpha}(\ell_2)$, then
\[
    \|au\|_{H_p^\eta}
    \le
    N\|a\|_{B^{|\eta|+\alpha}}\|u\|_{H_p^\eta},
\]
and
\[
    \|bu\|_{H_p^\eta(\ell_2)}
    \le
    N\|b\|_{B^{|\eta|+\alpha}(\ell_2)}\|u\|_{H_p^\eta},
\] 
where $N=N(\alpha,\eta,p)$. 
\item

Let $\Theta\in C_c^\infty$ be nonnegative with
$\int_{\mathbb{R}}\Theta(x)\,\mathrm{d} x=1$, and set $\Theta_k(x):=k\Theta(kx)$ for
$k\ge1$. Then, for every $u\in H_p^\eta$,
\[
    \|u*\Theta_k\|_{H_p^\eta}
    \le
    \|u\|_{H_p^\eta}.
\]

\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:51:12.736418+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_af1d08b927c9ea21eb34609c68751c499c0c6ce9ff671542dad490dcf3b0530d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 32 of arXiv:2605.02002, 'Glauber dynamics for random field Ising models on bounded degree graphs and MLSI'] Suppose that the graph $G=(V,E)$ has $\alpha$-stretched exponential growth for some $\alpha\in(0,1)$. Suppose that the RFIM measure $\mu_G$ on $G$ satisfies $\operatorname{WSM}(C)$ for some $C>0$. Then we can find $C_0=C_0(\alpha,C_\alpha,C)>0$ such that for any $p\geq 1$,

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:53:39.148280+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_af22fbed41e4f7db5532d301174d90570389b8674e499209098b344e8f3378ae","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 19 of arXiv:2608.26953, '2608.26953'] Let \(\widehat{\mathsf{DG}}_n\) be the full subcategory of \(\mathsf{DG}_n\) whose objects \((\Omega^\bullet,\wedge,d)\) satisfy the following conditions.

{"assumptions":["real variable on [-1, 1] for the extremal statements; the polynomials themselves are defined on all of R and C"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:31:12.479741+00:00","domain":"approximation theory","id":"claim_af2c306d13e82f8e10b1a499cd863744a70e37247652744c79e094c450f9b166","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"The Chebyshev polynomials of the first kind are defined on [-1, 1] by T_n(cos theta) = cos(n theta), n = 0, 1, 2, ...; equivalently T_0 = 1, T_1 = x and T_{n+1}(x) = 2 x T_n(x) - T_{n-1}(x). Facts: (1) T_n is a polynomial of degree n with leading coefficient 2^{n-1} for n >= 1, and T_n(x) = ((x + sqrt(x^2 - 1))^n + (x - sqrt(x^2 - 1))^n) / 2 for all real x (cosh(n arccosh x) for x >= 1); (2) |T_n(x)| <= 1 on [-1, 1], with T_n(cos(k pi / n)) = (-1)^k at the n + 1 extremal points and zeros at cos((2k - 1) pi / (2n)), k = 1..n, all in (-1, 1); (3) orthogonality: integral_{-1}^{1} T_m(x) T_n(x) dx / sqrt(1 - x^2) = 0 for m != n, pi for m = n = 0, pi/2 for m = n >= 1; (4) MINIMAX (Chebyshev): among all monic polynomials of degree n, 2^{1-n} T_n has the smallest maximum absolute value on [-1, 1], namely 2^{1-n}, and it is the unique minimiser; equivalently x^n is best approximated in the sup norm on [-1, 1] by polynomials of degree < n with error 2^{1-n}; (5) Chebyshev interpolation at the zeros of T_{n+1} has Lebesgue constant O(log n) and the Chebyshev series of a Lipschitz function converges uniformly, which is why Chebyshev nodes replace equispaced nodes (Runge's phenomenon) in numerical analysis. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:37:15.114475+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_af2c3c95794da284143e0e136508dbae4e474b0dd50b476922d619f82b134eff","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 3 of arXiv:2607.11773, '2607.11773'] A family $\Phi =
                           \left\{\Phi(t, \tau): t \in \mathbb{R}^+, \tau \in \mathbb{R}
                           \right\}$
  of mappings from $\left( \mathcal{P}_m(D_{\rho}), d_{\mathcal{P}(D_{\rho})} \right)$
  to itself 
  is called a non-autonomous cocycle on $\left( \mathcal{P}_m(D_{\rho}), d_{\mathcal{P}(D_{\rho})} \right)$
  if $ \Phi $ satisfies 
  the following conditions:
   for all $\tau \in \mathbb{R}$ and $t,s \in \mathbb{R}^+$:

  (i) $\Phi(0, \tau) = I$,
      where $ I $ is the identity operator on $\left( \mathcal{P}_m(D_{\rho}), d_{\mathcal{P}(D_{\rho})} \right)$;

  (ii) $\Phi(t+s, \tau) = \Phi(t,s+\tau) \circ \Phi(s,\tau)$.

  $ \Phi $ is continuous from  $\left( \mathscr{B} , d_{\mathcal{P}(D_{\rho})} \right)$
  to $\left( \mathcal{P}_m(D_{\rho}),  d_{\mathcal{P}(D_{\rho})} \right)$,
  then   $\Phi$ is 
  said to be continuous on bounded subsets of $ \mathcal{P}_m(D_{\rho}) $.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:42:16.236249+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_af301d480ff0d63b1823f79073205a288d43b79de86ce0d2782100e31d4bfd4e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem kpartW1 of arXiv:2607.00149, '\bf Uniform-in-time Propagation-of-Chaos for\\ Stein Variational Gradient Descent'] Let Assumption~(ass:w1-normalized-matern of the paper) hold and suppose the joint initial law of the particles is exchangeable. For fixed \(k\ge1\), define
the random \(k\)-fold empirical occupation measure
\[
        \widehat\mu_T^{N,k}
        :=
        \frac1T\int_0^T (\mu_t^N)^{\odot k}\,dt,
        \qquad
        \overline{\mu^{\otimes k}}_T
        :=
        \frac1T\int_0^T \mu_t^{\otimes k}\,dt,
\]
where
\[
(\mu_t^N)^{\odot k}
:=
\frac{1}{(N)_k}
\sum_{\substack{1\le i_1,\ldots,i_k\le N\\
i_1,\ldots,i_k\ {\rm distinct}}}
\delta_{\bigl(x_{i_1}^N(t),\ldots,x_{i_k}^N(t)\bigr)},
\qquad
(N)_k:=N(N-1)\cdots(N-k+1).
\]
Let \(W_1^{(k)}\) be the Wasserstein distance on \((\mathbb R^d)^k\)
associated with the product cost
\(
        d_k(x,y):=\sum_{\ell=1}^k \|x_\ell-y_\ell\| .
\)
Then, with $\gamma$ as in Theorem~(prop:uniform-time-averaged-w1 of the paper),
\begin{equation}
\lim_{M \to \infty} \, \limsup_{N \to \infty}\,\sup_{T>0}
\mathbb P\left(
W_1^{(k)}
\left(
\widehat\mu_T^{N,k},
\overline{\mu^{\otimes k}}_T
\right)
>
M(\log \log N)^{-\gamma/2}
\right)=0.
\end{equation}
Moreover, suppose the initial distributions satisfy (equation Gaussexp of the paper). 
Define, for $k \ge 1$,
\[
        \bar\mu_T^{N,k}
        :=
        \frac1T\int_0^T
        \mathcal L(x_1^N(t),\ldots,x_k^N(t))\,dt,
        \qquad
        \overline{\mu^{\otimes k}}_T
        :=
        \frac1T\int_0^T \mu_t^{\otimes k}\,dt ,
\]
where $L(x_1^N(t),\ldots,x_k^N(t))$ denotes the joint law of $(x_1^N(t),\ldots,x_k^N(t))$.
Then there is \(C_k<\infty\) such that, for all sufficiently large \(N\),
\begin{equation}
        \sup_{T>0}
        W_1^{(k)}
        \left(
        \bar\mu_T^{N,k},
        \overline{\mu^{\otimes k}}_T
        \right)
        \le
        C_k(\log\log N)^{-\gamma/2}.
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:15:34.384792+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_af372d3b39aa2d94abe5b55051fe70d5ed1b8b33d50692877fdf63145a880933","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 14 of arXiv:2609.03248, 'Connections between colored restricted $b$-ary and ordinary partitions'] Let $b\geq 2$ and $\rho\geq 1$ be integers. For each $i=1, 2, \ldots, \rho$, 
let $(z_{i,1}, z_{i,2}, \ldots)$ be an infinite sequence of parameters 
satisfying $|z_{i,j}|\leq r^j$ for a fixed real $r\geq 1$, and let $Z$ denote 
the collection of all $z_{i,j}$. Then we define the sequence
$C_b^\rho(n;Z)$ by the generating function
\begin{equation}
\sum_{n=0}^\infty C_b^\rho(n;Z)q^n =\prod_{j=0}^\infty\prod_{i=1}^\rho
\left(1+z_{i,1}q^{b^j}+z_{i,2}q^{2\cdot b^j}+z_{i,3}q^{3\cdot b^j}+\dots\right).
\end{equation}
When $z_{i,j}=1$ for all $1\leq i\leq\rho$ and $j\geq 1$, we set
$C_b^\rho(n):=C_b^\rho(n;Z)$, so that
\begin{equation}
\sum_{n=0}^\infty C_b^\rho(n)q^n =\prod_{j=0}^\infty
\left(1+q^{b^j}+q^{2\cdot b^j}+q^{3\cdot b^j}+\dots\right)^\rho
=\prod_{j=0}^\infty\frac{1}{\left(1-q^{b^j}\right)^\rho}.
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:30:52.739233+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_af450bf1c04dd962777a373b3274ebb387b0a16402a997837b1c21544c9d132b","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 9 of arXiv:2506.10494, 'Geometric Jensen-Shannon Divergence Between Gaussian Measures On Hilbert Space'] [\textbf{Alpha Log-Determinant divergences between positive definite trace class operators - \cite{Minh:LogDet2016}}]
			
			Assume that {$\dim(\H) = \infty$}. For {$-1 < \alpha < 1$},
			
			the Alpha Log-Det divergence 
			
			$d^{\alpha}_{\logdet}[(A+\gamma I), (B+ \mu I)]$ between  $(A+\gamma I) > 0, (B+\mu I) > 0$,
			$A, B \in \Tr(\H)$, $\gamma,\mu \in \R$, 
			
			is defined to be
			
			\begin{align}
				&d^{\alpha}_{\logdet}
				[(A+\gamma I), (B+ \mu I)]
				\nonumber
				\\
				& = \frac{4}{1-\alpha^2}  
				\log\left[\frac{\detX\left(\frac{1-\alpha}{2}(A+\gamma I) + \frac{1+\alpha}{2}(B+\mu I)\right)}{\detX(A+\gamma I)^{\beta}\detX(B + \mu I)^{1-\beta}}\left(\frac{\gamma}{\mu}\right)^{\beta - \frac{1-\alpha}{2}}\right],
				
			\end{align}
			where {$\beta = \frac{(1-\alpha)\gamma}{(1-\alpha) \gamma + (1+\alpha)\mu}$}.
			
			
			
			
			
			
			
			
			
			
			
				
				
				
				
				
				
				
				
			
				
				
				
				
				
				
				
				
				
			
			The limiting cases $\alpha \approach \pm 1$ are defined by
			\begin{align}
				&
				
				d^{1}_{\logdet}[(A+\gamma I), (B+\mu I)] = \left(\frac{\gamma}{\mu}-1\right)\log\frac{\gamma}{\mu} 
				\nonumber
				\\
				&\;\;\;\;\;+ \trX[(B+\mu I)^{-1}(A+\gamma I) - I] - \frac{\gamma}{\mu}\log\detX[(B+\mu I)^{-1}(A+\gamma I)].
				
				
				
				\\
				&
				
				d^{-1}_{\logdet}[(A+\gamma I), (B+\mu I)] = 
				\left(\frac{\mu}{\gamma}-1\right)\log\frac{\mu}{\gamma} 
				
				\nonumber
				\\
				&+ \trX\left[(A+\gamma I)^{-1}(B+\mu I) - I\right] - \frac{\mu}{\gamma}\log\detX[(A+\gamma I)^{-1}(B+\mu I)].
				
			\end{align}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T00:15:09.103457+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_af455860804200f9da1e82a3da978bc5e17d63f809a5d79200dcfcf3d2487a6d","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition Quotient graph induces by graph of arXiv:2411.11341, 'Ultra high order cumulants and quantitative CLT for polynomials in Random Matrices'] Let $G_1,\\dots,G_n$ be unoriented graphs with set of vertices and edges $(V_i,E_i)$ for $1\\leq i\\leq n$. We denote the vertices $\\{v_i,v_j\\}$ associated with the edge $e\\in E_T$ by $V(e)$.  \nWe call the triple $T=(V_T,E_T,\\{V(e)\\}_{e\\in E_T})$ a \\textit{graph of the graphs} $G_1,\\dots,G_n$. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:09:43.682340+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_af46b4cf56dd51b7cb69e8bc90c8cf2f734de6ab113c1193e9b207638b55d439","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma NEW-l:pre-Gron of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] Consider Lipschitz diffusion  coefficients $(b,\sigma)$ as defined in Definition~(NEW-d:lip_assum of the paper). Let $\{X[x]\}_{x\in{\cal X }}$ and $\{X'[x]\}_{x\in{\cal X }}$ be two families of  continuous  processes in $\mathbb{R}^{d'}$ adapted to the filtration generated by the family of i.i.d. standard Brownian motions $\{Z_x(\cdot)\}_{x \in {\cal X }}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d'}$ on $[0,t_0]$ 
and $\mathbb{E} [\|X[x]\|^2]<\infty$, $\mathbb{E} [\|X'[x]\|^2]<\infty$ for all  $x\in{\cal X }$.
Consider  the family of stochastic processes $\{Y[x]\}_{x\in{\cal X }}$ on $\mathbb {M} $, defined on $[0,t_0]$ by
\begin{equation}
   
Y(x,t):= Y(x,0)+\int_0^t b(t, X[x], X[N_x])\, \mathrm{d} t + \sigma(t, X[x], X[N_x])\, \mathrm{d} Z_x(t),
\end{equation}
along with the family of stochastic processes $Y'(x,t)$ on $\mathbb {M} $ defined as above but with $X'$ instead of $X$.
These processes are indexed by the vertices $x\in{\cal X }$, they utilize the graph neighborhood $N_x=\{y\in{\cal X }:y\sim x\}$ on a given graph $\Psi({\cal X })$
and they share the same initial conditions $Y(x,0)=Y'(x,0)$.
Then for any $x\in{\cal X }$ and $t\in[0,t_0]$, we have
\begin{equation}

\mathbb{E}  [\| Y[x,t] - Y'[x,t] \|^2]
\le 32\max(t,1)K_t^2\int_{0}^t \max_{y\in\mathfrak{B}_1(x)} \mathbb{E}  [\| X[y,s] - X'[y,s] \|^2]\, \mathrm{d} s,
\end{equation}
where $\mathfrak{B}_1(x)$  is graph ball on  $\Psi({\cal X })$ of radius $1$ centered at~$x$
and where $K_t$ is the Lipschitz diffusion constant given in Definition \ref
{NEW-d:lip_assum}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["i.i.d. nonnegative weights on Z^d, d >= 2","F(0) < p_c(d), so the time constant is a norm and the shape is bounded","E min{t_1^d, ..., t_{2d}^d} < infinity, equivalently E[Y^d] < infinity for Y the minimum of 2d independent copies of tau_e - and this condition is necessary, not just sufficient","no curvature, strict convexity or differentiability of B_nu is asserted; those are open"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.542575+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_af7572591de074922b3c8bcd06ef7d3cfa5df7ed73222e70cd4667e68059f97c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Consider i.i.d. first-passage percolation on Z^d, d >= 2, with edge-weight law nu. Assume the two conditions (i) E min{ t_1^d, ..., t_{2d}^d } < infinity, where the t_i are 2d independent copies of tau_e - equivalently E[Y^d] < infinity where Y is the MINIMUM of 2d copies, the two being the same because x -> x^d is increasing on [0, infinity) - and (ii) F(0) < p_c(d). Let B(t) = {x : T(0, x) <= t}, the random ball. Then there is a DETERMINISTIC, convex, COMPACT set B_nu in R^d with NON-EMPTY INTERIOR, symmetric about the axes, such that for every eps > 0, P( (1-eps) B_nu is contained in B(t)/t which is contained in (1+eps) B_nu for all large t ) = 1. The set B_nu is the unit ball of the time constant. Condition (i) is NOT merely convenient: if it fails then for every C > 0 the sum over x of P(m(x) > C|x|) diverges, where m(x) is the minimum weight over the edges at x, and Borel-Cantelli forces T(0,x)/|x| > C for infinitely many x almost surely, so the shape statement itself fails. Condition (ii) is what keeps the shape bounded: if F(0) >= p_c then zero-weight edges percolate, the time constant vanishes and B_nu is all of R^d. What is NOT known, and is repeatedly imported elsewhere as an unproven hypothesis: whether the boundary of B_nu is STRICTLY CONVEX, whether it is DIFFERENTIABLE, and whether it has uniformly positive CURVATURE. Those are open for every non-degenerate weight distribution in every dimension, which is why the Newman-Piza exponent bounds and the directed-geodesic results carry non-constructive curvature or differentiability hypotheses. B_nu is not computed explicitly for any non-trivial F. [Cox and Durrett (1981), verified against Auffinger, Damron and Hanson, 50 Years of First-Passage Percolation, Section 2.2]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["k >= 3 (for k = 2 the bound is trivial)","the random colouring is uniform and independent over edges; the argument uses only the expectation","the bound is on the diagonal Ramsey number; the off-diagonal case R(3,k) has a different order, of k^2 / log k"],"created_at":"2026-09-02T07:51:33.049085+00:00","domain":"Ramsey theory and the probabilistic method (hand-authored statement with hypotheses, 2026-09-02)","id":"claim_af7faf3b27b053c03395f6d63edc5d5d5ce31c728526823043a89ac793dcdeb1","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Erdos (1947): R(k,k) > 2^{k/2} for every k >= 3. Colour the edges of the complete graph on n vertices red or blue independently and uniformly at random. The expected number of monochromatic k-cliques is C(n,k) 2^{1 - C(k,2)}; when n = floor(2^{k/2}) this expectation is below 1 for k >= 3, so some colouring has no monochromatic k-clique, and R(k,k) > n. This is the first-moment method (a union bound over the C(n,k) cliques); only linearity of expectation is used, and no clique needs to be independent of another. With Stirling's formula the same count gives R(k,k) >= (1 + o(1)) (k / (e sqrt 2)) 2^{k/2}; the Lovasz local lemma (Spencer 1975) improves the constant to (1 + o(1)) (sqrt 2 / e) k 2^{k/2} and nothing better than the exponent k/2 is known. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:04:59.434011+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_afa7a9ab0ad47e1dd2adb6cdd3822de9b096a30633e178dcc501fd1e7b1ec702","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:concentration-mf of arXiv:2605.20697, 'Uniform-in-time propagation of chaos for \\ Second-Order Consensus-Based Optimization'] Fix \(q>2\), and assume that the objective function \(f\) satisfies
    (assumption:bounded of the paper). Consider \(J\) independent mean-field processes
    \((\overline X_t^j,\overline V_t^j)\), initialized with i.i.d.\ samples from
    \(\overline\rho_0\in\mathcal P_{2q}(\mathbb R^{2d})\).

    Define
    \[
        \overline Y_t^j
        :=
        \overline X_t^j-m_{\overline X}(\overline\rho_t),
        \qquad
        \widehat{\overline Z}_t^j
        :=
        \bigl(\overline V_t^j-m_{\overline V}(\overline\rho_t)\bigr)
        -
        \frac1\gamma\overline Y_t^j,
    \]
    and let
    \[
        \overline L_2^j(t)
        :=
        \psi_2(\overline Y_t^j,\widehat{\overline Z}_t^j),
        \qquad
        \overline L_2^J(t)
        :=
        \frac1J\sum_{j=1}^J \overline L_2^j(t).
    \]
    Assume the parameter conditions needed for
    (prop:ito-mfl-centered-lyapunov-differential of the paper) at \(p=2\) and \(p=2q\).
    Let \(\kappa\) satisfy
    \[
        0<\kappa<\min\left\{\lambda_{2},\frac{\lambda_{2q}}q\right\},
    \]
    and assume the concentration noise absorption condition
    \begin{equation}
        \sigma^2
        \leqslant
        \frac{m^2 c_1^{(2)}(\lambda_{2}-\kappa)}
        {2\tau(S)(1+C_{\mathrm{lem}})}.
    \end{equation}
    Then, for every threshold \(A>0\) and every \(J\in\mathbb N_+\),
    \begin{equation}
        \mathbf P\left[
            \sup_{t\geqslant0}
            \e^{\kappa t}\overline L_2^J(t)
            \geqslant
            \mathbf{E}[\overline L_2^J(0)]+A
        \right]
        \leqslant
        \frac{C_{\mathrm{Bad}}^{\mathrm{MF}}}{A^q}
        J^{-\frac q2}\,
        \overline{\mathcal L}_{2q}(0).
    \end{equation}
    Consequently, by the coercivity bound for \(\psi_2\),
    \begin{equation}
        \mathbf P\left[
            \sup_{t\geqslant0}
            \e^{\kappa t}
            \mathfrak M_2(\mu_{\overline X_t^J})
            \geqslant
            \frac{\mathbf{E}[\overline L_2^J(0)]+A}{c_1^{(2)}}
        \right]
        \leqslant
        \frac{C_{\mathrm{Bad}}^{\mathrm{MF}}}{A^q}
        J^{-\frac q2}\,
        \overline{\mathcal L}_{2q}(0).
    \end{equation}
    The constant is
    \[
        C_{\mathrm{Bad}}^{\mathrm{MF}}
        :=
        3^q
        \left(
            \overline C_{\mathrm{MZ}}
            +
            C_{Z,q}
            +
            C_{\mathrm{Mart}}
        \right),
    \]
    where
    \[
        \overline C_{\mathrm{MZ}}
        :=
        \frac{C_{{\rm MZ},q} C_\phi^q 2^{q-1}}{c_{1,2q}},
    \]
    \[
        C_{Z,q}
        :=
        \frac{
            2(2K_{\mathrm{tr}})^q C_{{\rm WM},2q}
        }{
            c_{1,2q}\ell^{q-1}(\lambda_{2q}-q\kappa)
        },
        \qquad
        \ell
        :=
        \frac{\lambda_{2q}-q\kappa}{2(q-1)},
    \]
    and
    \[
        C_{\mathrm{Mart}}
        :=
        \frac{
            2^{q+1}C_{\mathrm{BDG},q}C_{\sigma,q}
        }{
            \lambda_{2q}-q\kappa
        }
        \left(
            \frac{q-2}{\lambda_{2q}-q\kappa}
        \right)^{\frac q2-1}.
    \]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:28:31.998495+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_afb4969a1c1d9576129aa4f19cf2827a29f438b1abfbe733ed54ea64ded251e2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 5 ({Lemma 3.5 in \cite{vanwerde2024recovering}}) of arXiv:2512.02661, 'Worst-case mixing estimates for Brownian motion with semipermeable barriers'] Suppose that $\delta < 1/2$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:49:05.486331+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_afdf83da9723c1103761759b9ff4e4308e5736777232d05673399dc0c58c92a8","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Deff sobolev-spaces of arXiv:2601.19145, 'Stochastic Persistence in Infinite Dimensions'] For $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and $1 < p < \infty$ we define the Sobolev spaces recursively by $W^{0,p} \coloneqq L^p$ and
    $$W^{k,p} \coloneqq \{u \in L^p \mid \partial_iu \in W^{k-1,p} \text{ for } i = 1,\dots, N\}$$
    endowed with the norm
    $$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}} \coloneqq \sum_{i=1}^N\|\partial_i u\|_{W^{k-1,p}} + \|u\|_{L^p} \,.$$
    In the definition, it is implicit that the weak derivatives $\partial_i u$ exist. For $s > 0$ (not necessarily an integer), we define $W^{s,p}$ via complex interpolation, see [interpolation-simple] with the domain $\mathbb{R}^n$, but the results also hold for our domain $D$ via extension operators.

    If $D = \mathbb{T}^N$, we also define $W^{-s,p}$ to be the dual of $W^{s,p^*}$, where $1/p + 1/p^* = 1$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:53:53.199577+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b02fd5d34763cd070fdcc8423370ba67d5c5e32dc81514e3e73bc040065eb529","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 12 of arXiv:2606.11774, 'Martingale Solutions to a Stochastic Keller-Segel System with nonlocal Source and Super-li'] [Compactness criterion] 
    Let $\mathbb{H}$ be a real separable Hilbert space, $\mathbb{U}$ be a real reflexive Banach space such that the embedding  $\mathbb{U}\hookrightarrow \mathbb{H}$ is continuous and dense. Let  $\mathbb{U}'$ be the  dual space of $\mathbb{U}$   such that  the embedding $\mathbb{U}\hookrightarrow \mathbb{H}\cong \mathbb{H}'\hookrightarrow\mathbb{U}'$  are continuous.
         Let $E,\mathbb{V}$ be real reflexive  Banach spaces  such that the embedding $\mathbb{V}\hookrightarrow  E\hookrightarrow\mathbb{U}'$ are continuous and the embedding $\mathbb{V}\hookrightarrow E$ is compact.
          Let \begin{align}
    \mathcal{Z}
:= C([0,T];\mathbb U') \cap L^{q}_{w}(0,T;\mathbb{V}) \cap L^{p}(0,T;E) \cap C([0,T];\mathbb{H}_{w}),\,1<q\leq p<\infty,
\end{align} with the topology $\mathcal{T}$ induced by the supremum of  corresponding topologies. The definition of these functional spaces and the corresponding topologies can be found in \cite[Section 2.1]{law2014existence}. Then a set $\mathcal{K}\subset \mathcal{Z}$ is $\mathcal{T}$-relatively compact if the following
four conditions hold
\begin{itemize}
    \item[(a)] 
$\sup_{v\in \mathcal{K}}\sup_{s\in[0,T]}\|v(s)\|_{\mathbb{H}}<\infty,$
\item[(b)]
$\sup_{v\in \mathcal{K}}\int_{0}^{T}\|v(s)\|_{\mathbb{V}}^{q}ds<\infty,
\quad \text{i.e. } \mathcal{K} \text{ is bounded in } L^{q}(0,T;\mathbb{V}),$
\item[(c)]
$\sup_{v\in \mathcal{K}}\int_{0}^{T}\|v(s)\|_{E}^{r}ds<\infty,
\quad \text{i.e. } \mathcal{K} \text{ is bounded in } L^{r}(0,T;E)$, where $r>p$,
\item[(d)]
$\lim_{\delta\to 0}\sup_{v\in \mathcal{K}}\sup_{\substack{s,t\in[0,T]\\ |t-s|\le \delta}}
\|v(t)-v(s)\|_{\mathbb U'}=0$.
\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:20:07.898636+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b0420ba83e86da50a5f04757999deb6d59929e3883f02bab1358bbddbe2146ea","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma majorization_property_sylvester of arXiv:2608.23765, '\texorpdfstring{Tight Majorizations and Convergence Rates\\ of Nuclear Norm Minimization I'] \mbox{}\\
	Let $\mathbf{Z} \in \R^{d_1 \times d_2}$ be arbitrary but fixed.

    be orthogonal projection matrices.
    Denote by $\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{U},\bot} := \mathbf{I} - \mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{U}}$

    Assume that

    Define the operator
    $\mathcal{C}: \R^{d_1 \times d_2} \to \R^{d_1 \times d_2}$
    by 
    $\mathcal{C} (\mathbf{A}) 
    := \mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{U}} \mathbf{A} \mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{V}} + \mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{U},\bot} \mathbf{A} \mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{V},\bot}$
    for any matrix $\mathbf{A} \in \R^{d_1 \times d_2}$.
    Then the following statements hold true:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item The equation
        \begin{equation}
             \mathbf{L}_{\mathbf{U}}  \mathbf{W} 
            + \mathbf{W}  \mathbf{L}_{\mathbf{V}} 
            =

        has a unique solution $\mathbf{W} \in \R^{d_1 \times d_2}$.
        \item

For a balanced d-colour generalized Polya urn with replacement matrix R and balance lambda, Neri and Pinto (arXiv:2607.07309, Remark 3.7) asked whether the form w -> <w(R - lambda I), w> is negative definite on the sum-zero hyperplane H for the Euclidean inner product on all d coordinates or on the first d - 1 (their Proposition 3.6 with p = d or p = d - 1). \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item If \(I\subset\{1,\ldots,r\}\) is the set of nonzero replica couplings,
then the corresponding twisted polynomial de Rham complex has cohomology
only in top degree, of rank \(\mu^{|I|}\).  Integrating the inactive Gaussian
variables gives compatible finite reduction maps for all inclusions of
supports.  Thus the zero-coupling boundary is a rank-changing family over

lattice of rank \(\mu^{|I|}\).  Writing \(G\) for the leading rescaled

basis of descending thimbles, and any finite family of continued

  \Pi_{\mathrm{sel}}
  =

  \mathcal P_{\mathrm{th}}\,

\end{equation}
Here \(B_{\mathrm{Jac}}\) is a rational-algebraic change from Jacobi normal

{"assumptions":["N>=5,d=2,K=3,r=2,ell=0,n=6; two A/S pairs and remaining known S contexts","Actual iid factual samples without tags; p uniform on contexts then true candidates; all A truth supports allowed","Each data-dependent generator robustly exact-level source-calibrated at zero in every compatible world","Conditional V(D) maximizes after data; global Gamma_N maximizes over a fixed world before data"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T21:04:18.141881+00:00","domain":"statistical learning; calibrated generation; global minimax and actual iid data","id":"claim_b06700a866ade064c72020029c1c0095e0197f769e2a689f4972776a20807bd5","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Own-work draft; proof (unaudited), independent mathematical, priority and target-scope review pending. # A genuine zero-budget global averaging obstruction from repeated facts

T379-C020 v2, proof (unaudited), exact all-world checks PASS; audit pending.
Target 1, secondary target 2: auxiliary-route obstruction, not an exact
global frontier. This concerns actual iid training, not only an
artificial conditional posterior or a handpicked world.

## Experiment and objectives

Fix any N>=5. Set d=2,K=3,r=2,ell=0,n=6. There are two A/S pairs,
one A and one S each, and N-4 fixed S contexts. A has an arbitrary
uniform two-element truth support; S has all three truths. Source p
chooses contexts uniformly and then truths uniformly. Observe six
iid factual samples WITHOUT orientation labels or verifier information.
Require every data-dependent generator to have source Mis_infinity=0
in EVERY world compatible with its observed facts, at exact score bins.

For data D let V(D) be the conditional minimum over robustly calibrated
generators of their maximum compatible-world false mass. Let

 B_N=E_w[V(D)],
 Gamma_N=inf_policy max_fixed_world w E_w[H(policy(D))].

B_N is independent of the fixed actual world w: sibling permutations
and within-context candidate permutations map any world to any other,
preserve the model and compatibility, and carry source calibration,
false mass and V(D) with them. The data laws are carried along by the
same bijections. Thus V(D)'s distribution is identical in all worlds.

The candidate strict inequality is

 Gamma_N <= B_N-5/(1008*N^7) < B_N.                      (1)

No numerical value of B_N or Gamma_N is claimed. The point is that
expected conditional worst-world risk overstates global expected
minimax risk even at ZERO source calibration budget.

## Finite conditional selectors exist

There are finitely many actual worlds and finitely many score
partitions of the NK atoms. For a zero-calibrated g its score partition
Pi satisfies g=p_w,Pi for every compatible w, so a fixed Pi admits at
most one such g. Merging equal-score cells preserves this property.
The one-cell uniform generator is always feasible, so each V(D) is
attained among finitely many candidates. Choose any deterministic
conditional minimizer g*_D by a fixed tie rule. This selector is an
existence construction, not a claim of computational efficiency.
For every actual w it satisfies H_w(g*_D)<=V(D) pointwise.
Datasets incompatible with every source world may use the uniform
fallback; they have probability zero under every actual world.

## Observable rare event and its conditional value

Let E be the event that all six samples have this pattern:

* Four copies of ONE candidate in ONE context of one pair;
* one fact in each of the two contexts of the other pair;
* no other observations.

The pair roles, repeated context, candidate identities and sample
order are unrestricted. E is recognizable from the data alone.
Its known-truth counts are (1,0) in the repeated pair and (1,1) in
the other pair, all strictly below r=2. Thus C017's exact zero-budget
frontier, with pairwise minima 0 and 1, gives

 V(D)=1/(3N)+7/(24N)=5/(8N) on E.                        (2)

For clarity, the (1,0) pair's zero-calibrated bins must contain whole
contexts: support swaps make each uncertified set constant-score and
orientation invariance with the zero-known sibling leaves no known
truths available to peel from that context. Forgetting the repeated
fact therefore preserves all source-bin and false-count information.
The resulting balanced (0,0)/(1,1) game has artificial mean densities
1/(3N),7/(24N) on its residual groups, with false risks 1/6,1/4;
safe densities are higher. The per-bin low-density tail argument
gives the lower value (2), and the invariant-group mean attains it
worldwise. This is a conditional worst-world assertion, not an
actual-orientation posterior calculation.

## A causal calibrated generator on E

Let x be the observed four-repeat context. Let a,b be the two contexts
of the other pair and let their single observed candidates be c_a,c_b.
Form B from ALL THREE atoms of x plus the four atoms of a,b other
than c_a,c_b. Its source mass is 1/N+7/(6N)=13/(6N) in every
compatible world; its seven atoms get score q=13/(42N).
Give the two observed atoms in a,b score 5/(12N). Give every other
atom score lambda=1/(3N), including the untouched sibling of x and
all fixed S contexts. The group masses sum to one. All source group
masses are invariant across orientations and supports, so exact-score
mergers preserve source Mis_infinity=0. The rule uses observed context
counts and observed truths only; it never reads the hidden orientation.

If x is actually A, false mass is H_A=2q=13/(21N).
If x is actually S, false mass is H_S=q+lambda=9/(14N).
These identities hold for every compatible truth-support choice.

## Fixed-world event probabilities, not a posterior shortcut

In ANY fixed actual world, summing over the repeated candidate
identity gives repeated-four-fact weights proportional to

 r*(1/(Nr))^4=1/(N^4*r^3) for the A context,
 K*(1/(NK))^4=1/(N^4*K^3) for the S context.

Consequently, conditional on E, the repeated context is actually A
with probability K^3/(K^3+r^3)=27/35, uniformly in every fixed world.
The exponent is THREE, not four: the number of available true
candidate identities must be included. The other pair's one sample
per context contributes 1/N^2 after its identities are summed out.

There are two choices of repeated pair and 6!/(4!1!1!)=30 orders.
Thus in every fixed world

 P_w(E)=60/N^6*(1/8+1/27)=175/(18N^6),                  (3)
 E_w[H_pool|E]=(27/35)*13/(21N)+(8/35)*9/(14N)
             =153/(245N),
 V(E)-E_w[H_pool|E]=1/(1960N).                           (4)

These are ordinary disjoint-event sums under the fixed sampling law;
no independence of learned events or hidden labels is assumed.

## Global policy and strict separation

Use the explicit pooling generator on E and g*_D otherwise. Every
outcome is robustly zero-calibrated. For every fixed actual world,

 E_w H <= E_w[1_{not E}V(D)]+P_w(E)*153/(245N)
       =B_N-P_w(E)/(1960N)
       =B_N-5/(1008N^7).

Taking the maximum over w proves (1). At N=5 the exact strict gap
certified by this construction is 1/15750000. This is an upper bound
on Gamma_N relative to B_N, not an exact value for either objective.

The result complements C014's positive-budget example and C015's
single-outcome pointwise control. Here the improvement is realized
under actual iid data, uniformly for EVERY fixed world, at zero
budget. A global expected lower bound must therefore use a valid
fixed-prior/per-world argument rather than average conditional maxima.
Primary statistic: Kalai--Vempala 2311.14648v3 Definitions 1--2 pp.8--9.
Independent mathematical, priority and target-scope audit pending.

Exact verification: logs/zero_budget_global_separation_check.json
checks all 36 fixed worlds and all 108 rare-event histograms for
N=5,6,9, totaling 6480 positive-probability source-calibration checks
and 108 exact event expectation checks. Another 108 checks verify
whole-source-family transitive relabeling. In every fixed world some
event outcomes worsen risk, so the improvement is genuinely in
expectation. A three-repeat fault produces the wrong sign in all
108 world/parameter cases. The general finite-selector and symmetry
proof supplies the global conclusion; neither B_N nor Gamma_N is
estimated numerically.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:59:53.361405+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b0a2d98bce1f63e7d800279235190f5a0a228fa89de95d2ed01f22d5153b060c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:onepoint of arXiv:2607.24705, 'Derangetropy Operators'] Let $m(q) := \mathbb{E}[W^{q}]$ and $\lambda(q) := \log m(q)$, for
		the canonical step law $W = 2\sin^{2}(\pi U)$. Then:
		\begin{enumerate}[label=\normalfont(\roman*), leftmargin=*]
			\item for $q > -\tfrac12$,
			\begin{equation}
				m(q) = \frac{2^{q}\,\Gamma(q+\tfrac12)}{\sqrt{\pi}\,\Gamma(q+1)},
				\qquad
				\lambda(q) = q\log 2 + \log\Gamma(q+\tfrac12)
				- \log\Gamma(q+1) - \tfrac12\log\pi,
				
			\end{equation}
			and $\mathbb{E}[(S_{n}'(z))^{q}] = m(q)^{n}$ exactly, for every
			fixed $z$;
			\item $\tfrac1n\log S_{n}'(z) \to -\log 2$ almost surely, and
			\begin{equation}
				\frac{\log S_{n}'(z) + n\log 2}{\sqrt{n}}
				\;\xrightarrow{\ d\ }\;
				\mathcal{N}\Big(0,\ \frac{\pi^{2}}{3}\Big),
				\qquad
				\frac{\pi^{2}}{3} = \lambda''(0)
				= \psi_{0}'(\tfrac12) - \psi_{0}'(1),
				
			\end{equation}
			with $\psi_{0}$ the digamma function, and
			$\tfrac1n\log S_{n}'$ satisfies a large deviation principle with
			rate the Legendre transform of $\lambda$;
			\item the tangents of the free energy are the information constants
			of the deterministic theory,
			\begin{equation}
				\lambda'(0) = \mathbb{E}\log W = -\log 2,
				\qquad
				\lambda'(1) = \mathbb{E}[W\log W] = 1 - \log 2,
				
			\end{equation}
			the relative entropies of the identities~(equation eq:kl-identities of the paper),
			while the deterministic sharp Lipschitz constant $2^{n}$ of
			Proposition~(prop:intertwine of the paper) is the almost sure envelope
			$S_{n}' \le 2^{n}$ and the limiting slope
			$\lambda(q) = q\log2 - \tfrac12\log q + O(1)$ as $q \to \infty$.
		\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:54:12.500599+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b0a9c4400f89d7bf0f9de264f9645f1d8099ff75a1b398ee464dfd27ee8d3162","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:chawdl of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] Fix $\rho\in \mathbb{R}$. Consider a random function $\mathcal{M}^\rho: \mathbb{Q}^4 \cap \mathbb{H}^2_\uparrow \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying the following three conditions:
		\begin{enumerate}
			\item (Triangle inequality) For any $o = (x, s)$, $p = (y, r)$, $q = (z, t) \in \mathbb{Q}_{\ge 0} \times \mathbb{Q}$ with $s<r<t$, we have
			$\mathcal{M}^\rho(o; p) + \mathcal{M}^\rho(p; q) \le \mathcal{M}^\rho(o; q)$.
			\item (Independent increments) For any $s_1<s_2<\cdots<s_k \in \mathbb{Q}$, the increments $\mathcal{M}^\rho(\cdot, s_i; \cdot, s_{i+1}):\mathbb{Q}_{\ge 0}^2 \to \mathbb{R}, i \in 1, \ldots, k-1$ are independent.
			\item (KPZ fixed point marginals) For any $f: \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} \to \mathbb{R}\cup \{-\infty\}$, with $f(\mathbb{R})\subset\mathbb{Q}\cup\{-\infty\}$ and $f^{-1}(\mathbb{R})$ being finite, $s<t \in \mathbb{Q}$, and finite $Y\subset \mathbb{Q}_{\ge 0}$, we have
			\[
			(\max_{x\in\mathbb{Q}_{\ge 0}} f(x) + \mathcal{M}^\rho(x,s;y,t): y\in Y)
			\stackrel{d}{=} ( \max_{x\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}} f(x) + \mathcal{L}^\rho(x,s;y,t): y\in Y).
			\]
		\end{enumerate}
		Then $\mathcal{M}^\rho$ has a continuous extension to $\mathbb H^2_\uparrow$, which has the same law as $\mathcal{L}^\rho$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}
