{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:35:10.786930+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d838148ea03da798b7b29810cff92e1234c7fadf7972598ea311113e2b892c7c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 7 of arXiv:2604.00630, 'The contact process on a bipartite spatial network'] Assume that~$(\gamma_1,\gamma_2) \in \mathcal S$ and~$a > 0$. 	
Let
\begin{align*}
	&\mu_{\mathsf S} := \frac{1}{\gamma_1}+\frac{1}{\gamma_1}a,\qquad \mu_{\mathsf B} := \frac{1}{\gamma_1\gamma_2} + \frac{\bar{\gamma}_2}{\gamma_1\gamma_2}a,\qquad \mu_{\mathsf D} := \frac{\gamma_2}{\Delta} + \frac{\bar{\gamma}_2}{\Delta}a,\\
	&\nu_{\mathsf S} := \frac{1}{\gamma_2} + \frac{1}{\gamma_2}a,\qquad \nu_{\mathsf B} := \frac{\bar{\gamma}_1}{\gamma_1 \gamma_2} + \frac{1}{\gamma_1 \gamma_2} a,\qquad \nu_{\mathsf D} :=  \frac{\bar{\gamma}_1}{\Delta} + \frac{\gamma_1}{\Delta}a.
\end{align*}

Also define
	\begin{equation}
	\mu_\star:= \mu_{\mathsf S}\wedge \mu_{\mathsf B}\wedge \mu_{\mathsf D},\qquad \nu_\star:=  \nu_{\mathsf S}\wedge \nu_{\mathsf B}\wedge\nu_{\mathsf D}
	\end{equation}
	and
	\begin{equation}
		A_\star:=\mu_\star \wedge (1+\bar{\gamma}_2 \nu_\star)\wedge (1+a-\Delta_2 \nu_\star+\bar{\gamma}_1 \mu_\star).
	\end{equation}
	
	Then, there exists~$C > 0$ such that, for~$\lambda$ small enough, the survival probability~$\theta(\lambda)$ of the contact process with infection rates~$(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)=(\lambda,\lambda^a)$ on~$\mathcal G$, started from only the root infected, satisfies:
	\[
		(\log \tfrac{1}{\lambda})^{-C} \cdot \lambda^{A_\star} \le \theta(\lambda) \le (\log \tfrac{1}{\lambda})^{C} \cdot \lambda^{A_\star}.
	\]
	
	Moreover,~$A_\star$ is given explicitly by the following:
	\begin{itemize}
	\item[$\mathrm{(Ia)}$] $\gamma_1 > \frac12$ and~$\gamma_2 \le \frac{\gamma_1}{1+\gamma_1} $, then
		\[
			A_\star = \mu_{\mathsf S}. 
		\]
	\item[$\mathrm{(Ib)}$] If~$\gamma_1 > \frac12$ and~$\frac{\gamma_1}{1+\gamma_1} < \gamma_2 \le \frac12$, then
		\[
			A_\star = \begin{cases} \mu_{\mathsf S} & \text{if }  a \le \frac{\gamma_1-\gamma_2}{\gamma_2-\gamma_1+\gamma_1\gamma_2};\\[.2cm]
				1+\bar{\gamma}_2 \nu_{\mathsf S} & \text{if } a >\frac{\gamma_1-\gamma_2}{\gamma_2-\gamma_1+\gamma_1\gamma_2}. 
			\end{cases}
		\]
	\item[$\mathrm{(II)}$] If~$\gamma_1 \le \frac12$ (and consequently~$\gamma_2 > \frac12$), we have
	\[
			A_\star = 1 + \bar{\gamma}_2 \nu_{\mathsf S}.
		\]
	\item[$\mathrm{(III)}$] If~$\gamma_1,\gamma_2 > \frac12$ and~$\frac{1}{\gamma_1}+\frac{1}{\gamma_2} > 3$, then
		\[
			A_\star = \begin{cases}
				1+\bar{\gamma}_2 \nu_{\mathsf S}&\text{if } a \le \frac{\bar{\gamma}_2}{\Delta_2};\\[.2cm]
				1+\bar{\gamma}_2\nu_{\mathsf B}&\text{if } a > \frac{\bar{\gamma}_2}{\Delta_2}.
			\end{cases}
		\]
	\item[$\mathrm{(IV)}$] If~$\frac{1}{\gamma_1}+\frac{1}{\gamma_2} \le 3$  (and consequently~$\gamma_1, \gamma_2 > \frac12$), then
		\[
			A_\star = \begin{cases}
				1+\bar{\gamma}_2 \nu_{\mathsf S}&\text{if } a \le \frac{\bar{\gamma}_1 \bar{\gamma}_2}{\gamma_1\gamma_2 + \gamma_2 - 1};\\[.2cm]
				1+\bar{\gamma}_2\nu_{\mathsf D}&\text{if } \frac{\bar{\gamma}_1 \bar{\gamma}_2}{\gamma_1\gamma_2 + \gamma_2 - 1} < a \le \frac{\gamma_1\gamma_2 + \gamma_1 - 1}{\bar{\gamma}_1 \bar{\gamma}_2};\\[.2cm]
				1+\bar{\gamma}_2\nu_{\mathsf B}&\text{if } a > \frac{\gamma_1\gamma_2 + \gamma_1 - 1}{\bar{\gamma}_1 \bar{\gamma}_2}.
			\end{cases}
		\]
	\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X and Y are topological spaces and X x Y carries the product topology","for the equality: both X and Y are second countable (a countable base of open sets); separable metric suffices","B(X) tensor B(Y) denotes the sigma-algebra generated by measurable rectangles, not its completion","the inclusion B(X) tensor B(Y) inside B(X x Y) needs no countability hypothesis"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:13:10.402216+00:00","domain":"measure theory and topology, Borel structures on products","id":"claim_d85e091e5868ae9cbf056305f26be57cebf2da93d681eeb18aff1182d687f85d","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X and Y be topological spaces and give X x Y the product topology. Write B(Z) for the Borel sigma-algebra of a space Z and B(X) tensor B(Y) for the product sigma-algebra, i.e. the sigma-algebra on X x Y generated by the measurable rectangles A x B with A in B(X) and B in B(Y). Then: (i) ALWAYS B(X) tensor B(Y) is contained in B(X x Y), because the two coordinate projections are continuous, hence Borel measurable. (ii) If X and Y are both SECOND COUNTABLE (each has a countable base of open sets), then equality holds: B(X x Y) = B(X) tensor B(Y). In particular this applies to separable metric spaces, so B(R^(m+n)) = B(R^m) tensor B(R^n), and to Polish spaces and to countable products of second countable spaces. Practical consequence: for second countable targets, a map into X x Y is Borel measurable exactly when both components are, and Borel functions of two variables are jointly measurable in the product sense - which is what lets Fubini-Tonelli be applied to Borel functions. WHERE IT FAILS: second countability is not a technicality. Let X be a set of cardinality strictly greater than the continuum equipped with the discrete topology, so that B(X) is the full power set and X x X is discrete. The diagonal {(x,x)} is closed, hence Borel in X x X, but by a classical theorem (B. V. Rao) the diagonal of X belongs to P(X) tensor P(X) if and only if the cardinality of X is at most the continuum. So B(X x X) strictly contains B(X) tensor B(X). The underlying reason is structural: every set in a product sigma-algebra is already measurable with respect to a countably generated pair of sub-sigma-algebras, so a product sigma-algebra can only see countably many 'coordinates' at a time, while the product topology of a non-second-countable space produces open sets that need uncountably many. A second warning of the same kind: for Lebesgue sigma-algebras the analogous equality is FALSE - the Lebesgue sigma-algebra of R^(m+n) is strictly larger than the product of the Lebesgue sigma-algebras of R^m and R^n; it is its completion.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["All restricted four-point, unit-norm centered-ReLU teacher and paired nonzero initialization assumptions of C010","Independent label noise amplitude sigma_e=c_e sqrt(kappa) eta_e^(1/4)~sqrt(kappa)e^(9/4)","Noise-averaged clean risk; simultaneous both-layer GD step 1/2; fixed nu in (0,1]","Even width limit precedes feature-scale limit; local windows only; eta_e is spectral ratio, not GD step size"],"created_at":"2026-10-22T00:34:50.829441+00:00","domain":"learning theory","id":"claim_d89b9de19b9c660b1053843fd221195d71bd568e8a0d66ceffe03289fef81a6d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"# Joint low-noise central-window bifurcation

T267 / Target 2 / C012 / proof draft (unaudited); novelty unestablished.
This is a local, rescaled noise-onset result in C010's restricted model.
It is not an exact global two-critical-noise-level theorem.

## 1. Precise scaling and result

Use C010's four-point stratified design, centered unit-norm ReLU teacher,
paired nonzero initialization with fixed nu in (0,1], both-layer GD with
step 1/2, and label-noise-averaged clean risk Q. Let alpha=alpha_e and
let b_h denote C009's full-kernel rates. Set

eta_e=(b2+b12)/b1 ~ e,
rho_e=kappa sqrt(eta_e), kappa>0 fixed,
sigma_e=2alpha sqrt(rho_e),
t0_e=log(1/sqrt(eta_e)).

Here sigma_e is the amplitude of independent symmetric label noise.
It is asymptotic to sqrt(kappa) e^(9/4). The network step size remains
1/2; eta_e in this proof is a spectral ratio, not that step size.

Let F_e(z) be the continuously interpolated frozen risk divided by
alpha^2. Define its central-time version
G_e(s)=F_e((t0_e+s)/b1). Then, uniformly on compact real s intervals,

G_e'(s)/(2 eta_e) -> H_kappa(s)
       =kappa exp(-s)-exp(-2s)-1,
G_e''(s)/(2 eta_e) -> H_kappa'(s)
       =-kappa exp(-s)+2exp(-2s).

Equivalently, the normalized value differences converge locally uniformly:

[G_e(s)-G_e(0)]/(2 eta_e) -> V_kappa(s)-V_kappa(0),
V_kappa(s)=-kappa exp(-s)+(1/2)exp(-2s)-s.

If kappa>2, define z_+=(kappa+sqrt(kappa^2-4))/2 and
z_-=(kappa-sqrt(kappa^2-4))/2. The frozen curve has a central strict local
minimum at scaled time tending to s_min=-log z_+, and a subsequent strict
local maximum at scaled time tending to s_max=-log z_-.
In small fixed neighborhoods of those two points there is exactly one
frozen stationary point of the indicated type for sufficiently small e.
The actual nonlinear discrete-GD risk has strict descent-rise-descent
witnesses near these points, with probability tending to one in the
iterated even-width-then-feature-scale limit. Its interval minimizers and
maximizers on these separate neighborhoods have the same scaled limits.
Its resulting central local peak obeys

b1 k_peak-t0_e -> s_max,
k_peak ~ (2pi/nu^2) e^(-1) log(1/e),

in that iterated probabilistic sense. The first assertion refers to every
maximizer in a chosen sufficiently small neighborhood of s_max; it does
not assert that all actual extrema are unique.

For 0<kappa<2, the FROZEN interpolated risk is strictly decreasing on any
fixed compact central s window for sufficiently small e. No monotonicity
of actual finite-width risk is asserted. At kappa=2 the leading derivative
has a degenerate zero; this proof does not resolve its finite-e unfolding.
Thus 2 is a threshold for this limiting central-window shape, not a proved
global critical noise level or a global absence theorem.

## 2. Uniform derivative limit

The exact frozen curve is
F_e(z)=rho_e(1-exp(-b0 z))^2
      +sum_(h=1,2,12)[exp(-2b_h z)+rho_e(1-exp(-b_h z))^2].
Its nonconstant h derivative with respect to z is
2 b_h q_h [rho_e-(1+rho_e)q_h], q_h=exp(-b_h z).
At z=(t0_e+s)/b1, q1=sqrt(eta_e)exp(-s). Therefore its contribution to
G_e'(s)/(2eta_e) is exactly
kappa exp(-s)-(1+kappa sqrt(eta_e))exp(-2s).

For h=2,12, b_h/b1=O(eta_e) and
q_h=1+O(eta_e log(1/eta_e)), uniformly on compact s sets. Their combined
contribution to G_e'(s)/(2eta_e) tends to -1, since their b_h/b1 weights
sum to eta_e. Differentiating with respect to s makes their contribution
tend to zero: the extra b_h/b1 factor is O(eta_e).
The constant-mode term and its s derivatives tend to zero after division
by eta_e. Indeed b0/b1 is of order 1/e, t0_e is of order log(1/e), and
exp[-(b0/b1)(t0_e+s)] decays faster than every power of e on compact s
sets. These exact formulas prove both uniform derivative limits.
Integration from zero proves the uniform value-difference limit.

## 3. Limiting stationary points and risk witnesses

Writing z=exp(-s)>0, H_kappa=kappa z-z^2-1.
For kappa>2 its roots are z_+>1 and z_-<1 with product one.
At s_min=-log z_+, H_kappa'=z_+ sqrt(kappa^2-4)>0;
at s_max=-log z_-, H_kappa'=-z_- sqrt(kappa^2-4)<0.
Thus V has a strict minimum then a strict maximum. Compact uniform
convergence of H and H' gives a unique frozen critical point near each,
of the same type; the derivative is bounded away from zero outside small
root neighborhoods inside a fixed central compact window.

Choose delta>0 sufficiently small. The four scaled times
s_min-delta, s_min, s_max, s_max+delta are increasing and have strict
limiting value inequalities descent-rise-descent. Rounded integer times
floor((t0_e+s)/b1) have scaled grid error at most b1, which tends to zero.
The associated frozen risk differences therefore have strictly positive
margins of order alpha^2 eta_e. The same value convergence provides a
strict gap away from the unique minimum or maximum in each separate
small neighborhood.

For 0<kappa<2, completion of the square gives
H_kappa=-(z-kappa/2)^2+kappa^2/4-1<0 for every z>0.
Its maximum is strictly negative, so compact uniform derivative
convergence implies the stated frozen decrease on each fixed compact
s window. This does not control scaled times escaping all compacts.

## 4. Actual nonlinear GD and order of limits

For each fixed e, rho_e, alpha_e and all interval endpoints are fixed
numbers, and all involved integer times lie below T_e=ceil(e^(-5/2))
for sufficiently small e. Labels remain bounded. C010's independent-pair
finite-horizon comparison therefore controls every involved actual risk
uniformly through T_e as width grows, including all sixteen noise
patterns. Multiplication of the error by the fixed positive factor
1/(alpha_e^2 eta_e) preserves convergence to zero for this FIXED e.
It follows, first taking width to infinity then e to zero, that the
actual risk value differences converge to the same V differences and
inherit the strict four witnesses. The positive local value gaps transfer
the interval minimizers and maximizers to s_min and s_max. No derivative
comparison for the actual nonlinear network is needed or claimed.

Finally eta_e~e, b1~nu^2 e/(4pi), so t0_e~(1/2)log(1/e) and the displayed
peak time follows. This theorem concerns a different joint-noise regime
from C011's fixed-rho phase comparison; neither proof exchanges limits.

## 5. Exact concrete witness certificate, kappa=5/2

Here z_+=2, z_-=1/2. Use z values 3,2,1/2,1/4 in decreasing order,
so the corresponding s=-log z and integer times increase. The primitive
values are respectively

-3+log 3, -3+log 2, -9/8-log 2, -19/32-2log 2.

Their required margins are
log(3/2), 15/8-2log 2, log 2-17/32, all strictly positive.
For fully checkable bounds, log(3/2)>1/3 and
7/12<log 2<3/4 follow from integrals of 1/t: the lower bound splits
[1,2] into [1,3/2] and [3/2,2] and uses right-endpoint rectangles.
For the upper bound write t=1+x and use
1/(1+x)<=1-x/2 on [0,1], strict in the interior, since the difference
has numerator x(1-x)/2. The margins exceed 1/3,3/8,5/96 respectively.
This certifies a specific joint-noise witness choice by exact rational
bounds, not a floating-point estimate of a bifurcation.

## Remaining scope

The exact finite-e global onset, the degenerate kappa=2 case, interaction
with the initial constant-mode transient, iid sampling, fixed-positive
noise and all-time nonlinear dynamics remain open. These restrictions
matter: a central-window derivative result cannot imply that no other
double-descent pattern occurs elsewhere in time. Pairing and finite
support remain as in C010. Dependencies C009/C010 and this argument
await independent mathematical review; specialist novelty is unestablished.","status":"unverified"}

$$

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:24:34.421240+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d8b5cf3682c22bd5699ad777224252b9045437a827737f1d7ff7b7050f12b1cb","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 6 of arXiv:2608.31145, 'Gauge-compatible tensors on statistical manifolds: splitting and submanifold geometry'] Let $(M,g,\nabla,\nabla^{*},\Theta)$ be a Levi-Civita-parallel
$\Theta$-statistical manifold. Assume that the tangent bundle admits the orthogonal decomposition
\[
TM=\ker\Theta\oplus\operatorname{Im}\Theta.
\]
Then both distributions are preserved by
\[
\nabla^{g},\ \nabla,\ \nabla^{*},
\]
and
\begin{equation}
K_XY=0
\end{equation}
whenever one of $X,Y$ belongs to $\ker\Theta$ and the other belongs to
$\operatorname{Im}\Theta$.

Consequently, every point of $M$ admits a neighborhood $U$ for which
\[
(U,g,\nabla,\nabla^{*})
\cong
(U_0,g_0,\nabla^{0},(\nabla^{0})^{*})
\times
(U_1,g_1,\nabla^{1},(\nabla^{1})^{*}),
\]
where
\[
TU_0=\ker\Theta,
\qquad
TU_1=\operatorname{Im}\Theta.
\]
Thus the two local factors inherit statistical structures.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:22:08.454945+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d8c5986edf949bfd1af35d138d65024daeca0c97e574410b48b8e81128710dc5","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'] \label[lemma]{calYzero_sufficient}
Let $f \in \Sym$ with $\@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{\supp(f)} \ge 3$. 
At least one of of the following holds: 
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $H(f) > H(X)$
\item $g = \big(\sum_{k \in S^0} f(k)\big)^{-1} f \mathds{1}_{S^0} \in \Sym^0$ and $H(g) \le H(X)$.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{proof}
Note that $S^0 = 2 \mathbb{Z}$. 

By (large_median_at_zero of the paper), $c = \sum_{i \in 2\mathbb{Z}} f(i) > 0$, 
so $g \in \Sym^0$ by (lem:Sr_restriction_of_symmetrizers_produces_symmetrizers of the paper). 

If $c = 1$, $H(g) = H(f) \le H(X)$. 
Otherwise, $c \in (0,1)$ and 
$ f = cg + (1-c)h $,
where 
$ h = \frac{f-cg}{1-c}$ is a PMF according to (lem:Sr_restriction_of_symmetrizers_produces_symmetrizers of the paper). 

Noting that $h(0) = 0$, (large_median_at_zero of the paper) shows that $H(h) > H(X)$; by concavity of entropy, therefore, 
\[ H(f) > cH(g) + (1-c)H(h) > cH(g) + (1-c)H(X) .\] 
Thus either $H(f) > H(X)$ or $H(X) \ge H(f) > cH(g) + (1-c)H(X)$. 

\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:51.726283+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis / dispersive PDE","id":"claim_d948b0ea69eecd49bd6d6367620cfaf6003daf10d9fece613e380a2beca5623f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: the Christ–Kiselev lemma passes from an untruncated space-time bound L^p_t → L^q_t to its causal truncation ∫_{s<t} only when p < q strictly. At p = q the truncation can be unbounded even when the full operator is bounded. Concrete counterexample on L²(R): let K(t,s) = sin(t−s)/(t−s) (continuous, locally bounded). The full operator is convolution with the sinc kernel, whose Fourier multiplier is π·1_{[−1,1]}(ξ) (up to normalization), so it is bounded on L² with norm ≈ π. Its causal truncation is convolution with k(u) = 1_{u>0} sin(u)/u, whose multiplier is m(ξ) = ∫_0^∞ e^{−iuξ} sin(u)/u du; using ∫_0^∞ sin(u) sin(uξ)/u du = (1/2) log |(1+ξ)/(1−ξ)|, the imaginary part of m is −(1/2) log|(1+ξ)/(1−ξ)|, which is unbounded as ξ → ±1. A convolution operator on L²(R) is bounded if and only if its multiplier is in L^∞, so the truncated operator is unbounded on L²: p = q = 2 fails. Consequence for PDE: the retarded (Duhamel) Strichartz estimate at the double endpoint q = q̃ = 2 cannot be obtained from the untruncated estimate by Christ–Kiselev; it is exactly the case Keel–Tao had to prove directly. Any proof that claims the double-endpoint inhomogeneous estimate 'by Christ–Kiselev' is misapplying the lemma.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["for the smoothing transform: existence of alpha solving E[sum_i T_i^alpha]=1 in the admissible range, plus regularity conditions such as E[sum_i T_i^alpha log^+ T_i]<infinity from Durrett-Liggett/Biggins theory","for Poisson-Dirichlet: a well-defined subordinator, or fragmentation/coalescent structure, whose ranked, normalized jump sizes are being studied","independence of (T_i) from the i.i.d. copies (W_i) in the smoothing transform equation","non-degeneracy conditions ruling out the trivial Dirac-mass-at-0 solution"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.998030+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d95edc3570f77641129fb8247438ed5ea704bbccb6be4cad5233917af61c0692","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). The smoothing transform concerns fixed points of the distributional equation W =_d sum_i T_i W_i, where (T_i) is a given, typically random, sequence of nonnegative weights and (W_i) are i.i.d. copies of W independent of (T_i); such fixed points arise as limits of branching random walk martingales, including derivative martingale limits, or of Mandelbrot multiplicative cascades, and their tail behavior, characterized by a power-law index alpha solving E[sum_i T_i^alpha]=1 or a related equation, governs the limit's regular variation. Durrett and Liggett characterized the solution set of the smoothing transform equation, establishing existence, uniqueness up to a scaling constant, and the precise tail index under moment conditions on (T_i), a result foundational for analyzing branching random walk boundary and derivative martingale limits and related models such as the random energy model. Separately, Poisson-Dirichlet distributions PD(alpha,theta) arise as the limiting law of ranked, normalized jump sizes of a subordinator, of ranked cycle lengths in random permutations, or of ranked masses in fragmentation and coalescent processes, characterized via the stick-breaking (GEM) construction or via a Poisson process of jumps of a stable subordinator normalized by its total mass. Neither result gives an explicit closed-form density for the general fixed point or limit; the smoothing transform's fixed point is typically characterized only implicitly, through its tail index and functional equation, and both results require specific moment or regular-variation conditions on the input weights or subordinator to hold. Typical failure: Assuming the smoothing transform has a unique nontrivial fixed point up to scale without checking that the characteristic equation E[sum T_i^alpha]=1 actually has a solution in the admissible range, or without the Durrett-Liggett/Biggins regularity conditions, particularly in boundary cases such as the critical branching random walk where the derivative martingale, rather than the ordinary martingale, is the relevant object; applying the generic smoothing-transform tail behavior in a boundary or degenerate parameter regime without re-deriving it is a common source of incorrect tail-index claims. Canonical reference: Durrett and Liggett, 1983, Zeitschrift fur Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie und verwandte Gebiete; Biggins and Kyprianou, 2005, Electronic Journal of Probability; Pitman and Yor, 1997, Annals of Probability.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T21:00:30.493241+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d9619f115929734baab046145a93d1ace1842cc7f20f5d61cfb6bb39e4756f86","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 10 (Gelfand-Tsetlin facts, {\cite[Proposition 2) of arXiv:2607.04138, 'Hives from deformed GUE minor processes'] {NarSheffTao}}]
Let \(\lambda=(\lambda_1\geq \cdots \geq \lambda_n)\in\Spec_n\).  For
\(a\in\mathbb R^n\), let \(\GT_{\diag(\lambda)\rel a}\) denote the real
Gelfand-Tsetlin polytope of triangular arrays
\[
        \Gamma=\{\lambda^{(k)}_i:1\leq i\leq k\leq n\}
\]
satisfying
\[
        \lambda^{(k+1)}_i
        \geq
        \lambda^{(k)}_i
        \geq
        \lambda^{(k+1)}_{i+1},
        \qquad
        1\leq i\leq k<n,
\]
with top row \(\lambda^{(n)}=\lambda\), and diagonal boundary condition
\[
        \sum_{i=1}^k \lambda^{(k)}_i
        =
        \sum_{i=1}^k a_i,
        \qquad 1\leq k\leq n.
\]
Let \(\GT_{\diag(\lambda)\rel *}:=\bigcup_a\GT_{\diag(\lambda)\rel a}\).
Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] If \(a\in\mathbb R^n\), then the Schur--Horn relation
\(\diag(\lambda)\rel a\) holds if and only if
\(\GT_{\diag(\lambda)\rel a}\) is nonempty.
\item[(ii)] The \(\binom n2\)-dimensional volume of
\(\GT_{\diag(\lambda)\rel *}\) is \(V_n(\lambda)/V_n(\tau_n)\).
\item[(iii)] If \(A\) is Haar-uniform on the unitary orbit with spectrum
\(\lambda\), then the eigenvalues of the northwest principal minors of
\(A\) form a uniformly distributed point of
\(\GT_{\diag(\lambda)\rel *}\). Its boundary vector \(a\) is the diagonal of
\(A\).
\item[(iv)] If \(\Lambda\in\Spec_n\) has large gaps,
\[
        \min_{1\leq i<n}(\Lambda_i-\Lambda_{i+1})
        >
        \lambda_1-\lambda_n,
\]
then for every \(a\in\mathbb R^n\) there is a volume-preserving linear
bijection
\[
        \GT_{\diag(\lambda)\rel a}
        \longleftrightarrow
        H_n(\Lambda,\lambda;\Lambda+a).
\]
Under this bijection, a Gelfand-Tsetlin pattern
\((\lambda^{(k)}_i)_{1\leq i\leq k\leq n}\) is sent to the hive \(h:T_n\to
\mathbb R\) given by
\[
        h(i,j)
        =
        \Lambda_1+\cdots+\Lambda_j
        +
        \lambda^{(j)}_1+\cdots+\lambda^{(j)}_i .
\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-23T07:57:26.241377+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_d962bfc29dc542358b270c0f14017f7f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematics, the connective constant is a numerical quantity associated with self-avoiding walks on a lattice. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:20:55.630262+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d96947cd68bd5a5cba0c9976d9426dcee217294ab6bc482eb84c16efc072bdf6","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:biregular of arXiv:2411.07809, 'Pirogov--Sinai Theory Beyond Lattices'] Suppose $G$ is bipartite, one-ended, vertex transitive within each

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T00:37:20.359243+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d97463c8425c5edb42e765bd3f1c5bbad743dd782303dfb3731256ff50b17e30","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn de.2 of arXiv:2411.13099, 'Long time behavior of killed Feynman-Kac semigroups with singular Schr{ö}dinger potentials'] Let  $\mathbf F: \mathscr V\to [1,+\infty]$ be a measurable function. 
   We say that  $(Q^{\mathfrak X}_t,t\ge 0)$ is    $\mathbf F$ {\rm compact-ergodic} over $\mathscr V$   if:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item[\textbf 1.] There exists a unique q.s.d.  $\rho$ for  $(P^{\mathfrak X}_t,t\ge 0)$ in   $  \mathcal P_{\mathbf F}(\mathscr V)$.  
 \item[\textbf 2.] 
  For all $t>0$, $Q^{\mathfrak X}_t:b\mathcal B_{\mathbf F}(\mathscr V)\to b\mathcal B_{\mathbf F}(\mathscr V)$ is compact and there exists $\lambda\ge  \inf_{\mathscr V} \mathbf V$   such that $\mathsf r_{sp}(Q^{\mathfrak X}_t|_{b\mathcal B_{\mathbf F}(\mathscr V)} ) =e^{-\lambda t}, \ \forall t>0$. 
  Furthermore,  $\rho    Q^{\mathfrak X}_t =e^{-\lambda t}\rho$, for all $t\ge 0$, and $\rho (O)>0$ for all nonempty open subsets $O$ of $ \mathscr V$. In addition,  there is a unique   function $\varphi \in \mathcal C_{b\mathbf F}( \mathscr V)$   such that  $\rho   (\varphi )=1$ and $
      Q^{\mathfrak X}_t \varphi= e^{-\lambda  t} \varphi  \text{ on } \mathscr V, \forall t\ge0$.  
 Moreover, $\varphi>0$   everywhere on $\mathscr V$.
\item[\textbf 3.] There exist   $\mathfrak m_1>0$, and   $\mathfrak m_2\ge 1$, s.t.  for all  $t>0$ and all   $\nu\in \mathcal P_{\mathbf F  }( \mathscr V)$:
$$
\sup_{\mathcal A\in\mathcal B(\mathscr V)}\big |  \nu P^{\mathfrak X}_t(\mathcal A)-\rho  (\mathcal A)\big |\le \mathfrak m_2 \, e^{-\mathfrak m_1 t} \frac{\nu(\mathbf F )}{\nu(\varphi)}.
$$
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:53:10.208004+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d97a0074343288447573f4c2a666289f70fb11a057de0030bc516601727f38ff","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defi Def:W-Homo-Equiv of arXiv:2608.29013, 'Weighted Homology and Cohomology of Weighted Polyhedra'] Suppose $(X,\lambda)$ and $(X',\lambda')$ are two weighted polyhedra of the same type. We say that $(X,\lambda)$ is \emph{W-homotopy equivalent} to 
  $(X',\lambda')$ if there exist W-continuous maps
  $$f: (X,\lambda)\rightarrow (X',\lambda'), \ \ 
  g : (X',\lambda')\rightarrow (X,\lambda)$$
such that $g \circ f$ and $f \circ g$
 are W-homotopic to $\mathrm{id}_{X}$ and 
 $\mathrm{id}_{X'}$, respectively. The map $f$ is called a
 \emph{W-homotopy equivalence} from $(X,\lambda)$ to $(X',\lambda')$, and $g$ is called a \emph{W-homotopy inverse} of $f$.  \vskip 0.1cm
 Moreover,
  $(X,\lambda)$ and $(X',\lambda')$ are called 
  \emph{strongly W-homotopy equivalent} if in the above definition,  $f$ and $g$ are both weight-preserving, and $g \circ f$ and $f \circ g$
 are strongly W-homotopic to $\mathrm{id}_{X}$ and 
 $\mathrm{id}_{X'}$, respectively. If so, we call $f$ and $g$ \emph{strong W-homotopy equivalences}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-02T00:34:53.675639+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_d97be235d01df4d78b67ce6366ce4d108aa22374e33abc12f3ab6cb220eb967c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In calculus and real analysis, absolute continuity is a regularity property of functions that is stronger than uniform continuity, and hence continuity. The notion of absolute continuity allows one to obtain generalizations of the relationship between the two central operations of calculus—differentiation and integration. This relationship is commonly characterized in the framework of Riemann integration, but with absolute continuity it may be formulated in terms of Lebesgue integration. For real-valued functions on the real line, two interrelated notions appear: absolute continuity of functions and absolute continuity of measures. These two notions are generalized in different directions. The usual derivative of a function is related to the Radon–Nikodym derivative, or density, of a measure. We have the following chains of inclusions for functions over an interval:Lipschitz continuous ⊆ absolutely continuous ⊆ uniformly continuous ⊆ continuous","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:41:19.322996+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d9879ec63d0dbd32ed7b5f45e477dbbdb43103b95918e0086cb6ce778da349f8","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:conditional-bridge-functional-limit of arXiv:2609.03532, 'Airy limit for the Jack process and topological expansion'] [Xu]

Fix $x>0$ and $h_0,h_1\geq0$, and set
\[
  L_N=\lfloor xN^{2/3}\rfloor,
  \qquad
  H_{a,N}=\lfloor h_a\sigma N^{1/3}\rfloor,
  \quad a\in\{0,1\}.
\]
Normalize $\operatorname{wt}$ on
$\mathcal W(H_{0,N},H_{1,N},L_N)$ to a probability measure, and define
the right-continuous step process
\begin{equation*}
  \widehat W_N(u)
  :=\frac{W(\lfloor uN^{2/3}\rfloor)}{\sigma N^{1/3}},
  \qquad 0\leq u\leq x.
\end{equation*}
Then as $N\to\infty$, $\widehat W_N$ converges weakly in the Skorokhod space
$D([0,x])$, equipped with the $J_1$ topology, to the nonnegative
Brownian bridge of length $x$ from $h_0$ to $h_1$.  
If exactly one of $h_0,h_1$ is zero, the limit is the
corresponding three-dimensional Bessel bridge, interpreted by time reversal
when $h_1=0$; if both are zero, it is the normalized Brownian excursion. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:23:03.034516+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d98feba1bb71e6e4d6980179a25205901c9d83096617fcde4b9b35c89fed88d3","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 20 (SDE for the second Malliavin derivative) of arXiv:2605.03057, 'Uniform-in-time quantitative fluctuations of large scale interacting particle systems'] Assume that Assumptions \ref{ass:smooth},
and \ref{ass:second-malliavin-uniform} hold. Fix
$ 0 \le r \le s \le t $, $ u \in [s,t] $,
$ i,j,k \in \left\{ 1,\dots,N \right\} $, and
$ \alpha,\beta \in \left\{ 1,\dots,m \right\} $.
Then, the process $\left(
D_r^{k,\beta} D_s^{j,\alpha} X_u^{i,N}
\right)_{u \in [s,t]}$ solves the SDE
\begin{align}

D_r^{k,\beta} D_s^{j,\alpha} X_u^{i,N}
&=
\mathcal I_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\int_s^u
\left(
\partial_x b\left( X_\rho^{i,N},\mu_\rho^N \right)
D_r^{k,\beta} D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{i,N}
+
G_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)
+
R_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)
\right)
d\rho
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\int_s^u
\left(
\partial_x \sigma\left( X_\rho^{i,N},\mu_\rho^N \right)
D_r^{k,\beta} D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{i,N}
+
H_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)
+
S_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)
\right)
dB_\rho^i ,
\end{align}
where $\mathcal I_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}$ denotes the initial
condition given by
\begin{align*}
\mathcal I_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}
&=
\mathbf{1}_{\left\{ i=j \right\}}
\partial_x \sigma\left( X_s^{i,N},\mu_s^N \right)
D_r^{k,\beta} X_s^{i,N}
e_\alpha
+
\mathbf{1}_{\left\{ r=s \right\}}
\mathbf{1}_{\left\{ i=k \right\}}
\partial_x \sigma\left( X_s^{i,N},\mu_s^N \right)
D_s^{j,\alpha} X_s^{i,N}e_\beta
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\mathbf{1}_{\left\{ i=j \right\}} \frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_\mu \sigma\left( X_s^{i,N},\mu_s^N \right)\left( X_s^{\ell,N} \right)
D_r^{k,\beta} X_s^{\ell,N} e_\alpha
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\mathbf{1}_{\left\{ r=s \right\}}
\mathbf{1}_{\left\{ i=k \right\}}
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_\mu \sigma\left( X_s^{i,N},\mu_s^N \right)\left( X_s^{\ell,N} \right)
D_s^{j,\alpha} X_s^{\ell,N} e_\beta ,
\end{align*}
with $ e_\alpha $ denoting the $ \alpha $-th vector of the canonical basis of $ \R^m $,
\begin{align}

G_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)
&=
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_\mu b\left( X_\rho^{i,N},\mu_\rho^N \right)\left( X_\rho^{\ell,N} \right)
D_r^{k,\beta} D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{\ell,N},
\end{align}
and $H_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho) $ is defined by the same formula, with
$ b $ replaced by $ \sigma $, while
\begin{align}

R_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)
&=
\partial_{xx}^2 b\left( X_\rho^{i,N},\mu_\rho^N \right)
\left[
D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{i,N}, D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{i,N}
\right]
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_\mu\left[ \partial_x b \right]
\left( X_\rho^{i,N},\mu_\rho^N \right)\left( X_\rho^{\ell,N} \right)
\left[
D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{\ell,N}, D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{i,N}
\right]
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_x\left[
\partial_\mu b\left( \cdot,\mu_\rho^N \right)\left( X_\rho^{\ell,N} \right)
\right]\left( X_\rho^{i,N} \right)
\left[
D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{i,N}, D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{\ell,N}
\right]
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_v\left[

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:35:04.203652+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d9a3cf7ab6998ff45ad4b94a2b2234b8d395ccccb807531a21a1ebe345ac425a","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 18 (Parabolic and hyperbolic THP) of arXiv:2608.03575, '2608.03575'] Let \(P\) be an infinite THP, and let \(P^{\rm trun}\) be the polyhedron
obtained by truncating all ideal and hyperideal vertices. Let
\(\{K_n\}_{n\geq 1}\) be an exhaustion of \(\mathbb H^3\) by compact sets.

\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
    \item \(P\) is called \emph{parabolic} if
    \(P^{\rm trun}\setminus K_n\) tends to a single point in
    \(\partial_\infty\mathbb H^3\). Equivalently, the set of accumulation
    points of the boundary faces of \(P\) consists of one point.

    \item \(P\) is called \emph{hyperbolic} if
    \(P^{\rm trun}\setminus K_n\) tends to a half-sphere in
    \(\partial_\infty\mathbb H^3\). Equivalently, the accumulation points of
    the boundary faces form a circle in \(\partial_\infty\mathbb H^3\), and
    all faces of \(P\) lie in one of the two half-spaces bounded by the
    hyperbolic plane determined by this circle.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:42:55.331362+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d9e91310910fcb8afb8071542f99cc487ab965cba1c9e73055233371a03bfa20","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 7 of arXiv:2609.02416, '2609.02416'] Assume $q\equiv c>0$ and $V\in C_b(\R)$. Then
\[
\alpha d\,\cH\!\left(\frac{c}{\alpha d}\right)-\sup_\R V
\le\Lambda_D^\R(\alpha)\le
\alpha d\,\cH\!\left(\frac{c}{\alpha d}\right)-\inf_\R V.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\frac{\Lambda_D^\R(\alpha)}{|\log\alpha|}\longrightarrow\frac{c}{R_+}
\qquad(\alpha\downarrow0).
\]
Under the edge hypothesis of Theorem~\ref{thm:heteroHamiltonian},
\[
\Lambda_D^\R(\alpha)
=\frac{c}{R_+}\left[\log\frac{c}{\alpha d}
+p\log\log\frac{c}{\alpha d}-p\log R_+-\log(R_+A)-1\right]+O(1).
\]
If, in addition, $V\equiv a_0$, then
\[
\Lambda_D^\R(\alpha)=\alpha d\,\cH\!\left(\frac{c}{\alpha d}\right)-a_0
=\sup_{s\in\R}\{cs-\alpha d(M(s)-1)\}-a_0.
\]
If $s_\alpha>0$ is the optimizer, then $\alpha dM'(s_\alpha)=c$ and
\[
(\Lambda_D^\R)'(\alpha)=-d(M(s_\alpha)-1)<0,\qquad
(\Lambda_D^\R)''(\alpha)=\frac{c^2}{\alpha^3dM''(s_\alpha)}>0.
\]
Moreover,
\[
\Lambda_D^\R(\alpha)=-a_0+\frac{c^2}{2\alpha dD_2(J)}
-\frac{D_4(J)c^4}{24\alpha^3d^3D_2(J)^4}+O(\alpha^{-5})
\qquad(\alpha\to+\infty),
\]
and, under the edge hypothesis,
\[
\Lambda_D^\R(\alpha)=\frac{c}{R_+}\left[\log\frac{c}{\alpha d}
+p\log\log\frac{c}{\alpha d}-p\log R_+-\log(R_+A)-1+o(1)\right]-a_0
\]
as $\alpha\downarrow0$. Finally, for
$\cA_{\sigma,m,\R}u=\sigma^{-m}(J_\sigma*u-u)+cu'+a_0u$,
\[
\Lp(\cA_{\sigma,m,\R})=\sigma^{-m}\cH(c\sigma^{m-1})-a_0.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:15:54.876805+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d9f7687134244a6a8cc13fdfa0f9d7a84c6c96f25c1786e180487c8773efa003","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:c2fail of arXiv:2608.28007, 'Exact Risk Ratios for Weighted Data Selection in Linear Regression'] For $\varepsilon>0$ define directions in $\mathbb{R}^4$
\[
\begin{aligned}
d_0&=-\varepsilon(e_1+e_2), & d_1&=e_1,\ d_2=e_2,\\

d_6&=-\varepsilon(e_1+e_3), & d_7&=-\varepsilon(e_2+e_4),
\end{aligned}
\]
with masses $s_0=s_3=s_6=s_7=\frac1{4(1+2\varepsilon)}$ and

points have $t=1/\lVert v\rVert^2>1$ and all side points have $t<1$: no point is

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T16:46:51.518941+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_d9f8d662691360ba70c27634d29157ba859e2c7184c720c68306842f109cf517","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematics, the pigeonhole principle states that if n items are put into m containers, with n > m, then at least one container must contain more than one item. For example, of three gloves, at least two must be right-handed or at least two must be left-handed, because there are three objects but only two categories of handedness to put them into. This seemingly obvious statement, a type of counting argument, can be used to demonstrate possibly unexpected results. For example, given that the population of London is more than one unit greater than the maximum number of hairs that can be on a human head, the principle requires that there must be at least two people in London who have the same number of hairs on their heads.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:55:37.821578+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_da556587f6b3f72f6e0c09f708f5c5223b689dda072c04fb03354c3df659dbc7","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemstar lem:eigenfunctions of arXiv:2605.06488, 'Continuous-state branching processes with L\'evy-Khintchine drift-interaction: Laplace dua'] Let $\Psi$ be a  branching mechanism. Recall $\rho\in [0,\infty]$ its largest zero.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Assume $\Psi$ supercritical: $\Psi'(0+)\in [-\infty,0)$ and $\rho\in (0,\infty]$.  Let $u_0\in (0, \rho)$ be fixed. Define for all $\theta\in \big(0,-\Psi'(0+)\big)$,
\begin{equation}f(x):=\int_0^{\rho} (1-e^{-xu})\frac{\theta}{-\Psi(u)}e^{-\int_{u_0}^{u}\frac{\theta}{\Psi(v)}\mathrm{d} v}\mathrm{d} u,\quad x\in (0,\infty).
\end{equation}
This is a well-defined increasing function, in $\mathrm{C}^2((0,\infty))$, which satisfies $x\mathrm{L}^{\Psi}f(x)=\theta f(x)$ for all $x\in (0,\infty)$.
Moreover, 
\[f(x)\underset{x\rightarrow \infty}{\longrightarrow}\infty \Longleftrightarrow \int_0^{x_0}\frac{\mathrm{d} u}{-\Psi(u)}=\infty \text{ for some } x_0\in (0,\rho).\]
\item Assume $\Psi$ non-immortal (not necessarily supercritical): $\rho\in [0,\infty)$. Let $u_0\in (\rho,\infty)$ be fixed. Define for all $\theta\in (0,\infty)$, \[f(x):=\int_{\rho}^{\infty}e^{-xu}\frac{1}{\Psi(u)}e^{\int_{u_0}^u\frac{\theta}{\Psi(v)}\mathrm{d} v}\mathrm{d} u,\ x\in (0,\infty).\]
This is a well-defined decreasing function, in $\mathrm{C}^2((0,\infty))$, which satisfies $x\mathrm{L}^{\Psi}f(x)=\theta f(x)$ for all $x\in (0,\infty)$. Moreover, \[f(x)\underset{x\rightarrow 0}{\longrightarrow}\infty \Longleftrightarrow
\int_{x_0}^{\infty}\frac{\mathrm{d} u}{\Psi(u)}=\infty \text{ for some } x_0\in (\rho,\infty).\]
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:36:31.235220+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dab15ba146eefad594bfb1127aa334a49aadee8418addb6be53fcfc3f5cb9226","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 19 of arXiv:2609.00567, 'Hodge--Tate splitting and Akizuki--Nakano vanishing in positive characteristic'] Let \(\iota \colon X \to S\) be a morphism of $\F_p$-stacks.
Let
\[
X^{(1)} \defeq X\times_{S,F_S}S
\]
be the relative Frobenius twist, and let
\[
F_{X/S}\colon X \to  X^{(1)}
\]
be the relative Frobenius.
  \begin{itemize}
      \item   The \emph{(absolute) de Rham stack} of \(X\) is defined as a functor
  \begin{equation*}
    X^{\dR} \colon \CAlg^{an}_{\setF_p} \to \Ani; \  R \mapsto X(W(R)/^L p),
  \end{equation*}
  where \(W(R)\) is the ring of Witt vectors of \(R\), \(-/^L p\) is the derived quotient by \(p\), and \(X(W(R)/^L p)\) is the mapping space \(\Map_{\dSch_{\setF_p}}(\Spec(W(R)/^L p), X)\) in the \(\infty\)-category of derived schemes over \(\setF_p\).
  Since this is isomorphic to the relative Hodge--Tate stack \((X/\setZ_p)^{\HT}\) of \(X\) relative to the crystalline prism \((\setZ_p, (p))\) introduced in \cite{bhatt2022Prismatization}*{Construction 7.1}, this is a stack on \(\CAlg^{an}_{\setF_p}\) (\cite{bhatt2022Prismatization}*{Lemma 7.3}).

  This is equipped with natural morphisms
  \begin{equation*}
    \pi_{X} \colon X \to X^{\dR} \quad \text{and} \quad \nu_X \colon X^{\dR} \to X
  \end{equation*}
  of \(\setF_p\)-stacks: For each \(R \in \CAlg^{an}_{\setF_p}\), each morphism is given by precomposition of morphisms
  \begin{equation*}
    R \xrightarrow{\Phi_R} W(R)/^L p \quad \text{and} \quad W(R)/^L p \xrightarrow{\res} R,
  \end{equation*}
  where \(\Phi_R\) is the animation of the morphism \(a \mapsto [a^p] \bmod p\) and \(\res\) is the restriction morphism.
  Note that the composition \(\nu_X \circ \pi_X\) is the absolute Frobenius morphism \(F_X \colon X \to X\) of \(X\).
\item The \emph{de Rham stack} of $X$ over $S$ is defined by
\[
(X/S)^{\dR} \defeq X^{\dR} \times_{S^{\dR},\pi_S} S.
\]
We define natural morphisms
  \begin{equation*}
    \pi_{X/S} \colon X \to (X/S)^{\dR} \quad \text{and} \quad \nu_{X/S} \colon (X/S)^{\dR} \to X^{(1)}
  \end{equation*}
  of \(\setF_p\)-stacks as follows:
The morphism $\pi_{X/S}$ is defined by
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
X \arrow[r,"\pi_{X/S}"'] \arrow[rd,bend right,"\iota"] \arrow[rr,bend left,"\pi_X"] & X^{\dR} \times_{S^{\dR}} S \arrow[r,"\pr_1"] \arrow[d,"\pr_2"] & X^{\dR} \arrow[d,"\iota^{\dR}"] \\
& S \arrow[r,"\pi_S"] & S^{\dR}.
\end{tikzcd}
\]
The morphism $\nu_{X/S} \colon (X/S)^{\dR} \to X^{(1)}$ is induced by the following commutative diagram
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
X^{\dR} \times_{S^{\dR}} S \arrow[r,"\pr_1"] \arrow[d,"\pr_2"] & X^{\dR} \arrow[d,"\iota^{\dR}"] \arrow[r,"\nu_X"] & X \arrow[d,"\iota"] \\
S \arrow[r,"\pi_S"] \arrow[rr,bend right,"F"] & S^{\dR} \arrow[r,"\nu_S"] & S.
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\item We assume that $\iota$ is smooth representable.
Then the cotangent complex \(L_{X/S}\) is a locally free \(\cO_X\)-module concentrated in degree \(0\).  
We set
\[
\Omega^1_{X/S} \defeq L_{X/S},
\qquad
\Omega^i_{X/S} \defeq 
\bigwedge_{\cO_X}^i\Omega^1_{X/S}.
\]
The universal \(S\)-derivation
\[
d_{X/S}\colon \cO_X \to  \Omega^1_{X/S}
\]
extends uniquely to the relative de Rham complex
\[
\Omega^\bullet_{X/S}
=
\left[
\cO_X
\xrightarrow{d_{X/S}}
\Omega^1_{X/S}
\xrightarrow{d_{X/S}}
\Omega^2_{X/S}
 \to \cdots
\right].
\]

We define a morphism of complexes of $\cO_{X^{(1)}}$-modules
\[
F^{\dR}_{X/S} \colon \cO_{X^{(1)}} \to F_{X/S,*}\Omega^{\bullet}_{X/S}
\]
as follows:
We have
\[
d_{X/S}\circ F_{X/S}^{\sharp}=0
\]
by checking smooth locally on \(X\).  
Therefore, the morphism
\[
F_{X/S}^{\sharp}\colon
\cO_{X^{(1)}} \to  F_{X/S,*}\cO_X
\]
defines a morphism of complexes
\[
F_{X/S}^{\dR}\colon
\cO_{X^{(1)}}
 \to 
F_{X/S,*}\Omega^\bullet_{X/S},
\]
whose degree \(0\) component is \(F_{X/S}^{\sharp}\) and whose
positive-degree components are zero.
\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:55:27.258728+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dabd2d8a9c94c17b6e66ae3a98f56a0c89349c4f708e8d59a99c1a6e168d952a","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:dg of arXiv:2410.23509, 'Dynkin Games for L\'evy Processes'] Let 
$G_1(x)\leq G_2(x)$
be two real continuous payoff functions.
Consider a L\'evy process $X$ and a discount factor $r>0$, 
such that conditions (equation eq:ic of the paper) and (equation eq:limit of the paper) above hold.
Given two stopping times $\sigma$ and $\tau$, define the expected payoff

$$
{\operatorname{\mathbf{M}}_x}(\sigma,\tau)=\operatorname{\mathbf{E}}_x\left(
e^{-r\tau}G_1(X_{\tau})\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau\leq\sigma\}}
+
e^{-r\sigma}G_2(X_{\sigma})\mathbf{1}_{\{\sigma<\tau\}}
\right).
$$

The Dynkin game (DG) problem consists
in finding the value function $V(x)$ and two optimal stopping rules ${\sigma^*}$ and ${\tau^*}$ such that
\begin{align}
V(x)&=\inf_{\sigma}\sup_{\tau}{\operatorname{\mathbf{M}}_x}(\sigma,\tau)=\sup_{\tau}\inf_{\sigma}{\operatorname{\mathbf{M}}_x}(\sigma,\tau)={\operatorname{\mathbf{M}}_x}(\sigma^*,\tau^*).

\end{align}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:59:53.344842+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_daf1e28c9d6c98b0dabfc931156a104b3f647adab30159553e5fa19964d8a21b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:limit-law of arXiv:2607.24705, 'Derangetropy Operators'] Let $K$ be the Koenigs linearizer of $A$ at $\tfrac12$: the unique
		increasing solution of the Schr\"oder equation
		$K(2u) = A(K(u))$, $K(0)=\tfrac12$, $K'(0)=1$; then $K$ extends to a
		real-analytic increasing bijection $\mathbb{R}\to(0,1)$ and is the
		distribution function of a symmetric law $\mathcal{K}$ with analytic
		density. For every $f \in \mathcal{D}_{+}$,
		\begin{equation}
			2^{n} f(m)\,(X_{n} - m) \;\xrightarrow{\ d\ }\; \mathcal{K},
			
		\end{equation}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:46.149110+00:00","domain":"elliptic partial differential equations, maximum principles","id":"claim_db0bd50e4b1d3185e597734ebdf3437ca5f83b01bff6e16e23fd7c464aeb3f41","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: Omega bounded. The proofs use boundedness twice - the auxiliary function exp(gamma x_1) must be bounded on Omega, and the maximum must be attained on a compact set. On unbounded domains the conclusion is false even for harmonic functions with zero boundary data. Unbounded counterexample: on the half-space {x_n > 0} the function u(x) = x_n is harmonic and vanishes on the whole boundary, yet u > 0 inside; sup u = infinity while sup over the boundary of u = 0. Bounded counterexample (so boundedness of u does not rescue the statement in general): for n >= 3 let Omega = {|x| > 1} and u(x) = 1 - |x|^{2-n}. Then u is harmonic in Omega, continuous up to the boundary, bounded with 0 <= u < 1, u = 0 on the boundary sphere, and sup over Omega of u = 1 > 0 = sup over the boundary of u^+. In the plane, u(x) = log|x| on {|x| > 1} is an unbounded version of the same phenomenon. What restores the principle: treat infinity as a boundary point, i.e. assume limsup of u(x) as |x| tends to infinity is <= 0 (then the principle holds on any unbounded Omega, by exhausting with large balls), or impose a Phragmen-Lindeloef growth restriction adapted to the geometry. The admissible growth is set by the opening of the domain, and a thinner domain permits faster growth, not slower: in a plane sector of opening pi/a the threshold is exp(|x|^a), so a narrow sector allows faster growth than a half-plane, and in a strip of width d the threshold is exp(pi|x|/d), the extremal being exp(pi x_1/d) cos(pi x_2/d). The same caution applies to the H^1 weak maximum principle: its proof uses the Sobolev inequality together with the fact that the level sets have finite measure.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:56:21.583768+00:00","domain":"algebraic geometry","id":"claim_db5eb654cfadf445fa059f8bceb44a8415837ad88ca812a4513a0ade0f74de10","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a smooth projective curve of genus g over an algebraically closed field, equivalently a compact Riemann surface, and let D be a divisor on X. Write l(D) for the dimension of the space of meromorphic functions on X whose poles are bounded by D and which have no other poles, and let K be a canonical divisor of X. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:35:56.961006+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_db6f1f3f67070692d1b6450d41e2d7f9f5137d013b008fc1d32aeb790cb14589","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma main_lemma of arXiv:2604.05921, 'Simplicity of random hypergraphs'] Let $\delta_1,\delta_2 \in \mathds{N}$. Given (possibly non-unique) vertices $v_1,v_2,\hdots,v_{\delta_1} \in V$, let the unique vertices be denoted by $v'_1,v'_2,\hdots,v'_{u(\vb*{v})}$, for some $u(\vb*{v}) \in \mathds{N}$. Similarly, let the unique vertices in $w_1,w_2,\hdots,w_{\delta_2}$ be denoted by $w'_1,w'_2,\hdots,w'_{u(\vb*{w})}$. Let $D(\vb*{v})=\frac{\delta_1!}{\prod_{i=1}^{u(\vb*{v})} m_{v'_i}(\vb*{v})!}$ and $D(\vb*{w})=\frac{\delta_2!}{\prod_{i=1}^{u(\vb*{w})} m_{w'_i}(\vb*{w})!}$. Let $\hat{R}(\cdot)$ be as in (equation def:B_hat of the paper) and let $U$ denote a uniformly chosen vertex in $V$. For any functions $f_1^{(i)}(v):V \rightarrow \mathds{N}$, $f_2^{(i)}(v):V \rightarrow \mathds{N}$ and $w \in \mathds{N}$,
    \begin{align}
        
        &\sum_{\vb*{v} \in V^{\delta_1}}  \sum_{\vb*{w} \in (V\backslash\{v_1,\hdots,v_{\delta_1}\})^{\delta_2}} (D(\vb*{v})D(\vb*{w}))^w \prod_{i=1}^{u(\vb*{v})} f_1^{(m_{v'_i}(\vb*{v}))}(v'_i) \prod_{j=1}^{u(\vb*{w})} f_2^{(m_{w'_j}(\vb*{w}))}(w'_j) \nonumber \\
        &=\sum_{\substack{\vb*{a} \in \mathds{N}^{\delta_1}:\\ \sum_{i=1}^{\delta_1} ia_i = \delta_1}}  \frac{\delta_1!^{1+w}}{\prod_{k=1}^{\delta_1} k!^{(1+w)a_k}} \sum_{\substack{\vb*{b} \in \mathds{N}^{\delta_2}:\\ \sum_{i=1}^{\delta_2} ib_i = \delta_2}}  \frac{\delta_2!^{1+w}}{\prod_{k=1}^{\delta_2} k!^{(1+w)b_k} } \nonumber \\
    &\hspace{1cm} \times \sum_{\gamma(\cdot) \in \hat{R}(\vb*{a},\vb*{b})} (-1)^{\sum{\vb*{g} \in \mathds{N}^{\delta_1}, \vb*{h} \in \mathds{N}^{\delta_2}}( \sum_{i=1}^{\delta_1} g_i + \sum_{j=1}^{\delta_2} h_j -1) \gamma(\vb*{g},\vb*{h})} \nonumber \\
    &\hspace{1cm} \times  \prod_{\substack{\vb*{y} \in \mathds{N}^{\delta_1}\\ \vb*{z} \in \mathds{N}^{\delta_2}}} \Bigg( \frac{1}{\gamma(\vb*{y},\vb*{z})!} \Big(\frac{n\mathds{E} \big[\prod_{i=1}^{\delta_1} (f_1^{(i)}(U))^{y_i} \prod_{j=1}^{\delta_2} (f_2^{(j)}(U))^{z_j} \big] \big(\sum_{i=1}^{\delta_1} y_i + \sum_{j=1}^{\delta_2} z_j-1 \big)!}{\prod_{i=1}^{\delta_1} y_i! \prod_{j=1}^{\delta_2} z_j!} \Big)^{\gamma(\vb*{y},\vb*{z})} \Bigg).
    \end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:53:00.814024+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_db722a684036d88d3fed8ad5ff1061549c4e967a0edae2aee9aeb8f24e21e943","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition Type forest, type rays and paths of arXiv:2607.16911, 'Multipartite random graphs with given degrees: local limit, revisiting the giant, distance'] Consider the \\emph{Ulam-Harris forest} $\\mathscr{F}_S$ on the set of types $S$. That is to say, $\\mathscr F_S$ is an infinite forest, consisting of $|S|$ many infinite tree components $\\{\\mathscr T(s):s\\in S\\}$. For any fixed $s_0 \\in S$, the root of the tree $\\mathscr T(s_0)$ is $s_0$, and for any $v\\in \\mathscr T(s_0)$, it has $|S|$ many offspring $\\{vs:s\\in S\\}$. Observe that any $v\\in \\mathscr T(s)$ has the form of a word $v=s_0s_1\\dots s_k$. We call the forest $\\mathscr F_S$ the \\textit{type forest} corresponding to the set of types $S$. \n    \n    Furthermore any directed infinite path $\\pi=(s_0\\rightarrow s_0s_1 \\rightarrow s_0s_1s_2\\rightarrow \\dots)$ starting at the root $s_0$ is called a \\emph{type ray} in $\\mathscr T(s_0)$, and a finite directed path of the form $(s_0\\rightarrow s_0s_1 \\rightarrow \\dots \\rightarrow s_0s_1s_2\\dots s_k)$ is called a \\emph{type path} started at $s_0$. By $|\\pi|$ we denote the length of $\\pi$. Thus, if $\\pi$ is a type ray, $|\\pi|=\\infty$, while for $\\pi=(s_0\\rightarrow s_0s_1 \\rightarrow \\dots \\rightarrow s_0s_1\\dots s_k)$, $|\\pi|=k$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:36:04.961469+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_db75c2f89cf0c0e5614bf6efc2acc163da629893662959afc861c32c88072a49","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 2 of arXiv:2604.00642, 'Quantitative central limit theorem for an integrated periodogram via the fourth moment the'] Let
\[
f_\alpha(\lambda)=|\lambda|^{-\alpha}L(\lambda),
\qquad \lambda\in(-\pi,\pi),\quad \alpha\in\mathcal A,
\]
where $\mathcal A=[a,b]\subset[0,1)$, and assume that the true parameter value $\alpha_0$ belongs to $\mathcal A$. Suppose that $L\in \mathcal C^1([-\pi,\pi]\setminus\{0\})$ is positive on $[-\pi,\pi]$ and slowly varying at $0$.

Define the Whittle contrast by
\[
Q_n(\alpha)
=
\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}
\left[
\log f_\alpha(\lambda)+\frac{I_n(\lambda)}{f_\alpha(\lambda)}
\right]\dd\lambda,
\qquad \alpha\in\mathcal A.
\]
Let
\[
\widehat\alpha_n\in \arg\min_{\alpha\in\mathcal A} Q_n(\alpha)
\]
be any measurable minimizer of $Q_n$ over $\mathcal A$. Then
\[
\widehat\alpha_n \xrightarrow{\mathbb P} \alpha_0,
\]
and
\[
\sqrt n\,(\widehat\alpha_n-\alpha_0)
\;\Rightarrow\;
\mathcal N\!\left(0,\frac{4}{\sigma_0^2}\right),
\]
where
\[
\sigma_0^2
=
\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \bigl(\log|\lambda|\bigr)^2\,\dd\lambda.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:25:41.600281+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_db7d364cb00afeb71df457227830316d3af03b3c823ffcc7ab835243f64266b0","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary cor:mass-no-killing of arXiv:2608.11931, '\texorpdfstring{Nonlinear parabolic characterizations of stochastic completeness at infini'] Let $G$ be a graph with $\kappa=0$ and \(\mu(X)<\infty\).
Let $\phi\in\mathcal{I}$ with $\phi^{-1}(\mathbb R_+)\neq\emptyset.$ Then \(G\) satisfies
\hyperref[def:SC]{\textup{(SC)}}{} if and only if one, and hence all, of the
statements {\rm(ii)}--{\rm(iv)} of
Theorem~(thm:generalized-mass-characterization of the paper) hold, with the
generalized mass identity~\hyperref[eq:nonlinear-generalized-mass]{\textup{(MB)}}{} reducing
to the conservation of mass:
\[
    \mathsf M_u(t)=\mathsf M_{u_0}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.356901+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_db9918fbc671f11eee90cd6406606fa76cc6077e21fc89d28df52ffb173bfd87","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 237 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $\alpha,L,\epsilon,K>0$ and any sequence of $\epsilon$-approximate $L$-Lipschitz algorithms $(\cA_N)_{N\ge 1}$,
	\[
		\lim_{N\to\infty} \bbW_2\Big(\mu(\cA_{N[K]}), \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)\Big) 
		= \lim_{N\to\infty} \bbW_2\Big(\mu_{\sym}(\cA_{N[K]}), \cM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha;\epsilon)\Big)
		= 0\,.
	\]

\begin{proof}
	We only prove that the first limit is zero, as the second limit is proved analogously.
	Suppose for contradiction that there exists $\delta > 0$ such that $\bbW_2(\mu(\cA_{N[K]}), \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)) \ge \delta$ for infinitely many $N$.
	By \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l4} from Lemma~\ref{l:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound}, there exists $C = C(\alpha,L,K) > 0 $ such that for sufficiently large $N$, $\mu(\cA_{N[K]}) \in \cP_4(\R,C)$.
Then, for infinitely many $N$, we have
	\[\mu(\cA_{N[K]})\in
		S_\delta 
		\equiv \Big\{ \mu \in \cP_4(\R,C) : \bbW_2(\mu, \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)) \ge \delta 
		\Big\}\,.
	\]
	By Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.cPp.compact.Wq}, the space $\cP_4(\R,C)$ endowed with the $\bbW_2$ metric is compact.
	The set $S_\delta$ is closed with respect to the $\bbW_2$ metric, hence also compact. Therefore
 we may find $\mu \in S_\delta$ and a subsequence $(N_j)_{j\ge 1}$ such that
	\[
		\lim_{j\to\infty} \bbW_2\Big(\mu(\cA_{N_j[K]}),
		\mu\Big) = 0\,.
	\]
	As noted in Definition~\ref{d:truncated.lip.alg}, we have $\mu^{\Ising}(\cA_{N_j[K]}) = \mu^{\Ising}(\cA_{N_j})$: thus, since each $\cA_{N_j}$ is an $\epsilon$-approximate $L$-Lipschitz algorithm, so is each $\cA_{N_j[K]}$. It follows by omitting finitely many $j$'s that we have
	\[
	\WERR(\cA_{N_j[K]},\mu)
	=\max\bigg\{
	\bbW_2\Big(\mu(\cA_{N_j[K]}),
		\mu\Big),
	\bbW_2\Big(
		\mu^\Ising(\cA_{N_j[K]}),
		\cP(\{\pm1\})
		\Big)
	\bigg\}\le\epsilon
	\]
for all $j$. Recalling the definition \eqref{e:cM.Lip} of  $\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;L,\epsilon)$, this implies
	\[
		\mu \in \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;L,\epsilon) \subseteq \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)\,,
	\]
	which contradicts that $\mu \in S_\delta$.
\end{proof}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:43:44.242708+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dbc8babb32eb23f6e3ce1e9670842f005e215d3c0de85d384f47f9bcc66b30ab","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 4 of arXiv:2604.15152, 'The Multinomial Allocation Model and the Random Box Load'] Define
\[\Phi_n(r,t)=\binom{n}{r,t,n-r-t}
\Big(
 \rE\!\left[q_X^r q_Y^t (1-q_X-q_Y)_+^{\,n-r-t}\right]
- N^{-1} \rE\!\left[q_X^{r+t}(1-2q_X)_+^{\,n-r-t}\right]\Big)-\rE[\hat q_r]\rE[\hat q_t],\]
where $q_Y$ is an independent copy of $q_X$, and $(a)_+ := \max(a,0)$. 
Then for all $r \ne t$, 
\begin{align*}
\rE[\hat q_r]
&= \binom{n}{r}\, \rE\!\left[q_X^r (1-q_X)^{n-r}\right],\qquad
\rV[\hat q_r]
= \Phi_n(r,r)+N^{-1}\rE[\hat q_r],\qquad
\rC[\hat q_r ,\hat q_t]= \Phi_n(r,t).
\end{align*}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:36:31.222647+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dbd0d5759a727d7538da5d3816a778ec74338db6f0b32984dc664b1154ebf1eb","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 7 (Conditional unique limit at infinite time) of arXiv:2609.00501, 'Uniqueness of Finite-Time Varifold Limits for the M\"obius-Invariant Willmore Flow'] Let $F\colon[0,\infty)\times\Sigma\to\Sph^3$ be a smooth MIWF of a
compact torus.  Assume that there is one constant $c_0>0$ such that
\[
 \inf_{t>0}\min_{x\in\Sigma}|A_{F_t}^0(x)|^2\geq c_0,
\]
and, in addition, that
\begin{equation}
 
 \int_0^\infty\sqrt{-W'(r)}\dd r<\infty.
\end{equation}
Then there are positive Radon measures $\mu_\infty$ on $\Sigma$ and
$\lambda_\infty$ on $\Sph^3$ and a unique integral two-varifold
$\Var_\infty$ in $\R^4$, possibly the zero varifold, such that
\[
 \mu_t\longrightarrow\mu_\infty\quad\text{in total variation},
 \qquad
 \lambda_t\longrightarrow\lambda_\infty
 \quad\text{in }d_{\BL},
 \qquad
 \Var_t\rightharpoonup\Var_\infty
\]
as $t\to\infty$, and $\lambda_\infty=\lVert\Var_\infty\rVert$.
Writing $W_\infty:=\lim_{t\to\infty}W(t)$, one also has
\[
 H_{\Var_\infty}^{\R^4}
 \in L^2(\lVert\Var_\infty\rVert;\R^4),
 \qquad
 \frac14\int_{\R^4}|H_{\Var_\infty}^{\R^4}|^2
 \dd\lVert\Var_\infty\rVert\leq W_\infty.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:41:28.173115+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dbd1dca3c8072440538682ff80e8b1c8dd300ad26fc38ad37f7c4074747b89bf","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition Costly steps of arXiv:2510.26724, 'Sharp Fuss-Catalan thresholds in graph bootstrap percolation'] The $i$th step of the REA is called a {\it costly step}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:06:18.041687+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dbecbcb9b13f161904a3293a0fba4ae24ea22a3e38c1603cc1251089b13c41ad","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 34 (Finite spectral reduction) of arXiv:2608.15805, 'Spectral duality structures and the Fisher--Rao geometry of reset distributions'] The reduction space, \emph{in symmetrised coordinates}, is exactly
the odd sector:
\begin{equation}
\widetilde V:=D^{-1}V = E_{\mathrm{odd}},
\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad
V = D\,E_{\mathrm{odd}} .

\end{equation}
The distinction matters: $D$ does not commute with $S$ unless
$p=q$, so $D\,E_{\mathrm{odd}}\neq E_{\mathrm{odd}}$ for a biased
walk --- consistently with the fact, noted above, that it is
$\widetilde\psi$ and not $\psi$ that is antisymmetric. The space
admits the canonical decomposition
\begin{equation}
\psi(\gamma)=\sum_{k\ \mathrm{even}} f_k(\gamma)\,\mathbf m_k,
\qquad
\mathbf m_k := D\,P_k\,D^{-1}\xi = D\,P_k\,\widetilde\xi,
\qquad
f_k(\gamma)=\frac{t}{1-\lambda_k t},
\quad t=1-\gamma .

\end{equation}
The directions $\mathbf m_k$ are nonzero and linearly independent.
As for canonicity, the symmetrised directions $P_k\widetilde\xi$ are
determined by $(\widetilde P,S,\widetilde\xi)$; their
original-coordinate images are determined by $(P,S,\xi)$ alone. For
the present irreducible tridiagonal $P$ the positive diagonal
symmetriser is unique up to an overall scalar --- the ratios
$D_{z+1}/D_z$ being fixed by the neighbour relations --- and the
conjugation $D P_k D^{-1}$ is unchanged under $D\mapsto cD$; so no
normalisation of the symmetriser need be fixed. In particular $\dim V = r$, and all $\gamma$-dependence is
carried by the elementary scalars $f_k$.

The notation is deliberate: these $\mathbf m_k$ are \emph{not} the
normal directions $\mathbf n_\nu$ of Section~\ref{sec:finite-reduction}.
There are $N$ of the latter, one per spectral mode, spanning a space
of dimension $r$ and therefore dependent; there are exactly $r$ of the
former, indexed by the even $k$ alone, and they are independent. Both
families span $V$, which is all the two routes are claimed to share.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:51.726371+00:00","domain":"hyperbolic partial differential equations","id":"claim_dbf122d5a238489aa083fdb44f89336d4d034fb877e0be5e3ba3b1dc4f1ae3c4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: 'the solution at (t,x) depends only on the data on the sphere ∂B(x,t)', i.e. sharp propagation on the light cone with no tail, holds only in odd space dimensions n ≥ 3. Finite speed of propagation (support in {|x| ≤ t + R}) holds in every dimension; the sharp inner edge does not. Counterexample n = 1: with u0 = 0 and u1 = 1_{[−1,1]}, d'Alembert's formula gives u(t,x) = (1/2)∫_{x−t}^{x+t} u1, so u(t,0) = 1 for every t ≥ 1 — the disturbance never leaves the origin. Counterexample n = 2: with u0 = 0 and u1 = 1_{B(0,1)}, Poisson's formula gives u(t,0) = (1/2π)∫_{|y|<1} (t² − |y|²)^{−1/2} dy > 0 for every t > 1 — a decaying tail behind the wavefront (this is why a splash on a pond is felt long after the front passes, while a sound pulse in three dimensions is heard once). Practical consequence: statements like 'the data inside B(x,t) do not matter' or 'the solution vanishes after the front passes' are valid only for odd n ≥ 3, and any argument that tacitly extends them to n = 1, 2 or to even dimensions (or to variable-coefficient / curved-background wave equations, where strong Huygens generally fails even in odd dimensions) is unsound.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:16:53.600084+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dc256567fe2e9178ffc3e664d5f0a3ae4ec6240edbfaa03b19b5239356ad256f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition proposition duality of arXiv:2412.05064, '\textbf{Sample path central limit theorem for the occupation time of the voter model on a '] For any integer $m\geq 1$, $y_1, y_2,\ldots, y_m\in \mathbb{Z}^d$, $0\leq t_1\leq t_2\leq \ldots\leq t_m$, $\eta\in \{0, 1\}^{\mathbb{Z}^d}$ and function $G$ from $\{0, 1\}^m$ to $\mathbb{R}$, we have

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-22T11:15:24.943680+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_dc42d571cabd4fbbbe8af6d7e0fbaf69","kind":"heuristic","schema_version":1,"statement":"Method for the bounded-density-of-a-quadratic-form conjecture. A cold arrival triggers deterministic setup tau>=0, which is never cancelled; arrivals during setup wait. Set p=exp(-lambda g), x=lambda tau and rho=lambda/mu. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:27:08.845617+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dc6b41a2e65e311eaddb446d8f516a18f90158f9f11f93d80d67fed31fc2a608","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defi 17 (Elliptical Brownian motions) of arXiv:2511.10535, 'Eigenvalues of Brownian Motions on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$'] Let $\rho>0$ and let $\zeta\in\C$ with $0<|\zeta|\le\rho$.  Define
\begin{equation}
    
    \theta = \frac12\arg \zeta \qquad a = \sqrt{\frac12(\rho+|\zeta|)} \qquad b = \sqrt{\frac12(\rho-|\zeta|)}. 
\end{equation}
Then $a^2+b^2=\rho$ and $e^{2\i\theta}(a^2-b^2)=\zeta$, so that $(a,b,\theta)$ satisfy \eqref{eq.rho.zeta}.  This yields a bijective mapping
\begin{equation} \{(\rho,\zeta)\colon 0<|\zeta|\le\rho\}\mapsto\{(a,b,\theta)\colon a>b\ge 0, \theta\in[0,\pi)\}. \end{equation}
We may extend the definitions of $a,b$ to allow $\zeta=0$, in which case $a=b$; here $\theta$ is undefined.

Let $(X^N(t))_{t\geq 0}$, $(Y^N(t))_{t\geq 0}$ be independent Hermitian Brownian motions of size $N$. 
We define the general {\bf elliptical Brownian motion} $(W^N_{\rho,\zeta}(t))_{t\ge0}$ by
	\[ W^N_{\rho,\zeta}(t) = e^{\i \theta} \left(aX^N(t) + \i b Y^N(t)\right). \]
    Similarly, if $(x(t))_{t\geq 0}$ and $(y(t))_{t\geq 0}$ are freely independent free semicircular Brownian motion, the {\bf free elliptical Brownian motion $(w_{\rho,\zeta}(t))_{t\ge0}$} is defined as
    \[ w_{\rho,\zeta}(t) = e^{\i \theta} \left(a x(t) + \i b y(t)\right). \]
In both cases, when $a=b$ (i.e.\ $\zeta=0$), all values of $\theta$ yield the same distribution for the right-hand-side, so we may take canonically $\theta=0$ in this case.

Note that the laws of $W^N_{\rho,\zeta}(t)$ and $w_{\rho,\zeta}(t)$ are invariant under $a\mapsto-a$, $b\mapsto-b$, and $(a,b,\theta)\mapsto(b,a,\theta+\frac{\pi}{2})$.  It then follows from \eqref{eq.bijection} that $\rho>0$, $|\zeta|\le\rho$ paramaterize the laws of all possible elliptical Brownian motions.

To lighten notation we will often drop the subscripts $\rho,\zeta$ if there can be no confusion.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:19:42.478187+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dc7f92a47f72e853d6ed6052ff3725a3345f24c23d06c222b2e1bdf27fc0359c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 11 (Parametric weighted lattice-corner expansion) of arXiv:2609.03466, 'Least-Favorable Location for Binomial Top-$t$ Selection'] Let $U$ be a compact interval. For each $p\in U$, let $Z_p$ be a random vector supported by a fixed finite subset of $\Zz^d$, with masses that are positive and $C^{r+2}$ in $p$. Assume that the additive group generated by differences of support points is $\Zz^d$. Put
\[
 M_p(\lambda)=\Ee e^{\langle\lambda,Z_p\rangle}.
\]
Suppose there is a $C^{r+2}$ map $\lambda:U\to(0,\infty)^d$ satisfying
\[
 \nabla_\lambda\log M_p(\lambda(p))=0.
\]
Let
\[
 I(p)=-\log M_p(\lambda(p)),
 \qquad
 \Sigma(p)=\nabla_\lambda^2\log M_p(\lambda(p)).
\]
Let $w:\Zz_+^d\to\Rr$ be bounded and define
\[
 W(p)=\sum_{z\in\Zz_+^d}
 w(z)e^{-\langle\lambda(p),z\rangle}.
\]
For independent copies $Z_{p,1},\ldots,Z_{p,n}$, put $S_{n,p}=\sum_{i=1}^nZ_{p,i}$ and
\[
 \mathcal T_n(p)=\sum_{z\in\Zz_+^d}w(z)\Pp(S_{n,p}=z).
\]
Then, for $\varepsilon_n=n^{-1/2}(\log n)^{3r+6}$,
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal T_n(p)
 =\frac{e^{-nI(p)}n^{-d/2}}
 {(2\pi)^{d/2}\sqrt{\det\Sigma(p)}}
 \left[W(p)+O_{C^r(U)}(\varepsilon_n)\right].
 
\end{equation}
If $r\ge1$ and $I'(p_0)\ne0$, then
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal T_n'(p_0)
 =n^{1-d/2}e^{-nI(p_0)}
 \left\{-I'(p_0)
 \frac{W(p_0)}{(2\pi)^{d/2}\sqrt{\det\Sigma(p_0)}}+o(1)\right\}.
 
\end{equation}
If in addition $W(p_0)\ne0$, this may equivalently be written with a relative factor $\{1+o(1)\}$. If $r\ge2$, $I'(p_0)=0$, $I''(p_0)>0$, and $W(p_0)>0$, then
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal T_n''(p_0)
 =-I''(p_0)
 \frac{W(p_0)}{(2\pi)^{d/2}\sqrt{\det\Sigma(p_0)}}
 n^{1-d/2}e^{-nI(p_0)}\{1+o(1)\}.
 
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:06:18.036644+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dcb36ba39dd44d5895719498d4c735be156fcffb74b604526cb65b37c5bfa69f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 16 (The separatrix is the cone of square roots) of arXiv:2608.15805, 'Spectral duality structures and the Fisher--Rao geometry of reset distributions'] Suppose, as in Remark~\ref{rem:pi-mu}, that the underlying chain
is $(\sigma,\kappa)$-reversible with reversible measure
$\mu\propto\kappa^{-1}$. Then
\[
\Sigma\cap\Delta_{m-1}
=\Bigl\{\pi:\ \pi|_O\propto\sqrt{\mu}\,\bigl|_O\ \text{on each
orbit }O,\ \text{neutral weights free}\Bigr\},
\]
and the per-orbit constants (together with the neutral weights,
modulo normalisation) are global coordinates on $\Sigma$. Note that
the two pictures are of different kinds: in the $\pi$-coordinates
$\Sigma$ is an affine slice of the simplex, not a cone; it is in the
coordinates $x=2\sqrt\pi$ that it becomes a genuine cone, and the
name is to be read there. On the sphere, correspondingly,
\[
\Phi\bigl(\Sigma^\circ\bigr)
=\operatorname{cone}_{+}\bigl\{\mu^{1/4}\big|_O,\ \text{neutral
axes}\bigr\}\cap S^{m-1}_+(2),
\]
the \emph{positive} cone --- positivity and normalisation are part
of the statement, not decoration. The spectral square root
$\mu\mapsto\sqrt\mu$ and the geometric square root $\Phi$ thus
compose, and the separatrix is generated, in spherical coordinates,
by the fourth roots of the reversible measure.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:23:58.630342+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dcb9755e3b78d02e1ec93b76039e5957f028e8053edea20d6ae234b5f42a125f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 240 (Existence and continuation criteria for the characteristic initial value problem; \cite{speckyucharacteristicIVP}) of arXiv:2609.03101, 'The emergence of the Cauchy horizon from the crease for $3D$ compressible Euler flow'] \hfill

\medskip
	
\noindent \underline{\textbf{Local existence for the characteristic IVP}}. 
Recall that the classical solution is $C^{\infty}$ on $\twoargMrough{[\timefunction_0,0],[- \rightu,\leftu]}{0}$
and therefore induces $C^{\infty}$ data on the characteristic surfaces
$\ingoingcharacteristicsurfacetwoarg{\leftubar}{[\moreinterestingu_1,\moreinterestingu_2]}, \, \outgoingcharacteristicsurfacetwoarg{\moreinterestingu_1}{[\leftubar,0]}$; see Appendix~\ref{A:DATASSUMPTIONS}.
Then there exists a  
$\ubarlocal \in (\leftubar,0)$, depending on the data, such the characteristic data launch a unique $C^{\infty}$ solution
on $\characteristicdiamondtwoarg{[\leftubar,\ubarlocal)}{[\moreinterestingu_1,\moreinterestingu_2]}$,
and the change of variables map $(u,\ubar,x^2,x^3) \rightarrow (t,x^1,x^2,x^3)$
is a diffeomorphism from $\characteristicdiamondtwoarg{[\leftubar,\ubarlocal)}{[\moreinterestingu_1,\moreinterestingu_2]}$
onto its image in Cartesian coordinate space.

\medskip
	
\noindent \underline{\textbf{Continuation criteria for the characteristic IVP}}.

Assume the following: 
\begin{itemize}
	\item The assumptions of Theorem\,\ref{T:EXISTENCEUPTOCAUCHYHORIZONBYCONTINUATIONCRITERIA} hold.
	\item $\ubarboot < 0$.
	\item The ingoing eikonal function $\ubar$, the wave variables $\wavearray$, and the acoustic geometry variables $u, \, \chi$, etc. are classical solutions on $\characteristicdiamondtwoarg{[\leftubar,\ubarboot)}{[\moreinterestingu_1,\moreinterestingu_2]}$. 
	\item The bootstrap assumptions of Sects.\,\ref{S:BOOTSTRAPEVERYTHINGEXCEPTENERGIES} and\,\ref{SS:BOOTSTRAPASSUMPTIONSFORTHEWAVEENERGIES} hold for $(\ubar,u) \in [\leftubar,\ubarboot)\times[\moreinterestingu_1,\moreinterestingu_2]$. 
\end{itemize}

Then there exists a $\Delta \in (0,|\ubarboot|)$ such that the ingoing eikonal function $\ubar$, the solution variables $\wavearray, \, u$, and all of the other geometric quantities defined throughout the article can be uniquely extended to a strictly larger region of the form $\characteristicdiamondtwoarg{[\leftubar,\ubarboot + \Delta)}{[\moreinterestingu_1,\moreinterestingu_2]}$ on which all of the bootstrap
assumptions of Sects.\,\ref{S:BOOTSTRAPEVERYTHINGEXCEPTENERGIES} and\,\ref{SS:BOOTSTRAPASSUMPTIONSFORTHEWAVEENERGIES} hold.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["U open with lambda_1 > 0 on H^1_0(U) (e.g. U bounded, or bounded in one direction, or of finite measure)","g in L^2(U)","u the weak solution of the Dirichlet heat equation with u(0) = g","the equality case requires the infimum defining lambda_1 to be attained, e.g. U bounded"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:49.105957+00:00","domain":"parabolic partial differential equations","id":"claim_dccca23e6eedae7c488796bf4490a59edff019e1d479e546a6dbd3a3e781c655","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $U\\subset\\mathbb R^n$ be open with $\\lambda_1=\\inf\\{\\|\\nabla v\\|_{L^2}^2/\\|v\\|_{L^2}^2:v\\in H^1_0(U),v\\ne0\\}>0$; this positivity holds in particular when $U$ is bounded, when $U$ is merely bounded in one direction, and when $U$ has finite measure. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:30:50.719777+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dcd322992c63443755363911b4d69ea7f9ffeda5c3b0026ee2759aab501144b5","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:ensemble of arXiv:2609.02155, 'Exact Limits of Random Projections for Preserving Geometry:\\ Distance Recovery, Nearest-N'] Let $A_1,\dots,A_k\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d}$ be sketches applied to the same data.

\]

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:05:09.627779+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dce2388135a2e2a8b9cbf66da57e0489396ea0b66e60989dbe12db6c40d0a2cb","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:upper_lower_simple of arXiv:2411.03609, 'Asymptotically optimal Wasserstein couplings for the small-time stable domain of attractio'] Let $\alpha \in (0,2)\setminus\{1\}$, and suppose $\bm{Z}$ is $\alpha$-stable and $\bm{X}$ is in the domain of normal attraction of $\bm{Z}$.\\

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.176507+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dce2c5f1ca2ba7f115f24e4985d485e0ea81fbf2f9568b8bd5140a67410b7be1","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Ppn 71 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For fixed $q_0 \in [0,1)$ and $f \in L^\infty([q_0,1];[0,1/\alpha])$, the mapping $p \mapsto \cM(q_0;p,f)$, viewed as a function from $\incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ to  $P(\cP_2(\bbR))$, is uniformly continuous:
    \[
        d_\cH\Big(\cM(q_0;p,f),\cM(q_0;\tilde p,f)\Big)^2
        \le 6(1+\|f\|_\infty) \|p'-\tilde p'\|_1\,.
    \]
Here $\incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ is metrized by  $\mathsf{dist}(p,\tilde p) = \|p'-\tilde p'\|_1$, and we recall that  $P(\cP_2(\bbR))$ is metrized by the Hausdorff distance \eqref{e:hausdorff}. 

\begin{proof}
Let $p,\tilde p\in \incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ with $\|p'-\tilde p'\|_1 = \delta$.
Since $p(1) = \tilde p(1) = 1$, it follows by integrating that $|p(t) - \tilde p(t)| \le \delta$ for all $t\in [q_0,1]$, and so certainly we have $\|p-\tilde{p}\|_1\le\delta$. Recalling the notation of Definition~\ref{d:X.adm}, let $(b,\sigma)\in \Adm(q_0;p,f)$. We will construct modified controls $(\tilde b,\tilde \sigma) \in \Adm(q_0;\tilde p,f)$ such that the corresponding solutions to \eqref{e:formal.sde.main} approximate each other. Recall $s(t)\equiv (tp)'(t)^{1/2}$, and similarly denote
$\tilde{s}(t)\equiv (t\tilde{p})'(t)^{1/2}$.
We set $\tilde{b}=b$, and let $\hat \sigma$ be defined by the relation
	\[\hat{\sigma}_t-1
	= a(t) 
	(\sigma_t-1)\,,\quad
	a(t)
	\equiv 
	\frac{s(t)}{p(t)^{1/2}}
	\frac{\tilde{p}(t)^{1/2}}
		{\tilde{s}(t)}
	\]
for all $t\in[q_0,1]$. We note that 
	\[
	\frac{s(t)}{p(t)^{1/2}}
	= \frac{[p(t) + tp'(t)]^{1/2}}
		{p(t)^{1/2}} \ge 1\,,
	\]
so the ratio $a(t)$ can only be large if $p'(t)$ is very large, which occurs on a set of times of small measure. It is clear from the construction that $(\tilde b,\hat{\sigma})$ satisfies the budget constraint \eqref{e:budget-f} defining $\Adm(q_0;\tilde p,f)$, with the exception that $\hat{\sigma}$ is not necessarily non-negative. Let $X$ be given by \eqref{e:formal.sde.main} with controls $(b,\sigma)$, and $\hat X$ be given by \eqref{e:formal.sde.main} with controls $(\tilde b, \hat \sigma)$. We couple these processes with the same initialization $X(q_0) = \hat{X}(q_0) = 0$ and the same Brownian motion $B$. We will first show the endpoint laws of $X(1)$ and $\hat{X}(1)$ are close, then address the issue of $\hat{\sigma}$ being possibly negative. To this end, we recall from \eqref{e:formal.sde.main} that
  \[
        X(1) = \int_{q_0}^1 p'(t)^{1/2} b_t\,dt
        + \int_{q_0}^1 s(t)\,dB(t)
        + \int_{q_0}^1 s(t) (\sigma_t-1)\,dB(t)
        \,,
    \]
and similarly for $\hat{X}(1)$. This gives us a decomposition
$X(1)-\hat{X}(1) = \textup{(a)}+\textup{(b)}+\textup{(c)}$, and we proceed to bound each of the three terms:
    \begin{align*}\E[\textup{(a)}^2]
    &= \E \bigg[
    \bigg(\int_{q_0}^1 \Big(
        p'(t)^{1/2}
        - \tilde{p}'(t)^{1/2}\Big) b_t\,dt\bigg)^2\bigg]
    \le \bigg(
     \int_{q_0}^1\Big(
        p'(t)^{1/2}
        - \tilde{p}'(t)^{1/2}\Big)^2\,dt\bigg)
    \bigg( \int_{q_0}^1 \E[(b_t)^2]\,dt\bigg) \\
    &\le\bigg(\int_{q_0}^1 |p'(t)-\tilde{p}'(t)|\,dt\bigg)
    \bigg(\int_{q_0}^1 f(t)\,dt\bigg) 
    =  \delta \|f\|_1 \,,
    \end{align*}
having used the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality along with the budget constraint~\eqref{e:budget-f}. Next,
    \[\E[\textup{(b)}^2]
    = \int_{q_0}^1 \Big( s(t)-\tilde{s}(t) \Big)^2\,dt
    \le \int_{q_0}^1 \Big|s(t)^2 - \tilde{s}(t)^2\Big|\,dt
    \le \|p-p\|_1+\|p'-p'\|_1 \le 2\delta\,.\]
Lastly, using the above definition of $\hat\sigma$, we have
	\begin{align*}
	\E[\textup{(c)}^2]
    &= \int_{q_0}^1
    \Big( s(t) (\sigma_t-1)-\tilde{s}(t)(\hat{\sigma}_t
    -1)\Big)^2\,dt\\
    &= \int_{q_0}^1
    \frac{s(t)^2}{p(t)}
    \E[(\sigma_t-1)^2]
    \cdot p(t)
    \bigg( 1- 
    	\frac{\tilde{s}(t)}{s(t)} a(t)
    	 \bigg)^2
	\,dt\\
	&\le
	\|f\|_\infty
	\int_{q_0}^1
	p(t)
    \bigg( 1- \frac{\tilde{p}(t)^{1/2}}
		{p(t)^{1/2}}
    	 \bigg)^2
	\,dt 
	\le \|f\|_\infty \delta\,,
	\end{align*}
having used the budget constraint~\eqref{e:budget-f} along with the calculation from the bound on (a) above. Collec (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}
